en: Preface to the *Zhongzhi pinishi yiji yao* (Essential Collection on the Meaning of Matters Concerning the Vinaya):

The Dharma of the Tathāgata has vibrated throughout the eastern regions; from beginning to end, it must rely upon the regulations of the Vinaya. His compassionate edicts have been bestowed upon all sentient beings, remaining abundant and flourishing unto this day.

Yet, the rise and fall of the *mokṣa* (liberation) depends upon individuals. Now that a time of extreme decline has arrived, I am grieved that the transmission of the precepts throughout the land is [in such a state]. Much...
Failing to rely upon the regulations and the Dharma, I lament that those who transmit and receive the teachings throughout the land today rarely avoid erring themselves and misleading others;
this is entirely due to teachers who deviate from the fundamental instructions and fail to study the canonical codes.

Yet, the Venerable Master Qianshou Zhen, who has mastered the three schools and thoroughly understood their profound subtleties, traveled north to the state of Jin with his staff and, by the convergence of favorable conditions, was invited to reside at Qianshou.
Alas, these Vinaya teachings have been lost to transmission. For over ten years, he has vowed to turn back the calamity of this obscuration, prioritizing the study of the Vinaya.
Among those who have taken refuge at his feet, several have desired to practice these rules of training;

yet only the Bhikṣu Wuxia of Jinliao possesses exceptional natural talent and is uniquely devoted to the Vinaya school, having extensively read the *Vinaya* scriptures and thoroughly investigated the five [divisions].

Regarding the essential purport of this treatise: I regret that the commentaries on the Vinaya are not numerous, and as the entire Tripitaka is vast and extensive, even those who possess learning find it inconvenient to master.
Therefore, I have focused solely on the *Viniścaya-vinaya-śāstra*, which is deeply capable of addressing the maladies of the current age and sufficiently articulates the ultimate goal.
Consequently, I vowed to carve it into printing blocks for posterity, hoping only to respond universally to the capacities of all beings; thus my intention has accumulated over time.

Huai had never before been able to fulfill this aspiration. At that time, while he was at Guyi Chaoyang receiving the precepts, several bhikṣus who had inherited the Vinaya lineage gathered together to discuss the final age [of the Dharma].

They deliberated that if they were to once again edit the *Vinaya*, carve it onto wooden printing blocks, and circulate it, then perhaps this study of the Vinaya would provide hope for future generations.
At that time, there were nine venerable masters of the Vinaya: Huishi, Fobi, Qianshou, Taiji, and other senior upādhyāyas who upheld the discipline.
A number of individuals were selected to solicit funds and initiate the construction. Consequently, their resolve became as vast as the great void;
they did not shrink from toil and hardship, nor did they refuse the arduous journey. After two years of carving and engraving, this work was completed.

May all who see or hear of it rejoice and uphold it, hanging the sun of the precepts in the midst of heaven and erecting the True Dharma in this final age, so that we may not fail in our duty to the Dharma.
This is my humble aspiration, intended merely as a single drop from the ocean of repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
Preface to the *Zhongzhi pinishi yiji yao* (Essential Collection on the Meaning of Revising the Vinaya Matters), compiled by the Vinaya-studying Bhikṣu Zhìtái.
The Master was born on the third day of the fifth month in the year Jihai (1599), during the twenty-seventh year of the Wanli era, at the hour of Hai.
On the seventh day of the fifth month in the year Renxu (1622), at the age of twenty-four, he shaved his head and entered the monastic life.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month in the following year, he received full ordination before an image of the Venerable Master Yunqi. In the year after that, he received the Bodhisattva...
He received the *sāmaṇera* precepts before the stupa of Master Yunqi, with several eminent Dharma masters serving as his *ācāryas*.
In the spring of his twenty-seventh year, he read through the Vinaya once and recorded its essential meanings and principles in slightly over a hundred sheets of paper.
In the summer of his thirtieth year, he read the Vinaya for a second time and completed a record in four volumes. In the winter of his thirty-first year, he read it for a third time.
The Vinaya [commentary] was thus completed in six volumes, totaling eighteen fascicles.

In the summer of his thirty-second year, for the sake of Xinggu, Ruoshi, Xuehang, and Sanyou, he lectured on it thoroughly once; he subsequently added the first and last collections, making a total of eight volumes.
In his thirty-third year, the Dharma Master Jintai had them carved into printing blocks at Furi Temple on Gaotingshan. That winter, [he was] at...
At Lingfeng, he lectured on only seven fascicles; it was not until the following summer that he finally completed the lecture.

There were some ten or more listeners, but only the bhikṣu Cheyin was able to put it into practice. At the age of thirty-five, he entered the summer retreat at Xiaoshuhu Temple in the western part of Jinting.
Cheyin lectured on it once; there were nine listeners, but among them, only Cheyin and Zizhuan paid close attention.
It was by the grace of the Venerable Huanchan. In the winter of his thirty-sixth year, while at the Huanzhu Hermitage in Wumen, he gave another lecture;
only five or six people attended, including Ziguang, Sengju, and two bhikṣus who were capable of practicing it.
At thirty-eight, he entered Jiuhua; at forty, he entered Minzhong; and at forty-four, he arrived at Ti.
City. From this point on, for thirteen or fourteen years, he was personally unable to practice it, nor were there any others who would inquire about it.
Consequently, as the three monks with whom he had gathered also passed away one after another, he realized that the study of the Vinaya was truly nothing more than stagnant merchandise.
In the winter of his fifty-first year, he returned from Jinling to rest at Lingfeng. In the summer of the following year—
There were then more than ten people who had resolved to study the Vinaya and urged me to lecture on this text once again.
Consequently, I reflected that although I had previously compiled various excellent points from many sources, I had not yet reached a definitive synthesis for each of them.

Furthermore, I noted that the two works concerning phonology and semantics (*Wenbian* and *Yinyi*) had not yet been printed; it would be better to integrate these into the *Jiyao* (Essentials) and re-edit them, while also pruning [the text].
I have pruned away one or two points of prolixity and clutter to restore the work’s conciseness and directness.

It is my hope that those of dull faculties will not be moved to sigh of despair, like gazing out at the vast ocean from the shore. Written on the twenty-first day of the sixth month of the Gengyin year by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of Guwu. Preface.
Preface:
The Piṇḍanikāya (Vinaya-piṭaka) is the governing framework of the Buddha-dharma, the lifeblood of the Saṃgha, the bridge across the ocean of suffering, and the essential path to Nirvāṇa.
Since its first proclamation at the Kukkutārāma, when [the Buddha] summoned [Ānanda] with the words "Come hither" (*ehi bhikkhu*), the essence of the precepts was established.
It was thus established. When the *śāla* trees lost their luster [at the Buddha’s passing], the final testament (*guru-parideśa*) emphasized the gravity of Maudgalyāyana.

It was precisely because of transgressions that prohibitions were enacted; in essence, this accords with non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Whether in the opening of conditions or in subsequent regulations, its application further harmonizes with the wondrous perfection.

This is truly the common path for both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; how could it be the exclusive track of the Śrāvakas? Alas, in this age of the Semblance Dharma, those who have attained such understanding are rare.
The True Sect (Shinshū). The foolish are ignorant and deaf to its teachings; the mad cast it aside as something unworthy of concern.
Some use the subtleties of Zen to craft evasive excuses, while others use the Vaipulya (fangguǎng) scriptures as mere pretexts. Both rely solely on the literal text; who considers the true meaning?

For instance, when Master Huineng received the seal of the mind at Huangmei, why did he propagate the transformation [of beings] at Caoxi? He still utilized the formalities of ascending the dais and receiving [the transmission].
Complete. Master Guan propagated the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Mount Wutai; how could he have served as a model for the court and the commonalty without restraining himself with the Ten Vows?
For when the Great Hero (the Buddha) presides over the realm, the two treasures of Dharma and Saṅgha both radiate their brilliance through Perfect Enlightenment;
yet when the Sugata conceals his wondrous capacities, the two venerable ones—Dharma and Buddha—likewise rely upon the Saṅgha for their establishment. If there were only the ten grave [precepts]...
If one is treated with such contempt by the multitude, how does this differ from that of a layperson?

Were it not for the Five Categories and Seven Groups of precepts, how could one know the lofty standard of those who have left secular life? Thus we know that the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* encompasses all five realms of existence, excluding only hell;

by being universal in this way, it achieves its greatness. The Vinaya Piṭaka, however, restricts itself to human beings and still excludes those under various prohibitions; it does so precisely because it is limited.
To achieve such honor, one must certainly cause others to look up to and admire the Mahāyāna, finding no satisfaction in minor precepts.

Thus, one may naturally grow out one's hair and discard the robes, becoming an *utpala* lotus amidst the flames. If, however, one feels compassion for the Dharma-ending age and is determined to uphold it, how could one indulge one’s passions and abandon moral restraint, becoming a "body-worm" to the lion?
Zhi Xu reflects that his own hindrances are deep and he is unable to practice in emulation of these ideals.

Regarding the profound principle, I further lament that I was born too late; I have had no means to serve as an attendant to this sage. I grieve that the "gap-horse" (the fleeting moment) cannot be turned back, and thus I abandoned my compassionate mother to don the black robes of a monk.
Yearning for the Pure Land as a place to which I may return, I admire Master Tanyan and seek to learn from him in private.

I am eager to discern the essential tenets, always cherishing the spirit of Master Zibai; I am willing to sacrifice my life to protect the Dharma, vowing to continue the lineage of Mount Kuang. Upon seeing...

At that time, the current flowed with long sighs; reading the *Śāsanānuśāsana-sūtra*, my grief increased. Thus, in the final month of winter in the year of Jiǎzǐ, I paid homage at the Tower of Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*).
My resolve for the higher mind (*adhyāśaya-citta*) redoubled, and I requested the ancient virtuous Ācārya to serve as witness for my study of the Bodhisattva precepts.
Subsequently, I thoroughly examined both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Vinayas, adhering primarily to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* while also drawing from other schools, and compiled them into this record.
This brief summary of the essential meaning of the matter is merely the crude and ignorant view of a fool; how could it be worthy of being presented to the great masters?
It is intended only as provisions for those dwelling in mountain caves, nor do I have any intention of benefiting others as well. In the spring of the Wuchen year, I met Master Xuehang Ji.

He joyfully resolved to strictly observe the Vinaya. Reflecting that his previous collection, undertaken while his mind was preoccupied with entering the mountains, still contained many omissions and errors, he proceeded to the meditation cave at Longju.
There, he re-examined the texts of the Tripitaka; regardless of whether they belonged to his own school or other traditions, he extracted everything essential.
He carefully deliberated upon the propriety of gravity and lightness, fully elucidating what is permitted and what is prohibited.
This standard also references the *Mahā-vinaya*, providing detailed indications of what is distinct and what is common.

This is intended so that those who fear dogmatic adherence will not incur the calamity of slandering the Lesser Vehicle, while those who delight in vague generalizations will find it difficult to maintain their pretense of relying on the Great Vehicle. Having examined and finalized this work into a volume, its title was changed to *The Essential Compendium of the Meaning of Vinaya Matters*.
It was submitted for verification to the venerable Master Wengu of Zhenji, and by the Chan master Wuyi of Boshan.
The Master [Zhuhong] earnestly entrusted [the work] to the carving blocks for circulation.

Thereupon, he once again consulted with his two friends, Biri and Guiyi, to thoroughly investigate and refine the text, exhausting every nuance of its intent. Consequently, the Dharma Lord Jin Tai Furu joyfully ordered it to be engraved upon woodblocks.
Indeed, the arising of conditions for the Buddha-dharma surely has its own appointed time. Alas! Although this collection, regarding the subtle...
The substance of this lofty [teaching] is far greater than a mere mote of dust. For one of my own inferior and sluggish capacity, I have already exerted every effort.

What I regret is that my understanding and wisdom are shallow and mediocre, and my personal practice is deficient. Looking up, I feel ashamed before the sages of the past; looking down, I am abashed before the worthies of the future.

I only pray that my fellow students and virtuous friends will discern my sincere efforts and take pity on my shortcomings, maintaining a single-minded resolve to uphold and together support the destiny of the Dharma.

May this serve as a modest repayment of the Buddha’s kindness, even by a ten-thousandth part. Written by Zhi Xu in the first month of the Xinwei year at the ancient Yongqing Temple on Gaoting Mountain.
Original colophon.
The Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states: "If a son of good family wishes to establish the Buddha-dharma, he should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.

If he wishes to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time, he should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya. If he is terrified by the commission of offenses and seeks a refuge, he should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
If he does not wish to harbor doubt or regret and seek instruction from others [regarding his conduct], he should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya."
A person should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya. Those who wish to travel and transform beings in all directions without hindrance should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "The Vinaya has four meanings not found in other sūtras:
first, it is the level ground of the Buddha-dharma, from which all myriad virtues grow; second, all disciples of the Buddha rely upon it..."
Morality is the foundation; all sentient beings exist by virtue of morality. It is the initial gateway to the three realms and to nirvana.
It is the jeweled ornament of the Buddha-dharma, capable of adorning it. Possessing these four meanings, its merit is superior to that [of the aforementioned]. Alas!
How vast is the benefit of the precepts! Alas, the time since the Sage departed is so remote that errors have proliferated like "ru" for "nai" or "yu" for "jiu.
Beings of this final age rarely encounter the true wind of the Dharma. Since the raft of the precepts entered Zhendan (China), it first flourished under the Venerable Kai of the Cao-Wei dynasty;
thereafter, its excellence was inherited by Master Huaisu. Yet down to the present day, there has been a profound silence and no further renown. Occasionally, there are...
Certain eminent and versatile Mahāsattvas are neither like lions emerging from their caves, nor do they possess the discernment of the King of Geese who distinguishes milk from water.
They have recently abandoned the fundamental tenets of the five schools while peripherally adopting the trivial categories of question-and-answer manuals.

Thus, they treat what requires urgency with laxity and treat what requires patience with haste; their contradictions strike at themselves, and their loss of the Way grows ever more severe. Therefore, the heroic and eminent—

I, a common scholar, have never passed by his dwelling to inquire after him. By what means did he cause the moon of the precepts to shine brightly amidst profound darkness, and restore the collapsing web of discipline where its cords had snapped?

Having received the tally [of ordination], I have privately examined his surviving writings; every time I am stirred from sleep by them, I sigh with deep emotion for my virtuous elder brother, Master Xu.

My devotion to the Dharma is earnest and my compassionate resolve is profound. Having searched exhaustively through the Vinaya-piṭaka and extracted its essence several times over, I have taken the *Dharmaguptaka* (Four-Part) Vinaya as the skeletal framework, borrowing from other schools to clarify its meaning.
I have purified its source and tempered it with the nectar of truth, compiling this *Jiyao* (Essential Compendium) in several fascicles.
All of this follows ancient teachings and is not the product of mere personal speculation; it is my hope that those who drink even a single drop [of this water] may...
Chronic ailments can be cured; those who indulge in satiety will not contract new diseases. To purify once more the ocean of precepts depends upon this single act.
Looking back, what good fortune have I enjoyed in past lives that I may now attend the assembly for the Vinaya teachings? I feel profound joy at having dipped my finger to taste the flavor first.
I have appended these few words to the end of this volume. Among those who know the Dharma, there will surely be those who gather here spontaneously without prior consultation.
This unworthy one does not merely indulge his own preferences. Written with reverence by the junior disciple Youxi Shouchou of the Vinaya Society on a spring day in the year of Gengwu.

General Inquiry and Discernment.

Question: In the study of the Vinaya, the emphasis lies on sincere faith and diligent practice, and by strictly observing the Five Categories of Offenses, one can certainly secure rebirth among humans and devas.
Yet, if one’s merit is exhausted, what will become of them? Would it not be better to first open one's eyes through the teachings of the religious school?
The arising of the precepts co-arising with the Path is a matter of urgent importance. An ancient saying goes: "It is only the seeing of the Ground that is valued, not the practice of conduct.
Is this not so? Answer: The study of the Vinaya is the primary cause for transcending the world. The Perfection of Precepts (Śīla-pāramitā) is fulfilled only upon the Buddha-ground;

how could it be merely a matter of human or celestial merit? Though the words of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings may appear similar when they speak of "opening the eyes," they do so simply because they wish to transcend [worldly] precepts.
Let us set aside the discussion of religion. To set aside phenomena in search of principle is to fall into erroneous views.
Guishan said: "I have not yet even dared to enter the assembly for the Vinaya; how could I possibly discern the definitive meaning of the Supreme Vehicle? Jingxi said:

"Using the first four precepts as the object of contemplation, when viewed through the six contemplations, phenomena and principle are mutually identical. One should know that the articles and clusters [of the precepts] are one."
It must not be deficient. When those in the world disregard practical affairs while desiring to exalt profound principles, they should verify this through observation:

if [the mind] is solitary, empty, and without foundation, the object of contemplation is already deficient, and thus contemplation itself has no basis. Thus, whether from the perspective of the fundamental tenet (*zong*) or the teaching (*jiao*), the instruction is truly clear;
why do you not reflect upon it? What the ancients meant by "valuing the ground of insight (*jian-di*) rather than valuing conduct (*xing-li*)" was precisely because there is...
One who possesses the ground of realization must necessarily have practical cultivation; yet one who has practical cultivation does not necessarily possess the ground of realization.

Now, if you judge the unsurpassed precepts of the Tathāgata to belong merely to the realms of humans and devas, and abandon the *vinaya* discipline for empty talk of "path-dharma" (*mārga-sāṃvṛta*), then your right view is already destroyed and your practice is further neglected.
How could you dare to claim a share in escaping the three miserable destinies? Even if you wish to be born as a human, [it will be difficult].
[It is] heavenly [in its excellence], yet it cannot be obtained.

Question: In this degenerate age, those of dull faculties require only what is essential and concise. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka* is already feared by the world for its prolixity and fragmentation, such that it is placed on high shelves and neglected.
Now, this *Jiyao* (Collection of Essentials) cites various schools; why does it instead become even more confused and disordered?
"It would not be improper to take the *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Prātimokṣa Sūtra) as the primary text and add brief marginal annotations to resolve doubts.

What is wrong with that? The answer is: "To prefer brevity and dislike extensiveness is a universal malady of this degenerate age. To stubbornly cling to ignorance and dullness leads further and further downward;

ultimately, there will be no day when such doubts are resolved. Now, if one wishes to rescue them from their suffering, it is essential to study extensively and then return to the essentials; only then can success be achieved."

Ji: If one were to simply provide a brief marginal commentary on the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, how could one hope for a clear understanding of what is permitted or prohibited, and what constitutes an offense or its non-occurrence?
Those who delight in the Buddha-dharma would find it difficult to penetrate such a text, while those accustomed to indolence would likely remain indifferent.
Caught between these two outcomes, what benefit would there be?
Question: The single gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha (nienfo) is vast and simple; one should faithfully practice it.

If one can simply recite the Buddha’s name with a single mind, evil will naturally cease and wrongdoing will be prevented. Why then must one laboriously spend years studying these rules of discipline (vinaya), which are replete with names and categories and are thus anything but simple?
Furthermore, their ultimate fruit is that of the śrāvaka, which is not vast. I fear they are not as effective as focusing exclusively on the Pure Land.
This is the subtlety of the Dharma-gate of the Land of Bliss. Answer: Upholding the precepts and reciting the Buddha’s name are fundamentally one gate; they have never been divergent paths.

Pure precepts are the cause, and the Pure Land is the fruit. If one takes the practice of holding the name as the direct path and the study of the Vinaya as a circuitous route, one not only violates the sincere words of the final testament, but how could one ever achieve the Samādhi of Reciting the Buddha’s Name?
It is like the ocean, which has no shore; it is like treasure, which has no limit...
Is this not vast and great? To commit offenses and to cease them, or to maintain and uphold [the precepts], thereby securing liberation—is this not simple and easy?

Therefore, those who single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name are able to cease evil and guard against transgression; yet those who specialize in the study of the Vinaya even more strictly observe the Buddha’s clear instructions.
In the present life, they perpetuate and flourish the lineage of the Sangha; at the moment of death, they attain rebirth in the highest grade of the highest level. This is the gateway of the Dharma—
Excellent! What could surpass this?
Question: When the Tathāgata descended to birth in the Western Regions, the *vinaya* prohibitions against offenses of censure were all established because laypeople expressed reproach;
there were also precepts that followed local customs. Although these are not observed in this land today, it is not necessarily the case that laypeople would reproach [us for violating them].

[This would be] a violation. If one were to abandon even the subtle precepts, how would this contradict the holy teachings? Furthermore, as we are currently in the final age (*paścimaka-yuga*), external conditions are not abundant and internal causes are meager.
If one desires to avoid even the slightest transgression while expounding the teachings and propagating the great principles, then the Buddha-dharma cannot be widely disseminated.
To preserve minor details while losing the great benefit—how could this be the fundamental intention of a Bodhisattva who studies the truth of the One Vehicle?
"Is it so? He replied, "The Tathāgata possesses all-knowing vision and has universally established the precepts for the sake of sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm.

The group of six monks and others were likewise manifestations of great expedient means; they displayed the conditions for transgression by conforming to the dispositions of sentient beings in the final age.
It is precisely because people's hearts are indolent and they are unwilling to guard against both light and heavy offenses that the degenerate age has come to pass. Now, wishing to..."

In propagating the teachings of the Great Vehicle, one must take the observance of the precepts as the foundation. When the precepts are refined and strict, internal causes become pure and substantial, and external conditions naturally flourish.
That a single portion of light from within the *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft of hair) is by no means a deceptive word.

To regard the precepts as mere minor details is to slander the Dharma; to discuss the essence (*zong*) or explain the teachings (*jiao*) in such a manner is nothing but a state of confused and deluded ignorance. Even if one were to attain...
These external conditions are collectively termed demonic activities (*māra-karman*). What benefit do they provide to the True Dharma?
Question: The patriarchs of the Western Regions were thoroughly proficient in the three studies; here, however, the land is remote and time is distant, so few have heard of or seen them.
Only a few masters from the Tang and Song dynasties onward have had their traces so clearly manifest that all people look up to them with reverence.
Yet, when they were by the water’s edge or beneath the forest trees, they used three strips of bamboo and a single hoe as their means for pure self-sustenance;
but when they were guiding disciples and leading assemblies, they took the principle of "if you do not work for a day, you shall not eat for a day" as their true and fragrant legacy.
As for the transformation of others and the reception of disciples, they take a single staff or a single shout as the "upward" extraction of meaning;

thus, these practices no longer correspond with the Vinaya studies. Consequently, those who have left the household life with sincere hearts—whether traveling on pilgrimage, entering the mountains, or ascending the seat and donning the robes—have nothing but such things to emulate. Now, it is even permitted to follow...
Were the aforementioned patriarchs truly bhikṣus? If they were not bhikṣus, how could they have succeeded to the position of the patriarchs?

If they were bhikṣus, why did they not abide by the monastic regulations (*vinaya*)? Furthermore, those who succeed to the patriarchal position in the present day generally hold the study of the *vinaya* in low regard;
do you not recognize that the successive patriarchs of old also held it in low regard? Moreover, regarding those who succeed to the patriarchal position today...
Regarding those in high positions: although they do not personally observe the precepts, they still bestow them upon others.
One asks: "Do the successive patriarchs of old also bestow the precepts upon others? Answer: The successive patriarchs of old each fall into three categories.
The first consists of those who strictly purify the *vinaya* and establish a grand model for the three realms, such as Master Huiyuan, Zhiyi, Zuoxi, Yongjia, Jingxi, Damei, and Yongming.

Ming, Juefan, Gaofeng, Zhongfeng, Chushi, and others were such as these. It is recorded in their biographies that Juefan did not eat at improper times, and Zhongfeng wore but a single robe throughout both winter and summer;
their noble traces are thus clearly manifest. Such realized ones have existed from ancient times to the present.

They are also exceedingly numerous and worthy of our reverence and emulation. Second, because we are in this degenerate age and circumstances leave us no other choice, we follow the Buddha’s final testament by relinquishing minor precepts.
Thus, when dwelling in seclusion, we practice "sword-plowing and fire-seeding," and when leading a community, we clear the land and cultivate fields.
Nevertheless, regarding precepts such as those against eating at improper times, we continue to observe them ourselves; thus, they remain pure.
The regulations for evening use permit only medicinal tonics, not rice gruel; they allow only non-timely liquids, seven-day medicines, and lifelong medicines.
Furthermore, when Deshan went out with his alms bowl, he did so by observing whether it was early or late in the day; one should know that this was not eating at an improper time.
This is clear. Nevertheless, these types of practitioners do not dare to bestow the precepts upon others.

Therefore, since the Tang and Song dynasties, there have been Chan monasteries for Chan, lecture monasteries for exegesis, and Vinaya monasteries for discipline. When one first leaves the household life, [one enters one of these].
Most first study the Vinaya. If they achieve mastery in the study of the Vinaya, they become renowned as masters of the Vinaya.

If they do not achieve mastery in the study of the Vinaya, they abandon it to practice lecturing or Chan meditation. However, they may abandon minor precepts, but they do not abandon the grave precepts or the natural precepts (prakṛti-sāvadya).
Furthermore, there are those who are unable to study the Vinaya and instead directly enter the Chan teachings to practice; this is what is called "urgency in vehicle but laxity in precepts.
Nevertheless, they must certainly protect the five fundamental precepts, and there is no possibility that they would violate the heavy precepts.
I would never dare to call myself a bhikṣu, nor would I ever dare to hold the study of the Vinaya in low regard.
However, I feel ashamed that I have been unable to cultivate both paths simultaneously; thus, I take this as a source of my own humility.

Consequently, when it comes to appearing in the world to guide others, I may sometimes re-enter the ranks of the precepts so that both the prohibitive (śīla) and the natural (prakṛti-sāvadya) offenses are purified, as in the case of the Sixth Patriarch and others; or I may simply uphold the "upward" direction, engaging with individuals through a singular capacity.
For example, there was Shouchang and others. Someone asked Shouchang, "The Buddha ordained that bhikṣus must not dig the earth or harm grasses and trees.
Why do you now plow, sow, weed, and harvest for yourselves?

He replied, "We have merely awakened to the Buddha-mind and are capable of transmitting the Patriarchal intent. We simply point it out to those present so that they may recognize their own mind-nature. If, however..."
According to the standards of the True Dharma, I can only be called a "tonsure layman" (mundaka-gṛhapati); how would I dare to assume the name of a bhikṣu?
He asked again, "If there were someone in these times who was able to carry out the duties of a bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma, how would you regard such a person?
He replied, "If such a person truly existed, I would revere them as a Buddha and treat them with the etiquette due to a teacher."
It is not that we do not wish to do so; it is truly that we have been unable. Furthermore, throughout his life, the Great Master Zibai took only one meal of gruel and rice, consuming no other food.
For over forty years, he did not let his side touch the mat;
yet, because he felt he had still not been able to maintain even the most subtle precepts, he never dared to bestow the *śrāmaṇera* or *bhikṣu* ordinations upon others. He would certainly not...
Once [the precepts] have been received, one is then granted the Dharma of the Five Precepts. Alas! The various patriarchs of antiquity regarded the study of the Vinaya with such reverence;
how could one dare to treat it lightly? Those who hold the Vinaya in contempt certainly belong to the category of those with false views; they are not true masters of the lineage.
Third is the manifestation of great function: observing the capacities of beings to benefit them, shattering the doubts and attachments of others, and not being bound by conventional rules.
This is exemplified by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, who brandished a sword to confront the Buddha; by spending the summer retreats in three different locations;

by sitting with a woman while reprimanding the monk Zhongsheng; and by causing [others] to realize non-arising. It extends even to Hanshan and Shide’s rebukes of the Vinaya Master, and to Guizong and Nanquan.
The slaying of the snake and the killing of the cat were both provisional expedients that could not be avoided at that particular time.

They are like a skilled physician using arsenic to treat a disease, or a great general employing a clever stratagem to eliminate bandits; one may resort to them occasionally, but they cannot be established as a standard rule.
Furthermore, all instances of reviling the Buddha, cursing the Patriarchs, striking with heavy blows, or shouting harshly were likewise [expedients] that could not be avoided.
Subsequently, they were put to use. That which is called "the military" is an inauspicious instrument; it is not comparable to cloth, silk, beans, or grain.
If it is employed appropriately, then its outward appearance may seem to contravene the precepts, yet in reality it truly upholds the precepts, because it captures the essential intent of the Dharma.
This is, for example, like the Lady Mallikā who drank wine to save lives; the Buddha praised her as one who truly observed the fast.

Regarding the precepts: the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Bodhisattva-jie ben) also states that if a bodhisattva perceives the appropriate conditions (*jī*), they may engage in acts such as killing or stealing without violating the bodhisattva precepts, and instead generate great merit.
If one employs these [precepts] inappropriately, making them a mere matter of formal display, it is like You Meng’s imitation of Shu Ao;
the lineage is not the true lineage, and the discipline is not the true discipline—this is to slander the Great [Vehicle].
The Prajñā [scriptures] have misled later students; how could they possibly escape the severe retributions of the three miserable realms?
Even if they were to entice the ignorant toward the Three Jewels to perform various meritorious deeds, it is only by the sustaining power of such merit that they do not immediately fall into ruin.

In the end, they will become followers of external paths and the retinue of Māra, rather than disciples of the Buddha. In the final age, many such demonic and heterodox beings will delude and mislead the world;
supported by Māra, they will receive abundant offerings. Often gathering crowds of hundreds or thousands, their followers and descendants will spread throughout the world.
They will violate the precepts and destroy the teachings, subverting the true Dharma of the Tathāgata.
The True Wheel of Dharma. Ignorant and foolish people, envying its fame and glory, vied with one another to imitate it.
Consequently, those who had left the household life with a sincere heart all fell into their faction; seeking elevation, they instead descended. How tragic and heart-wrenching!

Nevertheless, because they still took the Triple Gem as their object of focus, when the time comes for their retribution for sins to end, they will once again rely on the power of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, and the precepts.
Thus they attain liberation. It is like one who has fallen to the ground rising from that very ground;
compared to those who have not even heard the names of the Triple Gem, they are superior by one measure. Therefore, the Māra said to the Buddha:
"In your age of the Dharma’s decay, I shall cause my kinsmen to eat your food, wear your robes, and destroy your Dharma. The Buddha said: "You shall only destroy yourself; I—"

The Dharma is indestructible. If you now wish not to fall into the three miserable realms and instead ascend directly to the fruits of sainthood, you must certainly begin with the observance of the precepts.
Even if you cannot fully observe them, you must at least praise them and feel a sense of shame within yourself.

If you have already been registered as having received the precepts yet hold the dharma of the precepts in contempt, and if you neither maintain the precepts with diligence nor act as a teacher for others, [you will surely suffer].

Regarding the conferring of precepts: although you have extensively conferred the precepts upon others, you do not instruct them to study the precepts according to the Dharma, but rather say that the precepts belong to the Hīnayāna and need not be practiced.
By doing so, they will certainly fall into the three miserable realms and become followers of Māra;
they will suffer their own miseries, for no one can take their place. Yet, in the end, they will all surely attain Buddhahood. I dare not look down upon them.

General Principles for the Translation of the Vinaya Piṭaka: The original texts are generally verbose and repetitive. Now, wishing to facilitate the study of beginners, I have largely summarized the meaning and condensed the phrasing.
Although the text has been abbreviated, I dare not alter the meaning in the slightest. If you do not believe this, please consult the Vinaya Piṭaka itself.
Regarding the contemplation:
after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the compilation of the Vinaya Piṭaka originally contained no distinctions between various schools.

Later, due to differing attachments, it resulted in the formation of many schools. Once the lineages were divided, each followed its own single path; thus, Yi Jing alone propagated the fundamental [Vinaya].
Originally, Huaisu followed only the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and maintained that it was inappropriate to synthesize it with other traditions.

This was likely out of fear that such a synthesis would allow practitioners to evade or rely on one another, abandoning prohibitions (*pratikṣepa*) to adopt permissions (*anujñā*), or seeking the light while avoiding the grave. Now, following the intent of the Nanshan school, I have composed this synthesis.
My intention is that where the principle is superior, it shall be put into practice; this is truly not a matter of seeking or avoiding, accepting or rejecting.

It is intended to synthesize the great achievements of various schools, so that we may perhaps accord with the original intent of the Tathāgata. Question: When Master Xuán adopted [teachings] from various schools, he was still criticized by Huáisù.
On what basis do you now arbitrarily exercise selection and exclusion? If you were merely following the arbitrary views of an ordinary person, how could this possibly conform to the Great [Vehicle]?
The Venerable Fanggui replied: "The gradual formation of multiple schools due to disputes was indeed a sign of the decline of the Dharma-path.
To adopt the strengths of various schools is the intent of achieving a 'Grand Synthesis' (Dacheng). Although I harbor a simple disdain for such [sectarian] criticisms, my own position has its basis."
Furthermore, the Vinaya scholarship of Master Xuān cannot be entirely dismissed as erroneous. Moreover, the Buddha gave a clear instruction, saying:

"Those with great wisdom are able to discern what to adopt and what to discard, whereas those who are ignorant and deluded cannot make such distinctions. Thus, he clearly intended for his teachings to be synthesized into a comprehensive whole for the sake of future generations.
Therefore, this present compendium of essentials has extensively gathered the strengths of various traditions to serve as a reference, so that—may it be hoped that...
How could one possibly trace the current back to its source? It is not that I dare presume upon my own subjective views to decide what to include or exclude.
Regarding the distinction between natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), I rely solely on the *Sudarsana-vinaya* for judgment.

However, as to whether these distinctions appear under each individual precept or not, I have retained the existing tradition and have not dared to forcibly add them; this is because they may be inferred by analogy. Furthermore, that [text] refers to "regulation" (*saṃvara*).
Regarding the offenses (*āpatti*): here we employ the character "zhē" (遮). Although the characters differ, their meaning is the same;

this is done for the sake of ease of understanding. Beneath each precept, there is a specific origin story (*nidāna*), an explanation of the meaning, and a classification of the gravity of the offense.

Next follows a dialectical inquiry and resolution. Then, there may be citations of scriptural evidence, along with other points concerning monastic decorum (*vinaya-īryāpatha*) that are similar to the fundamental precepts.
These [sections] are likewise appended at the end. Regarding these six categories—whether complete or abbreviated—they will not be listed in detail again;
instead, they shall be designated by the six characters: *yuan* (condition), *shi* (explanation), *xiang* (characteristic), *bian* (discrimination), *zheng* (verification), and *fu* (appendix).
Regarding various translations where the meaning is identical but the phonetics differ, or where the textual characteristics are difficult to clarify, they shall be annotated as appropriate.
Should it be inconvenient to annotate them clearly within the main text, each shall be appended at the end of its respective fascicle for the purpose of consultation and examination.
Regarding the offenses prohibited for Śrāvakas, the Mahāsattvas study them all together;

however, when it comes to opening [these prohibitions] through skillful means for the sake of sentient beings, there are clear evidences throughout the sūtras. How could one possibly allow for a uniform and indiscriminate approach?
Now, based on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and the *Maitreya Bodhisattva Precept Text*, I shall briefly clarify each precept, following the intent of the Tiantai commentaries.
The fivefold Dharma-body is summarized by taking precepts as its reliance; among the three trainings of the outflows-free state, precepts are the foremost.
There is not a single Tathāgata who does not possess the essence of the precepts, nor a single Bodhisattva who does not cultivate the perfection of precepts, nor a single scripture that does not...
Praise for the Dharma of Precepts: There is not a single sage or noble one who does not strictly observe the conduct of the precepts.
Upholding the precepts is like the earth; all myriad virtues are generated from it. Upholding the precepts is like a city; demonic obstacles are kept at bay by means of it.

Regarding its supreme excellence, even one who has merely touched the level of the precepts is called a field of merit for the human world. As for its ultimate destination, it is found in the Buddha alone.

Only then can it be called the perfection of pure precepts. The four-tiered pagoda—each tier representing the sudden and perfect realm—and the eighty thousand subtle practices—each practice encompassing the entire Dharma-realm—if one does not maintain the precepts, then even if one can study the lectures, practice seated meditation, or perform various meritorious deeds, they will all become the works of Māra, and one will inevitably join the ranks of Māra.
Therefore, those who have left home with a sincere heart must certainly follow [the precepts].

The beginning of upholding the precepts is to accomplish both self-benefit and the benefit of others; all dharmas are fulfilled through this. Apart from this general path, there is no shortcut. Question:

The *Bhikṣu-vinaya-piṭaka* originally belongs to the Śrāvaka vehicle, whereas the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* constitutes the Mahāyāna teaching. Now, you claim that all four levels of ordination constitute the realm of the Perfect and Sudden (Yuan-dun).
If so, how are the Great and Small Vehicles distinguished? Furthermore, if they are called "Perfect and Sudden," then they must be of a single kind.
[Question: It is already sufficient. Why must there be four stages? [Answer: For a person of perfect capacity (*yuanren*) who receives the Dharma, there is no dharma that is not perfect.

Having received the purport of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation and manifestation, every single form and fragrance is none other than the Middle Way. How could there be any precepts or dharmas that are not perfect and sudden (*yuantun*)?
Thus, the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) states: "The revelation of the coarse means that the study of the *Vinaya* is itself the study of the Mahāyāna. The *Śikṣā*..."
"Śikṣā (Precepts) is precisely the primary meaning of the Mahāyāna. Light is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black.

The three refuges, the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, and the two hundred and fifty [monastic rules] are all the Mahāyāna. How could there be coarse precepts that separate one from the wondrous precepts?
Since the precepts are themselves wondrous, so too is the person. 'You are truly my son'—this is the meaning of this. This is called..."
The wondrous precepts are absolute and beyond dependence. Alas! Viewed from this perspective, the meaning of the successive stages of the Perfect and Sudden (Yuan-dun) becomes manifest.
In the Dharma of the Perfect and Sudden, the one and the many are non-obstructive; only then does it constitute the inconceivable.

If one were to claim that a single type [of teaching] is sufficient, then could one say that the *Avataṃsaka*—with its seven locations and nine assemblies—is also sufficient in just one location and one assembly? Furthermore, [the text] asks: Five...
Regarding the precepts—the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras, the bhikṣu precepts, and the bodhisattva precepts—they are like the four tiers of a multi-storied tower. Therefore it is said:
"It is impossible for one who has not received the five precepts to receive the ten precepts, and so on, up to one who has not received the bhikṣu precepts to receive the bodhisattva precepts.
Thus, the meaning of this sequential progression is clear. Why, then, is it now permitted for śrāmaṇeras to receive the bodhisattva precepts?
"Does this not contradict the sincere words from the Golden Mouth? Answer: "The analogy of the multi-storied tower was intended merely as a provisional illustration of their sequence.
If one were to insist upon it literally, then even an upāsaka would be unable to receive the bodhisattva precepts.
Since it is permissible for an upāsaka to receive them, why alone should a śrāmaṇera be denied? In fact, the śrāmaṇera should rather surpass the upāsaka."
Sengyai replied: "However, regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, their principles are broad and they are not merely enumerated for the seven classes of practitioners.

Furthermore, in the various monasteries of the Western Regions, the Mahayana and Hinayana traditions are distinct; how could it be that there are no śrāmaṇeras at all within Mahayana monasteries? Again, he asked:
'The three—Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya—are like the orchid in spring and the chrysanthemum in autumn, each excelling in its own beauty. Why do you now single out the precepts as being universal?'"

Tudu asked: "How is it that from antiquity these have been established as three schools? He replied: "Among the twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Heaven, there were none who did not fully uphold the Tripitaka.
It was only when the Dharma flowed eastward to this land that separate lineages and gateways were established.
Yet, throughout history, we have never heard of a true Chan master or a Dharma-preacher who neglected the rules of propriety or transgressed the boundaries of decorum."

Generally, those who have not yet studied the precepts often fear the difficulty of upholding them; this is precisely because they do not understand the dharma of the precepts and thus falsely give rise to thoughts of retreat and abandonment.

If one studies these precepts, one will finally realize that the Tathāgata’s great wisdom exhaustively accommodates human sentiments, such that what is permitted and what is prohibited is perfectly suited to the occasion, and guarding them is not difficult.
I recall when I first left the household life, I relied on my own fundamental purity and felt [deeply... (Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)
Fearing the trivialities of ritual practice, he was unwilling even to accept the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera, let alone the full or perfect ordinations.
It was only because he followed the custom of the monastic community that he was compelled to receive the ten precepts.

Subsequently, as he perused the *Prātimokṣa* and eventually read through the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, he finally came to believe that if one wishes to attain mastery and fearlessness, one must be thoroughly proficient in the Vinaya. Without having studied the Vinaya...
At every turn, one encounters obstructions. The Confucianist says, "Without learning the rites, there is no way to stand.

How profound these words are! The lands of the Western Regions are mostly hot and humid; grasses and vegetables do not grow there. Therefore, it was permitted for bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat.
In this land, there are many varieties of vegetables; one must certainly not eat meat.
Furthermore, while those in the various kingdoms of the Western Regions who practice only the Hīnayāna consume the five kinds of pure meat, in Mahāyāna lands, this is entirely prohibited.

Now that the Mahāyāna has spread throughout this realm of China, if anyone were to eat meat, public censure would boil over and the World-Protectors would express their reproach; nothing is more essential than this.
Even if one has not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts, one must certainly not eat meat. Should one eat meat, they are not a śramaṇa.
While both the Sūtra and Śāstra Piṭakas are valued for their wide circulation, the Vinaya alone is held as extremely precious and secret. For this reason...
This is solely the Dharma of the Great Sangha; it is not something that outsiders may share. Therefore, the *Mūla-vinaya* states:
"Lay followers may hear the two piṭakas—the Śāstras and the Sūtras—but the Vinaya teachings are the disciplinary code for those who have left the household life."
It is not appropriate for the laity to hear [these matters]. The Preface to the *Śīla-hetupratyaya-sūtra* states: "In India, those who uphold the Vinaya do not disclose [the texts] to everyone.
Only those who are practitioners of the twelve dharmas and are firm and clear-minded may open the seals and transmit them to one another.
When Yaśas saw this entrustment, he was deeply instructed: "People may be made to follow [the path], but they cannot be made to know it. These words were most earnest and profound.
I only pray that those like me will be especially cautious regarding what is transmitted. Do not grant it to anyone under five years of age who is not a holder of the Vinaya.
From observing what is stated in these two Vinayas, one can know their gravity.

Therefore, if a śrāmaṇera understands the five categories of offenses, he may immediately undergo the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) provided there are no prohibitions or obstacles. This present *Jiyao* (Essentials) is specifically intended for those who delight in brevity.
This [text] is intended for those who have already received the precepts to practice and uphold; do not allow those who have not yet received them to peruse it prematurely.
Should a śrāmaṇera examine it, you must immediately rebuke and stop him. If you do not do so, both parties will incur transgressions. Question:

The World-Honored One’s teaching is like the moisture of a single rain; all who are moistened by it obtain benefit. Formerly, there was one who heard half a verse of a sutra and was thereby spared from [rebirth].
They fall into the womb of a dog. As for those who carry great scriptures like oxen and later become śramaṇas:
why is it that the Vinaya Piṭaka alone is treated as a precious secret? Is it that it cannot benefit people, or is it that one does not wish to benefit them?

Furthermore, even if a person has not yet received full ordination, should they resolve to read the Tripiṭaka, how could they know of the Buddha’s prohibition and fail to examine it? Moreover, there are those who transcribe and carve [the texts].

Those of such a class must have already passed before your eyes. If they later resolve to develop the aspiration for enlightenment and receive the precepts, should they be permitted to undergo full ordination (*upasampadā*), or should they be considered subject to the ultimate obstacle (*antarāyika-dharma*)?
If they were considered subject to the ultimate obstacle, then within the Buddha-dharma there would be a trap of limitation, and the nectar of immortality would instead become a poisonous drug.
Answer: The Sūtras value universal circulation, so as to establish the seeds of hearing-perfuming (*śruta-vāsanā*). The Vinaya, however, ought to be cherished...

Secret. This is for the purpose of preventing the transgression of "thieving residence" (賊住). One secret and one disclosure together constitute the Tathāgata’s skillful application of the four *siddhāntas*.

As for those who read through ignorance or by mistake, or where the text has been engraved before their eyes—since there was no intention to steal the Dharma, this should not be considered a grave offense.
However, those who write or engrave the text may not necessarily understand it; they can still be reconciled [with the teaching]. But as for those who read the *Tripitaka*...
One must certainly come to a thorough understanding; this requires strict prohibition. It is up to those who know the Dharma to provide skillful guidance.

Furthermore, it was asked: "If the *vinaya* categories and clusters (*pien-chu*) are not permitted for laypeople or *śrāmaṇeras* to know in advance, for what reason did the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly of humans and devas at the *Nirvāṇa* assembly, extensively explain the five categories and seven clusters, and entrust them [to others]?"
"Kun! Do not let [others] transgress. Is it not the case that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was also spoken specifically for bhikṣus, and thus cannot be circulated among the world at large?
Answer: "At the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa*, there were exclusively a multitude of great Bodhisattvas; there were certainly no evil persons who would steal the Dharma.
Therefore, regarding the names of the categories of precepts (*pīn-zǔ*), they were not concealed at all. Nevertheless, while their names were merely mentioned, they were not [fully detailed]."
Regarding the meaning of this matter: at present, when preaching on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is not necessary to provide a detailed explanation. Furthermore, it was asked:

"If one says that a śrāmaṇera understands the five categories of offenses, does he thereby become subject to the obstacles and difficulties for receiving full ordination? Now, suppose there is a person who wishes to receive the precepts."

First, one should examine the five chapters to determine whether they constitute obstacles or prohibitions. Answer: Regarding the dharma of the bhikṣu precepts, one should only undertake their observance after having received them;
one should not examine them beforehand without having received them. Even if one examines them by mistake without knowing this, the circumstances may still be excused.
However, if one knows this and deliberately violates it, it is difficult to grant leniency.

The personhood of a bhikṣu is most venerable; the customs of the common world are exceedingly defiled. Reciting sutras and performing repentance may still be called the "gift of Dharma" (dharma-dāna).
But blowing the sheng flute and beating the cymbals—how does this differ from the antics of a courtesan or a performer?

If the Lotus Sutra permits offerings to the Buddha, it was originally intended for laypeople. Since one’s physical appearance and deportment already place one within the ranks of the Sangha, how could one allow oneself to be so profaned? Thus, then:

When changing from the Vinaya (Yuan) tradition to the Chan tradition, one must permanently sever all matters such as music and performance. If these are not severed, it is a profound violation of the Buddha’s regulations.

Question: If you claim that blowing the sheng flute or beating the gong is comparable to performing for a lay troupe (*you*), yet the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states that during great assemblies and the *pravāraṇā*, there are drums, music, banners, flowers, and incense offerings at various shrines—since this is logically consistent with the former, why is it not permitted? If [it were permitted],...
If one merely causes another to perform [a prohibited act], what distinction is there between doing it oneself and instructing another? Would this not constitute a transgression? Answer:

The five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and the ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala*) are natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) according to worldly nature; therefore, instructing another to commit them is categorized as the same offense as committing them oneself.

However, dancing, singing, and performing as entertainers are prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) for those who have left the household life. Causing others to perform music remains termed a "meritorious deed" (*puṇya-karman*); it cannot be classified as a natural offense.
This is an example of a transgression.
Regarding the precept against eating at improper times, both the sūtras and śāstras fully demonstrate its inappropriateness; none of the vinayas permit it.

To refer to late-day meals as "medicinal food" (yao-shi) was originally not the word of the Buddha, though it may have been a skillful expedient of ancient practitioners. Even for those who are physically weak...
I am frequently ill. I already possess non-timely drinks, seven-day medicines, and lifetime medicines that can sustain me.
Why then would I willingly violate this great precept? Unless it is a circumstance where my life is at stake, I cannot strictly observe [the rule].
Otherwise, I may relinquish the names of Bhikṣu or Śrāmaṇera and simply act as a Bodhisattva Upavāsastha, or [observe] with earnestness every half-month.
I repent deeply and vow never again to transgress; I am content to be called a Master of Precepts. Question:

Regarding the precept against eating at improper times, it is termed *zhāi* (fasting). It certainly must not be violated. However, among the masters of old, there were many who were unable to maintain it.
Even if one’s fundamental [precepts] are pure, if the remaining aspects of the precepts are somewhat impure, does one still fall from them? Answer: One falls.

Violating the precepts and breaking the fast are both termed unwholesome dharmas. If one merely protects the root precepts, how can one hope to avoid the retribution for receiving offerings while being in debt?

As for those of the past who were true spiritual friends—those whose practice was swift in the vehicle but lax in the precepts—they certainly possessed a sense of shame and would never act as precept masters;
examples include Zibai and Shouchang. Furthermore, there are contemporary spiritual friends who do not observe the minor precepts, yet mistakenly [assume authority].
Even those who serve as teachers for others are not necessarily subject to downfall, for they are sustained by other particularly superior meritorious deeds.

Thus, their names contradict one another. This serves as a metaphor for the *Pañcaśata-praśna*, which is internally inconsistent with the Vinaya Piṭaka.

General Principles:
Regarding the intent of the Nanshan school, Vinaya Master Daoxuan resided on Mount Zhongnan; therefore, the world refers to the Vinaya tradition as the Nanshan school.
Although Master Xuan took the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka* as his primary authority, he frequently collected the strengths of various other schools.

Regarding natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*): even prior to the formulation of the precepts, there were naturally sinful acts according to worldly conventions;
these are called natural offenses, such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and the four types of verbal misconduct.
The World-Honored One established the rules of discipline (*śīla-dharma*) to protect monastics from worldly reproach; these are called prohibited offenses, such as keeping extra robes overnight.
Eating [food] such as that dug from the ground which damages the grass and other vegetation is prohibited by the Buddha. One who commits it incurs an offense;

therefore, it is called a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offense) and is also termed a *prajñapti-sāvadya* (prescribed offense), meaning that the offense is incurred in accordance with the Buddha’s prescription.
Regarding the offenses prohibited by the Śrāvakas, the Mahāsattva studies them all together with them. The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states:

"The Vinaya establishes prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) for the sake of protecting sentient beings, so as to cause those without faith to have faith, and to increase the faith of those who already possess it; thus one trains together with the Śrāvakas.
Why is this? If even the Śrāvakas, who seek only their own liberation, do not abandon the protection of others, how much more so must this be true for a Bodhisattva?"
For the sake of sentient beings, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* skillfully employs expedient means to provide an opening [for certain rules]. It states:

"Furthermore, regarding those prohibitions where one dwells in little benefit, performs little activity, and employs little skillful means, a bodhisattva does not train in these precepts in the same manner.

Now, according to the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu, there are only six matters concerning forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) that are opened up [as permissible] for the bodhisattva precepts.

The rest are not to be opened [or used] falsely. Regarding the six matters: first, begging for robes from those who are not relatives; second, receiving more than permitted during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony;
third, keeping an extra alms bowl; fourth, having a weaver who is not a relative weave a robe;
fifth, keeping bedding made of silk-cotton; sixth, accepting gold and silver. These are all for the sake of sentient beings; they are not permitted for one's own personal use.

In his *Yìshū* (Commentary on the Meaning), the Great Master Zhìzhě, within the "Mind-Ground" chapter of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, uniquely extracts and expounds upon the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts of the dharma-practice.
This work is titled the *Yìshū*. Beneath each precept, he invariably provides a comparative analysis (*liàojiǎn*) of their similarities and differences with those found in the Hīnayāna.

The three trainings in the outflow-free states (*anāsrava-śikṣā*) are summarized as having morality (*śīla*) as their foremost. The *Buddhottama-sūtra* states: "From morality arises concentration (*samādhi*);

from concentration issues forth wisdom (*prajñā*). This is what is called the three trainings in the outflow-free states. It further states: "Even if one possesses meditative concentration and abundant wisdom..."
First, if one does not cease sexual misconduct, one will inevitably fall into the realm of Māra; if one does not cease killing, one will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits, and so forth.
*Śikṣā* is translated here as "training."
The five kinds of pure meat are: not seeing the killing, not hearing of the killing, and not suspecting that it was killed for one's sake; meat from animals that died naturally;
and meat left over by birds. The twelve dharmas refer to the twelve *dhūta* practices.
Yeshé is likely the same as Buddhayaśas, who translated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* together with Zhu Fonian.
The phrase "one may cause a person to follow it, but one cannot cause them to know it" originally derives from the *Analects*; it is used here by adaptation.
It means that a person who has newly received the precepts may only be made to practice in accordance with the Vinaya, but they cannot yet be made to study the Vinaya in detail.

It appears that the six groups of bhikṣus were all manifestations of great expedient means (*mahopāya*), intentionally demonstrating the conditions for transgression for the sake of the degenerate age.

This was done out of sincere concern that the ignorant might fail to understand and mistake these events for actual occurrences, thereby concluding that even during the Buddha’s own lifetime such things occurred—let alone in the present day—and consequently allowing their minds to run wild with license.

Next, regarding the origins and lineages of the various schools (*nikāya*): each school possesses both general and specific names.

This translates as "skillful governance" (*shan-zhi*), also translated as "subduing" (*tiaofu*), and also translated as "extinction" (*weimie*).

The Dharma of Precepts consists of three types: first, the precept of restraint (saṃvara-śīla), also called the prātimokṣa-precept;

second, the precept concomitant with meditative concentration (dhyāna-sahaja-śīla), also called the dhyāna-precept; and third, the precept concomitant with the Path (mārga-sahaja-śīla), also called the untainted precept (anāsrava-śīla).

Regarding the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint): "restraint" (*saṃvara*) means to prohibit; "conduct" (*vṛtta*) refers to physical demeanor. Because it can stop various evils within one's physical conduct, it is called "precept" (*śīla*).
It is also termed "dignified conduct" (*īryāpatha*). "Dignity" (*īryā*) means being pure, solemn, and awe-inspiring; "conduct" (*patha*) means being a model that may be followed as a standard.
It is also called "the Tamer," meaning that it causes the activities of the mind to become disciplined and wholesome.

*Prātimokṣa* is translated here as "preserving liberation" (*baohuatuō*) and also as "individual liberation" (*biébiéjiětuō*). This is because it can ensure that the practitioner escapes the ocean of birth and death;
furthermore, by observing and maintaining each individual precept without violation, one attains liberation in each respective instance. These are the two [meanings].
The one hundred and fifty rules of training (*śikṣāpada*) and the attendant monastic decorum (*vinaya-īryāpatha*). "Concentration" (*samādhi*) means stillness and withdrawal;

at the time of entering concentration, one naturally becomes disciplined and virtuous, preventing all evils. "Path" (*mārga*) means that which enables penetration; after the realization of truth has arisen, there is naturally no further transgression.
It is like a field being plowed for the first time where insects remain four inches away; this is the power inherent in the Path. Since these two methods of precept (*śīla-dharma*) have already...

This is the superior function of the mind; its power is able to give rise to the precepts (*śīla*). Since the path (*mārga*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) arise concurrently with the restraint (*saṃvara*), they are called "concomitant.
Now, the Vinaya Piṭaka primarily elucidates the restraint, yet it also encompasses meditative concentration and the path.

Because the merits of dhyāna-concentration and wisdom arise from upholding the pure precepts, the restraint serves as the cause, while meditative concentration and the path serve as the fruit. This is due to [the distinction between] dhyāna and the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding power: when both natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) are entirely purified, then the *prātimokṣa* is the fruit, while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*) serve as the conditions.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "This *prātimokṣa* precept exists only when the Buddha is in the world; when the Buddha is not in the world, it does not exist.
The dhyāna-precept and the untainted precept (*anāsrava-śīla*) exist at all times. Thus ends the section on the *prātimokṣa* precept.
The precepts of dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) precepts are not obtained through instruction;

as it is said, the *prātimokṣa* precepts exist only among the disciples of the Buddha, whereas the dhyāna precepts are possessed by both Buddhists and non-Buddhists alike. Indeed, it is these [latter] that are able to sustain the Buddha-dharma.
There are seven classes of practitioners in the world, and the succession of the fruits of the path of the Three Vehicles remains uninterrupted;

all of these take the *prātimokṣa* as their root. This is not the case for the meditative (*dhyāna*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) precepts. Therefore, among the three types of precepts, it is the most excellent.

According to the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the Buddha himself recorded that after the extinction of the Dharma by Puṣyamitra, a descendant of King Śuṅga, there would be a king of exceptionally virtuous character who would restore the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus would become fond of fame and frequently give rise to disputes, [and they would] excerpt...
They administered my Vinaya, expanding and enlarging what Kāśyapa had codified. They split into separate factions, each claiming right and wrong, and sought the King’s adjudication.
The King assembled the two groups and distributed voting tallies; those who took the old [version] were numerous and were called the Mahāsāṃghika (meaning "The Great Assembly").
Those who took the new [version] were few, yet they were the Sthaviras (meaning "The Elders") and were called the Tāmraśāṭīya (meaning "The Red-Robed Ones").
Thereafter, due to disputes, further schools arose. Over the course of three or four hundred years, they branched out and divided again and again until they became numerous.
After a long period of transmission, whether correct or incorrect, only five schools remained.
Each extolled its own strengths and designated itself by the color of its robes: the Mahāsāṃghika school diligently studied the various sūtras and proclaimed the true meaning.
Because their position is central, they should wear yellow robes. The Dharmaguptaka school (i.e., the Dharmagupta) masters the flavor of principle;
they provide guidance for the benefit of others and manifest what is sublime; they should wear red robes. The Sarvāstivāda school...

The Mahīśāsaka school, being broad-minded, versatile, and sagacious, employs these qualities to guide the transformation through the Dharma; they should wear black robes. The Kāśyapīya school, being diligent and courageous, protects and gathers in sentient beings;
they should wear madder-dyed robes. The Mahīśāsaka school, through meditative contemplation, enters into the subtle and thoroughly elucidates the profound and esoteric;
they should wear blue-green robes. As for the Mahāsāṃghika school, its flavor is pure and correct; as for the other schools...
It is like when the gods drink [the mixture] containing nectar; they drink only the nectar and discard the water.

When humans drink it, they take both the water and the nectar together; sometimes this leads to a swift recovery, and sometimes it results in illness. It is the same for those who recite [this teaching]:
those with great wisdom are able to discern what to accept and what to reject, whereas the ignorant are unable to make such distinctions.

The *Bhikṣu-vinaya* was divided into five schools (*nikāya*). Subsequently, it indeed became divided into five: first, the Dharmaguptaka school;
second, the Sarvāstivāda school—this is translated as "Proponents of All Existence"—the name of whose Dharma is the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*;
third, the Kāśyapīya school—this is translated as "Revering the Contemplation of Emptiness"—of which only one fascicle of the *Vimukti-śīla-sūtra* has reached this land.
Fourth is the Mahīśāsaka school; this is translated as "the School of Contemplation that Does Not Adhere to Being or Non-being. Its legal texts are known as the *Pañcavargika* (Five-Part Vinaya).
Fifth is the Vātsīputrīya school; this is translated as "Child of the Ox" (*Gokula*). The original Vinaya of this school has not been transmitted here.

These five schools are the branches, while the Mahāsāṃghika is the trunk; generally speaking, there are six schools. Furthermore, according to the *Nanhai Jiguishi Chuan* (Record of the Inner Sea Sent Home), regarding the various lineages of these schools: [text follows].

and fourth, the noble Saṃmitīya school, which branched out into four schools. Among these, there were further divisions and sub-divisions.

first, Dharmaguptaka; second, Mahīśāsaka; and third, Kāśyapīya. As for what are called the *Daśabhāṇavāra* and the *Caturvarga*, [these belong to the former two].

Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) is not actually the Mūlasarvāstivāda [vinaya]. King Bimbisāra dreamed that a single lock of hair split into eighteen strands and that a golden staff was broken into eighteen pieces;
terrified, he questioned the Buddha. The Buddha said: "More than one hundred years after my parinirvāṇa..."
There was King Aśoka, whose majesty extended over Jambudvīpa. At that time, the bhikṣus (i.e., monks) taught eighteen different paths to liberation;
yet their ultimate aim was one and the same. This was precisely the omen [of what was to come]; let not the King be distressed by this.
