The second [section] clarifies the essence [of the precepts]. First, it clarifies non-arising; next, it clarifies the two virtues of cessation and cultivation.

Regarding the first clarification of non-arising, Master Tiantai said: "As for the essence of the precepts, it is simply non-arising. If it arises, it is the nature [of the precepts], which is unconditioned (asamskrta) and fictitious matter (avijñapti-rūpa).
Master Qing explained: "This means that as for this essence of the precepts, if it does not arise, that is it; if it arises, it is entirely the nature. And as for the nature..."

When cultivation reaches completion, there must be non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*). Once this non-informative [matter] has been produced, one spontaneously ceases from evil and spontaneously practices good;
after it has been performed once, it does not require repeated performance, and is therefore called "non-informative" (*avijñapti*). (Text) Regarding what is called non-informative matter:

among the eleven types of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), each has both conventional and substantial aspects. Within the category of matter subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is exclusively determined...

Resultant matter is called substantial matter (*dravya-rūpa*). Manifest and non-manifest matter are both called conventional matter (*prajñapti-rūpa*). Regarding the two types of precepts, wholesome and unwholesome, each has both manifest and non-manifest forms.
The manifest is termed "action" (*vijñapti*), and the non-manifest is termed "non-action" (*avijñapti*).

For now, I shall explain the wholesome precepts. Kneeling on one knee with diligent effort is called bodily manifestation (*kāya-vijñapti*). Reciting the request for the precepts three times is called vocal manifestation (*vāg-vijñapti*). [The Sangha...]

The assembly gathers at the site of the precept platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*). This is also called "bodily intimation" (*kāya-vijñapti*). The formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is also called "vocal intimation" (*vāk-vijñapti*).

Through this ritual act, one receives and attains the pure essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*), becomes a bhikṣu by nature, and [this state] becomes the object-condition (*ālambana*) for the mental faculty.
Because one spontaneously and constantly attains both the virtues of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), it is said: "Once performed, there is no need for it to be performed again;
this is called non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*). This essence of the non-informative precept is obtained at the conclusion of the third *karmavācana*.
One obtains the quality of non-lustful form with respect to all males and females, and one obtains [the quality of non-harming] with respect to all sentient and insentient beings.
One does not steal forms; regarding all sentient beings, one attains the quality of non-killing; regarding all sentient beings, one attains the quality of non-deception;
even regarding all ground, one attains the quality of non-digging; regarding all grasses and trees, one attains the quality of non-destruction;
regarding all intoxicants, one attains the quality of non-drinking. Thus there are two hundred and fifty [precepts].

Each and every precept of the Dharma individually pervades the entire Dharmadhātu. Therefore, the *Sutra on the Merit of Leaving Home* clarifies that the merit of observing the precepts for a single day and night is inexhaustible;
this is precisely because these wondrous and virtuous precepts universally take the Dharmadhātu as their object.
Thus, the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) essence of the precepts is a form belonging to the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana-rūpa); it is an outflow-free (anāsrava) form. It is established.

The treatise states that the "non-material, non-mental aggregate" (avijñapti) is mentioned to refute the two difficulties regarding the mind—namely, that there would be no loss or gain [of karma], and that the fruit [of Buddhahood] would lack both the insentient and the wholesome.

(The *Yishu* says: "Non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is explained differently in the sūtras and śāstras; there is debate over its existence or non-existence. One view holds that the mere mental vow not to commit evil is itself called 'receiving the precepts,' and that there is no such thing as non-manifest form at all.

Furthermore, if there were a distinct insentient-wholesome factor within the causal stage that together constitutes the cause of Buddhahood, then in the stage of Buddhahood there should likewise be a distinct wholesome factor that together constitutes the fruit of Buddhahood. This argument—that because the fruit lacks an insentient-wholesome factor, the precepts must be material phenomena—is based on the false views of the Hīnayāna.)

This is because non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is reckoned as a real form external to the mind. One school says: "The sutras and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna all contain [the doctrine of] non-informative action. If one were to take the mind alone as the precept, then upon the mere arising of the thought [to observe it], one should immediately obtain the precept. Why, then, are those who have committed the seven grave offenses unable to obtain the precept?"

Furthermore, there is absolutely no such thing as "non-action" (*avijñapti*). Why, then, is one said to have lost their precepts upon committing a grave offense? This is because the mind itself has neither gain nor loss; the precepts are a mental phenomenon (*cittadharma*). The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* establishes a category that is neither matter (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), which can simultaneously refute both difficulties.

Therefore, the Vinaya masters of antiquity relied upon this principle. According to what is clarified in the Mahāyāna, the precepts are "provisional matter" (*prajñaptirūpa*). Relying on a teacher, one receives them once, and they persist until reaching Bodhi. In accordance with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*), one vows to cultivate all virtues and vows to deliver all sentient beings.

It is also because the power of this mental force is great that it separately gives rise to the goodness of the precepts, serving as an object of focus (*ālambana*) for the practitioner to cease all evils. In reality, they are obtained through the influence of the mind, and are manifested by borrowing the form of matter. Thus...
The Mahāyāna tradition states: When the first *karmavācanā* is completed, the sublime and virtuous precepts of the ten directions, through the power of the mental karma, cause all things to tremble.

When the second *karmavācanā* is completed, the sublime and virtuous precepts of the ten directions appear in the void like clouds or canopies, covering the crown of the practitioner’s head. When the third *karmavācanā* is completed, the ten...

The wondrous and virtuous dharma of the precepts flows from the crown of the practitioner’s head into their body and mind, filling the primary retribution (the physical form) so that it serves as the seed of Buddhahood forever until the end of the future.
Although this matter is not explicitly mentioned within the Vinaya Piṭaka, it is also stated therein:
"When the *karmavācanā* is accomplished, one is said to have attained the locus. One should know that this refers to the contaminated five aggregates and the physical body.

The support is the untainted five aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*). The support for the body of precepts (*śīla-kāya*) is the tainted physical body (*sāsrava-rūpa-kāya*), which is born from the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood;
this is a conventional form (*rūpa-āyatana-prajñapti-rūpa*). The untainted body of precepts is obtained through the *karma* of the three masters and seven witnesses;
this is a conventional form within the sphere of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana-prajñapti-rūpa*). For this reason, the *upādhyāya* is called "one who gives birth by power," because he is truly able—

One receives the name [of a monk] only by giving rise to the aggregate of precepts (śīlaskandha). Having attained this aggregate of precepts, one becomes equal to the Jewel of the Sangha, enabling devas and nāgas to pay respectful homage and spirits and ghosts to receive it with reverence.
If the mind does not delight in the Path, it is called "weakness of the precepts" (śīla-klība).

If one declares to others that one renounces them, it is called "returning the precepts. If one truly lacks this unmanifest (avijñapti) essence of the precepts, then for what reason would celestial deities offer their respect?
Furthermore, why are they called "feeble" (*līna*) and "abandoned" (*prahīṇa*)? Question:

Since there is feebleness, abandonment, and also breaking [of the precepts], how can they be called "spontaneous cessation of practice"? Answer: It is like a bridge; it can spontaneously ferry people across.
Regarding the pond and well: they can be drawn upon spontaneously. If one were to dismantle the bridge or block the inlet, their functional capacity would be lost;
otherwise, they remain available at all times without needing to be recreated. Therefore, they are called "unconditioned" (*avijñapti*).

Next, to clarify the two virtues of restraint (*saṃvara*) and practice (*caryā*), as stated in the *Śata-śāstra*: the cessation of evil and non-performance [of it] is termed "restraint," while faith, acceptance, and cultivation [of virtue] constitute practice.
Cultivation is termed "practice" (*caryā*). Although the teachings of the Buddha are numerous, they are fully encompassed within cessation and practice.

Now, regarding these wholesome precepts: if they do not arise, that is one thing; but if they do arise, they strike down evil. All of these possess the meaning of cessation, and all possess the meaning of progress.

As for "striking down evil," this refers to the root afflictions and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) which give rise to the seven branches of body and speech; these are the causes of evil, leading to the intense sufferings of the three miserable realms.
This is the evil fruit. This collection of the Vinaya consists of ten points of meaning (as explained in detail below).

For the sake of the bhikṣus, he establishes the precepts so that those who receive and uphold them will eliminate the causes of evil and cause the fruits of evil to vanish; this is called "eradicating evil. As for "advancing forward":
To restrain the sense faculties, maintain mindfulness without confusion, always unify the mind, and practice all wholesome dharmas—
thereby spontaneously eliciting the provisional rewards of human and celestial realms, up to the ultimate fruit of supramundane liberation— is the meaning of "progressing forward."
The second section, on the determination of the essence, is concluded.

The third section, the critical analysis, is further divided into two parts: first, distinguishing attainment and relinquishment in relation to the Mahāyāna; second, distinguishing depth and shallowness according to the characteristics of the teachings.
Regarding the first, the distinction between attainment and relinquishment: the Mahāyāna emphasizes internal causes, whereas the Hīnayāna emphasizes external ones.
Because the internal cause is paramount, one must first resolve to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) before being fit to receive the precepts.

If one does so within a state of mind that is unwholesome or neutral, no non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is produced; therefore, for those who have no teacher even a thousand *li* away, it is permitted to receive the precepts before an image.

Because external conditions are paramount, there must be a preceptor, the monastic boundary, and the ritual procedures, all of which must accord with the regulations. If any one of these conditions is lacking—

If the conditions are not complete, one is not said to have attained the precepts; yet once all conditions are met, the attainment of the precepts pervades the three types of mind (meaning that the precepts arise simultaneously within states of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral mind).

Furthermore, after the single attainment [of the precepts], in the Mahāyāna they persist until the attainment of the Buddha-body, whereas in the Hīnayāna they last only for the duration of one's life.

In the Mahāyāna, if one commits a grave transgression involving the ten heavy offenses with superior fetters (*paryavasthāna*), or if one regresses from the Mahāyāna bodhicitta, it is termed "losing the precepts."

In the Hīnayāna, if one commits any of the four grave prohibitions (*catur-śīla-skandha*), it is termed "losing the precepts" (*śīla-hāni*). If the mind no longer delights in the Path and one renounces them before another person, it is termed "returning the precepts" (*pratyākhyāna-śīla*).
After losing the precepts in the Mahāyāna, if one perceives auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*), re-receiving them is permitted.

In the Hīnayāna, there is no provision for re-receiving once the precepts have been lost; however, provided that one never again conceals the offense, one may merely undergo the *karmavācanā* ritual and be granted the status of a trainee (*śikṣādattaka*).

(Regarding legal offenses, this is clarified within the Dharma itself). If one abandons the precepts, it is permitted to receive them again; however, after returning to lay life three times, one’s connection to the path is severed. Question:

Since the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*) is explained according to the Mahāyāna, yet the analysis of their acquisition and abandonment still distinguishes between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, does this not constitute a contradiction in the fundamental tenets?

Answer: Explaining [the precepts] according to the Mahāyāna as being without a creator does not violate the substance of the precepts themselves. This is in contrast to the [distinctions made between] the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

To discern what is to be attained and what is to be relinquished is not to destroy the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. If one violates the substance (*tattva*) of phenomena, then their characteristics have nothing upon which to rely;

if one destroys the characteristics of phenomena, then their substance has no means by which to manifest. Therefore, after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* revealed and clarified [the truth], the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* continued to support the precepts and regulations.

The rules and procedures of the *vinaya* have not been altered in the slightest. This is precisely what is meant by "knowing the constant within this very [reality]"; only then can it be called the wondrous state that transcends all dependencies.
That the fundamental tenets and their realization mutually support one another can be understood through reflection. Furthermore, it was asked:

Since the Mahāyāna places such importance on internal causes (*adhyātma-hetu*), when a Vinaya master nowadays confers the Bodhisattva precepts upon others, how can one know whether their internal cause is genuine or not? If it is not genuine...

Is it considered that one has obtained the precepts? If one has not obtained the precepts, then even if one commits the ten grave offenses, is one’s transgression determined by those ten grave offenses?
Answer: Within the *Karmavācanā* of Maitreya Bodhisattva, there is fully contained the method for observing the suitability of the recipient.
If one cannot discern the internal causes [of ordination] yet rashly transmits the precepts, one cannot avoid the fault of acting as a master without understanding.

Nevertheless, although the person receiving the precepts does not generate the formal vow within a state of unwholesome or neutral mind, they have nonetheless improperly assumed the title of "Bodhisattva" and must therefore be judged for their offense according to the Vinaya;
this is not the same as the case of one who has failed to obtain the Bhikṣu precepts.
In the end, he was judged according to the rules for one who feigns ordination (*caura-vāsa*). Next, to distinguish the levels of depth:

this belongs to the teaching of the "taste of curd" (*dadhi-rasa*), because it first disciplines ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) so that they may enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*). If one explains this by means of the mutual fusion of the five flavors, it can also be interpreted according to the four teachings (*catuḥ-śāsana*).
That is to say, firmly and steadfastly upholding all prohibitive precepts and being forever free from fetters—this is the teaching of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka).

If one realizes that offenses are like illusory diseases and the precepts are like illusory medicines, such that both upholding and violating are fundamentally empty and body and mind are pure, this is the teaching common to all vehicles (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*).

If one relies upon faith in the Middle Way, using these precepts first to sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), then subsequently engaging with the mundane world to benefit sentient beings, and finally awakening to and entering the Middle Way, this is the distinct teaching (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*). If the precepts are the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), then all...
The Dharma leads toward the precepts; this path does not exceed them. Abiding in the secret treasury of the precepts, one clearly perceives the Buddha-nature within each and every precept;
this is precisely the teaching of the Perfect Dharma. Furthermore, the Tathāgata established these precepts through the four *siddhāntas*, in accordance with the world.
To protect sentient beings and cause them to give rise to joy is the world-realm *siddhānta*. To produce goodness is the person-realm *siddhānta*.
To eliminate evil is the remedial *siddhānta*. To enable the True Dharma to abide for a long time is the ultimate *siddhānta*.
Furthermore, since one has received the teaching that reveals and clarifies [the truth], these precepts belong solely to the One Vehicle and are no longer the three previous vehicles. Therefore...

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, if there are people with gentle and supple minds, such individuals as these have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.
It further states: "That which you practice is the bodhisattva path.
Moreover, even before the [Great Vehicle] was fully revealed, Mahāyāna bhikṣus were required to study together; thus, the *Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa-sūtra* says: "If a bodhi..."

Śāriputra, within the Tathāgata’s *prātimokṣa*, the *vinaya* establishes prohibitions against offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) for the sake of protecting sentient beings, so that those without faith may gain faith and those with faith may increase and expand it. This is the same as the training of the *śrāvakas*. Why is this?
Because even the *śrāvakas*, who seek only their own liberation, do not fail to protect others; how much more so must this be true for the Bodhisattvas, whose ultimate aim is the liberation of all?
Furthermore, it says: "If a bodhisattva views things in this way and speaks thus, saying, 'A bodhisattva should not listen to the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas;
they should not accept them, nor should they study them. Of what use are the śrāvaka teachings to a bodhisattva?
This is called committing many offenses. It is an offense arising from defilement. Alas! One should reflect upon this. The initial title concludes.
II. Entering the Text has three parts: first, the introduction to the precepts; second, the formal enumeration of the precept categories; third, the conclusion, exhortation, and dedication.

In the first part [the introduction], there are four sections: first, the verse of praise; second, the inquiry and formal announcement; third, the formal recitation of the introduction to the precepts; fourth, the concluding inquiry. In the first section [the verse of praise], there are six parts:
first, taking refuge in and relying upon the Triple Gem; second, admonishing the assembly to listen attentively; third, the teacher...

1. The resources for transmission and reception; 2. The four similes admonishing against disparagement; 3. The manifestation that the precepts should be taught; 4. The praise of excellence and the concluding indication.
Now, the first:
I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas, as well as to the Dharma and the Sangha of Bhikṣus.
At the commencement of any ritual practice, one must first pay homage and respect to the Triple Gem (*triratna*) in order to seek their empowerment.

To prostrate is to show reverence through the physical action (*kāyakarman*). When the body pays homage, one recites the names of their virtues with the mouth while maintaining visualization in the mind;

this constitutes the offering of the three karmas (*trikarma*). The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are called the Triple Gem because they are worthy of honor and veneration. "Buddha" means awakening.

Regarding "Meaning" (*artha*): it refers to awakening oneself, awakening others, and the perfection of the practice of awakening; thus, one is called a *Buddha*. Regarding "Dharma": it carries the meanings of "track" (*niyama*) and "sustenance" (*dhāraṇa*).
It is called "Dharma" because it tracks and gives rise to understanding, and because it sustains its own intrinsic nature. Bhikṣu contains three meanings:

first, the meaning of a mendicant (*bhikṣu*), which means abandoning the ways of wrong livelihood, supporting the body with a single bowl, and cultivating oneself through the three types of wisdom to abandon the stains of ignorance.

Second is the meaning of "terrifying Māra. At the moment one first receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), once the *karmavācanā* ritual is completed, the earth deities immediately raise their voices and proclaim:
"In this place, a son of good family has received full ordination; may the devas increase and the asuras diminish.
Upon hearing this, the benevolent deities who roam the air likewise raise their voices and proclaim it in succession. In an instant—
He then reached the Brahma Heaven. When Pāpīyān heard this, he immediately felt terror; thus, he is called "the one who terrifies Māra. Third is the meaning of destroying evil:
by cultivating the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), one cuts off the delusions of views and thought.

Because these three meanings are present within the causal stage, one subsequently attains at the fruit-stage the titles of "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat), "Non-arising," and "Slayer of Thieves"; thus, one is named an Arhat. Furthermore, in comparison...
"Kiu" (丘) is translated here as "remover of hunger" (chujin). Because he serves as a great field of merit and opens the great Dharma-gift, he is named "Remover of Hunger.
As for "Seng" (僧), the full term is *saṃgha*; this is translated as "harmonious assembly. This is a designation for four or more bhikṣus. There are two meanings of harmony:

first, harmony in principle (*lihe*), meaning they equally realize cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, harmony in practice (*shire*), meaning they harmoniously cultivate the precepts together.

They see in harmony and share the same understanding; they dwell together in bodily harmony; they share equally in benefits; they are harmonious in speech and free from contention; and they are harmonious in mind and share mutual joy.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are five kinds of saṃghas: first, the shameless saṃgha, which consists of those bhikṣus who break the precepts;
second, the sheep-like saṃgha, which consists of ordinary persons of dull faculties and no wisdom, like a flock of sheep gathered together."
1. There is one group who does not know the *poṣadha*, does not know the *poṣadha-karman*, does not know the recitation of the precepts (*śīla-uddeśa*), and does not know the Dharma assembly.

This is the first type of separate community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha-vibheda*): within a single boundary (*sīmā*), they perform various formal acts (*karman*) separately in different locations. 2. The pure community of monks (*pariśuddha-saṃgha*):

this consists of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who maintain the precepts, as well as ordinary persons who are victors (*jina*). 3. The true community of monks (*tattvika-saṃgha*): this consists of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Among those [three types of Saṃgha] being venerated here, one truly venerates only the latter two.

This is because the Saṃgha of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-saṃgha*) enables the ultimate Dharma (*paramārtha-dharma*) to endure for a long time, while the Saṃgha of purity (*viśuddha-saṃgha*) enables the conventional Dharma (*saṃvṛti-dharma*) to endure for a long time.
As for the former three types, they can perform illegal formal acts (*adharma-karman*) and cause the True Dharma to be destroyed; therefore, they are not objects of veneration. Furthermore...
Next, there are the three jewels of the institutional tradition (*saṃpradāya*), which include the three jewels of the single essence (*ekatva*). Regarding the term "institutional tradition":

when the Buddha was in the world, his attainment of the Way under the King of Trees was the Buddha-jewel; his preaching of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths was the Dharma-jewel; and his ordination of the five bhikṣus and others was the Saṅgha-jewel.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [the Buddha-jewel consists of] images cast in metal, molded from clay, or depicted on paper and silk with ink and colors; the yellow...

The three baskets of the holy teachings, written upon crimson scrolls, constitute the Dharma Jewel. Those who shave their hair, don dyed robes, and succeed to the flourishing of the Buddha’s transformation constitute the Sangha Jewel.
Because these three abide in the world without interruption, they are called the "Abiding Three Jewels. Yet, all images are identical to the true body;
wherever the scriptures reside, that is the *dharmakāya* relic. Even ordinary monks of the present day are capable of bearing this responsibility.
Those who carry the True Dharma and serve as fields of merit for the world should also all be honored with prostrations.

Furthermore, the term "all Buddhas" refers generally to all Great Teachers currently seated at the site of enlightenment throughout the ten directions; because the essence of awakening is omnipresent, they are so even though they reside in other lands.
They are able to act as benevolent protectors within this land; this also refers generally to all World-Honored Ones who appear successively throughout the three periods of time.
Because the nature of awakening is eternal, although they manifest in the past and future, they are able to bestow their responsive grace in the present.

The same applies to the Dharma and the Sangha. As for the term "one essence," it means that through the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are neither [merely] empty nor [merely] existent.

It is not existent; it is both empty and existent. When both [existence and emptiness] are simultaneously forgotten and simultaneously illuminated, the three wisdoms are perfectly awakened—this is called the Buddha Jewel.

The principle of the dharma-nature that is thus awakened, complete with the three truths, is called the Dharma Jewel. This awakened wisdom, in harmony with both principle and phenomena, is called the Sangha Jewel.
Furthermore, the single thought-moment of the present inherently possesses the three truths while one is in delusion.
Non-awakening is the Dharma Jewel. The wisdom that can awaken to the Three Truths is the Buddha Jewel.
The union of the Truth and wisdom is the Sangha Jewel. The single character "and" (及) precisely reveals the meaning of the Three Jewels as being of one essence.
Furthermore, regarding the term "reverent salutation": it does not exist apart from the one essence, nor is it separate from the manifest maintenance [of the teachings].

To speak of them as a single essence while remaining within the realm of phenomenal characteristics, if one performs acts of reverence while being ignorant of the principle of this single essence, one merely achieves mundane goodness;

it is not called "true reverence. This is because the meaning of "reverence" (li) is "essence" (ti); since one has not yet realized that the three spheres are essentially quiescent, it does not accord with the meaning of "essence.

Conversely, if one discards the characteristics of provisional maintenance to discuss a single essence, one falls into a nihilistic misconception of emptiness and cannot be said to have realized the principle.
To abide in principle apart from phenomena is not yet to know that the whole phenomenon is itself principle, for they are not of a single meaning.

The word "and" (*yi*) precisely reveals the principle that they are neither one nor three, yet are both three and one; this is the essential purport of the sequential arrangement and the perfect fusion of phenomena and principle.
II. Admonishing the Assembly to Listen:
Now I shall expound the Vinaya Dharma, So that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. The precepts are like a boundless ocean;
Like jewels, they are sought without satiety. Those who wish to protect the noble wealth of the Dharma— Assembly, gather and listen as I speak!
To eliminate the four *pārājika* dharmas and to extinguish the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas—those who obstruct the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules, assemble and listen as I expound them.

"Expounder" (*yanyuǎn*) refers to one who proclaims and circulates [the teaching]. Regarding the *vinaya* dharma, as explained in the section on defining terms, the "True Dharma" (*zhèngfǎ*) emerges...
This is the Noble Path of the world. When the True Dharma abides in the world, the three aspects of teaching, practice, and fruit are all fully present.

Now, by expounding this Vinaya, the aggregate of precepts (*śīlaskandha*) is accomplished, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) arise; thus, the great fruits of a śramaṇa can be expected.
Therefore, it causes the True Dharma to abide for a long time. This half-verse clarifies the meaning of gathering in sentient beings. As for "like the ocean without limit":
The *Poṣadha-vastu* states: "The waters of the great ocean possess eight extraordinary qualities, for which reason the asuras dwell there in enjoyment.
First, all streams flow into it; second, its tides do not miss their appointed times;
third, when the five great rivers enter the sea, they lose their original names; fourth, all rivers and heavy rains return [to it] without..."

[The first seven are: (1) increasing and decreasing [in size]; (2) having the same salty taste; (3) not receiving corpses; (4) abounding in rare treasures; (5) being the dwelling place of large-bodied beings;
(6) the same salt taste; (7) not receiving corpses; (8) producing many rare treasures; (9) being inhabited by those of great form.
Within my Dharma, there are likewise eight wonders, so that when my disciples see them, they may find delight therein. First, my disciples study the precepts progressively. All...
First, they return to my Dharma and train therein in all wholesome dharmas. Second, my disciples abide in the precepts and do not transgress them until death.
Third, members of the four castes who leave the household life are all called śramaṇas.
Fourth, within my Dharma, those who with firm faith leave the household life to study the Path enter the realm of nirvana without remainder; and as for that realm of nirvana—

5. There is neither increase nor decrease. 6. Those who violate the precepts and engage in unwholesome dharmas, though they sit among the assembly, are always far removed from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is likewise far removed from them. 7.
They produce many precious treasures, namely the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path. 8. They receive a great form, namely:

The four stages of approach and the four fruits. Furthermore, at the very moment one first receives the precepts, one immediately and universally attains within the *dharmadhātu* the forms of non-lust, non-theft, non-killing, and so forth.

Thus, each of the two hundred and fifty precepts, the three thousand modes of deportment, and the eighty thousand subtle practices—each individual pure form of the precepts—is individually pervasive throughout the *dharmadhātu*. Moreover, from this point onward, in every thought-moment, [this continues].
The virtuous form of the spontaneously accomplished precepts pervades the entire *dharmadhātu* and is inexhaustible;
therefore, it is said to be "boundless like the ocean. Regarding "seeking jewels without satiety": "jewels" refers to the king of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*).
This jewel can, in every moment of thought, rain down all the requisites for happiness sufficient to fill Jambudvīpa, yet the essence of the jewel is never diminished.

It diminishes. The precepts are likewise: within every moment of thought, they give rise to all dharmas such as the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path, up to and including all the noble fruits of the three vehicles;

yet the essence of the precepts never undergoes change. Furthermore, regarding these precepts, the more one studies them, the more one perceives their refinement; the more one cultivates them, the more one attains their [purity].

Because it is beneficial, it is said that one seeks it like a treasure without satiety. As for the "sacred wealth of the Dharma," briefly stated, there are seven types: faith, precepts, learning, renunciation, wisdom, shame, and remorse.

Elaborated upon, they include the six perfections, the myriad practices, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the one hundred and eight samādhis, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and so forth.
Among all such treasures of the Dharma, none do not take the precepts as their guardian.
Guarding the precepts is like having excellent soldiers and valiant generals; it is also like a sturdy city with deep moats; it is like laws and statutes;
and it is like the "Treasure of the Minister of the Treasury. They ward off external insults so as not to be oppressed; they guard against treacherous thieves so as not to be plundered;
they organize and settle [the precepts] so that they are not allowed to be destroyed; and they manage income and expenditure so that [virtue] may increase.

This is called the meaning of "protection" (*rakṣā*). This single verse clarifies the meaning of "gathering wholesome dharmas" (*kuśaladharmasaṃgraha*). "Abandoning," "discarding," "extinguishing," "residual," "obstructing," "stopping," "renouncing," and "falling away" clarify the meaning of "gathering the code of discipline" (*saṃvara-saṃgraha*).
The explanations for "abandoning" and so forth will appear in the subsequent text. [Now] we inquire regarding the names of the three aggregates (*triskandha*).
This is not shared with the Lesser Teachings; how could you dare to judge and interpret it based on this? Answer: Before the [truth] was revealed, there was the reality but no name;
once it has been revealed, both name and reality exist together. These three meanings are manifest; how could they be subject to arbitrary judgment?
III. The Transmission from Teacher to Disciple.
Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni— These World-Honored Ones of Great Virtue have explained this matter for me.
I now wish to speak well; may all you worthy ones listen together.
Vipaśyin—alternatively called Vīra—this translates as "Victorious Vision. Śikhin—alternatively called Śikhi—this translates as "Fire.
Viśvabhū—alternatively called Suyāma or Viyūra—this translates as "Pervading All Oneself."

Regarding these three World-Honored Ones: at the end of the *Ratnavyuha-kalpa* (Adorned Eon), there was Krakucchanda—also called Krakutsunda, which translates as "that which should be severed" or "active function";
Kanakamuni, which translates as "Golden Silence" or "Golden Sage"; Kāśyapa, also called Kāśyapa, which translates as "Drinking Light"; and Śākyamuni, also called...
Śākyamuni is translated as "The Able Sage" (Nengrou) and also as "The Able Benevolent One in Silent Stillness" (Nengren Jimo).
These four Tathāgatas appeared in succession during the Bhadrakalpa. The reason these seven Buddhas are mentioned in various places is twofold:

first, because they were all seen by the inhabitants of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens within a single hundred minor kalpas; second, because it was for the sake of [the present Buddha] acting as the Teacher who cultivated the karma for the primary marks and secondary signs.
Because it begins from the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, the World-Honored One is endowed with the ten titles and is venerated by the nine realms.
"Virtuous One" (Bhadanta) refers to one whose causes are perfected and whose fruits are fulfilled, such that none in the world can equal them.

Furthermore, the term "Virtuous One" may also be applied generally to a bhikṣu, as they possess vast and extensive virtuous conduct. As for "this matter," it refers to the four matters and the thirteen matters. And so forth.
Regarding matters such as following the Vinaya, those who speak well should explain in accordance with the Dharma and in harmony.

As for those who listen together, everyone from those with no years of seniority (*anuvassa*) up to those with a hundred years of seniority (*śata-varṣa*) should assemble to listen. From the *Śīlaskandha* (the introductory section on precepts) down to the verses and sūtras, all should listen attentively.
○ Four Similes Admonishing Against Destruction:
Just as a person who destroys their feet Is unable to travel anywhere, So it is with one who destroys the precepts:
They cannot be born among gods or humans. If you wish to be born in the heavens, Or if you wish to be born in the human realm, [you must protect the precepts].
One should always guard the feet of the precepts, Do not allow them to be damaged or destroyed.

Just as a charioteer entering a perilous path Is filled with anxiety over a lost axle-pin or a broken shaft, So too it is with the violation of the precepts; At the time of death, one harbors fear and dread.
The first two verses provide an admonition regarding obstacles to rebirth in a favorable realm; the final verse provides an admonition regarding death and falling into the evil destinies. Birth.
Death is like a perilous road; the precepts and the Dharma are like the linchpins and axles.

When one violates the precepts, the signs of rebirth in the evil realms appear at the time of death, just as one who loses a linchpin or breaks an axle on a dangerous road has no place to set it down before or behind, and is thus terrified and distraught.
The *Chapter on Vows and Practices* states: "It closes all gates to the evil realms and opens wide the correct path to the human and celestial realms and nirvana."
The precepts truly fulfill their function. However, the *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"Those who diligently practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) with the wish for the human realm or the pursuit of the heavens will be reborn among humans or devas and briefly experience happiness; yet after the end of that life, they will enter hell.
Therefore, one should seek *nirvāṇa* in order to practice the holy life; do not delight in the human or heavenly realms, lest you bring about weariness."
Suffering. Furthermore, the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "There are two perilous paths: first, birth in the heavens; second, the evil realms.

Although one may experience various supreme pleasures by being born in the heavens, once that retribution is exhausted, one falls back into the evil destinies. Thus, even the human and celestial realms are not what should be desired.
As for the reference in the second verse, there are briefly two meanings: first, the feet of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāda*).
Because it is indestructible; if it were destroyed, even humans and devas would have no share in it, let alone *nirvāṇa*. Second, it is because it gathers in those of inferior lineage:
when told of *nirvāṇa*, they are terrified, but when told of the realms of humans and devas, they rejoice.

First, one uses the hook of desire to draw them in, and later causes them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom. Furthermore, speaking according to the facts of reality, if one is able to maintain the precepts, [one will attain the fruit].
It cannot be destroyed. Even if one lacks meditative concentration and wisdom, one will certainly not lose the body of a human or a deva.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the metaphor of the precepts as feet means there is nowhere they do not reach.

Whether one wishes to ascend to the lotus thrones of the highest grade, or to serve the Buddhas of the ten directions, or to adorn and purify boundless Buddha-lands, or to universally enter the profound Dharma-realm—[the precepts are the foundation].
There is no gate that does not take this as its initial expedient means.
Fifth, the manifestation of the precepts shall now be explained:
Just as when a person looks into a mirror, joy or sorrow arises according to whether they see beauty or ugliness; so too it is with the recitation of the precepts.
Complete destruction gives rise to sorrow and joy, like two armies fighting together; there is advance and retreat according to courage or timidity.
The recitation of the precepts is also like this: purity and impurity give rise to peace and fear.
Sorrow and joy belong to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*); peace and fear manifest in bodily conduct. If the precepts are entirely pure, then within one is not... [disturbed].
Having a sense of shame, one does not feel ashamed before others; thus the mind is joyful and the body is at ease.
If the precepts are violated or defiled, then one brings blemish upon oneself within and pollution upon the Sangha without; therefore, one harbors sorrow and stands in awe of the assembly.
6. Praise of Excellence and Conclusion:
Among kings, the world-ruler is supreme; Among all streams, the ocean is supreme; Among all stars, the moon is supreme;
Among all noble ones, the Buddha is supreme. Among all codes of discipline, The Sūtra on Precepts is the highest and most excellent.
The Tathāgata established the prohibitive precepts and proclaimed them every half-month;
those who receive these precepts are called "Great Śramaṇas. "Great" (mahā) is the Sanskrit term, which contains three meanings:
first, "great," because they are honored among devas and humans; second, "much," because they are richly endowed with merit and wisdom; third, "superior," because they transcend [the mundane].
Because of the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the first line now praises [the precepts] by means of a great analogy; the second line praises them by means of many analogies;
the third line praises them by means of superior analogies; and the fourth line praises them by means of a comprehensive analogy.
The subsequent half-verse correctly applies these to the Dharma: since this Precept Sūtra alone is supreme, those who receive it likewise become supreme.
"All disciplinary codes" refers to the correct laws of the world, as well as the codes held by non-Buddhists and others.
Furthermore, the five precepts, eight precepts, and ten precepts are not considered supreme in the same way that the bhikṣu precepts are.

Moreover, the dhyāna-precepts and the untainted (anāsrava) precepts do not compare to the prātimokṣa precepts, which serve as the structural framework for the Buddha-dharma. Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka...

Among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the precept sutras (*śīla-sūtra*) alone are supreme. If one does not firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts, then even if meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and abundant wisdom manifest before one, they will all become the works of Māra.
Therefore, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "The Buddha taught the teachings of the Tripiṭaka."
The *Vinaya* is the foremost. Furthermore, the first phrase is a metaphor praising the Sūtras of the Teaching, for they were spoken solely by the Tathāgata himself.
The second phrase is a metaphor praising the Sūtras of Practice, for all dharmas converge upon the precepts. The third phrase is a metaphor praising the Sūtras of Principle;
the unconditioned essence of the precepts is as cool as the moon, appearing to wax and wane according to the observance or violation of them.

Because, in reality, there is neither increase nor decrease. This is the fourth phrase. It is illustrated by the *Phala-sūtra* (Sutra on the Fruits), which states that one not only achieves the fruit of a śrāvaka but also accomplishes the path of a Tathāgata.
Question: The essence of the unconditioned precept (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*) is received from a teacher.

Even if one commits an offense against the first category of rules (*pārājika*), provided there is absolutely no intention to conceal it, one is merely permitted to remain under training (*śikṣamāṇa*); yet they will never again possess the functions of a monk. If, by means of the essence of the moon...
If one uses "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) as the essence, how does it differ from the "original nature" (*prakṛti*)?
If being called "unconditioned" merely means receiving [the teaching] from a teacher, then there would still be increase and decrease. Answer: Unconditioned is the essence of the actual entity;
original purity is the essence of the basis. Unconditioned belongs to cultivation; original nature belongs to the fundamental attribute. Unconditioned is the phenomenon (*vastu*).
The intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) is the principle (*li*). The unconditioned essence (*anabhisaṃskāra-śarīra*) is the tenet (*zong*). The essence of the intrinsic nature is the substance (*ti*).

Now, as for the tenet and the substance, they are neither identical nor distinct. The enlightened person realizes the substance by means of the tenet; the deluded person is ignorant of the substance and simultaneously confused about the tenet.
Since this sutra is now praised through the metaphor of the moon to illustrate the principle, it precisely points to the unconditioned precepts as the substance upon which they rely.
One should know that whether there is gain or loss, these are all matters of surplus and deficit at the periphery; they cannot be said to involve an increase or decrease in the nature [of reality].
Furthermore, from the analogy of a person whose feet are destroyed up to the *Śīla-sūtra* as the supreme and highest, these possess the four *siddhāntas*.
"Opening the path for humans and devas, and closing the gates to the evil realms" refers to the *loka-prasiddha* (worldly consensus) *siddhānta*.

"The two metaphors of the mirror" refers to the two types of *pudgala-prasiddha* (for individuals) and *pratipakṣa* (remedy) *siddhāntas*, because they respectively provide the two benefits of generating wholesome states and extinguishing unwholesome ones.

"The four supreme metaphors for morality" refers to the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth) *siddhānta*, because the essence of this morality is the pure *dharmakāya*. Thus the Tathāgata established [this].
Regarding the prohibitions and precepts: within the great trichiliocosm, the Buddha is the Lord of the Dharma, and the Vinaya is the Buddha’s decree. Only the Sage established these;

all others of lower rank may only rely upon and uphold them. This is truly because the Tathāgata’s practice and fruition are perfectly consummate, having fully exhausted the nature of the light and heavy karmas of sentient beings—something that those from the stage of Equal Enlightenment downward are simply not yet capable of. Question: The Sūtras state...

It applies to five classes of people. As for the Vinaya, only the Buddha himself may expound it—just as when rites, music, and the power of military punishment issue from the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords fold their hands and await his commands.
Now, the Great Ming Code is the regulation established by the Son of Heaven;
there are none among the civil and military officials who do not study it, and even a common farmer may peruse it. Why, then, is this Vinaya dharma permitted only to... [the ordained]?
When a bhikṣu reviews the texts, he does not permit śrāmaṇeras or laypeople to observe them. The answer is:
The Vinaya was established solely by the Buddha in order to manifest the dignity of the Dharma-way. However, it is not only the monastic rules that are called "Vinaya";

all precepts, including the five precepts, the ten precepts, and the bodhisattva precepts, are also termed "Vinaya. Their universal application to the seven classes of disciples is just like the promulgation of the Great Ming Code.
The world at large is thus. As for the monastic precepts and the Dharma, they are like the secret archives of the inner treasury or the official manuals on governance and selection;
these are matters that ordinary people do not dare to hear of. Regarding the bi-monthly recitation, the two months of the waxing and waning phases represent the two types of karma—good and evil.
One desires the white (the good) to be full and the black (the evil) to be exhausted. Furthermore, white represents wisdom.
Virtue. It is the virtue of severing black [deeds]. Regarding this, the precepts are recited so that one may examine oneself. Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"As for the method of the *poṣadha*, every half-month, all bhikṣus gather in one place and reflect upon themselves:
'What offenses did I commit during the day? What offenses did I commit during the night? Since the last *poṣadha* was recited, have I not committed any offenses? If..."
If you have committed an offense, you should confess it according to the Dharma before a fellow bhikṣu who shares your resolve and maintains pure precepts.
If you cannot find such a bhikṣu of pure precepts, you should cultivate the thought: "I shall obtain one later," and you should confess according to the Dharma.
By doing so, you abide securely in wholesome dharmas and abandon the unwholesome roots and miscellaneous matters. Thus I instruct you: every half-month, you should recite [the Prātimokṣa].
The Prātimokṣa—know that this is your great teacher and your refuge;
it is no different from my remaining in the world.

Appendix: The Fourth Division states that there are five qualities by which one is called a holder of the Vinaya: first, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what does not constitute an offense;

third, knowing what is light; fourth, knowing what is heavy; and fifth, extensively reciting the precepts of the two divisions. There are another five qualities, four of which are as previously stated.

four are as before, and the fifth is to be skillful in eliminating disputes when they arise. A person who upholds the Vinaya possesses five merits:
their precept-category is firm; they are skilled in overcoming all enemies; they are fearless in making decisions within the assembly; and if there is doubt...
Repentance can bring about resolution and cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time. It is further said that there are five factors that cause the True Dharma to perish quickly:
first, receiving and reciting [the teachings] without careful attention, being prone to forgetfulness and errors, and teaching others with incomplete texts;
since the texts are incomplete, their meaning is deficient. Second, acting as a superior person among the Sangha, such as a senior elder (sthavira), within a single country...

They follow this as their primary tenet, yet for the most part they do not uphold the precepts; they merely cultivate various unwholesome dharmas, abandon the practice of the precepts, and fail to apply themselves with diligence.
Younger bhikṣus born later imitate and practice their conduct.

Thirdly, there are those who possess great learning and uphold the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā, yet they do not transmit the teachings they have recited to the other four assemblies, and then pass away (upholding the Dharma means knowing...).

The Sūtra-piṭaka is held by those such as Ānanda; the Vinaya is held by those who know the Piṭaka of Discipline, such as Upāli; and the Mātṛkā is held by those skilled in instruction and who govern the profound principles, such as Mahākāśyapa.
Fourth, there are bhikṣus who are difficult to instruct; they do not accept wholesome words and are unable to practice forbearance, so that other virtuous bhikṣus simply abandon them.

Furthermore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if bhikṣus do not revere the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts and meditative concentration, then the True Dharma will quickly perish.
If one has left the household life within the Dharma and Vinaya, yet does not preach the Dharma for others with a sincere heart, nor... [does not practice it oneself].
One listens to the Dharma with the mind and retains it; yet even if one firmly upholds it, if one cannot contemplate its meaning and intent, that person does not understand the meaning.
Unable to practice in accordance with the Dharma, they neither benefit themselves nor others. By these causes and conditions, the Dharma is caused to perish quickly.
Conversely, for those who act in the opposite manner, the True Dharma will abide for a long time. The Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya states: If...
Faithful sons of good family who wish to obtain five benefits should fully receive and uphold this Vinaya.
What are these five? They are: wishing to establish the Buddha-dharma; wishing to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time;
not having doubts or regrets that require questioning others; and acting as a refuge for all bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who are terrified by their transgressions.
"If you wish to travel and transform beings in all directions without hindrance, you must all fully receive and uphold this Vinaya. Furthermore, it says:
Mahākāśyapa addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "Venerable ones, the relics of the World-Honored One are not our concern.

Furthermore, it is said that when a pure bhikṣu preaches the precepts without violating the Dharma, it is called the "Dharma abiding in the world. It is also said that there are five benefits to upholding the Vinaya:

Regarding the dharmas that do not obstruct the path, the *Mūla-nidāna* states:

As for these bhikṣus, the robes they wear are worth one hundred million gold coins; the dwellings and rooms they occupy are worth five hundred gold coins;
the food and drink they consume are complete with a hundred flavors. Such matters as these I have permitted them to receive, and you are all capable of digesting [the merit of] them.
However, if there is a bhikṣu who has broken a grave precept, even within the monastic residence...
A single mouthful of food will not digest; a single footstep will not find room upon the grounds of the saṃghārāma.
You should know that for one who has broken the precepts, there are ten kinds of faults: they know themselves to be a person of evil conduct who has broken the precepts, and others know it as well;
all the devas do not come to associate with them, and those who practice the holy life and virtuous people who understand the Dharma all give rise to [contempt].

They will be held in contempt; their evil reputation will be known throughout the four quarters; those who have not yet realized the truth will no longer be able to realize it, and those who have already realized the Dharma will all fall away from it.

After they pass away, they will be reborn in the hells. Furthermore, O Bhikṣus, you should know that this is what is experienced [as a result].
There are five types of utilization: first, utilization as a master, referring to Arhats who have eternally eliminated the three poisons;
second, utilization of parental wealth, referring to those in training (śaikṣas) who still possess residual afflictions;

third, utilization by permission, referring to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) of pure virtue who diligently practice meditation and recitation with a mind free from indolence regarding the purity of their precepts.

Fourth is enjoyment like that of one in debt: this refers to those who, though they guard their prohibitive precepts, do not diligently cultivate the wholesome dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
Fifth is enjoyment like that of a thief: this refers to those who, among the four grave prohibitions (*catur-āpattika*), commit any one of them.
Therefore, you all should practice and study [these]. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "Noble sons who leave the household life with a sincere heart..."

by relying upon the Vinaya-piṭaka, one personally maintains the precepts and is able to sever the doubts of others. When entering the Saṃgha, one is free from fear.

Yoga holds that there is nothing external and everything internal, such that all things are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).

Both of these systems strictly follow the sacred teachings; which is right and which is wrong? Both lead equally to Nirvana; which is true and which is false? The intent is simply to sever afflictions and delusions.
To save sentient beings, how could one wish to extensively cause confusion and further increase entanglement? If one acts in accordance with the teaching, all shall ascend to the other shore;

if one rejects and turns away from it, all shall drown in the flow of birth and death. In the Western Land, these two practices proceed together; in principle, there is no contradiction or conflict between them.

Furthermore, it is said that the life-preserving bag must not leak—this is the fundamental intention of a Bodhisattva. Do not treat even minor transgressions lightly, for they may yet result in the final song of regret.

To guard against minor transgressions while contemplating the Great Emptiness, and to gather sentient beings while clarifying the mind—what fault could there be in this? Fearing that I might delude myself or lead others astray, I have briefly set forth this single perspective in accordance with the teachings.

There are six root afflictions (kleśa) and secondary afflictions (upakleśa), namely: greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and the five views.
The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) number twenty and are further divided into three categories. First, there are eight major secondary afflictions (*mahābhūmika-upakleśa*), namely:

lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), lethargy (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), and distraction (*vikṣepa*). Third, there are ten minor secondary afflictions (*parīttabhūmika-upakleśa*), namely: anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), malice (*pradāsa*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), pride (*māna*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*).

Furthermore, before an image of the Buddha, one asks: "Are you a Bodhisattva? To which the other should reply: [Yes].
"Yes. "Have you yet made the vow for bodhicitta? One should answer, "I have already made it.

Regarding the "grave entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*) that constitute the violation of the ten grave precepts—namely, the ten grave precepts of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*—"entanglements" refers to the ten entanglements:
first, anger; second, concealment; third, drowsiness; fourth, sleep; fifth, restlessness; sixth, regret; seventh, envy; eighth, stinginess; ninth...
Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*). "Of the highest degree" refers to extremely heavy afflictions. The *Karmavācanā* text states:

"Having transgressed the grave precepts, they repeatedly manifest [such conduct] without any sense of shame or dread of blame, deeply generating attachment and delight therein, and regarding it as a merit."
One should know that this is called an offense committed through intense fetters (*adhimātra-paryavasthāna*).

Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned as wrong livelihood, there are four types of food for wrong livelihood: first, food obtained by means of the mouth, namely, seeking favors and acting as a messenger.
The second is horizontal-mouth sustenance, which refers to incantations and divination. The third is upward-mouth sustenance, which refers to observing the stars and constellations.

The fourth is downward-mouth sustenance, which refers to cultivating fields and gardens. Furthermore, there are five kinds of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*): the first is for the sake of gain and offerings.

1. Falsely manifesting extraordinary and unusual signs; 2. Speaking of one's own meritorious qualities; 3. Divining auspiciousness and misfortune through physiognomy and predicting destinies for others while preaching the Dharma;
4. Raising one's voice and manifesting an air of majesty to cause others to feel awe and reverence; 5. Speaking of the offerings one has received to stir the hearts of people.
The three types of wisdom are: first, the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), which refers to listening to the Dharma with a sincere mind and understanding its verbal meaning;

second, the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), which refers to reflecting deeply after hearing so that the Dharma enters the mind; and third, the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), which refers to practicing according to the teachings so as to attain realization.
Pāpīyas means "evil" (in Chinese) or "the slayer"; it is the name of the Māra King.

To realize *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (analytical cessation) is precisely to realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of analytical cessation. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "By the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*)."
It is called "analytical cessation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) because it extinguishes all defilements and is ultimately realized through discernment.
"Ordinary beings and victors" refers to the seven types of noble persons, consisting of the outer ordinary beings and the inner ordinary beings. The outer ordinary beings comprise:

(1) those with the five stabilizing practices (*pañca-vastu-sthiti-citta*), (2) those with mindfulness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*), and (3) those with mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*). The inner ordinary beings comprise: (1) the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*), (2) the stage of summits (*mūrdhan*), and (3) the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
The fourth is the stage of the candidate for the first fruit; these constitute the inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The ultimate true Dharma refers to the paths and fruits of the three vehicles.
The conventional true Dharma refers to the legal codes and instructions.
After Prince Siddhārtha had attained the Way following six years of ascetic practice, he accepted the supreme offering of milk-rice from a cowherd girl.
He spread auspicious grass and sat beneath the Pippala tree; beholding the morning star, he realized perfect enlightenment.
Consequently, this tree was named the Bodhi Tree, and it is also called the King of Trees.
To preach the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, the Buddha went to the Deer Park. There, he first turned the Wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths three times for the five bhikṣus.
First, the turning of demonstration: "This is suffering; its nature is oppression. This is the origin;

its nature is provocation. This is cessation; its nature is realizability. This is the path; its nature is cultivability. Second, the turning of exhortation: "This is suffering; you should [understand it]..."
"Know this: 'This is the origin; you should abandon it. 'This is cessation; you should realize it. 'This is the path;
you should cultivate it. A third turning of the wheel states: "This is suffering; I have known it. This is the origin; I have abandoned it. This is cessation..."
"I have realized it; this is the path. I have cultivated it.

Thus he spoke to the five bhikṣus, beginning with Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya. *Ājñāta* translates as "one who has known" (*ji-yi*) or "one who has understood" (*jie*), because he was the first to understand the Buddha's Dharma. *Kauṇḍinya* is also called *Kauṇḍina* or *Ku-lin*.
1. This is translated as "Fire-vessel. His ancestors served fire, and his clan was named after this. 2. Aṅgīrasa, also called Aśvajit;
this is translated as "Horse-Winner" and also as "Master of Horses. 3. Bāṣpa, also called Vatsa; this is translated as "Little Wise One.
4. Daśabala-Kāśyapa, also named Bhārgava. 5. Kaulita-rāja-putra, Cunda-Kāśyapa.
Two [of these] belong to the maternal lineage of the Buddha; the remaining three belong to the paternal lineage of the Buddha.
*Śarīra* is sometimes called *śilira* or *śelira*; this translates as "sacred bone" (*linggu*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Fragmented bones are the relics of the physical body (*janma-kāya-śarīra*); sutra scrolls are the relics of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya-śarīra*)."
Regarding the five great rivers flowing into the ocean, other sutras state that four rivers enter the sea:
the Gaṅgā in the east, the Sindhu in the south, the Vakṣu in the west, and the Sītā in the north; all emerge from Lake Anavatapta. The mention of "five" [rivers] here is likely an error.
The four castes are: first, the Kṣatriya, who are the royal lineage; second, the Brāhmaṇa, who are those of pure conduct—similar to the Confucian scholars here [in China];
third, the Vaiśya, also called Viśa, who are merchants and traders; and fourth, the Śūdra, who are those whose occupation is agriculture and fieldwork.
Jambudvīpa: *Jambu* is the name of a tree; *dvīpa* means "continent. Because this tree exists upon the continent, it is named after it.
This translates as "Superior Gold" (*shèngjīn*). The *Xīyùjì* (Records of the Western Regions) states that its correct pronunciation is *Nánzhānbùzhōu*.
*Xiānzhāng* (Constitutional Charter): *Xiàn* (Constitution) refers to law; *zhāng* (Charter) refers to articles; *diǎn* (Canon) refers to constancy; and *xíng* (Punishment) also refers to law.
This denotes the laws, decrees, and institutional systems transmitted through successive generations by the state.
The *Gṛhapati-ratna* (Treasure of the Steward) is one of the seven treasures of a *cakravartin* (Wheel-Turning King).
[The character] *hu* is pronounced with the *ba* and *qie* tones; its sound is the same as *ha*. It refers to the iron at the head of a chariot axle.
The character for *zhou* (axle) is pronounced *zhu*; it refers to the hub of the chariot wheel.
"Arriving at the sound of the precepts" means "to reach.
The True Dharma of the world refers to the Five Constant Virtues of the human path, the ten wholesome actions of a Wheel-Turning King, and so forth.
The twelve divisions [of the scriptures] are: first, prose; second, verse; third, prophecy; fourth, chanting; fifth, unrequested [discourse];...

These are: (1) *Sūtra* (discourses), (2) *Geya* (verses in response to prose), (3) *Vyākaraṇa* (prophecies), (4) *Gāthā* (stanzas), (5) *Udāna* (inspired utterances), (6) *Nidāna* (causal origins), (7) *Avadāna* (parables), (8) *Itivṛttaka* (past events), (9) *Jātaka* (birth stories), (10) *Vaipulya* (extensive teachings), (11) *Adbhutadharma* (marvels), and (12) *Upadeśa* (exegesis).
These are also known as the twelvefold division of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
The "Great Trichiliocosm" refers specifically to the Sahā world.

Four great continents, sharing one sun and moon and one Mount Sumeru, are called a single "four-continent system" (cāturdvīpaka). One thousand such four-continent systems are called a "small chiliocosm.
One thousand small chiliocosms are called a "medium chiliocosm," which is one million worlds. One thousand medium chiliocosms are called a... [Great Trichiliocosm].
A great trichiliocosm consists of one hundred million four-continent worlds, one hundred million suns and moons, and one hundred million Mount Sumerus;
these are collectively termed a "trichiliocosm" (three thousand great thousand worlds), all of which are governed and transformed by Śākyamuni Buddha.
Yet, when viewed from the perspective of the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu), this great trichiliocosm is merely like a single infinitesimal atom.
The name "Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment in the Stage of One Life Remaining" refers to those such as the present Bodhisattva Maitreya.

From the perspective of those on lower stages, they are equal to a Buddha; yet because they still have one most subtle grade of ignorance that has not been exhausted, they are still called Bodhisattvas.
*Mātṛkā* is fully transcribed as *Mātṛkya*, also as *Mātṛka*, and also as *Matṛka*.
It is also named *Mudraka*. This translates as "Mother of Wisdom" (*jñānamātṛ*), because it is capable of giving birth to wisdom.

Those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have already ascended to the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*) are called the assembly of "similar-born" (*sabhāgajana*); those who have not yet entered the stream of the noble ones are called the assembly of "dissimilar-born.
"Pure goodness" (*śubha*) refers to the exclusive cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
First is Madhyamaka and second is Yogācāra. Madhyamaka is the school of Nāgārjuna, which the world calls the Dharma-nature (Faxing) school.
Yogācāra is the school of Dharmapāla, which the world calls the Dharma-characteristics (Faxiang) school. It is named Yogācāra because it takes the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* as its fundamental authority;
this term translates as "correspondence" (*xiāngyìng*).
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that it is like one who carries a life-preserving bag while wishing to cross the great ocean;
this refers to the upholder of the precepts, who relies on the power of these precepts to cross the ocean of suffering in birth and death, just like a life-preserving bag.
Even if a rākṣasa were to beg for the entirety of it, or for half of it, or for as much as a palm, or for as much as a finger—
Not even so much as a speck of dust may be given to them. It is the same with the observance of the precepts:
one must not allow oneself to be led astray by the rākṣasas of craving and views to violate anything from the first to the fifth category of offenses. Not even a speck of dust of these may be broken;
for if even a single atom is violated, the vital breath will gradually leak away, and one will no longer be able to float.

Part Two: Questions and Answers and Formal Announcements.

Is the Saṃgha assembled? (Answer: "The Saṃgha is assembled. Is it in harmony? (Answer: "It is in harmony. Let those who have not received full ordination depart. (If there are any, they are sent away; answer: "Those who have not received full ordination have already departed.
If there are none, say: "There are no persons here who have not received full ordination. Do the bhikṣus who did not attend state their *chanda* and purity?

(If someone states their *chanda*, say: "So-and-so and others state their *chanda* and purity. If no one transmits their *chanda*, say: "In this assembly, there is no one who states their *chanda* and purity. Who has dispatched the bhikṣu?

[Question: A bhikṣuṇī has come to request instruction and admonition. [Answer: [Reply: "There is no bhikṣuṇī here to request instruction and admonition. [Question: The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what should be performed? [Answer: [Reply:
"The formal act (karmavācanā) for reciting the Prātimokṣa."

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today is the fifteenth day of the waxing moon (or the fifteenth day of the waning moon, or the fourteenth day of the waning moon). The community of monks shall recite the Prātimokṣa.
"If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, hear me: we shall recite the precepts in harmony. This is the motion.
The *Khandhaka on the Recitation of Precepts* states: "The Great Kāśyapa was staying at the Black Rock Mountain in the Abode of the Rishis.
While reflecting in a quiet place, he thought: 'Whether I go to the recitation of the precepts now or do not go, I am always [the foremost]...'"

First, Purity. At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, vanished from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa as swiftly as a strong man might bend and extend his arm, appearing suddenly before Kapphiṇa, where he spread out his seat and sat down.
Then Kapphiṇa paid homage at the feet of the World-Honored One and sat to one side. The World-Honored One, knowing this, asked him intentionally:
"Did you not have this thought while sitting here? He replied, "I did. The Buddha said: "The method for reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*) should be treated with reverence, respect, and service.
If you do not revere, respect, and serve the *poṣadha*, who then shall be revered?"
"Out of respect and service, you should go to recite the precepts; you must not fail to go. You should go on foot;

you must not travel by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). I, too, shall go. At whatever location there may be, whether the number of people is large or small, you should assemble in one place to recite the precepts.
To recite the precepts without being in harmony constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense, O young bhikṣus."

On the day of the *poṣadha*, one should first go to the hall where the precepts are recited (*sīma-śālā*), sweep and sprinkle it, spread out the seating mats, prepare the pure water jar and the foot-washing jar, light the lamps, and provide the *śalākā* (translated as "counters" [còu];
the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states they should not be thicker than a small finger and not thinner than a hair).

If anyone does not know how to do this, the senior monk (*sthavira*) should instruct them; if he does not instruct them, or if they do not follow his instructions, all such persons commit a *duṣkṛta* offense. Once the recitation of the precepts is finished...
One should collect [the utensils]. If a single bhikṣu dwells alone, on the day of the *poṣadha*, he should go to the *śīla-saṃghāṭa* hall and sweep and sprinkle it as described above.
If visiting bhikṣus arrive—whether there be four or more than four—he should first announce [their arrival] and then recite the precepts.
If there are three or two, they should each recite them facing one another, saying: "Now, the Saṃgha..."
On the fifteenth day (or the fourteenth), for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), I, [name], am pure. Thus it is said three times.
If there is but one person present, they should likewise recite this three times mentally and verbally.

One must not perform an illegal separate assembly (*adharmika-bhinna-saṃgha*), an illegal united assembly (*adharmika-sāmagrī-saṃgha*), or a legal separate assembly (*dharmika-bhinna-saṃgha*) for the formal act (*karma*) of reciting the precepts (the explanation of these is found in the *Karmavastu*). One should instead perform a legal united assembly (*dharmika-sāmagrī-karma*).
When the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts) is being recited, if one is ill or there are matters concerning the Three Jewels, it is permitted to give consent (*chanda*) and purity (*śuddhi*).
One should do so by speaking with the mouth; if one does not manifest the physical signs or speak with the mouth, the giving of consent and purity is not established.
If, after having received the consent and purity, one passes away or becomes subject to formal acts such as expulsion (*pravāsanīya*), [the procedure remains valid].

The formal act of granting consent and purification (*chandapariśuddhi*) is accomplished if one is asleep, in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), or has forgotten, provided it was not done intentionally; this is termed "the accomplishment of granting consent and purification.
If one does not speak [of it] intentionally, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one is unable to do so, one should support the sick bhikṣu and bring him to the midst of the Saṃgha.
If there is concern that he might die, the entire Saṃgha should go to the place where the sick bhikṣu is and surround him.
They circumambulate and perform the *karmavācanā* (formal act). If there are many sick persons, it is well if they can assemble in one place;
if they cannot, the monks should go outside the boundary to perform the *karmavācanā*. There is no other expedient for performing a *karmavācanā* as a separate assembly (*bhinna-saṃgha*).

One should not grant consent (*chanda*) or purity (*śuddhi*) by referring to the specific matter; rather, one is permitted to grant consent for a formal monastic act (*dharmika-saṃghakārya*) in accordance with the Dharma.

Regarding "purity" (the term *śuddhi* refers to: "I give my consent regarding this matter; I do not give my consent regarding that matter"). It is permitted to receive the consent and purity of many people.
If the recipient has business, it is permitted to transfer the consent and purity. Once the business is concluded, one should go in person.

At the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), if the eight types of calamities arise or there are other circumstances, a brief recitation of the precepts is permitted. The eight calamities are: kings, thieves, water, fire, disease, [famine, non-human beings, and spirits].
Regarding "evil insects," "humans," "non-humans," or other circumstances: if a large assembly has gathered but there are few seats;
or if many are ill; or if the canopy is not complete and it rains; or if there is a matter of dispute;

or if the night has already been spent preaching the Dharma—one should perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts before the appearance of the dawn. There are five ways of reciting the precepts; the first is the [full] recitation.

The introduction: The remainder is made known as being commonly heard by the Sangha. Second, the introduction and the four *pārājika* rules are explained. Third, the explanation proceeds up to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules.
Fourth, the explanation proceeds up to the *aniyata* rules; in all these cases, the remainder is made known as being commonly heard by the Sangha.

Fifth, from the recitation of the introduction until the conclusion: if any one of the eight obstacles arises, the recitation should be expanded or abbreviated according to the proximity or distance of the obstacle.
If no such obstacles exist, it is not permitted to abbreviate the recitation.

If a bhikṣu is mentally disturbed, insane, or deluded—whether he remembers the recitation of the precepts or not, or whether he attends or does not attend—one should perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for one who is insane or deluded.

[The bowl] is polished; the illness has ceased; it should be understood. One who has committed an offense may not recite the precepts, nor hear the precepts, nor confess toward a bhikṣu who has committed an offense.
One who has committed an offense may not accept the confession of another. Only after one has confessed according to the Dharma may the precepts then be recited.
If a bhikṣu, while the precepts are being correctly recited, either knows he has an offense or [is aware of it in his mind]...
