Because Devadatta had intended to harm the Buddha and further incited Ajātaśatru to kill his father, his ill repute spread and his offerings were cut off.
He then went with his own five disciples from house to house to beg for food.
Since the Buddha had prohibited eating separately from the community, Devadatta conceived this thought: "Gautama has cut off people's food; I should rather..."
He split the Saṃgha’s wheel and taught the bhikṣus with five practices for as long as he lived:

begging for food, wearing rag-robes, sitting in the open air, abstaining from ghee and salt, and abstaining from fish and meat. He caused them to have faith and delight in these ways, using skillful means to split that Saṃgha’s wheel.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of censure (*pratiśāraṇīya-karman*) against him, and thus established this precept.

The third section states: Devadatta cast the voting sticks (*śalākā*), saying, "Which elders among you who approve of these five points as being the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the teaching of the Buddha, take up a stick.
Thereupon, five hundred newly ordained, ignorant bhikṣus took up the sticks and followed Devadatta away. Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana then manifested the teaching of the Dharma.
The general returned. The Buddha ordered that he perform a *sthūlātyaya* confession. [Commentary:
"In harmony" means performing the same *karmavācanā* and reciting the *Prātimokṣa* together. "Sangha" refers to four bhikṣus up to an infinite number.

There are eighteen matters for causing a schism: regarding what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, what is Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya, what is an offense and what is not an offense, and whether it is light or heavy.

If it is grave; with remainder or without remainder; coarse or not coarse; habitual or not habitual (the *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* says: expiation through formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) or expiation without formal procedure; the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says:

habitual actions include the single-announcement procedure (*jñapti-karman*), the two-announcement procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), the four-announcement procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, and the establishment of the fourteen types of formal procedures);
prescribed or not prescribed; spoken or not spoken; and those who abide in the methods for causing a schism in the Saṃgha—these constitute the eighteen [grounds].
Regarding the matter, the third section states: "There are two things that cause a schism in the Saṃgha: false speech and similar speech.
Furthermore, there are two things that cause a schism in the Saṃgha: performing a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) and taking up voting tallies (*śalākā*).
Even if one, or even two or three bhikṣus, should employ such expedients, they cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha. Nor can bhikṣuṇīs and others cause a schism in the Saṃgha. If this...
If a group of four or more, or if a group of four or more, proceeds to cast the voting sticks for schism and performs the *karmavācanā*, this constitutes the breaking of the harmonious Saṃgha;
such a person shall suffer punishment in the hells for one *kalpa* without remedy. One who is able to reconcile them shall obtain the merit of Brahmā and enjoy happiness for one *kalpa*.
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "I do not see any other dharma that destroys a person as much as this."
Regarding the intention for the Path: as for fame, reputation, gain, and offerings, it was for the sake of these that Devadatta caused a schism in the Saṃgha.

Because Devadatta accomplished eight unrighteous acts, he caused a schism in the Saṃgha: gain and lack of gain, praise and lack of praise, honor and dishonor, delighting in evil, and following evil associates.
There are four matters termed "causing a schism in the Saṃgha": preaching the five points, distributing voting sticks oneself, and taking up the voting sticks.

To perform monastic affairs separately within the boundaries [of the saṃgha]. Furthermore, if a king, a great minister, or other groups of six persons cause the saṃgha to be discordant but not schismatic;
or if from one bhikṣu up to seven bhikṣus are in discord.
Nor is it a schism. If one performs monastic affairs without consulting the Elder, this constitutes a lack of harmony, yet it is not a schism in the Saṃgha.
If they do not eat together, sitting separately during the mealtime and quarreling or reviling one another, this is likewise not called a schism.
It must involve eight or more bhikṣus within a single boundary (*sīmā*), who divide themselves into two groups and perform monastic affairs separately;
this is what constitutes a schism (*saṃghabheda*). One who acts as the leader in this act shall fall into the great hells for one kalpa, from which there is no salvation.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are two kinds of schisms: the schism of the ritual procedure (*karmabhedaka*) and the schism of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakrabhedaka*). Regarding the schism of the ritual procedure: within a single boundary...
To perform the *poṣadha* ritual separately within [the community] is what constitutes "breaking the wheel of the Dharma. The "wheel" refers to the eightfold noble path;
it causes people to abandon the eightfold noble path and enter onto a false path. The *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* states: "It breaks the wheel of the Saṃgha."

Committing a crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya) is a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) that cannot be remedied. Breaking the *saṃgha* through formal ritual (karmavācanā) is a grave offense that is not a crime of immediate retribution and can be confessed.
To break the wheel of the *saṃgha*, there must be at least nine persons; one person claims to be a Buddha, thereby breaking the ritual *saṃgha*.
At the very least, this applies to eight persons. One does not claim to be a Buddha oneself. Regarding the breaking of the wheel of the Saṃgha, it is broken both within and outside the boundary;

regarding the breaking of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) of the Saṃgha, it must be performed by conducting a separate *karmavācanā* within the boundary. The breaking of the wheel of the Saṃgha necessarily involves a *bhikṣu*;

however, a *bhikṣuṇī* can also break the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha. Furthermore, the breaking of the Saṃgha according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the breaking of the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha are likewise [possible].

The schism of the Saṃgha of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-saṃgha*) and the breaking of the wheel of the Dharma (*dharmacakra*) occur only in Jambudvīpa. The schism of the Saṃgha regarding formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*) extends throughout the three continents.

Regarding the confession: if one abandons [the offense] after the third *karmavācanā* has been completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If one abandons it after two *karmavācanās* have been completed, there are three *sthūlātyaya*s.
If one abandons it after one *karmavācanā* has been completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya*s. If one abandons it after the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been completed, there is one *sthūlātyaya*.

If one stops [the procedure] before the initial motion (*jñapti*) has been completed and then abandons it, or even if one undergoes the formal act for causing a schism in the Saṃgha (*saṃghabheda*), it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If, while the Saṃgha is delivering a formal reprimand and admonition, one instructs them not to abandon [their position], it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if one does not deliver such a reprimand and admonition, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for a bhikṣuṇī: there is no offense if she relinquishes [the position] immediately upon the first admonition;
this also applies when she breaks with those who are contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, contrary to harmony, or who are all evil associates. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"If other monks know that a certain bhikṣu intends to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, they should appoint one monk who is close and friendly to go and admonish him. If he relinquishes it, there should be one *duṣkṛta* offense."
He should repent. If he does not relinquish [the offense], two or three bhikṣus should be sent to admonish him. If he relinquishes it, there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If he still does not relinquish it, the Saṃgha should go to admonish him. If he relinquishes it, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses.

If he still does not relinquish it, one should further admonish him through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. If he relinquishes it after the motion (*jñapti*) has been made, there is one *sthūlātyaya* and three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
It is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This continues until the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*; whether he relinquishes it or not, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If, after the three admonitions are completed, he does not relinquish [the view], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. That bhikṣu must then enter the midst of the Saṃgha and announce it himself."
Venerable Elders, I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. It would be well if I were to confess it immediately;
if I do not confess it, from this moment on, the number of days shall be counted as days of concealment. Furthermore, it is said that one must first issue a gentle admonition.
If one issues a formal injunction through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the person performing the *karman* incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one expels [the individual] before the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been performed, the person performing the *karman* incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. This applies even if the injunction has not yet been issued by means of the three-fold proclamation (*tri-vācika*).
If one separately requests individuals within the boundary to perform a *karmavācanā*, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense due to the causal conditions for schism in the Saṃgha;
if the Saṃgha is aware [of this], the Saṃgha incurs an offense.
Appendix: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If one knows that a person intends to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, the bhikṣus should say to him:
"Venerable sir, do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; the offense of causing a schism is grave, leading to rebirth in the evil realms and the hells.

We shall provide you with robes and alms-bowls, transmit the scriptures to you, read them with you, answer your questions, and instruct you. If he nevertheless does not desist, they should speak to those who have power.

The lay follower Śreṣṭhin said, "Long-lived one, this man wishes to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should go and admonish him, instructing him to desist. Lay followers, you should say to the Venerable One:
'Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha. The offense of causing a schism is grave; it leads to rebirth in the evil destinies and entry into hell.
I shall provide the Venerable One with robes, alms-bowls, and medicinal broth for times of illness. If you do not find delight in practicing the holy life, [I shall provide for your needs]. "
"You may return to secular life; I shall give you my wife and provide for all your necessities. If he still does not desist, one should pull out his tally and expel him.
Once he has been expelled, one should announce: "Venerable sirs, a schismatic has arrived; you should take note of this yourselves.
If, despite such precautions, he still causes a schism, this is called "causing a schism. If one makes offerings within such a [schismatic] group...
Therefore, it is called a "noble field of merit. Receiving full ordination therein is therefore called "properly receiving full ordination. If one awakens [to this], one should depart;

if one does not depart, they are called a "companion in the schism of the Saṃgha. As a partisan of those who cause a schism in the Saṃgha, for as long as life lasts, one should not converse with them, dwell with them, or eat together with them.
One should not share in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, nor share in the *poṣadha*, the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), or other communal rites.
At will. Regarding the *asādhāraṇa-karman* (unshared formal act): one may speak to other non-Buddhist renunciants. If there is a bed or seat, they may sit upon it as they please;
one must not tell them to sit.
Discourse on the Question: If the *saṃgha* wheel has already been split, why is it still called a "field of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*)?

Why is it still said that one has "properly received full ordination"? If one has properly received full ordination, why must one depart once [the truth] is realized? Answer: Splitting the *saṃgha* is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

He has never lost his precepts; therefore, it is said that he remains a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Just as a golden staff remains gold at both ends even if it is broken, since he has not lost his precepts, he is still a member of the *saṃgha*.
At the time of his initial ordination, he was unaware [of the transgression];

having received the precepts from him, how could he not have obtained them? However, if he later becomes aware [of the fault], he should not willingly become an associate of one who has split the *saṃgha*.
Therefore, one should depart. ○ Eleventh:
The precept against causing a schism in the Saṃgha by not relinquishing one's faction. The gravity of this offense in the Mahāyāna is the same as above.
If a bhikṣu has companions—whether one, two, three, or even countless—this bhikṣu speaks to them...
The bhikṣus said, "Venerable sirs, do not admonish this bhikṣu. This bhikṣu is a speaker of Dharma;
he is a speaker of Vinaya. What this bhikṣu says, we delight in; what this bhikṣu says, we accept."
That bhikṣu said: "Venerable sir, do not speak thus. Do not say that this bhikṣu is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya;
that we delight in what this bhikṣu says and that we approve of what this bhikṣu says.
For this bhikṣu is not one who speaks according to the Dharma, nor is he one who speaks according to the Vinaya. Venerable sir, do not seek to cause a schism."
"You have caused a schism in the Saṃgha. You should desire harmony with the Saṃgha, O Venerable One;

let the Saṃgha be united, joyful, and free from dispute, studying under one teacher like water and milk blending together. Within the Buddha’s Dharma, there will be increase and a dwelling in peace and happiness."
When that bhikṣu, being thus admonished, persists and does not relinquish [the matter], that bhikṣu should be admonished three times so that he may relinquish it.
If he relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
On account of Devadatta’s faction, they said to the bhikṣus, "Do not admonish Devadatta. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of admonition (*karmavācanā*) and thereby established this precept.
Commentary: The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "Dharma-speech" refers to speech whose phrasing is complete and perfect;

"Vinaya-speech" refers to speech that accords with reason without deviation and can lead to the realization of true meaning—this is called Dharma-speech. To produce words that are gentle and supple is called Vinaya-speech.
The gravity of the offense is the same as above. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one bhikṣu is expelled and four bhikṣus follow him, it is called 'schism' (*saṃghabheda*).

If there is a person of great virtue who is widely learned, well-known, and possesses extensive knowledge, clearly understanding the meaning of the Tripiṭaka, one should not carry out an expulsion against him for failure to acknowledge an offense. If one does so, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. (Nearby)
Because it causes a schism in the Saṃgha. Furthermore, it is said: if one person expels one person, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense;

if one person expels two, three, or four persons, one incurs two, three, or four *duṣkṛta* offenses respectively. It is the same if two, three, or [more] persons expel two, three, four, or one person.
If four bhikṣus expel four bhikṣus, they incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense, because it constitutes a schism.
Regarding the causes and conditions concerning the Saṃgha:
Question—If one bhikṣu is expelled and four bhikṣus follow him, this is called "schism in the Saṃgha.
To whom does this offense of schism belong: to the one who expels, to the one who is expelled, or to those who follow? Answer: If it is the one who expels...
If the action is performed according to the Dharma, the offense belongs to those who carry out the suspension and those who follow them in doing so.

If those who perform the suspension act contrary to the Dharma, the offense belongs to those performers and the Saṃgha. Nevertheless, even if a bhikṣu who acts according to the Dharma is unjustly subjected to suspension, he will certainly not separately conduct Saṃgha affairs within the boundary.
Furthermore, it was asked: "If one is highly learned and widely known, should one not be granted [the right to participate]?"
If one carries out a formal act of suspension (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*) against such persons, they are indeed at fault; how could they possibly be granted pardon? Answer:

When those with many acquaintances commit an offense, although it cannot be pardoned, one must instead employ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to exhort and guide them so that they recognize their transgression.
If one were to hastily perform the formal ritual (*karman*), it would inevitably lead to the fault of causing a schism in the Sangha; therefore, one incurs guilt.
○ Twelfth, the offense of refusing to submit to the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*). This is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna.

"Defiling the families of others" refers to the precepts concerning seeking profit from profit and managing the affairs of laypeople. "Engaging in evil conduct" refers to the precepts concerning improper mental activity and wrong livelihood.
To say that "the Saṃgha possesses attachment and so forth" is subsumed under the precept against slandering the Saṃgha.

If a bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon a village or a town and defiles families, committing evil deeds—such that his defiling of families is both seen and heard of, and his committing of evil deeds is also both seen and heard of—the other bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir, you defile families and commit evil deeds; your defiling of families is both seen and heard of, and your committing of evil deeds is also both seen and heard of."
[He] hears: "Venerable sir, you have defiled families and committed evil deeds; you must now depart from this village and need not remain here.
That bhikṣu says to that other bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, the bhikṣus possess affection, hatred, fear, and delusion.
There are bhikṣus who commit such identical offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not. The bhikṣus...
The Buddha replied: "Venerable One, do not speak such words as 'there is attachment, there is aversion, there is fear, and there is delusion.

There are bhikṣus who have committed the same offense, yet some are expelled while others are not; this is because the bhikṣus are without attachment, without aversion, without fear, and without delusion.
Venerable One, you have defiled families and committed evil deeds; that you have defiled families has been both seen and heard, and that you have committed evil deeds..."

If a bhikkhu both acts and speaks thus, and when he is being admonished in this manner persists in his refusal to desist, that bhikkhu should be admonished up to three times so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Regarding the connection: there were two bhikṣus who were bound together, one named Aśvaka and the other named Punarvasu.
They engaged in unrighteous conduct: they planted flowering trees themselves and instructed others to plant flowering trees; they irrigated them and plucked the flowers;
they even performed singing, dancing, and theatrical performances, playing drums, blowing conchs, and accepting payment for their jesting and merriment. At that time, there were many bhikṣus...

The two bhikṣus were begging for alms in a continuous line, maintaining a dignified and orderly manner, with their eyes cast downward as they walked straight ahead. The lay devotee (gṛhapati), however, considered this to be a transgression.

When the two bhikṣus became aware of this, they reported the matter in full to the Buddha. The Buddha dispatched Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana to perform the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against them.
At that time, the two bhikṣus spoke as follows. Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana returned and informed the Buddha. The Buddha—
The Sangha was instructed to perform the formal act of censure and admonition (*karma*), and thus this precept was established.
*Explanation:* There are four ways of defiling another's household: first, defiling a household by means of that household. This refers to taking goods from one family and giving them to another;
the family from which the goods were taken is displeased upon hearing of it, while the family to whom they were given thinks of seeking retribution.
"Indeed," he said, "if someone gives to me, I shall repay them; if they do not give to me, why should I give to both [families] who defile the household with their offerings?
If a bhikṣu receives gains in accordance with the Dharma—even down to the remnants in his alms bowl—and gives some to one layperson and not to another, the one who receives it should reflect thus:"
Requiting gratitude is as described above. Third, defiling the household by relying on friends and associates:
if a bhikṣu relies upon a king, a great minister, or a single lay devotee—whether for one lay devotee alone or not—he thinks, "I must repay his kindness;
he who acts for my sake, I shall support with offerings; he who does not act for my sake, I shall not support. Fourth, defiling the saṃghārāma.
At home, if a bhikṣu takes flowers or fruits belonging to the Saṃgha and gives them to one layperson but not to another, or even refuses me, I will not make offerings.
One who practices such evil conduct may as well plant flower trees and the like himself.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "There are two causes and conditions by which one defiles another's household: first, cohabitation, such as sitting on the same bed with a woman or eating from the same dish;
second, shared enjoyment, such as jointly using tree leaves, flowers, fruits, and tooth-sticks. The *Vibhāṣā* says:
"In general, those who have left the household life are without conditioned activity and free from desire; they are pure and self-reliant."

One who maintains [the precepts] should take the cultivation of the Path as their primary concern. If one engages in the exchange of letters with laypeople, it will disrupt and disorder one's primary practice.
Furthermore, if one sends material gifts, it will destroy the impartial and virtuous intentions of those before one;

toward those who receive such things, one feels joy and respectful affection, yet toward those who do not receive them—even if they be sages—one fails to maintain a respectful heart, thereby losing the profound [trust] of others.
They receive abundant benefits and, furthermore, they bring disorder and confusion to the Buddha-dharma.
While it is the duty of laypeople to provide offerings to those who have left the household life, these monastics instead offer support to laypeople.

Moreover, laypeople constantly seek the pure field of merit within the Triple Gem, sacrificing their own flesh and blood to plant roots of goodness; yet, due to the circumstances of these monastics' gifts, [the merit is lost].

Therefore, one develops a longing for those who have left the household life, thereby destroying the pure faith and respect of others and losing all the various benefits and offerings due to a renunciant.

If one were to give even a small gift to a layperson—even if it were to erect a stupa made of the seven precious gems and adorned in every way—it would not equal the merit of sitting in quietude and purely upholding the precepts; this is true worship.

The Tathāgata’s true Dharma-body—if one were to bestow even a small gift upon a layperson, such that they were able to establish a vihāra as magnificent as Jetavana—it would not equal sitting in quietude and purely maintaining the precepts; this is itself the pure worship of the Triple Gem.
Even if one were to bestow small gifts upon laypeople, providing the four requisites until they filled the entire Jambudvīpa, it would still not equal this.
To all the noble assembly, there is nothing that compares to sitting in meditation while maintaining pure precepts; this is itself the purest form of making offerings to the entire noble assembly.
If there are those with great power who wish to destroy stūpas or damage images, one must provide gifts to ensure their complete rescue.
One may sell the land of the stūpa, its flowers, or its fruits; or, if there is money within the stūpa, or if goods are obtained through other circumstances, one should utilize them as appropriate.

Cease. If there should be those of great power who wish to cause dissension, disruption, or reduction within the *saṃgha*, or who would sell whatever items exist upon the grounds of the *saṃgha* to make money, acting according to circumstances—whether it be the regular *kaṭhina* robe-offering or the face-gate *kaṭhina* offering—one must respond accordingly.
If there is someone with great power who wishes to reduce [the amount], one should adjust it according to the goods that can be produced from this land.
Since parents are fields of merit, they are permitted to receive offerings. As for the labor of the *saṃghika* community, this should be provided to them.
If a donor wishes to provide food for the community of monks and desires to know the proper rules, this [instruction] should also be granted.
Out of a heart of compassion, one should give to all who are destitute, impoverished, or begging, even in the event of the death of parents.
At all times, weeping is not permitted; otherwise, the fourfold assembly commits a *duṣkṛta* offense, and a bhikṣuṇī commits a *pāyattika* offense, due to the depth of her attachment.
Therefore, the classification of the offense as light or heavy is the same as above. For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.

There is no offense if, at the time of the first speech, she desists (and thus does not incur the root offense). Nor is there an offense if [the gift] is given to one's parents, the sick, small children, or pregnant women.

[If it concerns] a woman; a person imprisoned in a jail; or a temple laborer (none of these constitute the offense of defiling another's family). Or if, for the sake of the Three Jewels, one plants flowers or trees;
or instructs others to gather flowers to make offerings to the Three Jewels; or if one flees to avoid danger; or if one leaps over ditches and canals.
If one whistles or calls out to companions while walking (this constitutes a transgression; it is one form of misconduct), the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If, before the formal act of expulsion (*ukṣepaṇīya-karman*) has been performed, one says that 'the bhikṣus act according to favoritism, anger, fear, and delusion,' it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is not something for which one should issue a formal admonition."
Appendix: The third division states: "One should not shave the hair of a layperson (*avadātavasana*), except for those who wish to leave the household life.
The fourth division states: "One should not pay homage to laypeople; one should not pay homage to the shrines or temples of laypeople, nor should one intentionally circumambulate them to the left.
One should not perform divinations for others, nor should one undergo divinations from others."
One should perform music oneself, such as blowing a conch shell, to make offerings to a stūpa; it is permitted to allow laypeople (avadātavasana) to do so.
One should not keep birds such as parrots, nor should one keep dogs. One should not ride on elephants, horses, carriages, litters, or palanquins, nor carry swords or blades.
However, for those who are old or ill, riding in a hand-pulled carriage is permitted. If a man is riding, he may ride an elephant to avoid danger.
Horse. A layperson may entrust a sword or blade to a monk for safekeeping. Within the Noble Dharma and Vinaya, singing and playing are like weeping;
dancing is like being mad; and frivolous laughter is like that of a child.

One should not go to the house of a layperson at twilight, except for the sake of the Triple Gem, for the sake of a sick bhikṣu, or when invited by a donor; one should always take pleasure in going [for such reasons].
There are five faults in returning to the homes of laypeople (*avadātavasana*): first, frequently seeing women; second, gradually becoming intimate with them;
third, becoming increasingly close and affectionate; fourth, giving rise to lustful thoughts; and fifth, committing either a mortal offense (*prāṇātipāta*) or a crime nearly as grave as that.
There are nine rules regarding the homes of laypeople which one who has not yet become a *dānapati* (donor) should not observe: if one goes to their home, one should not sit down. What are they?
Nine: Upon seeing a bhikṣu, one does not rise to greet him with joy; one does not joyfully pay him homage; one does not joyfully invite the bhikṣu to sit;
one does not rejoice when the bhikṣu sits. Even if he speaks, one does not believe or accept what is said.
If there are robes, food, drink, or necessary requisites, one treats the bhikṣu with contempt and does not give them; or if there is much, one gives little; or if there is anything refined...
Giving what is small when coarse and foul food is available, or giving with a lack of respect—these constitute nine [offenses].

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should not offer monastic fruit to a layperson; however, if they ask for it, one should give it. Regarding those who learn spells to bewilder people or spells to raise the dead, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu has five places where he should not go: [the house of] a child..."

A woman, a widow, a wife, a prostitute, and a bhikṣuṇī. Furthermore, there are five [other places]: the house of a thief, the house of a caṇḍāla, the house of a liquor-seller, the house of a prostitute, and the house of a butcher.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "There are five improper places where one should not stand or remain:
the house of a public crier, the house of a prostitute, the house of a liquor-seller, the royal palace, and the house of a caṇḍāla. The *Sudarśana-vibhāṣā* [states the same].

The Vinaya states: "If a *dānapati* invites a bhikṣu to accompany them to a funeral, he must not go. The *Nanhai Jiguai Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) states:
"At the time of death and mourning, one must not grieve in the same manner as the laity; rather, one should reasonably prepare a single room for the deceased, decorating it with purity."

Alternatively, one may temporarily provide a canopy as the occasion requires, recite the scriptures and chant the Buddha’s name, and fully arrange incense and flowers, hoping that the deceased soul may be reborn in a favorable realm;
only then does one become a filial son and truly repay their kindness. If it is a *bhikṣu* who has passed away, burn the body with fire;
those who escort the remains sit to one side and have a capable person recite half a sheet of the *Anityatā-sūtra*.
[Recite] one page [of scripture]; do not let yourselves become weary for too long. Then, each should contemplate impermanence and return to your quarters.
Outside the temple, bathe together with your robes on; use only old garments so as not to damage new ones. Once you have changed into dry clothes, return to your rooms.
Regarding the etiquette of clothing, there has never been even a slight distinction; how could one permit wailing for several months or wearing hempen garments for three years?
The *Mūla-nidāna* states: "One should not sell medicine.

If one is skilled in medical formulas, one should give medicine according to the illness, arising from a heart of compassion, and must not accept payment from others. The *Jiemen jingxun* says: "But simply..."

A corrupt mind involves the defilement of greed; to sell the Dharma for profit, to perform prostrations, recite scriptures, or practice fasting as a means of livelihood—all such gains from these activities are termed "wealth of wrong livelihood.
This is fundamentally contrary to the Buddha’s transformation of beings.
○ Thirteenth: The precept against not relinquishing a wicked disposition. This is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna.

If a bhikṣu is of a wicked disposition and does not accept the words of others, and after the bhikṣus have admonished him according to the Dharma regarding the rules of training, [he still refuses to comply].
He himself does not accept admonitory speech, saying: "Venerable sirs, do not speak to me of what is good or bad;
I, too, will not speak to the venerable sirs of what is good or bad. Venerable sirs, please desist; do not admonish me. Other monks should speak to that monk, saying:
"Venerable sir, do not yourself refuse to accept admonitory speech. You, venerable sir, ought yourself [to accept it]."
One should accept words of admonition. Venerable sirs, you should admonish the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, and the bhikṣus should likewise admonish you in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, the Saṃgha of the Buddha’s disciples prospers; they admonish one another, instruct one another, and confess to one another.
When a bhikṣu is thus being admonished, if he persists and does not relinquish his position, that bhikṣu should be admonished up to three times to relinquish it.
The case: Up to three admonitions. If he relinquishes [the behavior], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

The缘 (nidāna): Regarding the Venerable Chanda, who was of an evil nature and would not accept the words of others, the Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of censure (*pratisaraṇa-karman*) and thereby established this precept.

Regarding the gravity of the offense, it is the same as above. If, before the formal announcement (*jñapti*), one of a wicked nature refuses to accept the words of others, it is a *duṣkṛta* for a *bhikṣu*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* for a *bhikṣuṇī*, and a *duṣkṛta* for the other three assemblies (*parṣad*).
There is no offense if, when being admonished by someone of little wisdom, one says: "The conduct of your *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* was also like this; you may [proceed] further."
Regarding the study and recitation of the scriptures, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If bhikṣus do not raise [a fault] against one another, nor bring it to mind, and thus act in a manner that makes them unfit for communal discourse, they commit a *duṣkṛta* offense. This is because they ought not to fail to issue a formal admonition.

The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* explains: "To 'raise' means that a bhikṣu should say: 'Venerable sir, you have committed such-and-such an offense; you should confess it and must not conceal it. It continues: "One should act accordingly..."
Regarding the removal of the offense through recollection: the bhikṣu should say, "Venerable one, do you recall committing such an offense at such a time and in such a place?
The *Caturvargika* states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "I shall describe to you eight types of evil horses."
And there are eight kinds of evil persons. Or there may be a wicked horse; when the bridle and whip are given to it with the desire to make it go, it instead stumbles and refuses to move (1).
Or it leans back against both shafts and does not advance (2).
Or it rears up and falls to the ground, injuring its knees and breaking the axle (3). Or it even walks backward and does not move forward (4). Or...
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of evil horses: (5) those that stray onto improper paths, breaking the wheel and snapping the axle;
(6) those that show no fear of the driver nor the whip, using their teeth to bite the bit and charging headlong so they cannot be restrained; (7) those that stand on two legs and foam at the mouth;
or (8) those that crouch backward and lie down. These are the eight kinds of evil horses. Likewise, there may be a bhikṣu who brings forth [faults] based on what he has seen, heard, or suspected.
1. Upon committing an offense, one says, "I do not recall; I do not recall. Or, one neither says that an offense was committed nor says that no offense was committed, remaining silent (2).
Or, one says, "Venerable sir, you yourself have committed an offense; how can you remove the offenses of others? (3).
(4) Some say, "Venerable sir, you are yourself deluded; you still require instruction from others, yet you wish to instruct me.

(5) Or they answer by speaking of other matters, which in turn gives rise to anger. (6) Or, showing no fear of the Sangha and no dread of committing an offense, they refuse to accept the words of the one who has charged them with a fault;
they then take their sitting mat, place it upon their shoulder, and depart, beyond reproach or restraint. Or they tuck up the edge of their robe on the left side.
Raising his hand in the midst of the assembly, he spoke loudly: "Do you intend to have me instructed by you? Or he might say:
"Venerable sir, you have not even given me robes, a bowl, bedding, or medicine; why then do you instruct me? Thereupon, he abandons the precepts.
Taking the lower path, he goes to where the bhikṣu is and speaks these words: "I have abandoned the religious life; is your mind at ease?
(8). These are the eight kinds of evil persons, no different from those wicked horses whom the Buddha compassionately pities.
[The Third Summary Question:
Venerable sirs, I have recited the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas: nine offenses that are complete upon the first transgression, and four that require up to three admonitions.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these dharmas and knowingly conceals it, he should be compelled to undergo *parivāsa*.
Having completed the *pārivāsa*, he is granted an additional six-night *mānatva*. Having practiced the *mānatva*, there remains the formal rehabilitation (*ābṛti*).
This bhikṣu’s offense must be rehabilitated before an assembly of twenty monks.
If even one person is missing and the assembly does not number twenty, the rehabilitation of this bhikṣu’s offense cannot be achieved; the other bhikṣus likewise [cannot be rehabilitated].
"Ha! This is the proper time. Now I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this matter? (Ask three times.
Since the Venerable Ones are silent, they are pure in this matter. Thus shall this matter be held."
The *Śāriputra-vinaya* (Shi sengqi lü) states: The Buddha rebuked the bhikṣu who concealed his transgression, saying, "Foolish man!
This is an evil deed. Having violated the precepts, you do not even feel a gradual sense of shame; how can you claim to feel remorse? He then spoke this verse: 'That which is covered leaks;
that which is opened does not leak. Therefore, all who conceal [their faults] should always open them so that they do not leak. *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*."
The Vinaya states: *Mānatva* means, in the language of Han, "to humble arrogance," and it is also called "lowering one's mind. To "lower one's mind" means to serve the community of monks.
*Ābhāṣaṇa* means, in the language of Han, "calling in," and it is also called "extracting from sin. Why is it called "calling in" and "extracting from sin"?
Because one is permitted to participate in the *poṣadha*, the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*), and the *pravāraṇā*; since one shares in these communal ritual affairs, it is so named.
Regarding the entry into the removal of offenses: the *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā* states that "submitting one's mind to all bhikṣus" is called *mānatva*;
"lifting [the offender] from an unwholesome state and placing them in a wholesome state" is called *āpattivyutthāna*.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "*Mānatva* is, in the language of Qin, 'joy of mind. It means rejoicing in one's own mind, and also causing the assembly [to rejoice]."
The Saṃgha rejoiced. Regarding *āpohana* (rehabilitation): it gives rise to pure precepts and attains pure liberation;
within these precepts, one is pure and free from transgression.

Question: For those who have committed offenses of the second category (*dvitīya-pārājika*), the removal of the offense requires twenty monks. Yet, now that we are far removed from the Sage, [how is this to be understood?]
The Vinaya laws have long been overgrown with weeds. If one commits such an offense and there are not twenty monks present, how can one be cleared of the offense? Answer:

Although there may not be twenty monks to perform the formal act of absolution, if there are four pure monks, one may likewise perform the *pārivāsika*, *mūlāpakarṣa*, and *mānatva* *karmas* according to the Dharma.
Having acted in accordance with the law, one subsequently encounters [twenty monks].
When a quorum of ten members is complete, one may again seek absolution from the offense; even if such an assembly is not encountered, one is still considered pure.
This is as explained in detail in the section on the methods for treating offenses. Second: the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas are concluded.
III. The Three [Sections]: 1. General Introduction; 2. Specific Enumeration; 3. Concluding Inquiry.
I. General Introduction:
"Venerable sirs, these two *aniyata-dharmas* (undetermined rules) are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*."
II. The second part consists of two sections: first, three dharmas that are indeterminate; second, two dharmas that are indeterminate.
Regarding the first section on the three dharmas that are indeterminate: these are natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and are shared by the Mahāyāna.

If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place, a screened place, or a place suitable for sexual intercourse, and speaks improper words, and a faithful upāsikā states one of three charges against him—namely, a *pārājika* offense;
[or a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika]; [then he is to be dealt with according to that charge].
If it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*, and the monk who was sitting there confesses, saying,
"I have committed this offense," then among these three rules— one being a *pārājika*, one a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and one a *pāyattika*—
he should be dealt with according to the law in accordance with what the laywoman of faith (*śraddhā-upāsikā*) has stated. This is called [the rule of] non-...
The established rule concerns Kāḷudāyin.

While he was exchanging intimate glances with a female lay follower (*upāsikā*) who was a friend of his wife, he went to her house during his alms-round and sat upon a single bed with her, speaking improper words. [This was reported to] Visākhā, the Mother.
[The Buddha] heard the sound and looked through the opening. He informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.
*Explanation:* "Alone" means one bhikṣu and one woman. There are two kinds of concealment:
first, concealment by sight, such as when there is dust, mist, or darkness; second, concealment by hearing, even to the point where they can hear each other’s constant conversation.
Regarding the sense-sphere of sound and the sense-sphere of obstruction: these refer to obstructions such as trees, walls, fences, clothing, or other objects.

A laywoman (*upāsikā*) who abides in faith—one who properly remembers and maintains the Three Refuges and Five Precepts without error or falsehood—is described in the *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* as follows:
"If a person says to her, 'If you speak falsely... [the rest of the sentence would follow].
"I will not harm your life by speaking falsely; however, if you speak falsely, I shall take your life. He then thought:

"If I do not speak falsely, it will mean the destruction of this physical body and the end of this single life. But if I speak falsely, it will mean the destruction of infinite lives as well as the harm to my Dharma-body.
I vow not to speak falsely. The man spoke again: "If you speak falsely, I will spare the lives of your parents and brothers."
"Sisters and all my kinsmen—if I do not speak falsely, you will all kill me. Yet I reflect:
if I do not speak falsely, I shall destroy these relatives of mine for only this single lifetime within the cycle of birth and death.

But if I speak falsely, I will wander through the three evil realms and forever lose my kin and retinues throughout successive human and celestial lifetimes; I will also lose the noble and holy companions who transcend the world. Therefore, I vow not to speak falsely."
She spoke again, saying: "If you speak falsely, I shall give you precious jewels and various kinds of wealth;
if you do not speak falsely, I shall not give them to you. She then thought, "If I do not speak falsely, I will lose these worldly riches;
but if I speak falsely, I will lose the wealth of the Noble Dharma. I vow not to speak falsely. This is called a trustworthy upāsikā.

Regarding the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence): If a bhikṣu himself declares the destination he was heading toward, declares the place he reached, declares that he sat, declares that he lay down, or declares that he acted, he should be dealt with according to the bhikṣu’s own words.

If he does not declare that he acted, does not declare that he lay down, does not declare that he sat, and does not declare the place he reached, but only declares the destination he was heading toward, [he should be dealt with accordingly].
Wherever one may be—whether sitting or lying down—one should treat the matter according to what the upāsikā has stated. There is no fixed rule regarding this;
therefore, it is called "undetermined" (aniyata). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"If one does not confess the existence of such an offense oneself, one should perform a *yathādṛṣṭa-karman* (act of searching for the truth) based on the words of a trustworthy upāsikā. Once it has been performed, one should act accordingly."
Regarding the conferring of full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others and so forth, if one acts contrary to the Dharma, one shall not be released from this *karmavācanā* for as long as life lasts.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* states: "Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, if one confesses a prior offense, the *karmavācanā* should be dissolved, and one should be disciplined according to the gravity of the offense.
If one does not confess it, the *karmavācanā* shall not be dissolved for as long as life lasts."
2. Two dharmas are indeterminate. The conditions are the same as before:
if a bhikṣu sits with a woman in an exposed place, in a location where sexual intercourse is not possible, and utters coarse and wicked words.
If there is a laywoman who dwells in faith, she may declare one of two offenses regarding each case: either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*.

If the monk sitting there confesses himself as having committed this offense, he should be dealt with according to one of those two rules—either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*—exactly as declared by the laywoman who dwells in faith.
This bhikṣu should be dealt with according to the Dharma; this is called an *aniyata-dharma*.
[End of section. Third, the formal inquiry:
"Venerable sirs, I have already recited the two *aniyata-dharmas*. Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?"
(Recited three times. Venerable sirs, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent. Thus I shall hold it to be so.
(Three times. The two indeterminate rules are concluded.
IV. The Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas. 3. First, the general heading; second, the detailed enumeration; third, the concluding inquiry.
I. General Heading.
Venerable sirs, these thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month in the *Śīla-sūtra*.
From the middle [section]. Explanation:
*Niḥsargika* is translated here as "to abandon" (*she*). *Pāyattika* is translated as "falling" (*duo*). This refers to the thirty matters;
all constitute offenses arising from material objects. These objects must be abandoned, and the *pāyattika* offense must be confessed and removed.

II. The detailed enumeration of the thirty [precepts]: from the first, the precept against keeping extra robes, to the thirtieth, the precept against diverting the property of the Saṃgha for one’s own use.
I. The first, the precept against keeping extra robes: this is a prohibitory offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). In the Mahāyāna, however, it is permitted for the sake of sentient beings.
Although they do not study the same texts, both must likewise perform the rite of *śuddhi* (purification). The *Jingmen jingxun* states:

"The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* says that a bodhisattva first, regarding all requisites he possesses, because they are not pure, relinquishes them with a pure mind to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, just as a bhikṣu relinquishes his current clothing and belongings."

Regarding [the keeping of] preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and *ācāryas*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Although one may listen to, receive, and keep [these items], they must be given as pure gifts (*viśuddha-dāna*) by donors (*dānapati*) of sincere faith.

In the present age, those who lecture and study are solely intent on profit and fame; they do not feel shame for the five types of heterodox conduct (*pañca-kudṛṣṭi*), and they keep many of the eight impurities (*aṣṭa-kaṣāya*).
They merely follow the drifting customs of the world; how could they contemplate the words of the Sage? From the moment one descends from the ritual platform (*maṇḍala*)... [text continues].
It has been many summer retreats since we have attained the pure Dharma; not even once has it touched our bodies.

How could we know that what we rely upon for daily use is nothing but defiled things, and that what we accumulate in chests and bags is entirely wealth obtained through transgression? To be arrogant toward the Dharma and deceive one’s own heart is to bring calamity upon oneself.
Those who study the Vinaya knowingly commit such offenses; as for those of other schools, they need not even be mentioned. Who knows the retribution that awaits?

It is accomplished according to the mind. How could one not believe that the fruit is produced from the cause? We see now that while the *kāṣāya* is separated from the body, in the future iron leaves will wrap around the body.
As a human, one will be born into poverty, with clothes soiled and filthy;
as an animal, one will fall into impurity, with fur and feathers foul and rank. Moreover, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are collectively termed "pure dharmas. If one harbors...
With deep faith, how could one hesitate to practice accordingly? Thus, the *Fuxingji* (Record of Aiding Practice) by Jingxi states: "Some people say:

'Regarding all things that exist, if one regards them as not being one's own property, one may use them whenever they are beneficial; what is the need for the ritual of "purifying through declaration" (*shuo jing*)?
Now I ask: if these are not one's own wealth, why not entrust them to the four seas? If they are used when beneficial, why not directly bestow them upon the two fields [of merit]?"

If one places [the object] in a deep room as an offering to the field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*) or the field of respect (*guru-kṣetra*), seals it in a bag or casket, and harbors thoughts of another’s property, one will inevitably incur the fault of theft.

If, however, one suddenly regards it as one's own wealth, this still violates the rite of *viśuddhi* (purification). If one performs the *viśuddhi* and then gives it away, what harm is there in principle?
Following their own arbitrary attachments, later generations imitated them. Thus we know that not reciting the *śuddhika* (purity) formula deeply violates the Buddha’s regulations;
it is not encompassed by the Two Vehicles and is not subsumed within the Three Roots of Goodness. If this is what constitutes leaving the household life, is it not a futile waste?
If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having had the kaṭhina robe suspended, keeps an extra robe for ten days without performing the *aviśuddha-dāna* (pure giving), he may keep it;
if it exceeds ten days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (the word "extra" is pronounced in the departing tone).
The Buddha permitted monks to possess three robes, but not in excess.
The group of six monks possessed extra robes—either morning robes, midday robes, or afternoon robes—and thus [the rule] was established.
Ānanda obtained a piece of discarded refuse-rag (pāṃśukūla) which he wished to offer to Mahākāśyapa; however, Kāśyapa was absent. Ānanda informed the Buddha, who then questioned Kāśyapa.
"When will you return? He replied, "In ten days. Thus, he was permitted to keep [the extra robes] for ten days. The *Cīvaravastu* states:
The Buddha saw various bhikṣus traveling on the road carrying many articles of clothing and thought, "I should establish a regulation regarding the quantity of robes;
one must not possess more than this. Then, during the first watch of the night, the Buddha sat in the open air wearing a single robe. At midnight...
Feeling cold at night, he put on a second robe; feeling cold again during the latter part of the night, he put on a third robe, and thus dwelt in peace and security.
He then permitted the bhikṣus to possess three robes, but not more than that. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"My disciples shall limit themselves to these three robes. They are sufficient to ward off great cold and great heat, to protect against flies, mosquitoes, and gadflies, and to cover the shame [of the body]."

[One should feel] shame. One shall not destroy the noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*). If one’s nature cannot endure the cold, it is permitted to wear old, worn-out garments; one may, according to one’s wish, have them quilted with layers of cotton.
"Having finished [making] the robes" refers to the three robes (the *kaṭhina* robe—translated here as "robe of merit"—the explanation of which follows later in the text). Regarding "extra robes":

if they are eight fingers long according to the Tathāgata’s measure, or four fingers wide (which is sixteen inches in length and eight inches in width), they may be used to make the strips for the three robes. Thus says the Vinaya.
The *Śāstraparigraha* states: "It should be understood that the three robes have distinct functions for use.

When performing manual labor, when traveling on the road, or while inside the monastery, one should regularly use the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*). When performing prostrations or during meals, one should wear the seven-strip robe (*saptakaṣāya*)."
To ward off the cold, when entering a village to beg for food and eat, or when performing prostrations before a caitya, one should wear the *saṃghāṭī*.
The latter two robes should be made by cutting [the cloth into strips]. If one is poor, these latter ones must necessarily be cut [into patches]. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
There are ninety-six kinds [of heterodox teachers], and among them there is no dharma for pure giving (*śuddha-dāna*).

Because of the Buddha’s great compassion and the power of his skillful means (*upāya*), he taught the method of pure giving so that his disciples might possess surplus wealth (*atireka-lābha*) without violating the precepts. Question:

Why did the Buddha not simply permit the possession of surplus wealth, instead of forcefully establishing this precept and setting up such a skillful means? Answer: The Buddha’s Dharma is characterized by moderation.
Desire is the root; therefore, the precept was established prohibiting the accumulation of surplus wealth. Yet, the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ:
some may accumulate much beforehand and subsequently practice the Path to realize the noble Dharma.
For this reason, the Tathāgata first establishes the precepts and subsequently provides skillful means, so that there is no obstruction regarding the Dharma and sentient beings may obtain benefit.

Regarding the mark of the ten-day period: whether one has obtained the robe-cloth or not, when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, it becomes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense requiring forfeiture).

This applies equally whether the cloth was formally dedicated (*pariṣkāra-datta*), not formally dedicated, sent to another person, lost, destroyed, made into something other than a robe, taken with the intent of a close friend, or forgotten and left behind.
"Formally dedicated" means truly giving it to another or declaring it as pure (*śuddhi*) to another; anything other than this is not so.

This is called "impure giving. If one sends [the robe] to another person, it becomes "successively pure giving" (*kṣepa-viśuddha-dāna*). [The robe is considered lost] by theft or by being separated overnight and so forth; [it is considered ruined] by being worn out, torn, and so forth; or by being made into something other than a robe; or by being made for another's use;

or by taking it with the intent of a close friend, meaning it is taken away by a close friend. In this context, from the first day after obtaining the robe up until the tenth day, during which interval there may be days on which one obtains more or days on which one does not, regarding those acquisitions—whether they were given as pure gifts or impure gifts—it is solely due to the power of the robe obtained on the first day that all such surplus robes (*atireka-cīvara*) held during the ten-day period become subject to the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* at the appearance of dawn on the eleventh day. This applies even if one causes what was previously obtained...

Regarding the object: having performed the ritual of purification (*śuddha-dāna*) and so forth, and there being no other surplus cloth, if one obtains another garment after a lapse of one day, that very day shall be considered the first day; one may then keep it at will for up to ten days without committing an offense.

If one does not relinquish a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (forfeiture) garment, but instead exchanges it for another garment, there is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense and one *dukkaṭa* (transgression) offense.

This garment should be relinquished to the Saṃgha—whether to many people or to a single person—but it must not be relinquished to a separate group (the relinquishment should follow the number of people residing at that location).
[If] few [are present], they should assemble in one place and then relinquish it). If the relinquishment is not accomplished, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, prostrate toward the Elder, kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally kept such a number of extra robes for more than ten days; I have committed an offense involving forfeiture. I...

"I now relinquish this to the Sangha for wearing. Having completed the relinquishment of the robe, one must perform the confession (*pratideśanā*). The person receiving the confession shall make the formal motion (*jñapti*): 'Venerable Sangha, listen.

This bhikṣu so-and-so has intentionally kept such a long robe in excess, thereby committing an offense involving relinquishment and forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). He now relinquishes it to the Sangha.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent that I receive the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so. The motion is as follows."
It is so. He should speak thus to this person: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept these extra robes beyond the permitted period; I have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Having already relinquished the robes to the Saṃgha, I now confess all the *pāyattika* offenses before you, venerable sir. I dare not conceal them. Through confession there is peace and happiness; through non-confession..."
Confessing with a restless mind, one recalls the offense and discloses it; knowing it, one does not conceal it. "Venerable Sir, please remember my pure body of precepts;
I am fully endowed with the purity of the *poṣadha*. Thus he should say three times. The other should speak to him, saying:
"Reproach your own heart," and he should reply, "So be it. If the Saṃgha is difficult to assemble, or if this bhikṣu wishes to travel far away, he should ask [for the *poṣadha*].
He says: "To whom shall I give this robe? He should give it according to whatever he says. The Saṃgha should then return this robe to that bhikṣu by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

It should be given in this manner: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu named so-and-so has intentionally kept an extra robe for such a length of time and has committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha permits, [the Saṃgha] shall take this..."
"I give this robe to that bhikṣu [Name]. That bhikṣu [Name] shall return it to this bhikṣu. Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal act) is performed. If, after having relinquished it, one does not return it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If someone says, "Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one makes it a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*), or sends it to another person, or takes it to make the three robes (*tricīvara*), or makes...
Regarding the *pālikara* robe (the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: *cīvara-pālikara*; in the Chinese language, it means "variegated or miscellaneous fragments"):
if it is intentionally damaged, burnt, made into something other than a robe, or worn until repeatedly ruined, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
There is no offense if, within ten days, one performs a *śuddha-dāna* (pure gift), gives it away to another, or has the perception that it was seized, lost, burnt, or swept away.

If one makes a "pure gift" (*śuddhadāna*) but does not hand it over to another person, and the recipient of that entrusted robe subsequently dies, goes abroad, leaves the monastic life, encounters the danger of bandits, is harmed by wild beasts, or is swept away by water—then, because the pure gift was not handed over to another person, there is no offense. The *Cīvaravastu* states:
"If the robes of the Saṃgha remain for more than ten days, there is no offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If [it is] for the sake of the Buddha..."
If one gathers items in one place for the purpose of making offerings to the Saṃgha, there is no offense even if they have not been used for a long time.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "If one keeps clothing for the sake of the Three Jewels, it is not an offense. Or, if a donor says, 'This is my property;
you should use it,' then even if one does not distinguish [the items] (i.e., perform the ritual of *śuddhi*), using them is without offense. (Fundamental Text)
The Vinaya states: If one commits an offense involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika), yet does not forfeit the object; or if, although one has forfeited it, one does not confess the offense;

or if, although one has confessed it, one does not wait until the end of the night—whatever one subsequently acquires constitutes a forfeiture offense as well, because of the prior defilement. However, if one forfeits the robe and confesses the offense...
After one night has passed, it is considered that no offense has been committed. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One must not give [the extra robe] away to another person or to a non-human being.

Only after having relinquished it may one then perform the confession of the transgression (*pāpadeśanā*). If one confesses the transgression without first relinquishing it, the offense becomes even more grave.
With the exception of the three long robes, if any other extra robe—even down to a hand-towel—is kept for more than ten days, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). If it is purified..."
[If one] gives [the robe], there is no offense. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

"If one obtains a robe on the first day and is not subjected to the act of *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), or if the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* is not performed (that is, the formal censure and confession have not been carried out), or if one is subjected to the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* for not abandoning evil views;

or if one is deranged, distracted, or has a mind impaired by illness such that even if the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* is not lifted, one does not regain one's original state of mind until the end of life—there is no offense against this precept. Once the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* is subsequently lifted, [one may receive the robe]."

Regarding the fundamental intent: even if one calculates the days to determine the offense, if on the first day one obtains a robe and ascends to a celestial palace, traveling as far north as Uttarakuru, and remains there until the end of one's life without violating this precept, then upon returning to one's original location, the offense is calculated according to the number of days elapsed.

If one obtains a robe on the first day and does not see the formal act of suspension (*pravāsanīya*) until the fifth day, and subsequently the suspension is lifted, one regains one's original mind, and returns to one's original location,
then the five previous days are counted together with the subsequent five days, after which the offense is completed.

○ Second, the precept against staying overnight separated from one’s robes. This is a *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offense). It is likewise regulated in the Mahāyāna, as it is included among the eighteen items.

If a bhikṣu, having finished his robe-making and with the *kaṭhina* period having ended, stays overnight in a different location separated from any one of his three robes—unless by formal authorization (*jñapti-karman*) of the Saṃgha—it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The Case: Six groups of bhikṣus went traveling among the people. They entrusted their robes to bhikṣus who were their acquaintances, who then dried them repeatedly.
Other bhikṣus, having learned the reason for this, reported it to the Buddha, who then established a precept.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu suffering from consumption who wished to travel among the people; however, his paṃsukūla saṃghāṭī was heavy, and he was unable to carry it on his journey.

The companion informed the Buddha. The Buddha permitted the Saṃgha to grant the "non-loss of robe" (*akalpiya-cīvara*) status to a sick bhikṣu through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. The procedure is as follows:
if one leaves one's robe inside a monastery and stays overnight under a tree or in another location until the appearance of the dawn light.

If he goes out and remains separated from the robe for which he was subject to *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. If he leaves the robe in another location and spends the night at a monastery, it is likewise.

With the exception of the three robes, to be separated from any other robe constitutes a *dukkaṭa*. Once the robe has been relinquished and the confession performed as above, the Saṃgha should immediately return this robe to the bhikṣu by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement).
If they do not return it, then for every instance of him wearing it again until it is worn out, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if she holds the robe with her hand before the dawn light has appeared; or if she discards the robe;

or if she stands within the distance reached by a thrown stone (the "robe-boundary"); [in the case where the robe-boundary is narrow, she must hold the robe close to her body; in the case where the robe-boundary is wide, it suffices to stand within the distance reached by a thrown stone, and this is termed "not being separated from the robe"].

Alternatively, if she is unable to hold the robe and cannot stand within the distance reached by a thrown stone, she must, while the dawn light has not yet appeared, form the intention to discard the robe. By thus discarding the robe, she incurs only a *duṣkṛta* offense for lacking the robe.

If one does not set it aside, one commits the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense of being separated from one's robe. Therefore, one should avoid the heavy and adopt the light. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
Regarding the *karmavācanā*, if an illness has not yet been cured, one may remain separated [from the robe] overnight.

If the Sangha has performed the *karmavācanā* and one has gone elsewhere separated from the robe, and the illness is cured and one wishes to return, but the road is dangerous and difficult so that one cannot return—provided one constantly maintains the intention to return, even though the illness is cured, the robe is not lost. If...
Having resolved not to return, he loses his robe. After ten days have passed, he commits the offense of keeping an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*).

If he travels to another region, recovers from his illness, and returns to the place where the robe was, but the illness breaks out again and he wishes to go to yet another region, he may rely on his previous *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) and need not perform the *karmavācanā* again.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one has re-sewn the three robes (*tricīvara*), even if there is a cause for [removing them], one should tear [the seams]."
Regarding the practice of partial retention (*parihāra*): it is called "not staying overnight separated from one's robe. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:

"If one goes elsewhere for a short time with the intention of returning immediately, one may leave the robe behind as one pleases. Furthermore, if one goes out for a short while intending to return, but reaches there at twilight and returns after night has fallen, one might be harmed by insects or bandits;
in such a case, one should stay the night there. One must not travel at night. This applies to the robes that are being retained."

One should mentally resolve upon relinquishment (*cetanā-tyāga*). One may borrow the remaining three robes from fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*) and maintain them for the sake of the practice.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Wherever one dwells, one should always have the three robes with one; carrying the alms bowl while begging for food, they are always with the body, like the two wings of a bird."

**Discrimination:** Question: Since it is said that the robe and the alms bowl are always together like the two wings of a bird, why does one incur an offense for being separated from the robe, yet not incur an offense for being separated from the bowl?
Answer: The robe is for covering the body, and the bowl is for begging food; both ought to be constantly with one’s person.
However, during the regular meals of the Saṃgha or when receiving invitations, it is still permissible not to use one's own bowl. As for the robe, however...
There is no further principle by which [the fetters] could be abandoned;
thus, there are those that are bound and those that are not. *Chóngzhì píní shìyì jíyào*, Scroll Four, Glossary of Pronunciations and Meanings.
King Udayana—also called Udāyana or Udrayana—is translated as "One Who Has Received [the Mandate].
Chandaka, formerly called Channi, was the name of the groom who was ordered to lead the horse when the Buddha left the city to renounce the world;
he was thus known by the title "Horse-Attending Slave. He is also called Chandraka.
*Ḍavama-ra-putra* is also called *Tāpīya*, or translated as "Strong Power" (*Śrībala*).
*Devadatta* is also called *Tiāodá*. This is translated as "Heavenly Heat," because when he was born, the hearts of the assemblies of devas and humans were all struck with alarm and fever.
It is also translated as "Heavenly Bestowal" or "Heavenly Gift," meaning that he was obtained through a request made to the heavens.
Therefore, he was the Buddha’s younger cousin and Ānanda’s biological elder brother.
Ajaśatru— translated here as "Unborn Enemy"—
and Maudgalyāyana (also called Maudgalika)— translated here as "Bean-Gatherer"— were the names of the Venerable One’s clan.
His name was Kauṇḍinya, which is the name of a tree; he was born after praying to this tree, and thus it became his name.
He was foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and served as the preceptor (*ācārya*) to Rāhula.

The *karmavācanā* for appointing fourteen persons refers to the formal procedure for appointing individuals to serve as temple administrators (*vihārasvāmin*), treasurers, and so forth, down to those who distribute rice gruel.
Regarding "receiving retribution in *niraya* for one *kalpa* without relief," *niraya* is the hell realm; this term is translated here as "that which does not exist" (*wu you*).
It is devoid of joy and bliss; it lacks flavor, and because it is without delight or benefit, it is either translated as "base" or "degraded.
An eon (*kalpa*) refers to one complete cycle of the world's formation and destruction. The Sanskrit term *kalpa* is also rendered as *kap*. This is translated as "distinguishing time periods.
There are three types of eon-measurements: small, medium, and great. [When] human life expectancy is eighty-four thousand years...
The lifespan decreases until it reaches ten years, and then gradually increases again until it reaches eighty-four thousand years.

One such decrease and one such increase is called a *kṣudraka-kalpa* (small kalpa). Twenty small kalpas constitute one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*). The periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness each consist of one intermediate kalpa;
these four intermediate kalpas together constitute one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). This is stated with reference to the Sahā world-system.
The durations of kalpas in other directions vary in many ways, as explained extensively in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Those who do not seek treatment cannot be saved.
Among the remaining six groups of renunciants and the seven groups of disciples, only the community of bhikṣus is capable of causing a schism in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus.
The others are all incapable [of doing so].
Regarding the three types of admonition: first, a single bhikṣu uses gentle speech; second, two or three bhikṣus use gentle speech;
third, the Saṃgha issues an admonition through formal ritual action (karmavācanā).
Jili (羈連) is the name of a town; "ji" (羈) is pronounced like "ji" (饑).
Aśvā is translated here as the "Horse Mansion" (馬宿);
Pūrṇavasu is translated here as the "Full Mansion" (滿宿).
"Zengyi" (gifts) refers to the offering of sounds and positions; it means to present or send.

"Changla" (constant offerings) refers to the property of the resident monks (*sthavira-saṃgha*), while "mianmenla" (offerings at the gate of the face) refers to the property of the monks currently present.
In the *Vibhāṣā*, items for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and items belonging to the Buddha’s stūpa are also collectively termed "la. It is not yet clear why this is so.
The meaning is as follows: "Or it is taken to mean 'using the mind according to the occasion.
*Lian* (輦) [pronounced with the initial *lì* and the final *zhǎn*]: a carriage drawn by footmen. *Yu* (輿): pronounced *yú*, a carriage."
The four matters of the first section constitute offenses equivalent to capital crimes; because those who commit them cannot be saved, they are termed "capital crimes.
The thirteen matters of the second section possess some possibility of redemption, and are thus termed "near-capital crimes."
"Changling-jia" refers to households that employ actors, jesters, and musicians for entertainment; their lewd sounds and beautiful forms delude the human mind.
"Zanghuī" (pronounced zānghuì) refers to the name for goods received by corrupt officials; it also denotes what is stolen or plundered by thieves.
This is the name for an object. Now, those who have left the household life and seek profit with a crooked mind also receive this name.
*Lè* (勒) is pronounced as the combination of *lì* (歷) and *dé* (德). It refers to the head-stall and bit of a horse.
*Biān* (鞭) is pronounced as *biān*; it is made of leather and used to drive the horse.
*Zhì*: The pronunciation is *zhì*. It means to stamp one's feet and stop short, failing to advance.
*Yuán*: The pronunciation is *yuán*. It refers to the curved wood at the front of a carriage that hooks over the crossbar (*héng*).
*Lì*: The pronunciation is *gé*. It refers to the axle of a carriage.
*Jia* (pronounced *zé*) means "to bite.
*Viśākhā* is translated here as "Distinct Branches" (*biézhī*), which refers to the lunar mansion of that name. She was named after the lunar mansion under which she was born.
The six groups of bhikṣus were: first, Nanda; second, Upananda—these two were both excessively greedy for wealth and profit, yet they were both reborn in the heavens.
Third was Kālodāyin, whose nature was prone to lustful defilement;

it was only after being rebuked by Queen Mallikā that he attained the realization of the fruits [of the path]. He exhorted and converted couples until one thousand families had together realized the noble fruits. Fourth...

Chanda was of a wicked nature and difficult to converse with. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda followed the Buddha’s command and applied the method of silent exclusion (*tūṣṇīmbhāva-niḥsaraṇa*), and Chanda also attained the fruit of realization.
As for Pañcaśikha and Pūrṇaśikha, they defiled others’ households and practiced evil deeds; both fell into the Heat-Sand Dragon realm.
Originally, these six individuals were all from noble and wealthy lineages; after they had left the household life, they acted together as follows:
They formed factions; thus they were called the "Six Groups.
*Cetiya* is sometimes called *zhiti* or *zhiduō*; this translates as "a place worthy of offerings," or it is translated as "a place where evil is extinguished and goodness arises.
That which contains relics is called a *stūpa*; that which lacks relics is called a *cetiya*.
Regarding the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Regions, there are ninety-six types in total.
Some say that ninety-five of these are heterodox, while only one is orthodox.
*Ti* (pronounced *ti*) means to pick out or expose.
