○ The Precept Regarding Keeping an Extra Robe for More Than One Month: In the Mahāyāna, this is not an offense when done for the sake of the Saṃgha; however, it is an offense when done for oneself.
If a bhikṣu’s robes are finished and the kaṭhina period has ended, and that bhikṣu obtains an out-of-season robe, he may accept it if he needs it.
Having accepted it, he must quickly have it made into a robe. If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, he may keep [the extra cloth] for one month.
[The Buddha said: "For the sake of fulfillment. If one keeps [an extra robe] beyond that, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. The Circumstances:
A certain monk’s *saṃghāṭī* was worn out, and he could not provide for a replacement within ten days.

Fearing he might violate the preceding precept, his companion informed the Buddha on his behalf. Consequently, [the Buddha] permitted the keeping of an extra robe until it was fulfilled. The group of six [monks] had...

Regarding paṃsukūla robes and other types of robes, if those of the same kind were insufficient, one should take a medium-quality paṃsukūla robe, wash and dye it, and mark its four corners to purify it.

Having entrusted it to a bhikṣu friend and departed on a journey through the human world, the person who received the entrustment, because the traveler had not returned for a long time, took it out to dry.
When the other bhikṣus questioned him about this, they informed the Buddha, who then established a precept.
Explanation of "the time": If there is no *kaṭhina* robe, it is one month after the *pravāraṇā*;
if there is a *kaṭhina* robe, it is five months after the *pravāraṇā*. "The wrong time" refers to exceeding these limits.

Regarding the signs: if one has sufficient robes within ten days, one should immediately cut them, sew them together with thread, stitch them into a robe, give them as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*), or send them to another person.
Otherwise, when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense according to the number of robes possessed.
If one does not have sufficient robes on the tenth day but obtains sufficient robes by the eleventh day, one should [act accordingly] immediately.
The cutting and so forth are as described above. Otherwise, if the dawn of the twelfth day appears, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense according to the number of robes.

This applies likewise up until the twenty-ninth day. If it reaches the thirtieth day, regardless of whether the robes are complete or not, or whether they match or not, one must perform the cutting and so forth on that very day. Otherwise, at the dawn of the thirty-first day...
[If the robe] is finished, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The *Samantapāsādikā-vinaya* states:

"If on the twenty-ninth day one obtains the expected fine cloth, while the previous cloth was coarse and the previous cloth had been formally dedicated (*pariśuddha*), the newly obtained cloth may also be kept for one month."
Because they desire uniformity: if one expects to obtain coarse robes, one may further store them for one month.
In this manner, proceeding by successive stages according to one's own preference, because they desire uniformity, it must not exceed one month.
The fourth precept concerns receiving robes from a nun who is not a relative; this is a prohibitory offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).

In the Mahāyāna, one does not distinguish between relatives and non-relatives, but rather considers only whether something is acceptable or unacceptable to receive. Nevertheless, during the Dharma-ending age, it is especially appropriate to avoid such suspicions.
If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The缘 (nidāna):
There was a bhikṣu wearing a worn-out saṃghāṭī; the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā saw him.
Having already conceived a heart of compassion, she immediately exchanged the expensive garment she was wearing for it. Later, she went to see the Buddha wearing this tattered robe.
The Buddha said, "It should not be like this. I allow you to keep and wear five robes that are complete and sturdy;
as for any other garments, you may give them away as you wish. Why is this? Even when women wear fine, superior clothing, they still do not look beautiful, let alone [in such rags]."
Wearing tattered robes, he then assembled the community and established a precept. Thereafter, all the bhikṣus were cautious and fearful, not daring to take robes from their own relatives.
The Buddha said: "If they are relatives, one may take them after weighing the circumstances to know whether they have them or not; thus, taking them is permitted.
Furthermore, when the two divisions of the Saṃgha within Jetavana received a gift of robes and were dividing them together, at that time a bhikṣu made an error.
A bhikṣuṇī obtained a robe; however, she mistakenly received a robe belonging to a bhikṣu. The bhikṣuṇī took the robe to the saṃghārāma and attempted to exchange it.
The bhikṣus again informed the World-Honored One, whereupon he permitted such exchanges.
Commentary: "Relatives" refers to parents and their kin, extending even to those related through seven generations.

"Trading" means exchanging clothing for clothing, or exchanging clothing for non-clothing, or exchanging non-clothing for clothing; this includes items such as needle cases, knives, thread, and even a single pill of medicine.

[The] characteristics: for the other four groups [of practitioners], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. (If a *śrāmaṇera* takes the robes of a non-relative *bhikṣuṇī*, *śikṣamāṇā*, or *śrāmaṇerī*, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.

If a *bhikṣuṇī*, *śikṣamāṇā*, or *śrāmaṇerī* takes the robes of a non-relative *bhikṣu* or *śrāmaṇera*, it is likewise all a *duṣkṛta*). There is no offense if one takes them for the sake of the Saṃgha or the Buddha-temple.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Taking from a non-relative *śikṣamāṇā* or *śrāmaṇerī*..."
[Receiving] clothing [from one who is not a relative]: a *duṣkṛta* offense. If one takes clothing from a relative who has committed a transgression or holds wrong views, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: if the person is not a relative, and one perceives them as such, or if doubt arises, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If the person is a relative, but one perceives them as not being so, or if doubt arises, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. There is no offense if, for example, a nun offers clothing to the Saṃgha, or...
One gives for the sake of preaching the Dharma; or one gives at the time of receiving full ordination; or one gives upon seeing someone being robbed by bandits;

or when a nun has received abundant offerings, she takes her robes and belongings to the place where the bhikṣus are, places them on the ground, requests that they be accepted, and then departs, leaving them behind.
Taking [the items] also constitutes no offense. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "To take clothing that conforms to the prescribed measure constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
to take clothing or other items that do not conform to the prescribed measure constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."

○ The fifth precept concerning causing a nun who is not a relative to wash one's robes. This is a shared training rule for the Mahāyāna; it is especially a precept that must be observed during the Dharma-ending age.
If a bhikṣu causes a nun who is not a relative to wash an old robe, or to dye it, or to beat it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Pāyattika. The case involves Kālodayin, who sat with the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā in a state of nakedness; they gazed at one another with lustful intent, resulting in the discharge of impurity that soiled his lower robe (antarvāsaka).
The bhikṣuṇī requested that he wash it for her, and she took the impurity and placed it in her mouth.
[The semen] entered the vagina and the urinary tract. Subsequently, she became pregnant. The nuns questioned her and learned the reason;
they informed the bhikṣus, who in turn reported it to the World-Honored One. He rebuked them and established a precept.

Thereupon, the bhikṣus were each cautious and fearful, not daring to have nuns who were relatives wash, dye, or beat their old clothes. The Buddha further added the words "non-relative" [to the rule].
Commentary: Regarding "worn-out robes," this refers to those that have been worn on the body at least once. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states:
"One may have an ordained nun—even down to a granddaughter—wash them; however, one must not have an ordained wife or a daughter-in-law wash them, as they are not relatives."

Regarding the signs: if one causes [a robe] to be washed, dyed, or beaten, each constitutes one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense requiring forfeiture and confession). [If the robe is forfeited once, it is purified; there are three types of offenses involving falling away that must be confessed.
If one causes someone else to wash, dye, or beat [the robe], but they do not actually wash, dye, or beat it, each constitutes one *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one causes a non-relative *śikṣamāṇā* or *śrāmaṇerī* to [wash, dye, or beat it], it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one causes a non-relative *bhikṣuṇī* to wash, dye, or beat a new robe, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
*Dūṣkṛta*. For the other four assemblies, it is *duṣkṛta*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one has a nun wash a robe for the sake of the two teachers, it is a *vinayātikrama* offense; if for the sake of a stūpa or the Saṃgha, there is no offense.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) states: "If one first washes it oneself and then further orders [the nun] to wash it, etc., it is all *duṣkṛta*. The *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā-śāstra*...
The *Śāstra* states: "Regarding this precept, [the offense applies] to all cases of robes that are either of appropriate measure or inappropriate measure. The *Mātṛkā* states:

"If one causes a nun who is not a relative to wash a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). If she washes a bedspread, a pillow, or the like, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)."
Appendix: The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "In washing and laundering robes, there are five benefits: it removes foul odors; lice and nits do not breed;
the body is free from itching; the robe can accept dye; and it is fit for long-term use. For one who does not wash their robes, these are inverted into five faults.
There are also five benefits to wearing dyed robes: because they accord with the outward appearance and deportment of the Noble Ones (*ārya*), they cause one to abandon arrogance."
Because of pride; because it does not receive dust and grime; because lice and nits do not arise upon it; and because it is soft to the touch and easy to maintain.
There are five kinds of faults in washing clothes excessively: they cause the garment to wear out quickly and render it unfit for rigorous use.

Because it involves the exhaustion of mental effort; because it is a fruitless toil; and because it obstructs all categories of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*). There are likewise five faults in being attached to fine dyed robes:
they increase one's own arrogance and self-indulgence; they give rise to envy in others; they cause others to perceive one as merely grooming one's appearance for the sake of beauty;
they cause great hardship and suffering when seeking them; and they obstruct the practice of wholesome qualities. These exceed the [allowable] degree of dyeing.
Damaging the robe: because it is used when it is not durable. Excessive beating also has five faults as mentioned above.
○ Sixth: The precept against begging for robes from those who are not relatives. In the Mahāyāna, one does not train identically [to the Hīnayāna] because of the sake of sentient beings;
however, one must deliberate upon whether the donor is capable or incapable of giving.
If a bhikṣu asks for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The "appropriate time" refers to when a bhikṣu has had his robes taken away, lost, burned, or carried away by water;
this is called the appropriate time.
The Setting: There was a householder in Śrāvastī who went to a park for recreation. Turning his carriage toward the Jetavana Monastery, he saw the Śākya son Upananda.
He paid his respects and listened to the Dharma. Upananda preached the Dharma to instruct and transform him, exhorting him until he was filled with joy.
The householder asked what he required; Upananda replied that he required nothing. The householder pressed him further, and Upananda replied:
"Stop, stop! Even if I have something you require, I cannot give it to you. The elder invited him again, whereupon he said, "You may give me what you are wearing now.
At that time, the elder was wearing an expensive, wide, and long white cotton cloth garment (*karpāsa*).
He replied, "Come to my house tomorrow; I shall give it to you there. But Bāḍananda continued to press him, refusing to desist.
The householder was displeased; he took off his garment and gave it to him. The householder then entered the city by carriage, wearing only a single garment.
The gatekeeper suspected he had been robbed by a thief, but the householder explained the circumstances in detail. Because the layperson criticized and disparaged this, the rule was established.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus were cautious and fearful, not daring to ask for garments from their relatives. The Buddha further added the words "from those who are not relatives. Hereafter...
There were a number of bhikṣus who, having completed their rains retreat in the kingdom of Kośala, took up their robes and bowls and set out for the place where the World-Honored One was.
Because it was too hot to travel during the day, they traveled by night; however, they lost their way and were plundered by bandits.
They stood outside the gate of the Jetavana with their bodies exposed. The other bhikṣus, suspecting them to be Nirgranthas, informed Upāli, who questioned them and came to know [the truth].
Therefore, he immediately borrowed clothing and went to see the Buddha. The Buddha greeted him with inquiry, and he fully explained the circumstances.

The Buddha then established the rule that practicing nakedness constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. At such times, one should cover the body with soft grass or tree leaves and should go to the vicinity of the monastery.

If one already possesses an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*), one should take it and wear it. If one has none, and a companion monk (*kalyāṇamitra*) possesses an extra robe, one should take that and wear it.
If the companion has none, one should ask the Saṃgha, "What kind of robes are there to be distributed? If there are any, [one should take them].
One should give it. If there is none, one should ask whether there are bedding materials. If there are, one should give them.

If one does not give them, one should personally open the storehouse and look; if there are cushions, floor mats, woolen cloths, or blankets, one should tear them apart, take them, and cut them into robes to cover one's body.
When going out to beg for robes, the bhikṣus did not dare to carry [the materials].
When items from this place were taken to that place, the Buddha said, "It is permitted. At that time, the bhikṣus had their robes stolen, lost, burned, or washed away;

fearing transgression, they did not dare to wear the monastic robes. The Buddha said, "It is permitted to wear them. After they obtained new robes, they did not return the monastic robes to their original locations.
The Buddha said, "This should not be done. Once you have obtained new robes, you should wash, dye, and sew the old ones and place them securely back in their original location. If...
"No, it is not so; it should be dealt with according to the Dharma. At that time, there were bhikṣus who had their robes stolen, lost, burned, or carried away by water.
Fearing and being cautious, they did not dare to beg for robes from those who were not relatives. The Buddha said, "I permit it," and then further formulated this precept text.
[Regarding] the signs: for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in cases such as begging on behalf of another, when another begs on one's behalf, or obtaining [an item] without having requested it. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If one begs for oneself, causes another to beg, begs by making gestures of cold or heat, or begs while preaching the Dharma, whatever is obtained constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. This also applies if one begs for a water-strainer."
A bag; small items for mending clothes; objects for tying the head; dressings for wrapping wounds; and a *dié*—a single strip of cloth within a garment—all these do not constitute an offense.
If one begs on behalf of the two teachers (*ācārya* and *upādhyāya*), it is a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense. If one begs for the sake of a stūpa or the Saṃgha, there is no offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: at the time of begging, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense. Regarding the clothing obtained, whether in price, color, or quantity, if it is... [the text continues].

Regarding what is appropriate for the request: it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. Regarding what is inappropriate: there is no offense. The *Vibhāṣā* states: "If two people together request one robe, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To solicit on behalf of another, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one obtains a robe of proper measure, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one obtains a robe of improper measure, it is a *duṣkṛta*. To solicit from a relative who is impoverished, it is a *duṣkṛta*."

If one gives a small amount and subsequently demands a large amount, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If a person who is not a relative first invites one to accept a robe and later, being impoverished, asks for it back, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one gives a small amount and subsequently demands a large amount, it is a *duṣkṛta*. To demand on behalf of another is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Mātṛkā* states: "There is no offense in begging for a robe from a non-human, an animal, or a deva."

**Discrimination** Question: Regarding the four cases where begging for another person’s sake does not constitute an offense, the *Mahāsāṃghika* and *Sarvāstivāda* schools both classify it as a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense).
From what source is this derived? Answer: When one perceives the poverty and suffering of others and gives rise to compassion, the *Dharmaguptaka* school permits this without fault.

However, when one desires that another act on one’s own behalf and employs skillful means [to obtain goods], the *Vibhāṣā* therefore classifies it as a transgression. This must be discussed in terms of the underlying intention (*citta*).
Only then may it be definitively settled.

○ Seventh, the precept against receiving robes more than seven times. This is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). In the Mahāyāna, for the sake of sentient beings, one does not train in the same manner;
one should accept them according to what is offered.
If a bhikṣu has lost his robes, had them stolen, burned, or carried away by water, and a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative invites him and offers him many robes,
that bhikṣu should accept the robes with moderation. If he exceeds this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Case: A group of bhikṣus encountered bandits and lost their robes. Upon arriving at Jetavana, there was an upāsaka who possessed many fine robes.
He allowed the bhikṣus to take as many as they desired; however, because the bhikṣus already possessed their own three robes, they refused to accept them.
The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) bhikṣus said, "Why do you not take some and give them to us? Or would you rather give them to others? Thereupon, the bhikṣus took [the robes].
[The Buddha] gave [the robe] to him. Those of few desires criticized this and reported it to the Buddha; therefore, he established this rule. Commentary:

If one loses one robe, one should not take another. If one loses two robes, and there remains one robe—whether it be double, triple, or quadruple layered—one should tear it apart to make individual robes.
If all three robes are lost, one should accept only what is sufficient for one's needs.
Contentment is of two kinds: first, accepting whatever clothing a layperson provides (one should not ask for more);

second, the three robes (one should not accept anything beyond the three robes). If a layperson, being liberal, offers many robes—whether fine, thin, or of poor quality—one should take them and make them into double, triple, or quadruple layers;
they should be provided with borders and shoulder-straps.
One should affix hooks and buttons to places stained by grime or grease. If there is any remnant remaining, one should ask the layperson:
"What shall this leftover cloth be cut and made into? If the donor says, "I did not give it because the robe was lost;
I wished to give it to you, Venerable Sir," then if he wishes to accept it, he may do so.
[The offense of] *niḥsargika-pāyattika* for a bhikṣuṇī; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
○ The eighth precept concerning the seeking of a higher price for robes is likewise regulated in the Mahāyāna; that is, [the offenses of] evil seeking and excessive seeking.
If a bhikṣu, while staying at a layman’s home, and that layman’s wife has prepared the price for a robe for the bhikṣu, intending to buy such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu;
and if that bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation to choose freely, goes to the layman’s house and speaks thus: "Excellent, layman!
Buy such and such a robe for me and give it to me, so that it may be of good quality"; and if he obtains the robe—[he commits an offense].
*Naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The circumstances were as follows:
A certain bhikṣu entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms and arrived at the house of a lay devotee.
There he heard the husband and wife of that layman discussing and arranging the price for a robe for Baddhananda, and he returned to inform Baddhananda. Baddhananda...

He inquired about the man’s household and went to speak with him the following day, saying, "If you wish to give me a robe, it should be made large, new, fine, and sturdy, so that I may accept and wear it.
Because the householder criticized and complained, [the Buddha] established this rule.
Thereafter, when a householder invited a monk at his own discretion, asking, "Venerable sir, what kind of robe do you require? the bhikṣu, being hesitant and doubtful, did not dare to answer.
Furthermore, there was a lay devotee who wished to provide robes of high value. A bhikṣu, being content with his lot, desired something of inferior quality;
yet, harboring doubts in his mind, he did not dare to request it as he wished. The Buddha said: "If one has previously accepted a formal invitation (pravāraṇā), there is no offense."
**Explanation:** There are two kinds of seeking: first, seeking the price, even by increasing it by a single small coin; second, seeking the robe, even by adding a single thread.

If one obtains [the robe] through such seeking, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture); if not obtained, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three [groups], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
These constitute various *duṣkṛta* offenses. There is no offense in cases such as seeking [items] for others. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states:
"If one requests fine items from a relative, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:
"There is no offense in begging from gods and the like, or in begging for thread, silk, small pieces of cloth, and so forth."
○ Ninth: The precept against seeking to have cloth purchased for oneself. The origin of the rule, the offenses, and the non-offenses are all the same as before.
If a bhikṣu, two laymen or a laywoman provide the price for a robe for a bhikṣu, and [the bhikṣu] takes that price for such a robe...
"Buy such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu. That bhikṣu, having not previously received a formal invitation from the householder, goes to the two householders' homes and says:
"Excellent! Prepare such and such a price for a robe and give it to me."
If one makes a single robe together for the sake of its beauty, and if such a robe is obtained, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
○ The tenth precept concerning soliciting robes more than six times is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). This is likewise studied by those of the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu, or a king, or a minister, or a brahmin, or a householder, or a householder’s wife,

sends a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to a bhikṣu, saying, "Take this robe-price and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu," and that messenger arrives at the bhikṣu's location and says to the bhikṣu, "Venerable sir, this robe-price has been sent for your sake; please accept it."
The bhikṣu should speak to that messenger as follows: "I should not accept this price for a robe.
If I require a robe, I shall accept it when it is the proper time and it is pure. The messenger should say to the bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, do you have an attendant?
The bhikṣu who requires a robe should say: "Yes; there are monastery attendants or lay devotees (upāsakas); these are the bhikṣus' attendants."
Regarding the person acting as an agent: he constantly serves as the steward for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the messenger goes to the place of the steward, delivers the price for the robe, and returns to the bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir, I have already given the price for the robe to the steward you designated.
Venerable sir, please know the proper time; go there and you shall obtain the robe. The bhikṣu who requires a robe should then go to the steward.
If one has been reminded by another person two or three times, one should say, "I need a robe.
If, after being reminded two or three times, one obtains a robe, that is well. If one does not obtain a robe, one should stand silently before that person four, five, or six times.
If, after standing silently before them four, five, or six times, one obtains a robe...
This is good. If he does not obtain the robe, and should he seek to obtain a robe beyond this [limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he still does not obtain the robe, he may either go himself or send a messenger to the place where the price for the robe was received, saying:
"Previously you sent a messenger with the price for a robe to a certain bhikṣu; that bhikṣu did not ultimately receive the robe. You should take it back; do not [give it away]."
[This is] the occasion for [the rule against] causing loss.
At that time, a high minister of Rājagṛha sent a messenger with the price of a robe to give to Upananda.
Upananda took this messenger into the city and gave the price of the robe to a kinsman, an elder, to hold for him. Later, at another time...
The minister asked the messenger, "Has Vaḍḍhananda put it on? The messenger replied, "He has not. The minister immediately dispatched another messenger to demand the return of the price for the robe.
Vaḍḍhananda then hurried to the house of the elder to seek the robe. At that time, the elders of the city were assembled;
there was a regulation that those who did not attend would be fined five hundred coins. The elder said, "Venerable Sir..."

“Wait a moment; I shall return after attending the assembly. But Bhadanta did not grant this. Once the householder had finished making the robe and the assembly had already concluded, he paid five hundred coins.
Thereupon, he and the lay devotee began to reproach and disparage one another. Therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule.
The *Śāriputra-vinaya* (Shi sengqi lü) states: "When one has gone to request [the robe] three times, and has remained silent for six periods, the time may be extended or shortened.

What constitutes extension or shortening? If, when requesting the robe, the donor replies, 'Venerable sir, please come again in one month,' the bhikṣu shall go to request it after exactly one month has passed.
If they say again, 'Please come in another month,' he shall likewise go to request it after another full month has elapsed."
If it is further stated that one may come after another month, and one goes to request [the robe] once the full month has passed, one may not request it again after three months have elapsed.
If it is stated that one may come after half a month, ten days, or even for a brief moment (*muhūrta*), one may not request it again after three such moments have passed.
The same applies to remaining silent for six turns; after six months, or even after six moments, one may not request it again.
Go. When speaking to the owner of the object, if the owner says, "I previously gave this to a bhikṣu," one may seek it again through skillful means.
At that time, one may obtain it by speaking three times as before, or by remaining silent for six times.

The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If one does not seek by speaking, one may seek twelve times in silence; if one speaks once to seek it, two instances of silence are broken. [The same applies] for two [instances of speaking].
Regarding the "request for speech": it breaks four instances of silence; up to six requests for speech break twelve instances of silence.
This constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense for a bhikṣuṇī; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"After this bhikṣu has spoken to the owner of the robe, he may have further business that leads him to the place of the official in charge. If [the official] asks why he has come..."
He replied: "I have come because of other business. If they say, 'Take this robe and go,' he should reply: 'I have already informed the owner of the robe;
you may go yourself and settle the matter with him. If they say, 'Just take it and go; I myself will explain the matter to the owner.'"
At that time, if one accepts the robe and takes it away, there is no offense. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"If a bhikṣu has sent a messenger with a message, and that attendant comes and says, 'Venerable sir, you may accept this robe,' he should reply:
'I have already relinquished this robe; you should return it to the place from which it was sent. If he reports in this manner, it is well. If...
If one takes the robe, it is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya-pācittiya). However, if the attendant says, "Venerable sir, you may accept this robe;
I shall consult with its donor to ensure they are pleased," then taking the robe in such a manner is not an offense.

○ The eleventh precept concerns bedding made of silk and cotton wool. In the Mahāyāna, one may possess such items for the sake of sentient beings; however, one must not use them for one’s own personal enjoyment.

The *Jingxun of the Monastic Gate* states: The *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* says that if silks, cotton wool, furs, or other such items have been passed along from hand to hand until they leave the hands of those who killed the animals, and are then offered to a person observing the precepts, it is the dharma of a bhikṣu not to accept them.
To accept [fine garments] would not be compassionate. The two masters Nanyue and Daohui did not wear silk or cotton; both wore only mugwort and coarse hemp.
Thus, the Vinaya Master of the Southern Mountains said: "Since the Buddha-dharma first flowed eastward for nearly six hundred years, it has been only at these [sites of] Mount Heng that..."

"Compassionate conduct is that to which one should return. Question: Since you do not permit wild silkworm silk, yet allow the use of sheep’s wool and the like—both being parts of sentient beings—why is one permitted while the other is prohibited? Answer:

Although silkworm silk and wool are equally parts of sentient beings, the cocoon is boiled specifically for the sake of obtaining the silk, whereas the sheep is slaughtered not specifically for the sake of its wool.
Furthermore, regarding the requirements for bedding and furniture: if one calculates based on cotton, the number of living beings involved is extremely large;

if calculated based on wool, the number of living beings is relatively small. These precepts emphasize the careful consideration of human circumstances; it is not necessary to extend the logic to its absolute limit in every case.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding out of mixed wild silkworm cotton, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika). The occasion:
The group of six (ṣaḍvargika) bhikṣus made a new bedding out of mixed wild silkworm cotton. They went to a silkworm-keeping household and asked for cotton.
The host replied, "Wait until the silkworms are mature. The group of six remained nearby waiting; they watched as the cocoons were being dried, and the silkworm pupae made a sound.
The laypeople criticized and disparaged [this practice], so it was prohibited. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "The non-Buddhists felt contempt and spoke thus:
'If one uses this, many sentient beings are killed. How can one give fine food and clothing to those shaven-headed ones who sever the lives of living beings?
When the Buddha heard this, he therefore prohibited it."
Explanation of "various" (*miśra*): It refers to wool, cotton, *koccha*, *kṣauma* grass, *śāṇa*, or hemp.

therefore, they are called "one lacking a sense of shame. Conversely, when one lacking a sense of shame associates with a person possessing a sense of shame, they will surely reform their evil ways and cultivate goodness;
this is what is meant by "a person possessing a sense of shame. Third is the application of the Dharma, which refers to possessing a sense of shame.
People obtain [possessions] in accordance with the Dharma. Fourth is the improper use of things: this refers to those who lack shame and remorse obtaining things without relying on the Dharma;
if they obtain such items, it is no different from obtaining poison. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There was a bhikṣu..."
Taking a śrāmaṇera back to visit his relatives, they passed through a vast wilderness. Within it dwelt a non-human being who manifested in the form of a dragon;
he circumambulated the śrāmaṇera to the right, scattered flowers, and praised him, saying: "Excellent! You have gained great benefit by renouncing your home to leave the household life."
When the bhikṣu had visited his relatives' home and was about to return, the relative's wife said, "As you are now returning, the road is long and you will suffer much from lack of provisions;
take this money to purchase whatever you require. The śrāmaṇera accepted it and tied it to the hem of his robe.
On the way, a non-human being again transformed himself into a dragon, circumambulated the śrāmaṇera to the left, and threw dirt over him while speaking:
He spoke thus: "You have lost a great benefit. Having left the household life to practice the Way, you carry money with you.
The śrāmaṇera then wept. The bhikṣu asked him the reason for this, and he replied: "I do not recall having committed any transgression; yet I have been distressed without cause. The teacher said:
"Do you have anything in your hand? He replied, "I am holding this money. The teacher ordered him to discard it. Then non-human beings returned and made offerings as before.
The bhikṣu reported these circumstances to the Buddha. The Buddha said: "From now on, I do not permit śrāmaṇeras to hold gold, silver, or money.
If a bhikṣu causes a śrāmaṇera to first take hold of gold, silver, or money, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
Regarding the Vinaya offense: if one sees that a śrāmaṇera has already taken hold of something and subsequently causes him to take it, there is no offense.
○ Nineteen: The precept against buying and selling precious objects. This is likewise regulated in the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling of precious objects, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. The origin [of this rule]:
Upananda went to a marketplace and exchanged money for more money, taking it away; the laypeople criticized and disparaged him.
Therefore, eight types of currency were established: gold coins, silver coins, copper coins, iron coins, white tin coins, lead and tin coins, wooden coins, and hū-jiāo (foreign resin) coins.
The ritual for relinquishing [the object] is the same as above. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one uses money to purchase ornaments for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha, or if one exchanges ornaments for money.
Regarding matters for the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, the *Vinaya-viniścaya* states:

"If one manages the income and expenditure for the Three Jewels, or if a donor establishes an 'inexhaustible treasury' (*akṣayanīvī*), even if there is active pursuit of profit, it does not constitute an offense.

However, when such items yield interest, one must deposit a pledge equal to the principal amount and secure reliable guarantees. A formal contract must be drawn up clearly. At the end of the year, one should report [the accounts] to the superior."
The seating arrangements and the officials in charge shall all be made known to one another; or alternatively, inform those faithful upāsakas.
○ Twenty: The precept against buying and selling is likewise regulated in the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of trade, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*. The缘 (nidāna) is as follows:
Upananda was in the village of Anāthapiṇḍada; he took ginger and exchanged it for food before departing.
Śāriputra, while going on his alms-round, arrived at a house where rice was being sold, and the owner immediately asked for the price. Furthermore, there were non-Buddhists in Śrāvastī.
He obtained a garment of great value and took it to a monastery to trade for something else. Upāli (Bhadanta) said to him, "Come back tomorrow.
That very night, he washed his old garment, beat it, and pressed it until it shone like new. In the early morning, he exchanged it.
The heretic received the garment and returned to the park where he resided, showing it to the other heretics. Among them was one of wisdom who said to him: "You..."

He was deceived by another. Thereupon, that non-Buddhist practitioner took the robe and wished to return it, but Baddhālī did not consent. The non-Buddhist practitioner then criticized and disparaged him;
therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule. Commentary:
Regarding "various kinds of trading," this refers to exchanging what is timely for what is timely, exchanging what is timely for what is untimely, or exchanging it for a seven-day period.
Exchanging that which lasts for as long as one's life with that which lasts for a *pālikaḷa*; exchanging non-time [food] with non-time [food]; exchanging it with [food for] seven days;

exchanging it with [food for] as long as one's life or with timely [food], and so on, up to exchanging a *pālikaḷa* with timely, non-timely, and other such [foods]. To sell [it]: [these constitute offenses].
It is worth one *kārsāpaṇa*. As he repeatedly haggles up and down, increasing the stated price to three or five *kārsāpaṇas*, the purchase is likewise [fraudulent].
Regarding the signs: if he engages in various kinds of buying and selling and acquires [the goods], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; if he does not acquire them, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one exchanges with members of the five assemblies of renunciants, or if it is for oneself.

One should examine [the goods] to ensure they are of equal value and not trade with others. If one employs a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) to conduct the trade, the goods should be returned if there is regret.
If one exchanges ghee for oil, or oil for ghee, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If the items on the market stall already have a fixed price, and a bhikṣu brings the payment to purchase them, at the moment he places the money down, he should speak to the person regarding the goods."
The Master said: "This is the value; one must know this regarding the object. If one takes it away while remaining silent without speaking, it is an offense of *vinaya*-transgression (*vibhaṅga*).
If that object is worth fifty [coins] but the seller asks for a hundred, and the bhikṣu says, "I will take it for fifty," knowing its true value, such a case is not considered a low offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu knows that another person intends to purchase an object, he must not snatch it up and buy it. He must purchase it [properly].
This constitutes a *vinaya*-offense. If one thinks, "In the future, grain will be expensive," then at the time of purchasing it, there is a *vinaya*-offense;

at the time of selling it, there is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. If one fears that grain will be expensive at a certain time and thinks, "I shall purchase this grain now so that, by relying upon it, I may recite the sūtras, practice meditation, and cultivate the Path," and when the time comes the grain becomes very expensive, [one may] consume the surplus or give it to the two teachers, or employ it for labor.
Virtue. As for others, there is no offense in selling and making a profit. The same applies to buying bowls, medicine, and so forth. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one wishes to engage in trade, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) say: 'For my sake, exchange this item for that item.'"
Furthermore, one should reflect in one's mind: "May they obtain my profit, even if I do not obtain theirs.
If one engages in trade oneself, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense if done among the five groups of monastics or with laypeople (*avadātavasana*). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
If one buys for profit but does not sell for profit, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of purchase, but no offense at the time of sale.
If one does not buy for profit but sells for profit, there is no offense at the time of purchase, but there is a *nissaggiya pācittiya* (offense involving forfeiture) at the time of sale.
If one travels to another region to buy goods without originally seeking profit, even if a profit is gained when selling upon arrival, there is no offense. (*Vinayaviniścaya-saṃgraha*)

It is said: If, at the time of buying or selling, one does not speak according to the facts, or deceives another by using false or adulterated measures and scales, one incurs the offense of lying (*mṛṣāvāda*).
At the moment one obtains the goods, one commits the offense of theft (*steya*). Whenever one intends to buy or sell property, one must first fix the mind and have no desire for profit;
whatever profit is gained in the course of the transaction is entirely without fault. *Nidāna*.
It is said: A bhikṣu should not determine the price for another layperson, nor should he negotiate the high or low value of the price.
If there is no layperson to pay on his behalf, he may personally pay the price two or three times; beyond this, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: To purchase food with such impure items constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for every mouthful consumed; to purchase clothing constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for each article acquired.
If one exchanges goods with another and the other person later regrets the transaction, the goods should be returned. However, if more than seven days have passed, they need not be returned.
If one demands a high-priced garment in exchange for a lower-priced item, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If that specific item is absolutely necessary, [one may proceed] three times...
If the creditor is unwilling to relinquish it, one should seek out a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) to purchase it.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "It would be better to be a butcher than to engage in trade, for [trade] involves all manner of deception and harm.

Regarding goods obtained through such trade, even if they are used to prepare food for the Saṃgha, the monks should not eat them; nor may they dwell within a monastery built with such goods, nor use them to construct a stūpa or an image.
One should pay homage to it. Furthermore, it says: "However, one may pay homage through mental attention (*manasikāra*) [meaning that one need not perform the physical or verbal acts of prostration].

The reason for such a strict refusal is precisely the fear that shameless individuals might falsely consider making offerings to the Triple Gem to be meritorious, thereby seeking to compensate for their transgressions by chance. Any bhikṣu who maintains the precepts should not make use of these items.
If this bhikṣu dies, these items should be divided through *karmavācanā* (formal ritual action); since he is dead, he no longer possesses a mind of craving.
Because it has been kept for a long time, it remains the same as the property of a deceased bhikṣu; it shall be divided by means of a *karmavācanā*.
(21) The precept concerning the keeping of an extra bowl: in the Mahāyāna, because of [the concern for] sentient beings, this is not a training rule common [to all].

If a bhikṣu keeps an extra alms-bowl without having performed the ritual of "pure giving" (pariṣkāra-dāna), it may be kept for up to ten days. Should he keep it beyond that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
The origin story:
The group of six bhikṣus kept alms-bowls, holding onto those they liked and setting aside those they did not. A householder came to their quarters to observe them.
Observing that people would mock him as if he were a potter selling his wares in a shop, the Buddha established this rule:

Ānanda obtained a high-priced bowl from the kingdom of Soma and wished to offer it to Mahākāśyapa, but the latter was temporarily away; fearing he might violate this precept, the Buddha asked Kāśyapa when he would return.
Kāśyapa replied, "In ten days. Thereupon, the Buddha permitted the possession [of such an item] for a period of up to ten days.
Commentary: There are two kinds of almsbowls: iron bowls and clay bowls. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"The superior bowl holds two *śu* of cooked rice; the medium holds one and a half *śu*; the small holds one *śu*."

Regarding the bowl obtained during the ten-day period: whether it is acquired or not, when the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense requiring forfeiture).
The remainder is as explained in the precept on extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*). Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* for bhikṣuṇīs, the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states:

"If it is of deficient measure, or of excessive measure, or if it was intended to be given to another person who is seeking ordination or full admission (*upasampadā*), [it may be kept] to provide for them..."
If used [in this way], even if one does not distinguish [the vessels], there is no offense.
If for the purpose of storing soup or vegetables, or for drinking water, one keeps two small bowls, as well as a salt dish and a spoon, there is no offense in any of these.

Furthermore, if small bowls are placed within a large bowl according to what is required, keeping many is not an offense; however, one should keep one additional large bowl to prevent the possibility of being short of supplies.

Therefore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one keeps an extra white iron bowl, an unbaked clay bowl, or any bowl that does not conform to the prescribed measure, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The third section [of the same work] states: "Small bowls and secondary bowls may be kept without having been formally dedicated through the rite of *pariṣkāra* (purification).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one obtains two bowls, one should ask the teacher which one [is to be kept]."

Victory. If the teacher does not distinguish [the quality] well, one should use each for five days; once one knows which is superior, one should maintain that which is superior and give the inferior one to another.
[Section on] Debate. Question:
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* permits [the possession of] items that are either below or above the prescribed measure. If it accords with one's needs, is there no offense in possessing many?
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one keeps extra items such as white iron bowls and the like, all constitute *duṣkṛta* (offenses of wrong-doing).
From what source does this derive? Answer: It is said that in accordance with one's needs, there is a limit even for many items.
Since keeping white iron bowls and the like are not items suitable for use, they must stem from hoarding and greed; how then could there be no offense?
22. The precept against seeking a fine bowl while possessing one. This is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
If a bhikṣu possesses a bowl that has fewer than five mends and is not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its excellence, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
That bhikṣu must go before the Saṃgha and relinquish it; [the Saṃgha] shall take the lowest-ranking bowl from among them and give it to him. Let...
[The Buddha said: "One should hold [a bowl] until it breaks; one should hold it. This is the proper occasion.
The cause was this: Venerable Upananda’s bowl broke. He entered the city of Śrāvastī and went to the lay devotees to beg for a bowl.
Having broken one bowl, he obtained many bowls. At another time, the lay devotees gathered in one place and each said, "We have gained immeasurable merit."
Because he traded his bowl for that of Baddhananda, they immediately began to criticize and disparage him;
therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule. *Commentary*: Regarding "five patches," each patch is placed at intervals of two finger-widths.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "It is permitted to use either iron or copper to patch the bowl. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If it is difficult to obtain a bowl, one may repair it as desired."
If it can be easily obtained elsewhere, one should discard it and seek a better one.
If the robe has five full seams and is not leaking, yet one seeks a new one, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
For the other three groups [of monastics], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense if: it is less than five patches; one seeks it because it is leaking;

one seeks it for another; another seeks it for oneself; one obtains it without having sought it; one receives it as part of the distribution to the Saṃgha; or one purchases it at its own price and keeps it. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"This bowl should not be formally maintained (*parigraha*), nor should it be designated as one's own, nor should it be given away to others. One should keep two."
Regarding the alms-bag: if it is of good quality, place the long bowl (*dīrgha-pātra*) inside; if it is not of good quality, place the old bowl inside.
When going on alms-round, one should carry both bowls. If one receives dry rice, place it in the long bowl; if one receives moist rice, place it in the old bowl. One should eat from the old bowl.
First wash the long bowl, dry it in the sun, and set it aside; in all matters, the long bowl takes precedence. [It should be] placed in the niche and...

When fumigating with fire, one should always first place the extra bowl (*dīrgha-pātra*) in a secure location. When traveling on the road, one should have someone carry the old bowl while carrying the extra bowl oneself.
If there is no one to hold it for one, the extra bowl should be placed on the left side and the old bowl on the right side, and one should proceed while carrying them.
This disciplinary regulation shall remain in effect until the end of one’s life, or until the bowls are broken; they should be maintained well.
One must maintain and protect it; those who violate this incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmāpatti*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If a bhikṣu who maintains and repairs his bowl intentionally breaks it, it is a *pāyattika* offense. Alternatively, if his two teachers, spiritual friends, or others take pity on him because washing the bowl hinders his progress on the Path, [they may intervene].
Having hidden it so that it is no longer seen, begging for more incurs no offense. If one begs for and obtains one bowl, it should be kept and used.

If two bowls are obtained, one should be placed in the Sangha’s storehouse for pure goods (*śuddhavihāra*). This applies even up to ten bowls; nine should be placed in the Sangha’s storehouse for pure goods.
The same rule applies to begging for the price of bowls. The *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā* states: "If one begs for and obtains many bowls..."
One should relinquish that which is craved and enjoyed by the mind; as for the remainder, one should accord with the consensus.
*Zhongzhi vinīti shìyì jíyào*, Scroll Five, Phonetic Glossary.
In addition to the three robes (*tricīvara*), the five-robed *bhikṣuṇī* further possesses the armpit-covering robe (*kakṣāśāṭī*) and the shoulder-covering robe (*aṃsaśāṭī*).
The term *Nirgrantha* is fully rendered as *Saccaka Nirgrantha*; this translates as "Freed from Bonds," referring to the non-Buddhist ascetics (*tīrthika*) who practice self-starvation.
It is also translated as "unbound" (*asaṃyukta*). They pluck out their hair and expose their bodies, possessing no stored accumulations.
*Tié* (pronounced dié) refers to the remnants of weaving; *huì* (pronounced wèi) refers to the warp threads of a loom.
*Yǒng* (蛹): a silkworm in its cocoon.
*Chuì* (毳): the fine hair of an animal.
*Kābèi* (劫貝), also called *jiépōyù* (劫波育) or *jiāpōluó* (迦波羅): this is the cotton tree (*kapok*).
*Kucara* has no equivalent translation [in Chinese]. It is likely the same as *kusuma*, which is translated as "flower.
*Kṣoma* means "fine and soft" (*xi'nruan*); it is also a type of hemp.
*Kauśeya* refers to silk from silkworms. *Jianxun*:
"jian" is pronounced with the departing tone; "xun" is pronounced like *xun*, meaning spun thread.
*Nou*: pronounced as *nu hou*, meaning a wild sheep (a goat-like animal).
*Li-chi-tzu* (犁車子) is also called *Licchavi* (離車) or *Licchā* (離奢). This is translated as "Lord of the Borderlands" (*pratyantabhūmipati*).
It is also translated as "King of the Lineage of Sages" (*ṛṣivaṃśarāja*) and "One Who Transmits and Governs State Affairs."
*Zhé* (pronounced *zé*): To stretch out the fingers to measure an object;
the correct character is *jié*. *Jī* (same as *jī*, pronounced *jī*): To carry and deliver to another person; it means to pack, to send, or that which is used for travel.
*Bèn* (pén, fourth tone).
*Upāsaka* is the Chinese transliteration for *upāsaka*.
*Kaṃsa* is also called *jiàntí*, *jiàncí*, or *jiànzá*; this is translated as "shallow bowl. It is now colloquially referred to as a *tuó*.
Regarding the phonetics and definitions of the character "zǐ" (子): although it is commonly used as such, a thorough search of the Vinaya texts reveals no mention of a "zǐzi" (鐼子).
Furthermore, according to the *Haipian* (海篇), "dié" (鐼) is pronounced "fén," meaning iron or ornamentation; it is also pronounced "bēn," referring to a flat wooden tool.

Although the *Zihui* (字彚) gives the pronunciation "huǒ yùn qiè," it classifies it as belonging to the category of iron and notes that it is identical to "cuī" (錛), which is likewise a flat wooden tool. It is unclear from what source this name originated.
Who is this person? Nowadays, everyone within the Vinaya hall refers to him by this title. According to the Vinaya, it says: "The *kaṇḍola* fits into the small bowl;
the small bowl fits into the intermediate bowl; the intermediate bowl fits into the large bowl."
The phonetic transcription is clumsy; it is also redundant. It means "to connect.

23. The Precept Regarding Having Cloth Woven by One Who Is Not a Relative. In the Mahāyāna, this is not a training rule for the community.
If a bhikṣu personally solicits thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave three robes for him, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The缘 (nidāna): Upāli [Bhadanta] wished to sew a saṃghāṭī. He entered the city of Śrāvastī and went to the house of a lay devotee, seeking thread everywhere.
Having begged for a great deal of thread, he then had a weaver weave three robes for him. He personally wound the skeins and personally supervised the weaving.
When the lay devotee saw this, he criticized and disparaged him; therefore, the rule was established.
Regarding the characteristics: whether one watches another weave, wraps [the thread] oneself, or winds the skein oneself, it is all *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture); for the other three assemblies, it is *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if the weaver is a relative, or if the one who provides the thread is a relative, or if one weaves for oneself small articles such as a bowl-bag. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one weaves for oneself..."

To beg for thread: it is a *vyatikrama* (transgression) with mental remorse (*cittavipratisāra*). To obtain [the cloth]: it is a *vyatikrama* offense. To have it woven into fabric: it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If one causes a weaver who is not a relative to weave [it], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. If one begs for thread from someone who is not a relative, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one weaves it oneself, or causes the five classes of monastics to weave it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mūla-vinaya* states:
If one weaves [the cloth] in exchange for payment, there is no offense. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one has only a small amount of cloth, one should properly beg for more cloth;
one should not beg for thread to make a garment. However, if one must use thread to sew a garment or make a sash, there is no fault."
24. The precept against seeking fine robes by improper means. This is likewise prohibited in the Mahāyāna, as it constitutes evil and excessive seeking.
If a bhikṣu has a householder or a householder’s wife have a weaver weave a robe for that bhikṣu...
Without first accepting an invitation for a formal meal, he went to the weaver’s place and said, "Weave this robe for me;
weave it very well, making it wide, large, and firm. I shall give you a small amount as wages. The bhikṣu then gave him the wages.
Even for the value of a single meal, if one obtains a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The缘 (nidāna/origin): There was a householder in Śrāvastī who provided high-quality thread and had a weaver weave a robe for Baddhālaka.
The weaver said to Baddhālaka, "He has immediately dispatched me to weave something vast and of fine quality. The weaver...
He said, "The thread is insufficient. Upāli (Baddhālaka) went to the householder’s home and begged for more thread.
The householder’s wife brought out a box of thread, and he took at will whatever was best and gave it to the weaver. The weaver said, "The price is too low. He then agreed to give him a higher price.
When the householder returned from elsewhere, he saw that the cloth being woven was not what he had previously ordered. Upon questioning, he learned the reason. Thereupon...

Because they incurred criticism and reproach, [the Buddha] established this rule: "From now on, bhikṣus shall not, out of doubt, dare to accept an invitation for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, nor shall they dare to seek anything that is inferior.
The Buddha said: "One who has already accepted an invitation for the *pravāraṇā* does not commit an offense."

If one seeks to obtain clothing through such means, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. If not obtained, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if it is for another’s sake, if another acts on one’s behalf, or if it is obtained without having asked for it.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one merely goes to urge [the donor] and obtains clothing without [the donor] agreeing to the price, it is a *vyatikrama-vinaya* offense. (10)
The Vinaya recitation states: "There is no offense if one uses one's own property and has a weaver weave it.
(25) The precept against giving a robe and then angrily seizing it back is studied by those of the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another bhikṣu and later, out of anger, either seizes it himself or instructs another to seize it, saying, "Give me back my robe;
I will not give it to you," and the other bhikṣu returns the robe and he takes it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The occasion was that Nanda’s disciple, being well-skilled at exhortation, spoke to Upananda, saying, "Travel through the countryside together with me, and I shall give you a robe.
Other bhikṣus said to him, "For what purpose do you travel with Upananda?"
That foolish man did not know how to recite the precepts, perform the formal recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), or carry out the ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*).
Later, when that bhikṣu did not comply with his instructions, Upāli (Vāḍananda) demanded back his former robe. When the bhikṣu refused to return it, he became angry and forcibly seized it.

The bhikṣu cried out, "Do not do this! Hearing him, the monks in the neighboring cells gathered together to inquire about the cause. They reported the matter to the Buddha, who then established the precept.

If one seizes another's belongings and conceals them, or takes them and moves them from their original place, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. If one does not conceal them or move them from their place, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one does not act out of anger.
That person shall immediately return the robe; or another person may be exhorted to cause the robe to be returned.

If the one who borrowed the robe seizes it back without justification, or if there is fear that the robe will be lost, or fear that it will be damaged, or if that person has broken their precepts, broken their views, or broken their decorum;

or if they have been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), or have been expelled (*pabbājanīya-kamma*), or are liable for expulsion; or if, for the sake of this matter, there is danger to life or danger to the holy life—as in these cases... [as above].
This refers to taking everything away without storing it or setting it aside. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"Whether what was given collectively is taken individually, or what was given individually is taken collectively, or what was given collectively is taken collectively, or what was given individually is taken individually—if it is taken collectively, one incurs one *pāyattika*;
if it is taken individually, one incurs many *pāyattikas*. When giving the robes, one says: 'Stay...'"

If one gives to those who are biased and takes back from those who do not abide [in the Dharma], or says, "I give this to you because it suits my mind," and then takes it back when it no longer suits the mind;
or if one gives for the sake of receiving a scripture and takes it back when the scripture is not received—in all such cases, there is no offense.
Or if one sells a robe but has not yet received the price, and takes back the robe before the payment is finalized, there is no offense. Or if a disciple cannot be instructed or corrected.
If one seizes [the robes] for the purpose of subduing [the offender], and after they have been subdued returns them, there is no offense. The *Śāriputra Vinaya* (Shisong lü) states:
"If one succeeds in seizing them, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if one does not succeed, it is a *dukkaṭa*. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) states:

"Seizing the robes of the five classes of monastics, as well as those under training (*śaikṣa*), those undergoing *parivāsa*, *mānatva*, the blind, the deaf, the mute, or those who have been formally censured (*ukkhepaniya*)—in all such cases of seizing, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."

If one takes the robes of those whose minds are impaired by insanity, those who have committed the four pārājika offenses or the five ānantarya crimes, or those who have committed the five heinous acts, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī seizes the robe of a bhikṣu, it is *duṣkṛta*; if she seizes the robes of other bhikṣuṇīs and so forth, it is all a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If one has previously given a robe to another as a formal gift, but later, out of malice, temporarily takes it back, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The robe must be relinquished and returned to the other.

This is a *pāyattika* offense requiring confession. If one first gives a garment to another as a permanent gift and later takes it back as a permanent gift, one incurs an offense according to its monetary value (if it is worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, a grave offense is committed).
If one first lends a garment to another temporarily and later takes it back out of anger, wishing to cause them distress, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
However, if one takes it back temporarily for the purpose of subduing them and causing them to abandon unwholesome practices, there is no offense.
**Discrimination.** Question: According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there is no offense in taking back robes from those who have violated their precepts (*śīla*) or their views (*dṛṣṭi*).

However, according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, taking back robes—even from those under probation (*śikṣādattaka*) or those who have been formally censured (*utkṣipta*)—constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. From what source does this [latter] position derive? Answer:

If the robes were first given [to them], and subsequently taken back because they have violated their precepts or views, this constitutes an act of disciplinary subjugation (*nigraha-citta*); therefore, there is no offense. If...
Originally, these were things belonging to those who study; first they were given out of attachment, and later they were taken back out of anger.
This was merely to indulge in ordinary worldly sentiments, which is why it resulted in the accumulation of transgressions.
○ The twenty-sixth precept: Regarding medicine kept for more than seven days. This is a prohibitory offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) shared by Mahāyāna bhikṣus.
If a bhikṣu has medicinal remnants—namely ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar—he may consume them for up to seven days.
If he consumes them after the seventh day, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Due to the autumn winds, the bhikṣus suffered from wind-related illnesses; their bodies became withered and they developed malignant sores.

The Buddha permitted them to consume the five kinds of medicinal substances at both appropriate and inappropriate times. Piṅgiyānī, who resided in Rājagṛha, was widely known and had a large following of disciples.
He obtained a great quantity of ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar, which his disciples then accumulated.

[The medicine] was stored away and spread about everywhere; the rooms became foul-smelling and filthy. When the various householders saw this, they criticized and disparaged it. Therefore, [the Buddha] established the rule:

If one commits an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) regarding medicine and does not forfeit it, but instead exchanges it for other medicine, there is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and one *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. There is no offense in the following cases: if ghee or oil has been kept for more than seven days and is used as an ointment for the door-sill; or if honey [is used].
[He gives] rock honey to the garden keeper. When the seventh day arrives, he should give it to the bhikṣu to eat.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "It should be done before midday; having washed one's hands clean, one should receive that medicine and speak thus to a fellow practitioner of the holy life:
'Venerable one, please bear this in mind: I, the bhikṣu [Name], have this medicinal necessity for purification.'"
"Medicine: I now take possession of this for my own use within seven days, as well as for my fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Thus one should say three times. If one has already taken it for one day, one should immediately inform the fellow practitioners of the holy life, saying:
"This medicinal medicine has been taken for one day; six days remain. I shall take it," and so on, until the seventh day, informing them at each stage.
After seven days have passed, if there is still medicine remaining, it should be given away to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) or to a *śrāmaṇera* (novice).

The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: To seek a fine appearance, or for the sake of flavor, or to seek robustness, or with a deceitful mind, to consume various medicines constitutes an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If one has a serious illness, there is no offense; one may consume it.
When chewing the four types of medicinal fruits, one should reflect: "I am chewing these for the purpose of curing illness, not for the sake of delicious flavors.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should discard them to the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha shall then give them to laypeople or śrāmaṇeras.
If they are used to light lamps or as ointment for the feet, the monk who discarded the medicine may not use them; no bhikṣu whatsoever is permitted to consume them."
○ Twenty-seventh: The precept against seeking and using a rain-bathing robe at an improper time. This is shared with the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu, when one month of spring remains, seeks a rain-bathing robe, he should use it for bathing during the [subsequent] half-month.
If a bhikṣu seeks a rain-bathing robe more than one month before [the end of spring], or uses it for bathing more than half a month [before the appropriate time], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
[The Buddha] said: "It is a *pācittiya* offense. The Buddha was staying at Jetavana. The mother of Viśākhā invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha. At that time, it rained heavily.
The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to bathe in the rain. A maidservant came to announce that the time had arrived; seeing from afar the bhikṣus bathing naked, she became suspicious.
This was an outsider who returned and informed his mother. After the Buddha had accepted the offering, the mother requested eight vows:
that food be provided for visiting bhikṣus, for bhikṣus traveling from afar, for sick bhikṣus, for medicine for sick bhikṣus, and for those who attend to the sick.
The Buddha permitted monks to eat congee, and he permitted monks to wear rain-bathing robes and nuns to wear bathing robes.

At that time, the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks sought rain-bathing robes at all times and did not relinquish their summer rain robes, using them for other purposes instead. Therefore, this rule was established.
[The Characteristics: On the sixteenth day of the third month, one should seek [the robe]; on the first day of the fourth month, one should use it.

To seek it before that date, or to use it before that date, constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "This robe must not be accepted as one of the three formal robes (*tricīvara*).
It must not be given away as a pure gift (*pariśuddha-dāna*). One must not wear it to bathe in rivers or ponds. One must not wear it during light rain."
Regarding bathing: when it is raining heavily, one may bathe. If the rain suddenly stops, one may bathe in other water after removing the film of grime that has adhered to the body;
there is no offense. At other times, one must not bathe naked; one should wear a *saṃkakṣikā* or some other old garment.
One must not use a rain-cloak for various activities. If, at the time of eating, one wishes to smear oil on the body, or if one is ill, [there is no offense].
If it is in a place where many people pass through, one may tie both ends together to create a barrier; this must be relinquished by the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
A single bhikṣu shall announce within the Saṃgha: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today the Saṃgha relinquishes the rain-bathing robe. This is to be said three times.
If it is relinquished after the sixteenth day, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama*. Once relinquished, it may be used as [any of] the three [robes].

One may also perform the ritual purification (*śuddhi*) of robes, and one may enter other waters for bathing; there is no offense in making various [garments] for these purposes. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"A bhikṣuṇī may possess a bathing robe, but she may not possess a rain-bathing robe.

For a bhikṣu to possess a rain-bathing robe, there are generally two circumstances: first, during the rainy season, he may bathe within it while shielding the four sides; second, during times of intense heat..."
One uses it to shield oneself while bathing therein. Second, because there is much rain during the summer months, one constantly wraps oneself in the three robes while carrying them about.
If there is an intercalary third month, one should not seek [the robes] during the first three months. A bhikṣu incurs no offense if he does not keep a rain-bathing robe.
○ The twenty-eighth precept concerning the keeping of an urgent gift of robes past the [prescribed] time: In the Mahāyāna, one may keep such robes for the sake of sentient beings;
however, they must be purified through formal giving (*pariṣkāra-dāna*) as previously explained.

If a monk, while the ten days before the end of the three-month summer retreat have not yet expired, receives an urgent gift of robes (ātyayika-cīvara), and the monk knows it to be an urgent gift of robes, he should accept it.
Having accepted it, he may keep it until the time for making robes. If he keeps it beyond that time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The Setting: After the Buddha had completed his summer retreat at Pārileyyaka, a brahmin prepared an offering and presented robes.
The Buddha permitted the bhikṣus to accept these summer robes. Thereupon, the group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks began to constantly beg for robes at all times;

they begged for robes even before the retreat was finished, and they accepted them as well. Furthermore, after Upāli (Vadanyata) had completed his retreat in one location, he heard [news] from another location.

They obtained a great quantity of robes and, having distributed portions of the robes everywhere, they carried them into the Jetavana. A bhikṣu of few desires reported this to the Buddha, who rebuked them.
At that time, two ministers of Śrāvastī, Liśāda and Punnaka, had been commissioned by the king to suppress a rebellion.
Thinking to themselves that they did not yet know whether they would return alive, they wished to provide food for the Saṃgha and offer robes as alms.

The bhikṣus, because their *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) had not yet concluded, did not dare to accept the robes. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha permitted them to accept them, subsequently establishing the precept. Commentary:

Regarding "robes given as urgent offerings" (*ātyayika-cīvara*), one obtains them by accepting them; if one does not accept them, they are lost. Regarding "the time for robes" (*cīvara-kāla*), it is after the *pravāraṇā* (ceremony of invitation) has been completed.
If the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, one may accept an urgent gift of cloth for one month; if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread, for five months.
When ten days remain until the *pravāraṇā*, if an urgent gift of cloth is obtained, it should be accepted and kept until the time for making robes.

If nine days remain until the *pravāraṇā*, if an urgent gift of cloth is obtained, it should be accepted and kept until the time for making robes, with one additional day added. This continues down to when only one day remains.
One should accept offered robes and may keep them until the time for [receiving] robes, with an additional nine days permitted.

If one exceeds the former limit or passes beyond the latter limit, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. For a bhikṣuṇī, this also constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. There is no offense in cases such as when robes are seized or lost, resulting in exceeding the former limit;
or when, due to the perception that they have been seized or lost, one exceeds the latter limit. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If..."
During the summer retreat, if a donor wishes to give with their own hands, there is no offense in accepting it.

If one has been appointed as the monk in charge of storing robes, or if the donor says, "I will give with my own hands upon my return," there is no offense in keeping them even if the time limit has expired.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Except for the ten-day urgent gift of robes, all [other cases are subject to the rules]."
The *varṣā-cīvara* (rainy-season robe) must necessarily await the time of the *pravāraṇā*. If one divides [the robe] during the rainy season retreat, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
[Regarding] the twenty-ninth precept on being separated from the robe for more than six nights after the final month: Mahāyāna bhikṣus study this together [with the Hīnayāna].
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Before the three months of summer are completed. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "During the three months of the *varṣā*; before the eight months are completed."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Three months have passed; it has not yet reached the eighth month, nor is the year complete. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"One performs the latter *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) in an *araṇya* (forest hermitage). According to the term *kārttika*, it is translated as "merit" (*guṇa*) and also as "the constellation Mṛgaśiras.
Because the constellation Mṛgaśiras governs this month, the period from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month is called *kārttika*.
This refers to the month. Regarding the full term, it should be read in conjunction with the following sentence according to the other four sections:

those who undertake the later *anvārambhaṇa* (post-summer retreat), although they follow the assembly of the earlier retreat, must still complete this final month by dwelling in an *āraṇyaka* (forest hermitage) for the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
Because the conclusion of the later retreat is thus restricted, they are not permitted to be separated from their robes.
If a bhikṣu, at the conclusion of the three months of the summer retreat, during the final month of Kārttika,
remains in an araṇya that is full of doubt and fear, and while staying in such a place, wishes to leave one of his three robes behind in a village dwelling,
other bhikṣus may, for a valid reason, be separated from their robes for up to six nights. If they exceed this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Pāyattika. The缘 (nidāna):
