There is no offense in sitting on a stool with rotating legs, straight legs, curved legs, or no legs; nor when there is a covered floorboard or similar structure above. [End of] the Saṃgha [section].
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "If there is no one sitting beneath a pavilion, there is no offense. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

"In all matters of sitting and reclining, one must be composed and careful; if one is not careful and composed, one will inevitably cause injury and, moreover, ruin one's dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*)."
○ Nineteen: The Precept Against Pouring Water on Mud or Grass. This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). It is likewise prohibited in the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living beings, pours it onto mud or grass himself, or instructs another to pour it, he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
**缘 (The Circumstance):** Cunda built a large house using mud mixed with water containing insects. He instructed others to mix it. When the elders saw this, they criticized and reproached him;
therefore, the rule was established.

**相 (The Nature of the Offense):** For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. For the other three assemblies [of nuns], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense for one who did not know [the presence of insects].
There are insects. If the insects are large, one should touch the water with the hand to make them leave. If one strains the water and sprinkles it on the ground, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"Regarding water containing insects, that which is obtained by straining through a bag and that which is seen with the naked eye—if there are insects, and one perceives them as such, or has doubt, it is all a *pāyattika* offense.
If there are no insects, but one perceives them as such, or has doubt, it is all a *dukkaṭa* offense. This refers to using [water] that contains [insects].
External [use] refers to things such as food and drink; internal use refers to things such as pouring water, washing clothes, and bathing.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "For every insect that dies [as a result], it is a *pāyattika* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If a bhikṣu is constructing a dwelling and requires water—from a pond, a river, or a well—he must strain it, fill a vessel, and examine it [for insects]."
One should use [the water] only after it is free of insects. If there are still insects, one should filter it again with a cloth bag and examine it closely.
If there are still insects even after three layers of filtration, and if there are still insects despite this, one should construct another well and examine it as before.
If there are still insects, one should abandon the task at hand and go elsewhere. The birth of insects is impermanent; they may have been absent previously and now appear.
"Or that which exists now may later cease to exist. For this reason, monks should examine [the water] daily with careful attention and use it only when it is free of insects.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* (Sapoduo lun) states: "If one uses a triple-layered water filter and yet insects are still present, one should not remain in that place."
○ The twentieth precept concerning the roofing of a dwelling beyond three layers. This is a prohibitive offense (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya) shared with the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling, including doors, windows, and other decorative fittings, he must direct that the roofing of straw or tiles be limited to two or three layers.
If it exceeds this, it is a pāyattika offense.
The case: Channa constructed a large dwelling. After it was covered, there was still excess straw; he covered it again, and did so a third time without stopping. The roof then collapsed.
When the lay devotees saw this, they criticized and reproached him. Therefore, the rule was established.
[The offense is] a *pāyattika* for a bhikṣuṇī; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one reaches the fourth layer—whether covered with grass, tiles, or boards—it is a *pāyattika* for each [layer].
The preparatory effort (*prayoga*) and the time of burning or cutting are all *duṣkṛta*. The *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If it is fired bricks or..."
Stone and wood: if the donor wishes for the work to be completed quickly, there is no offense even if the weight exceeds the prescribed limit.
○ Twenty-one: The precept against going personally to instruct nuns. This is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). Mahāyāna bhikṣus share this same rule.
If one observes the capacity [of the recipient] and knows there will be great benefit, one does not commit an offense. Nevertheless, in the age of the Final Dharma, one must be especially cautious.
If a bhikṣu, without being appointed by the Saṃgha, teaches or instructs bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika.
The Setting: The Buddha was staying at Jetavana. Mahāprajāpatī requested that the Buddha permit the bhikṣus to provide instruction and preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs.
The Buddha commanded Ānanda to appoint a senior elder in due order to go; it then fell to the Venerable Panthaka to go.
The one verse she recited was repeated three times; then, she entered the fourth dhyāna three times.
All the bhikṣuṇīs were filled with great joy, while the group of six bhikṣuṇīs mocked her in jest. Thereupon, the Venerable One displayed his supernatural powers and departed.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went there themselves to instruct and admonish her, yet they did not speak the True Dharma, but instead spoke only all manner of worldly discourses. Thus...
When [the nuns] reached the point of laughing, dancing, and limping, the group of six nuns (ṣaḍvargikā) were greatly delighted. Mahāprajāpatī informed the Buddha.

The Buddha ordained that within the Saṃgha, a person must be appointed to instruct the nuns through a formal procedure consisting of one motion and two proclamations (jñapti-dvitīya-karman). Thereupon, the group of six went outside the boundary and appointed one another.
Mahāprajāpatī again informed the Buddha. The Buddha ordained that only after fulfilling ten qualities may one [be so appointed].
1. She is fully endowed with the precepts for instructing nuns. 2. She is learned and has mastered the recitation of both sections of the Vinaya.

3. She possesses decisive judgment and is free from doubt. 4. She is skilled in preaching the Dharma. 5. She is of noble lineage and has left the household life. 6. Her physical appearance is upright and handsome. 7. When the assembly of nuns sees her, they are filled with joy. 8.
She is capable of preaching the Dharma to the assembly of nuns and exhorting them to rejoice. She does not... [text ends]
(9) A monk who has gone forth and donned the dharma-robes but has committed a grave offense (saṃghāvaśeṣa). (10) One who is exactly twenty years of age or older.
To such persons as these, the instruction and ordination for nuns may be granted; thus this precept was established. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"The community should appoint one who possesses seven qualities to instruct the nuns: first, upholding the precepts; second, being learned; third, standing in the rank of seniority; fourth..."
1. She is skilled in the language of the capital city. 2. She has never defiled a nun with her body. 3.
She is well able to distinguish the eight *pārājika* rules. 4. She is well able to explain the eight *gurudharma* rules.

Commentary: Regarding the eight rules that must not be transgressed: (1) A bhikṣuṇī of one hundred years' seniority, upon seeing a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts, must go out to meet him, inquire after his well-being, prostrate, and invite him to sit. (2) She must not revile, scold, or slander a bhikṣu.
(3) She must not expose the offenses of a bhikṣu, nor obstruct another's search for their own offense, nor obstruct the *poṣadha*, nor obstruct the *pravāraṇā*.

(3) One should seek the conferral of the full precepts from the Saṃgha. (4) If one commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, one must undergo the mānatva penance for half a month within the two divisions of the Saṃgha.
(5) During that half-month, one should request an instructor from within the Saṃgha. (6)

One should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) where there are no bhikṣus (7). When the retreat is concluded, one should request the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) from the community of bhikṣus regarding three matters:
what has been seen, heard, or suspected (8). These eight matters should be respected, honored, and praised, and one should not violate them for as long as life lasts.
[This is] not a day for instruction. To go and preach the eight rules that must not be transgressed [on such a day] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one has been appointed by the Saṃgha to go, one should arrive at the appointed time; the *bhikṣuṇīs* should also meet them at the appointed time. If one does not arrive at the appointed time, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"In instructing the *bhikṣuṇīs*, one must not do so from sunset until the appearance of the dawn star, nor should one go too deep [into the matter]."
One must not go to a secluded place, nor to a place that is exposed. One should go to a place that is neither too deep nor too exposed—such as a lecture hall or beneath a tree.
One must not go on the fourteenth, fifteenth, first, second, or third day of the lunar month;
one should go to provide instruction and admonition from the fourth to the thirteenth day. One must not provide instruction to a community of nuns who are not in harmony. Having arrived...
One should ask whether the bhikṣuṇīs are in concord. If they say they are in concord, one should dispatch a messenger to summon them.

If they cannot be brought, one should grant them the formal expression of consent (*chanda*). One must not provide instruction to only some of them, nor should one provide instruction with protracted speech.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one who has not been appointed instructs bhikṣuṇīs, for every word so spoken, it is a pāyattika offense;

if one instructs other groups of two women, it is a duṣkṛta offense. The *Samantapāsādikā* states: "If one does not recite the Eight Respectful Rules but first recites other teachings [it is an offense]."
An *dukkaṭa* offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu should recite the bhikṣuṇī precepts so that they are not forgotten.
Why? Because women are prone to forgetfulness and their wisdom is scattered. After my parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣuṇīs shall inquire about the rules of the precepts from the great assembly of monks."

Appendix: The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu, without being appointed by the Saṃgha, enters the residence of bhikṣuṇīs for the purpose of instruction, except when there is a valid cause, it is a *pāyattika*.
A 'valid cause' refers to the illness of a bhikṣuṇī; this is called a valid cause.
If, without being appointed by the Saṃgha, he enters the residence of bhikṣuṇīs for the purpose of instruction, for every step he takes, [he incurs an offense]."
A *pāyattika*. If one enters the gate with only one foot [inside], it is a *dukkaṭa*. (This precept also exists in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, and is therefore appended here.
○ Twenty-second: The precept against instructing nuns until sunset. This is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, continues until sunset, it is a pāyattika. The circumstances were as follows:
Nanda—who possessed a beautiful voice (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states that this was not the Buddha’s younger brother, Nanda)—was preaching the Dharma to the nuns.

Because the listeners delighted in hearing it, he continued until sunset. When the nuns emerged from Jetavana and entered the city, the city gates were already closed; they were thus forced to take refuge against the city wall.
Staying overnight within the moat, one enters the city ahead at dawn. Various elders slandered [the monk], claiming he had stayed overnight with a bhikṣu;

therefore, it was established as a rule: except for the case of providing instruction, if matters such as receiving or reciting the scriptures continue until sunset, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If other women receive the scriptures and so forth until sunset, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense in the following cases:
preaching the Dharma at a ferry crossing where nuns listen; traveling together with merchants and preaching the Dharma at night while nuns listen; or preaching the Dharma within a nunnery.

If, on the day of the *poṣadha*, one comes to request instruction and admonition (*anuśāsana*), and happens upon a time when the Dharma is being preached, one should listen. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states:

"Even if it is within the proper time, if the nuns are standing rather than sitting, or if they are preoccupied with busy activities that have not yet ceased, or if there are other constraints, for one who preaches under such conditions, it is likewise called 'improper time' (*akāla*).
This includes the six permutations regarding the evening and the perception of the evening, and so forth.

Two cases are grave offenses; two are light offenses; and two are non-offenses. There is no offense if one preaches the Dharma throughout the night, or if the temple gates are close together, or if the city gates are not closed, or if both parties are within the city, or if the nuns are in the house of a layperson. In all these instances, there is no offense.
Regarding the person appointed to instruct the nuns: once appointed, they shall instruct them for as long as they live; there is no need to appoint another. ○ Twenty-third:
The precept against disparaging those who teach the nuns; this is studied by Mahāyāna practitioners alike.
If a bhikṣu says to other bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus teach bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food and drink," it is a pāyattika offense.
The缘 (nidāna): Having heard that the instructor was coming, the nuns went out half a yojana to welcome him, provided him with lodging, and prepared food, drink, and bathing facilities.
The group of six [monks], not having been appointed by the Saṃgha, became jealous and spoke as follows. Therefore, this rule was established.
If one speaks clearly, it is a *pāyattika* offense; if not clearly, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if the matter is actually so, or if one speaks while dreaming, or speaks erroneously.
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "If one says that for the sake of making offerings, one instructs a bhikṣu or the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If one says that a bhikṣu practices the twelve dhūta ascetic virtues, sits in meditation, recites the sūtras, or performs various meritorious deeds—
all for the sake of offerings and profit— each such statement constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
○ Twenty-fourth: The precept against giving robes to a nun who is not a relative. This is not a point of common training in the Mahāyāna;
nevertheless, during this age of the Semblance Dharma, one must exercise careful scrutiny.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for goods, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Circumstance: There was a bhikṣu who went for alms in Śrāvastī, who was fully endowed with dignified deportment.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī saw him and conceived a virtuous heart; she repeatedly invited the bhikṣu [to her home], but he did not accept.

On another occasion, when the Saṃgha was distributing robes and other goods, this bhikṣu took his portion of cloth and was leaving through the gate of Jetavana. Seeing the bhikṣuṇī approaching, he immediately gave it to her.
The [intending] recipient did not accept it, but the nun accepted it on her own initiative. Because the bhikṣus repeatedly associated with such people, they were criticized and rebuked;

therefore, this was established as a rule. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one gives clothing to a relative nun who has broken the precepts or holds wrong views, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If she is a relative, or one perceives her as a relative, even if she is not a relative, [it is a *duṣkṛta* offense]."

If one gives clothing with the intention [of helping], there is no offense. If one sees someone in distress who lacks clothing and gives it to them, or gives it because they have received the precepts, there is no offense.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "Giving clothing to the other two groups of women constitutes an offense in the same way."
25. The precept regarding making robes for a nun who is not a relative. This is shared with the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Case of Kālodayin: For the sake of a certain nun, Kālodayin fashioned a garment depicting the act of sexual intercourse between a man and a woman.

He folded it up and gave it to her, instructing her not to open it to look at it, nor to show it to anyone, saying, "When the time for the *poṣadha* arrives, you should wear this robe and walk behind the community of nuns.
The nun followed his instructions. When the lay devotees saw it, they mocked and ridiculed them greatly.
Āmrapālī questioned her and learned the reason for it. The nuns informed the bhikṣus, who in turn informed the World-Honored One, leading him to establish the precept.
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "At the time of taking the robe, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
When cutting [the cloth] and when dyeing it, it is all a *pāyattika*. When sewing it, for every stitch there is a *pāyattika*.
○ Twenty-sixth: The precept regarding sitting in private with a nun; this is studied by those of the Mahāyāna as well.
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
This was occasioned by Kāḷudāyin going to the place of Thullanandā and sitting together with her in one spot outside the door.
Because householders criticized and disparaged [this behavior], it was therefore prohibited.
Explanation: "In a secluded place" is as explained in the *Aniyata-dharma*. Regarding the characteristics:
if one is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense [in the following cases].
[This refers to one who] has a companion. If, while walking, one passes by and suddenly falls to the ground, and so forth; the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"To sit with two other women in a secluded place is also a *pāyattika* offense. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "Even if other modes of conduct [are involved], they are all equally offenses."
○ Twenty-seventh: The precept against traveling with a bhikṣuṇī. This is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*). It is shared by those who study the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel along the same road from one village to another, except at the appropriate times, it is a *pāyattika*.
The "appropriate times" are: when traveling with merchants, or when there is suspicion, fear, or terror; these are called the appropriate times.
At that time, the group of six monks and the group of six nuns were traveling through the human world together. Laypeople took offense at this, and so [the Buddha] established a rule.

Consequently, when they encountered one another unexpectedly on the road, they were apprehensive and did not dare to travel together. The Buddha said: "If it was not by prior appointment, there is no offense."
Furthermore, when a group of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs traveled from Śrāvastī to Vaiśālī, they were unable to travel together;
the bhikṣuṇīs fell behind and were plundered by bandits. For this reason, he further opened the allowance for [the rule] at other times.
Commentary: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are two kinds of doubt: first, the doubt of losing one’s robes and bowl; second, the doubt of losing one’s provisions.
If such doubts arise, a bhikṣu should take the robes and food of the bhikṣuṇīs and carry them away.
Upon reaching a safe place, he should return them and say: "Sisters, you may use these as you wish. They must not travel together.

Regarding the offense of association: if one makes an appointment with a nun to travel together, even as far as the boundary of a village, it constitutes a *pāyattika* for each instance according to the number of people involved and the number of boundaries crossed.
If they travel ten *li* through an open space, it is a *pāyattika*. If it is less than the distance of a village, [the penalty is determined accordingly].
If one shortens the distance by ten *li*, and if one proceeds with forceful intent, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense; for the other four assemblies, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in cases such as being constrained by force or power. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If traveling together with companions on a carriage, when stopping to rest or setting out again, one should call for the *bhikṣuṇī* so that she does not fall behind her companions; [if she does], it is a *pāyattika*. If [the companion] says, 'Go, go!'"
Do not cause them to lose their companions; there is no offense. This applies equally to asking for directions or inquiring about the house of a donor (*dānapati*).

The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "If one makes a pact while traveling on foot, but later travels through the air, or manifests one's form to meet at a rendezvous, or departs after concealing one's form—in all such cases, one incurs an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
The same applies to traveling by boat. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "To happen upon someone unexpectedly while traveling together on the same road [is not an offense]."
One should ensure that they are separated to a distance where their voices cannot be heard; if they can hear one another, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is likewise an offense to travel with two other groups of women. The *Śāriputra-vinaya* states: "If one travels together with a king’s consort, there is no offense."
Appendix: The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: A bhikṣu who has an enmity or grievance with another should not travel together with him.

If there is a necessary reason for traveling together, they should first perform an act of reconciliation (*kṣamāpanā*) before proceeding. Whenever traveling on a road, one should engage in discourse concerning the Dharma;
one must not utter harsh words, or else maintain noble silence so as not to allow the mind to become distracted. If one arrives at a shrine or temple of a deity...
Recite a Buddha-gāthā and proceed with a snap of the fingers. A bhikṣu should not offer worship to celestial deities.
Whenever he pauses briefly along the way, or at a place where water is drawn from a spring or pool, he should recite a gāthā.

At his place of lodging, he should recite the Threefold Salutation (triskandhaka). He should also carry a water-drawing rope with him. If there is a specific occasion, he may travel together with a bhikṣuṇī.
When traveling, a nun’s food should be carried by a bhikṣu. At mealtime, they should pass it to one another; if there is a sick bhikṣu, they should carry it together for him.
If there are few people, the nuns should also assist in carrying it. If they reach a village, they may go to seek medicine.
When begging for alms, they should have someone watch over their belongings and bring the food back to them. If a nun is ill, it should be understood that the same applies.
○ The twenty-eighth precept concerning traveling on the same boat with a bhikṣuṇī. This is shared with the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī agree to board the same boat together to travel upstream or downstream—except in the case of crossing directly across—a pāyattika offense is incurred.
The conditions are the same as before. Regarding "crossing directly": there were several bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who wished to cross the Gaṅgā River.

The bhikṣuṇīs were at the rear; a violent rainstorm caused the water to rise, and before the boat had returned, night had already fallen. They were plundered by bandits; therefore, [the rule] was relaxed.
If one makes an appointment to board a boat together—whether going upriver, downriver, or entering the vessel—it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot has already stepped onto the boat, or if one makes preparations with the intent to enter, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For the other four assemblies (*parṣad*), it is also a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if there was no prior agreement, or if one was bound [and unable to leave], and so forth. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one intends to cross directly but is carried away by the current..."
Offense.
○ Twenty-nine: The precept against receiving food through the commendation of a bhikṣuṇī. This is likewise prohibited in the Mahāyāna, as it constitutes wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).

If a bhikṣu, knowing that he has received food due to the cause and condition of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise and exhortation, eats that food—except when the donor had previously [intended it for him]—[he commits an offense].
If one does so intentionally, it is a *pāyattika*.
The circumstances were as follows: In Śrāvastī, there was a householder who invited Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana for a meal.
Thullanandā slandered them, calling them men of low birth, while praising Devadatta and his followers as "dragons among dragons. At that time—
When the two arrived, they immediately announced, "The dragon among dragons has arrived. After the two, Sthūlananda and the other, had finished eating, the householder reproached them.
They returned and informed the Buddha. The Buddha then rebuked Devadatta and others and established a precept.
Subsequently, the bhikṣus did not know whether there was an invitation to eat or not. The Buddha said, "If you do not know, there is no offense. Furthermore, at Rājagṛha...
In the city there was a great elder who wished to wait for the arrival of Upagupta in order to provide offerings to the assembly of monks.

Later, when Upagupta arrived at the city, a nun went to inform the elder, whereupon he immediately prepared a vegetarian feast. Fearing that he might violate the precepts, Upagupta would not accept the food;
therefore, [the rule] further excludes the case where a donor has previously expressed their intention.

Explanation: Those who teach and transform others include those who practice the twelve *dhūta* ascetic virtues, as well as those who are learned (*bahuśruta*), Dharma masters, upholders of the Vinaya, and practitioners of seated meditation (*dhyāna*).
Regarding food: one may obtain food from dawn until midday.

If one eats food obtained through the praise of a *paricārikā* (attendant nun), for every swallow, it is a *pāyattika*. If one obtains other items such as undergarments, lamps, or oil through her praise, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For the other four assemblies [of monastics], it is a *dukkaṭa*. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states:
"If one obtains and eats food through the causal condition of the praise of the other four assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If..."
One should not offer indirect praise for their merits; rather, one should simply state that the merit of giving to śramaṇas is exceedingly great, and that those who eat it incur no fault.
○ The thirty rules concerning traveling together with women. This is a shared precept of the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel along the same path, even as far as a village, it is a pāyattika. The occasion for this rule:
There was a woman from Vaiśālī who had married a man from Śrāvastī. Having a dispute with her mother-in-law, she was returning to her native country.
At that time, Anuruddha was traveling from Śrāvastī to Vaiśālī. That woman wished to accompany him, and [Anuruddha] agreed.

[The Buddha] granted permission for this. The husband pursued him and struck the Venerable One until he was nearly killed. The Venerable One stepped off the path and sat cross-legged in a secluded place, entering the *ābhāsvara-samādhi* (fire-light samādhi).
The husband waited for him to emerge from his meditative absorption, whereupon he prostrated and repented. The Venerable One preached the Dharma to him and departed.

Upon returning, he informed the community of monks, who reported it to the Buddha, leading to the establishment of a precept. Thus, there was no offense, as the circumstances were such [that the rule had not yet been promulgated].
The preceding offenses regarding their gravity are as stated before. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"If another sends a woman to lead the way, or if one is confused about the path and a woman provides directions, there is no offense."
○ The thirty-first precept: The Precept Against Accepting More Than One Meal. This is shared with the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu is at a place where a single meal is offered, a bhikṣu who is not ill should eat only one meal. If he accepts more than that, it is a pāyattika offense.

The Context: There was a village called Anāthapiṇḍika-āvāsa. A householder built a dwelling for the bhikṣus and regularly provided them with food and drink, stipulating that they should take only one meal per day.
The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) bhikṣus, however, obtained excellent food and drink and stayed for a second night, continuing in this manner to eat repeatedly.
Because the householder criticized and resented this, the rule was established. Later, Śāriputra obtained [alms] at that place.

"I am ill. Fearing that I might violate this precept, I have left while supporting myself through my illness; consequently, my condition has grown much worse. Thus, he further added the words "I am not ill.
The *Śāriputra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) states: "As for 'the sick,' it includes even those wounded by a single leaf of bamboo."
Regarding the *śikṣamāṇā* and *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense in cases where one intentionally requests to be detained, or when there are various obstacles and difficulties. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one stays overnight and does not eat, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one stays elsewhere and eats at midday, it is a *pāyattika*."
○ The thirty-second precept concerning eating in succession: This is a prohibitive offense (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya). Mahāyāna bhikṣus study this together.
If a bhikṣu eats in succession, except at other times, it is a pāyattika. "Other times" refers to the time of illness and the time of receiving robes.

This is called "other times" (the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Other times" refers to the time of illness, the time of work, the time of traveling on a road, and the time of receiving robes; these are the times).

There was a certain Śramaṇa brahmin who, with five hundred wagons fully laden with food and drink, followed the World-Honored One through winter and summer, waiting for an opportunity to present offerings.
However, he could find no such occasion. Ānanda informed the Buddha on his behalf, and the Buddha permitted him to prepare cakes and congee as offerings for the Saṃgha.
At that time, the lay devotees heard that the Buddha had permitted the Saṃgha to eat [these foods].

The porridge and the cakes were all received with great joy. There was a minister of little faith who, seeing that the Buddha and the Saṃgha had received such abundant offerings, conceived the thought of them as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
He prepared rich and delicious food and invited the Saṃgha;

however, because the monks had already eaten the thick porridge, they were no longer able to eat much more. The minister resented this. It was the same story with a musician of little faith and devotion in Rājagṛha.
The Buddha then established the precept. Consequently, at the places where the sick bhikṣus were invited to eat, there was no food appropriate for their illnesses nor medicine.
Even if such food and medicine were present, they feared transgression and did not dare to eat it. The Buddha permitted sick bhikṣus to eat by taking turns (to share meals).
Furthermore, after one householder had already invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, another householder also invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to offer alms.

Regarding food and clothing: A bhikṣu, being cautious and apprehensive, informed the Buddha. The Buddha permitted eating in succession (*krama-bhojana*) at the time of receiving robes. [Commentary]: As for "thick gruel" (*yavāgū*):
if one draws lines with a blade of grass and the portions do not join, it is not to be eaten. "Eating in succession" means an invitation. There are two kinds of invitations:

an invitation by turn of the monastic assembly (*saṃgha-paṭipāṭika*), and a private invitation (*pṛthag-āmantraṇa*). Regarding the time for giving robes, it is as explained in the section on the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* [offense].
[The Buddha] said: "Regarding the mark: if today one receives many invitations for meals, one should accept one invitation for oneself and give the remainder to others.
When giving it away, one should say: 'Venerable sir, I ought to go there; I now give this to you. If one does not relinquish it [in this manner], [it is a fault]."
If one accepts a subsequent invitation after having already accepted a prior invitation and eats, there is a *pāyattika* offense for every mouthful swallowed.

If one does not relinquish the subsequent invitation but accepts and eats according to the prior invitation, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense for every mouthful swallowed. There is no offense if what was invited is not food; or if the food is insufficient; or if there is no one to provide the food;
or if one obtains food again after having already finished eating; or if there are both a prior meal and a subsequent meal at the same location.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a sick bhikṣu cannot satisfy his hunger at one place of invitation, he should accept a second invitation.

If he still cannot satisfy his hunger at the second place, he should accept a third invitation. If he still cannot satisfy his hunger at the third place, he should eat gradually after having accepted it until midday;
he must not accept a fourth invitation. It is permitted to calculate the number of days."
Regarding eating multiple times: The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states that Ānanda had previously accepted an invitation from another, but at that time he forgot and did not remember it.
Later, while dining with the Buddha at the invitation of King Prasenajit, as he was placing food in his mouth, he remembered that there were two invitations.

Fearing that he would not give the other invitation to someone else, he did not dare to spit out the food out of respect for the Buddha; yet, he also did not dare to swallow the food, so as to maintain [the integrity of the precept].
Because of this precept, the Buddha knew that Ānanda’s mind was filled with regret, so he told him to mentally dedicate [the merit] to others and then eat.

Upāli asked the Buddha, “May other people also do likewise? The Buddha said, “With the exception of five types of persons: first, those practicing meditation (because their minds are focused on the Path);

second, those dwelling alone (because there is no one else to speak with); third, those traveling far (because they may have lapses of mindfulness while hastily setting out on the road; furthermore, according to the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, it is permitted for them to do so repeatedly).”
Because of eating [forbidden food]. Fourth, chronic illness. Fifth, staying with one's relatives during times of famine. In all other cases, it is not permitted.
The *Mātṛkā* states: "If one says to a bhikṣu, 'Eat here; I shall seek clothing and food for you,' and he eats, there is no offense."
He said to the bhikṣus: "Eat here; as for other places, you may eat according to your own preference. Thus eating, one does not commit an offense.
The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states: "Whether in a single house, within a monastery, or in an araṇya, if one seeks plumpness and vigor, or delights in fine food..."
If one eats frequently, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*. If one refrains from eating out of a contemptuous mind or through hypocrisy, one likewise incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

○ The thirty-third precept: Eating in a Group Apart from the Community (*pārivāsika-bhojana*). This is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). Mahayana bhikṣus share the same training in this matter.
If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense. "Other times" refers to: when one is ill; when making robes;
when robes are being distributed; when traveling on a road; when traveling by boat; when a great assembly has gathered; and when śramaṇas are distributing food. These are the [permissible] times.
**Context:** Due to Devadatta’s loss of offerings and gains, he went with five bhikṣus from house to house to beg for food; therefore, this rule was established.

**Explanation:** Regarding "eating in a separate group": if four or more than four people eat together—whether it be rice, parched grain flour, or dried cakes—it constitutes eating in a separate group.
Fish and meat. Regarding the sick, this includes those down to those with foot deformities such as lameness or being paraplegic; when making or giving robes, it is as described above.
Regarding travelers on the road, this includes those who have traveled even half a *yojana*; the same applies to those traveling by boat.

Regarding "śramaṇas who give food," this refers to all those who have left the household life outside of these śramaṇa sons of the Śākya, including those who have gone forth from among non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
Regarding the assembly of the great multitude (*mahājana*), it consists of at least eight persons: four resident bhikṣus and four visiting bhikṣus.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If within a boundary (*sīmā*) one separately invites four or more [bhikṣus], it is called 'separate-eating for a group' (*pṛthaggaṇa-bhojana*). If they are invited in succession..."
There is no offense. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Eating in a separate group" means eating individually. The *Vinayavibhaṅga* states:

"A separate group" refers to those who do not eat in the same place. If four bhikṣus are within the same boundary, even if only one person does not eat together with the others, they are all termed a "separate group.
The word "eating" here refers specifically to the formal meal (*bhojana*); as for other [foods]...
There is no offense regarding eating.
To analyze this "separate assembly" (*pṛthaggaṇa*), there are generally two meanings: first, being separate from the assembly, as clarified in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other texts;
second, being distinct from the assembly, as explained in the *Vinayasamgraha*. Thus, one must not beg for food [in such a manner].

When four people travel together, they must be dispatched according to the monastic order of seniority when accepting an invitation. Within the Sangha, pure food [is served] only after the *ghanṭā* has been struck;
invitations to private residences are not permitted unless there is a valid reason. The sacred regulations are clear and must not be transgressed.
Regarding the offense of eating separately from the community without a valid reason: for every swallow, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there is a valid reason and one does not declare it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*. The *Śāriputra-vinaya* states:
"It is for two benefits that eating separately from the community is prohibited: first, to protect and care for the donor out of compassion; second, to destroy various evil desires."
Due to the power and influence of the bhikṣus: if three bhikṣus eat separately in one place and a fourth person takes a portion of the food, there is no offense.
If traveling on a road or by boat, if they arrive yesterday, eat today, and depart tomorrow, eating today [in such circumstances] constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If three people eat and one person does not eat..."
If [the food] belongs to those who are fully ordained (*upasampanna*) or those who are not yet fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), there is no offense in either case.
If one sends food to them, even as little as a single spoonful of salt, and it is given to the community dwelling there, there is no offense in eating it.

Or, if a donor says, "I will give food to everyone who enters," or if a donor builds a separate room and donates it, saying, "I will give food to everyone who stays in my room"—in these cases as well, there is no offense.
There is no fault. The *Śīla-pratyaya-sūtra* states: "If a bhikṣu does not announce [his intention] within the assembly and goes privately to a gathering, he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
This was established because Visākhā, the Mother of Migāra, had personally invited five hundred monks.
Therefore, whenever one wishes to invite virtuous persons individually, one must necessarily invite the Saṃgha as well; even if there is but one person among the assembly who follows [this rule].
Next, regarding the acceptance of invitations: this is not termed "eating separately from the assembly.
An appendix to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: there are five causes and conditions for which one may accept an early invitation for food and eat it within one's own room:

first, being a newly arrived guest; second, being about to depart on a journey; third, being afflicted by the suffering of illness; fourth, being a caregiver for the sick; [and fifth, being on the way to receive food].

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that those who serve as administrators (*karmadāna*) may take their own portion of the midday meal first and eat it; there is no fault in this. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottarakarmaśataka* (Mukḍaka) says:
"If one is a supervisor, they should first take their own portion from the communal meal and eat it; this is without transgression."
○ Thirty-fourth: The precept against accepting more than three bowls when invited. This is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), shared with the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson and is invited by that layperson to receive cakes, parched grain flour, or cooked rice, and if the bhikṣu desires them:
One should accept two or three bowls [of food]. Upon returning to the monastery, one should share it with the other bhikṣus.
If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, accepts more than two or three bowls and, upon returning to the monastery, does not share it with the other bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Case of the Village Woman of Śrāvastī: She married into the kingdom of Ujjayinī and neglected her parents' home. She gave food to the bhikṣus;
when her husband summoned her back, the bhikṣus had already taken all the food she had prepared, so she had to prepare it again.
Her husband had already taken another wife. Furthermore, outside the city of Vārāṇasī, a caravan of merchants was staying overnight together with some... [bhikṣus].

The Buddha received food at the home of a merchant who had single-minded faith and joy. He passed the word along to other bhikṣus, requesting that they eat it all up so that the merchant would have to purchase more provisions.
His companions departed first, only to be robbed by bandits on the road; for this reason, he established the rule.
[The offense of] *pāyattika* for a bhikṣuṇī; for the other three assemblies, it is *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one accepts [food] because of illness, or even if the person brings it themselves.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "To take [food] beyond [the allotted time] is a *pāyattika*.
To go outside and see a bhikṣu who does not give [it] is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one takes another's food..."
If the amount exceeds four and a half *śē* (升) of cooked rice, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. However, there is no offense if the donor takes the liberty of determining the quantity.
The *Vinaya-viniścaya-saṃgraha* states: "There are five places where one should not beg for alms:
the house of a professional bard, the house of a prostitute, a tavern, the royal palace, and the house of a *caṇḍāla*. Furthermore, if one knows that it is a woman..."
He is by nature prone to lustful defilement; therefore, he shall not accept alms out of fear that it might give rise to affliction.

If one takes more than three bowls from a non-human or from those of a non-Buddhist sect, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). However, there is no offense if one eats more than three [meals] at that very seat;
or if, excluding cakes and parched grain, one takes only other items; or if the donor joyfully allows one to take as much as desired. In all such cases, there is no transgression.

There are three kinds of wasteful squandering of offerings given in faith: first, receiving what a donor has offered with faith to one who upholds the precepts, and then giving it to one who violates the precepts;
second, receiving what a donor has offered with faith to one who possesses right view, and then giving it to one who holds wrong views;
third, receiving in excess and not consuming it oneself, even if it is only a single handful of food received in surplus—unless the donor had previously intended it for that purpose.
There is the practice of eating at will (*yathāsukham*). These three matters are all termed wasteful squandering of the faithful’s offerings and shall invite evil retribution.

○ Thirty-fifth: The precept against not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food). This is a prohibitory offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). Mahāyāna bhikṣus study this together [with the Hīnayāna].
If a bhikṣu, having finished his meal, should at some time accept an invitation and eat without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food), it is a *pāyattika*.
The context:

The Blessed One praised the practice of eating a single meal (*ekāsanika*), and the bhikṣus followed this precept. Consequently, their physical complexions became emaciated and withered. The Buddha [thereupon] permitted...
He permitted eating in a single sitting until full. He further permitted eating rice, parched grain, and the other five kinds of food until full.
He also permitted sick bhikṣus to eat repeatedly, which led to the discarding of leftover food and caused various birds to clamor in competition for it.

He further permitted those who tend to the sick to eat leftover food, as well as permitting the performance of the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of making food permissible) upon receiving almsfood. He also permitted all bhikṣus...
The Buddha returned from that place carrying food. He performed the *kṛtapiṇḍa-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food) and ate it.
The *kṛtapiṇḍa-vidhi* should be performed as follows: one should say, "Venerable sir, I have already eaten my fill; know this and look upon this. This is the performance of the *kṛtapiṇḍa-vidhi*.
The other person should take a small portion of the food and say, "I have finished; you may take and eat it. This is called the *kṛtapiṇḍa-vidhi*.
At that time, there was a gluttonous bhikṣu in the kingdom of Śrāvastī who did not know whether he had eaten enough or not, nor did he know whether he had finished his meal or not;
he would eat whatever he obtained. Therefore, this rule was established.

**Commentary:** There are five conditions for "having finished eating" (*pūrva-bhakta*). One must know it is rice (referring to the five *bhojana* foods; other items are not termed "finished eating").

One must know it has been brought [and received from another person]. One must know the refusal [saying "it is not needed"]. One must know the deportment (*īryāpatha*)—that one may receive food while in any of the four deportments: walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.

One must know the relinquishing of deportment—when a walker stops, a stander takes a step, a sitter leaves the seat, or a recliner turns over and rises; this is called "relinquishing deportment. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "It is permitted for the sake of two benefits."
The Procedure for Receiving Leftover Food (i.e., the *khalupaścādbhaktika* rule). First, due to the circumstances of a monk who is nursing the sick;
second, because a monk has a reason for which his food is insufficient.
[The] Characteristics: Having finished eating to satiety, one abandons the formal deportment (*īryāpatha*) and eats without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food).

For every swallow, it is a *pāyattika*. If one has already eaten to satiety and performs the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* for another; or if one knows that another has already eaten to satiety and performs the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* toward them;
or if one takes food with one's own hand and performs the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta*; or if one places it on the ground and performs it; or if one causes [another] to...

If it is done by a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to prepare food), or if it is done in the presence of a *kappiya-kāraka*, or if one covers good food with inferior food while performing the ritual, or if one has accepted the *paramparā-bhojana* (food received from another) and carries it all away, in all such cases the *paramparā-bhojana* ritual is not accomplished; for each instance, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When preparing 'leftover food' (*vighasa*), if one prepares it as leftover directly upon the bowl, it is correctly designated as 'leftover food' only by the name of the bowl;
the food within the bowl itself is not so designated. If the liquid from the food in the bowl flows into the [other] bowl, both may be designated as 'leftover food.
If one seeks to prepare 'leftover food' using two bowls simultaneously, the person before one must cease eating."
Regarding "food in one bowl": when exactly one bowlful is designated as *vighasa* (leftover food), it is called *vighasa*.
If either cakes or vegetables are placed together, covering two bowls side-by-side, both are designated as *vighasa*. The same applies to various other types of vessels.
If a bhikṣu has already finished his meal and a great donor arrives bringing various kinds of food and drink, he should ask: "Is there any [left]?"
If the *karmadāna* or other administrative officers have not yet finished their meal, one should perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual for leftover food) from them.

If they have already finished their meal, it should be performed from among those beginning with the *sthavira* who have not yet finished. If the *sthavira* feels ashamed and is unable to do so among the assembly, [one should act otherwise].

When it is time to perform the *kṛtāvakāśa* (the formal declaration of having finished eating), one should go to a secluded place to do so. If the senior monk (*sthavira*) has already finished eating and a visiting monk arrives, one should ask him;

if he has not yet finished, one should perform the rite for him. If the visitor has already finished eating, the Sangha should employ skillful means so as not to violate the donor’s virtuous intention.
Alternatively, if there is a great *śrāmaṇera* among the assembly, one should lead him to the boundary field (*sīmā*) and [perform the rite] with him.
Having received full ordination and been instructed in the ritual for handling leftover food (*vighasa*), one may then eat (as stated in the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*). The *Vinayasamgraha* states:
there are five types of *pūsanī* that may be eaten: first, rice; second, wheat and bean porridge; third, parched grain flour; fourth, meat.
There are five types of *bim̐da* (soft foods). Furthermore, there are five types of *khādaniya* (hard foods) that may be chewed, namely: roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
If one first eats the five types of chewed foods, along with milk, curd, vegetables, and so forth, and subsequently eats the five types of soft foods, there is no offense.

If one first eats the five types of soft foods and then eats the five types of chewed foods, along with milk, curd, vegetables, and so forth, it is called an offense. One should know that there are five [categories].
"Unsatisfied speech" refers to when, at the time of receiving food, one does not yet require it;
one should respond by saying, "Wait a moment," "Go ahead," "Hold on," "Wait while I eat," or "Wait until I have finished. If the word "wait" (*qie*) is used, it is called "unsatisfied.
If the sound "wait" is absent, it constitutes a refusal of further food. If the intention is not for satisfaction, even if the words of satisfaction are uttered, they do not count as such.
[If one] eats [after having already finished], one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing), because the speech does not accord with the Dharma.
If one obtains additional food and partakes of it after performing the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*), one will dwell in personal ease and the donor will obtain merit.

When wishing to perform the ritual, one should wash one's hands and receive the food, then approach a bhikṣu who has not yet finished eating, or one who, though having finished, has not yet left their seat, and perform the ritual in his presence. If he himself...
If one has not yet finished eating, one should take two or three mouthfuls. Once one has satisfied oneself, it is no longer permissible to eat.

One should press down with the hand and say to the other person: "This is your portion; eat it as you please. There are five cases in which the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual for making food 'leftover') is not valid:
first, when one is within the boundary while the other person is outside the boundary; second, when they are out of reach of one another; third, when [one is]...
[The rules apply] when [the monks] are at one's side, or four are behind one, or five are ahead and have left their seats;
the opposite of these conditions constitutes a violation. If one person performs the ritual (*karmavācanā*) while others eat, there is no offense for anyone.

If, after having finished eating, one perceives that they have finished or suspects it, yet swallows food without performing the *atiriktapiṇḍa* (remaining-food) ritual, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. Even if one has not yet finished eating, if one acts as though one has finished...
If one eats while harboring doubt, in both cases one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). For the latter two [cases], there is no offense.

If it is fruit from the north, or celestial lotuses (*devapuṣpa*), or other such rare items, or during a year of famine when food and drink are difficult to obtain, eating them without performing the *atirittakamma* (the rite of making food leftover) is without offense.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: When a bhikṣu receives offerings from others, if he acts contrary to the Dharma, he falls because of those offerings.
There are two kinds of such falling: first, consuming the offerings of others while failing to practice the Path according to the Dharma, allowing the mind to run wild and become dissolute.

There is no merit to be recorded. Second, there is giving to those who, in turn, give to others; such giving is not in accordance with the Dharma. Because of these two cases, one shall fall into the three miserable realms. Regarding those to whom one should give:
if one's parents are poor and suffering, one should first cause them to receive the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten Wholesome Actions, and only then provide for them.
If they are not poor, although they have received the Refuges and Precepts, it is not appropriate to give to them. Furthermore, there is another kind of giving...
Those who repair stupas, those who serve the Saṃgha, and those who maintain monastic dwellings—having calculated their labor, one should provide them with wages.
If one gives them more than their due, it constitutes a downfall of giving. When giving food to the sick, one should act with a mind of compassion and give according to what is appropriate.
If one gives food by mistake, it constitutes a downfall of giving. [This applies to] infants, those imprisoned in jail, and those who are pregnant.
To such a person, one should give with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), without hoping for any return or reward. To those who come to a monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*) to beg:
if they already possess provisions, there is no need to give; if they have no food, there is no fault in giving.

If a bhikṣu does not practice meditation, does not recite the sūtras, and does not attend to the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṃgha, yet accepts offerings from others, he falls because of those offerings. If...
Those who lack these three types of karma may knowingly engage in such giving; yet both the giver and the receiver fall because of that gift.
It would be better to swallow iron balls and die than to eat the faithful offerings of others without observing the precepts.

If one has already eaten to satisfaction and eats more by force, it will neither increase one’s complexion or strength, but only increase one’s afflictions. Therefore, one should not eat without moderation.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "If all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and non-self, how can one give rise to the three kinds of evil karma—of body, speech, and mind—on account of food?

If, for the sake of craving food, one gives rise to these three types of evil karma, then regarding the wealth obtained thereby, everyone will say that when the fruit of suffering is experienced later, there shall be no one to share it. Furthermore, one should contemplate all sentient beings...
"Birth exists for the sake of food and drink; thus body and mind undergo suffering. How could I possibly give rise to craving and attachment toward such food?
Furthermore, it is because of food and drink that the body grows and increases. I have now left the household life to receive the precepts and cultivate the Way in order to abandon this body;
if I now crave this food, how shall I ever succeed in abandoning this body? Thus [he reflected].
Having observed this, although he still partakes of food, it is as if he were eating the flesh of his own son in a desolate wilderness; his mind feels revulsion and finds no pleasure in it at all.
He deeply contemplates the fault of physical food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) in this way. Next, he contemplates contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*), like an ox being flayed alive.
One is devoured by immeasurable worms. Next, one contemplates the food of thought (*manah-saṃcetanāhāra*) as being like a great mass of fire.
The food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) is like three hundred spears. If a bhikṣu goes for alms, he should beforehand form this thought: "May I obtain excellent [food]."
I pray that I may certainly obtain much, and I pray that I may obtain it quickly.
If one does not conceive a sense of revulsion toward food, the wholesome dharmas one cultivates will decline day and night, while unwholesome dharmas will increase.
When wishing to beg for alms, one should first make this aspiration: "May all who beg be fully satisfied; may those who give this food obtain immeasurable merit. I...
If one obtains food, one should use it to heal the body of its toxins, cultivate wholesome dharmas, and benefit sentient beings.
When making this aspiration, the wholesome dharmas one cultivates will increase day and night, while unwholesome dharmas shall be eliminated through shame.
36. Causing another to commit the offense regarding the rule on leftover food (vighasa-kalpa). This is a training rule common to Mahāyāna bhikṣus.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already finished his meal, persistently offers food to him without having performed the vighasa-kalpa, saying, "Venerable sir, please take this food," and does so for no other reason than with the intent to cause the other to commit an offense, it is a pāyattika.

"Ti. Regarding the condition: because a bhikṣu was rebuked by others, he harbored resentment in his heart and intentionally caused another to commit an offense; therefore, [this rule] was established.
Regarding the perception: if the other person eats it, for every swallow both [the giver and the eater] incur a *pāyattika* offense. If the other person does not eat it, the giver incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
The same applies to cases of mistaken perception or doubt. There is no offense if one was unaware that the person had already finished eating, or if one did not cause another to commit an offense.
○ The thirty-seventh precept against eating at improper times. This is shared with the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu eats food received at an improper time, it is a pāyattika offense.
The circumstances were as follows: Kālodāyin went out for alms at dusk. A pregnant woman was carrying food out of her door when she encountered the rain.
There was a clap of thunder and lightning. Seeing his face for a brief moment, [the man] was terrified and cried out, "This is a ghost! He immediately collapsed.

In anger, he said, "O śramaṇa son of the Śākyas, it would be better to break your own belly than to go begging for food at night. Therefore, the rule was established. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
When the group of seventeen monks entered the city to beg for food, they heard a woman uttering words that were shameful; they immediately endured their hunger and ceased their rounds.
In a certain household, there were lay associates enjoying a banquet in their garden. When the time for the midday meal had passed, they brought food to him so that he might eat his fill.
Upānanda asked them about it, and they replied, "We do not receive [food] before noon, nor do we eat after midday. How could we endure hunger and let our lives end?
When the Buddha heard this, he rebuked them and established a precept (*śikṣāpada*).

**Explanation:** Regarding "time," it refers to the period from the appearance of the dawn light until midday. Regarding "non-time," it refers to the period from midday until the dawn light has not yet appeared.

**Consequences:** For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; for the other three assemblies [of the Saṃgha], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. **Non-offense:** There is no offense if one eats black [food].
Regarding rock honey: when taking emetic or purgative medicines for an illness, one should boil barley so that the husks do not break, strain the juice, and drink it.

If it is spit out from the throat, one should swallow it back. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If it is at an improper time (*akāla*), and one perceives it as such, or if there is doubt [regarding the time], one falls into an offense."

If one perceives it as the proper time when it is not the proper time, or if one is in doubt, in both cases there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If it is the proper time and one perceives it as such, or if it is not the proper time but one perceives it as the proper time, there is no offense.
The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, there are some donors who build monasteries and provide abundant provisions to support the Sangha of future generations; they resemble those who have left the household life."
If one requests food from the person in charge of provisions at an improper time, what offense does the giver incur, and what merit does the original donor obtain?
The Buddha said: "One who eats at an improper time is a person who has broken the precepts; such a person is a thief."
One who gives at an improper time is also a person who has broken the precepts and is a thief. They steal the property of the donor;
it does not belong to the donor's intent, and thus the donor gains no merit because the object has been lost. There is only the merit of the initial resolve to establish [the offering].
Śāriputra said: "If one receives food at the proper time and eats it, but does not finish it, and then eats again at an improper time—or if one receives [food] at the proper time until..."
"Can one still obtain merit by eating at improper times? The Buddha said: "Those who eat at the proper time are pure;
they are the field of merit, they are the renunciants, they are the Saṃgha, they are the true friends of gods and humans, and they are the guides of gods and humans.
Those who are impure are like precept-breakers, robbers, or hungry ghosts; they are the dwelling place of sin. To seek food at an improper time is [to act as such]."
To give food at improper times or to give it haphazardly at improper times—such a steward of the provisions is called a Māra who retreats from the Path.
He is called a broken vessel of the three evil realms and a leper, because he destroys the fruits of goodness. O Brahmins, even you do not eat at improper times;
even the heterodox Brahmans do not eat perversely. How much more so for my disciples, who know the Dharma and practice the Dharma—how could they possibly...?
Is it so? Anyone who acts in this manner is not my disciple; such a person is one who does not follow the Dharma.

By stealing salt or vinegar, even in a single lump or a mere pinch, and receiving what was stolen, they die and fall into the Hell of the Scorched Intestines (*Jiao-chang*). There they swallow glowing iron balls.

Upon emerging from that hell, they are reborn among pigs and dogs, where they eat all manner of impurities. They are then reborn as evil birds, whose cries cause people to marvel in horror. Hereafter...
They are reborn as hungry ghosts, dwelling within the latrines of monasteries where they consume excrement and filth for hundreds of thousands of myriads of years.
Even when they are subsequently reborn among humans, they are poor, lowly, and base; whatever they say is not trusted by others.
This is more grievous than stealing the property of a single person, for by seizing the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) of many, one cuts off the path to transcendence.
Therefore, the *Mūla-nidāna* states: A certain sick bhikṣu was instructed by a physician to eat flour mixed with water as a non-time meal (*vikālabhojana*).
The Buddha said: "There are toothless oxen that eat barley; when they later excrete it, the grains remain entirely intact."

Use this as flour-meal; it should be taken at improper times. If it is not cured even after taking it, use raw wheat-flour meal, stir it with plenty of water, strain it through a cloth, and then it should be taken.
If it is not cured even after taking it, the Buddha said: "The physician has prescribed that one should take a flour-drink, whether thick or in the form of a bolus;
it should be taken according to one's preference. In all such matters, I act for the sake of the sick."
Regarding those who open [the storehouse] at improper times: after one has recovered from illness, none of these [stored fruits] should be consumed. The *Ekottara-karman* states:
"There are five kinds of fruit which, whether at the proper or improper time, and whether one is ill or not, may be eaten according to one's desire:
first, *harītakī*, which is called 'brought by the Lord of Heaven' in Chinese; second, *vibhītaka*; third, *āmalaka*, which is the *yu* (remnant) fruit of Lingnan."
The *karamarda* fruit resembles the *bīla* (areca nut) in shape; eating it removes wind [from the body]. The "fourth, coarse grain" refers to black pepper (*marica*).
The "fifth, *pi-pa-li*" refers to *kṛtānna* (vinegar made from fermented *piper betle*). The *Śānabū-karmapada* states:

"In the event of the cause and condition of thirst, one is permitted to receive non-timely liquids (*akālika-pāna*), such as fruit juices or honey syrups, provided they are clear like the color of water and purified by dripping water [into them] before receiving them. There is [this rule].
Due to causes and conditions such as wind or heat disorders, one is permitted to accept five kinds of seven-day medicines.

Due to various causes and conditions involving illness, one is permitted to accept medicines for life, namely all salty, bitter, sour, and pungent substances unfit for food, such as ginger, pepper, and so forth, up to powders, pills, decoctions, and ointments of *bai zhu* (Atractylodes).
However, non-time [afternoon] drinks must not be kept until [the next morning].
Regarding the "medicine for seven days": it must not be kept until the eighth day. The *Nanhai Jiguai Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) states:
"If food remains on the teeth or a film of grease persists on the tongue, until one has rinsed with pure water, saliva and phlegm must be discarded externally.
If the time limit has passed, one further commits the offense of taking food at an improper time (*vikāla-bhojana*). One who observes the water and observes the time is called a Vinaya Master."
Volume Seven of the *Chongzhi pinishi yiji yao* (Essential Collection on the Meaning of Matters Concerning the Vinaya).
Phonetic Explanations: *zé* (迮) is pronounced *zhé*; it means "to press" or "to constrain."
*Tian* (苫) is pronounced with the *shi* and *lian* finals. It refers to thatching a roof with grass.
*Bandha* is also called *Sagada*; this is translated as "Successor of the Way" (*jidao*), and it is also translated as "growing by the side of a small path."

Regarding the eight *pārājika* dharmas for nuns, there are eight offenses involving expulsion. In addition to those concerning sexual misconduct, theft, killing, and lying, four further rules are added:
touching [a man], the eight [instances of] concealing, and the four [instances of] following suit. These are explained in detail within the *bhikṣuṇī-śīla*.
*Nirvāṇa* is *nibbāna*. This is translated as "extinction" (*mie-du*).
The character for *bei* (卑) is pronounced *ji* (忌), or alternatively *qi* (其). It means "to lift up. The common usage of *yu* (舁)—read like *yi* (异)—is both erroneous.
Upāli (also transcribed as Wǔbālī) is translated as "Foremost" (shàngshǒu), because by upholding the Vinaya, he served as the guiding pillar for the assembly;
alternatively, it is translated as "Attendant" (jìnzhí), as when the Buddha was a prince, he served as his close personal attendant.
*Tiē* (pronounced tiē): to crave food. *Weina* (維那):
in Sanskrit, *karmadāna*; this translates as "one who knows affairs" (*shizhi*) or "one who gladdens the assembly" (*yuezhong*).

The two characters for *weina* combine both Chinese and Sanskrit terms: *wei* (綱維) is the Chinese term meaning "to maintain the framework," while *na* is the Sanskrit term, with the latter part [of the original word] omitted.
"Karma" refers to the three syllables.
"Fruit" refers to the naturally occurring non-glutinous rice and so forth in the northern continent of Uttarakuru.
"Lotus" refers to the lotuses within the celestial Anavatapta Lake.
Kavaḍīkāra-āhāra (edible food) refers to morsel food; it is also called "segmental food" because it exists in distinct portions.
Sparśa-āhāra (contact-nourishment) refers to the mental factor of contact associated with the first six consciousnesses.

It generates joy and pleasure upon encountering an object, such as when watching a theatrical performance, where one feels satiated even without eating all day. Furthermore, various cooling and refreshing contacts can provide nourishment.
The body [is sustained by] volition as food (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*). Volition, which is a mental factor associated with the sixth consciousness, gives rise to aspiration toward desirable objects;
this mental sustenance nourishes and moistens the sense faculties, causing them to grow. Furthermore, the thought of food and drink prevents a person from dying, as it is said: [like...]

The child looking at a bag suspended from a beam, or the case of quenching thirst by looking at plums, illustrates the manner in which the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) maintains [the body] through its cognition of food.
This consciousness is strengthened and becomes predominant by being supported by the power of the first three types of nutriment;
thus, it is able to sustain the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the sense organs. Furthermore, the seventh consciousness (*manas*) clings to the eighth consciousness.
It serves as one's own internal self; this is the cause for birth within the three realms and is termed "nutriment.

When one enters the meditative absorption of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it causes the afflicted portion of the seventh consciousness—the mind and mental factors—to cease, so that they no longer grasp the eighth consciousness as a self.
Consequently, one cannot remain long within the three realms; thus, it is known that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is nutriment (*āhāra*). If these are distinguished according to the six destinies:

humans and animals possess all four nutriments, with edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) being predominant. Ghosts and deities of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) exclude edible food and thus possess three nutriments, with contact-nutriment (*sparśāhāra*) being predominant.
Deities of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) exclude both edible and contact nutriments and thus possess two nutriments, with volition-nutriment (*manaḥsañcetanāhāra*) [being predominant].

The term "food" (āhāra) indicates superiority. In the realm of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and the Avīci hell, beings subsist solely by means of the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), excluding the three other nutriments—edible food, contact, and volition.
[The character] *chà* (啑) is pronounced with the first tone; it means to bite.
[Zàn] (矛*贊): Pronounced as guǎn, with the sound zhuàn; it refers to a *tián*. *Tián* (鋋) is pronounced shàn;
it is a small spear. *Máo* (矛) is pronounced móu; it is a weapon like a *tián* that has three edges.
The group of seventeen refers to the seventeen youths; the eldest was seventeen years old and the youngest was twelve.
They sought ordination together, and for this reason they were called the "Group of Seventeen Bhikṣus."
Upānanda is the same as Upananda.
The character *xian* (哯) is pronounced with the initial *qian* and the final *yan*.
*Qing* (圊) refers to a latrine; it means a privy or a place of extreme filth. One should always maintain such places, ensuring they are kept clean.
It is also [called] *jù*, pronounced like *jǔ*. It is a fruit that resembles the vine of the *wángguā* (bitter gourd). When the seeds grow large, the stalk becomes a persistent tendril (*liúténg*).
The fruit resembles a mulberry; its skin is black and its flesh is white. When eaten, it has a pungent fragrance. Nowadays, the people of Lingnan take its leaves and combine them with...

○ The thirty-eighth precept concerning leftover food kept overnight. This is a prohibitory offense (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya) shared by Mahāyāna bhikṣus.
If a bhikṣu eats food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika.
The Venerable Kāla was constantly seated in meditative reflection. At that time, alms were easy to obtain in the city.
Kāla thought to himself, "Why do I weary myself by begging for food every day? It would be better to eat whatever I first receive;
as for what I obtain later, I shall take it back. He acted exactly according to this thought. When the monks went out for their meal, they did not see him.
Kāla suspected that [the monk] had died or traveled far away; later, upon seeing him, he questioned him and learned the reason. He informed the Buddha, who established the precept.
Commentary: Regarding "storing food": having received it on this day, if it reaches the next day, it is entirely impure for all bhikṣus.
Purification.

The mark: for a bhikṣuṇī, this is a pāyattika offense. There is no offense if she has food remaining from what was received overnight and gives it to her parents, laborers, and so forth, and subsequently begs it back from them.
The *Śāriputra Vinaya* (Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya) states: "If a mahābhikṣu has not yet..."
To receive [food] with one's own hand and keep it overnight is called "storing indoors" (*antaḥśayita*). To eat it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one has received it with one's own hand, lifted it up, and kept it overnight, this is called "leftover food stored overnight" (*śeṣabhakta-śayita*). To eat it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

If one first takes fruit for oneself and later receives it from a *kalpiyakāra* (a pure person) before eating it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. There are two kinds of touched food that may be eaten without fault: first, that which is pure...
A pure bhikṣu may inadvertently touch [the food]. Two bhikṣus who have broken the precepts and lack shame or remorse may touch it.
Celestial food that has passed its proper time for consumption may be accepted for seven days. The *Mūla-nidāna* states: "Any remaining cakes or fruit should be given to a śrāmaṇera;
at dawn, one may receive them back and eat them. If there is a mind of expectation when giving, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of eating. At the time of eating...
One incurs a *pāyattika* offense. However, if one has no expectation of gain at all, there is no offense. The *Mūlakalpa* states:

"If a patient is poor, even if it is residual or touched *ghṛta* or oil, there is no offense in taking it. Furthermore, when a *bhikṣu* is traveling on a journey, he may have a *śrāmaṇera* carry provisions;
he may also lift them up for him or set them down. Moreover, when various *bhikṣus* are traveling on a road, they should carry their own provisions.
If there are neither laypeople nor novices present, one should urge the donor to give [the food]. If there is no donor either, one should take it oneself.
Later, upon seeing a layperson, one should exchange it with them for food. If there is no one at the place of exchange, divide it into two portions and say to the layperson:
"Take one portion. Once they have received it in their hand, one should say to them: "Take my food."
"I shall take your portion and exchange it for food. This will be difficult to obtain; on the first day, you must fast.
On the following day, if someone offers food, accept it and eat it. If no one offers any, take for yourself a handful the size of a tiger's paw and eat it.
When the third day arrives and again there is no one who offers anything, eat two such handfuls. By the fourth day..."
If there is no one to offer [the food], one may take it according to one's needs and eat until satisfied; there is no offense.

Later, when provisions for the journey are exhausted, if one sees ripe fruit fallen on the ground, one should take it and perform the ritual purification (*kappiya-karaṇa*). Having received it, one may eat it.

If a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who can perform the purification) is difficult to find, one should eat it after having formally accepted it. If there is also no one to offer it, one should take it oneself and eat it while maintaining the mental perception that one is in Uttarakuru.
Regarding fruit on a tree that has ripened but not yet fallen to the ground: one should climb the tree and shake it to make it fall, then take and eat it oneself.
