As for the aforementioned allowances, they are all permitted due to circumstances of hardship; if there is no such hardship, they are all strictly prohibited.
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If many bhikṣus are traveling together and there is only one young śrāmaṇera, the bhikṣus shall each carry [the provisions] themselves."

Regarding alms-food: when it is time to eat, each person divides their portion. Once a *śrāmaṇera* has received his share, he says to a *bhikṣu*, "I will now exchange my portion for yours, Venerable Sir.
Having received it, he exchanges it again with the second seat, continuing in this manner through many people;
in all such cases, eating is without offense. However, if the *śrāmaṇera* does not understand the rule, the *bhikṣu* may personally take his own food portion and give it to him.
If a *śrāmaṇera* exchanges food through successive transfers, he incurs no offense even if he obtains food. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

"If the food belongs to the Buddha’s *kaṭhina*, the face-gate (*mukha-dvāra*) *kaṭhina*, or the *pravāraṇā* *kaṭhina*, then even if one first takes it and later purchases it to obtain food, there is no offense because the perception of ownership has ceased."

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "It is impossible for one who has attained Arhatship—having exhausted all outflows—to eat leftover food that has been kept overnight while residing within a house.
This proves that there can be no Arhat whose taints are already exhausted who would [behave otherwise].
Residing in the homes of laypeople and eating leftover or stored food.
[The Master] asked: "If a śrāmaṇera does not eat leftover or stored food, can he realize the fruit of arhatship?
If he has already realized the fruit of arhatship, must he receive full ordination? He replied: "Among the eight types of bhikṣus, although there are those who have destroyed the fetters..."
As for the ordination of bhikṣus, following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of fourfold proclamation) must necessarily be taken as the essential core.
Therefore, even if a śrāmaṇera has realized the state of *aśaikṣa*, he may receive full ordination immediately without waiting until he has reached the age of twenty;
there has never been a case where one did not ascend the ordination platform to receive the precepts.
○ Thirty-nine: The precept against taking food by oneself. This is a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). It is shared among Mahāyāna bhikṣus.
If a bhikṣu, without having received it [from another], places food or medicine into his mouth—except for water and tooth-sticks—he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
The Circumstance: There was a bhikṣu in Śrāvastī who constantly went on almsround and wore robes made of discarded rags (pāṃśukūla).
At that time, various lay devotees (gṛhapati) in the city, for the sake of deceased parents and others, prepared food offerings and sacrifices at crossroads and even within shrines.
That bhikṣu took this food for himself and ate it. The lay devotees criticized and disparaged him; therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule. At that time...
The bhikṣus became doubtful and did not dare to take the tooth-sticks or pure water for themselves. The Buddha said, "There is no offense.
[Commentary: There are five ways of receiving: receiving with hand from hand; or receiving from one who gives by hand while holding an object;

or receiving an object from one who holds an object; or receiving with the hand from one who holds an object; or receiving by passing an object across from a distance. This applies to both the giver and the receiver.
Both are known. There is no obstruction or resistance within, so it can fall into the hand. Furthermore, there are five ways of receiving:

receiving with the body for a body, receiving with robes for robes, receiving with a bent elbow for a bent elbow, receiving with a vessel for a vessel; or, due to certain causes and conditions, it may be placed on the ground and given.
The six phrases concerning perception, conceptualization, doubt, and so forth are to be understood as usual. For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "Except for tasting food, one must not swallow it. It is permitted to receive food from a nāga, from a deva, from a preta, or from a monkey;
one may also receive food by means of the donor’s verbal instruction. However, one must not accept food that is thrown to one."

**Discrimination** Question: The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that if an object is passed from afar, the acceptance is valid; yet the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states that one may not accept food by tossing it.
From what source does this [discrepancy] arise? Answer: What the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* refers to as "passing from afar" likely indicates that there were certain underlying causes and conditions.
What the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* refers to as "tossing food," however, arises from an attitude of disrespect. The distinction between these two rules of prohibition lies precisely in this intention.
○ The forty-first precept: Prohibiting the solicitation of fine food when not ill. In the Mahāyāna, one must not consume fish or meat even when ill.
If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, solicits for himself such fine foods as delicious meals, milk, curd, fish, or meat, it is a pāyattika offense.
The缘 (nidāna): Upāli went to the house of a merchant leader to solicit various foods.

The merchant leader asked, "What ailment do you have? He replied, "I have no ailment; I simply wish to obtain various foods. The merchant leader censured him for this, and thus [the rule] was established. At that time, sick bhikṣus were fearful and cautious;
they did not dare to beg for themselves, nor did they dare to beg for the sake of the sick, and having obtained food, they did not dare to eat it. Therefore...
Listen. This is the rule for the confession of offenses by bhikṣuṇīs. For the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Śāriputra Vinaya* states:
"If one obtains [what was requested], it is a *pāyattika*; if one does not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "To beg from someone who is not ill..."

If one eats while ill: when begging for it, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing); at the time of eating, there is no offense. If one begs for it while ill but eats it while not ill, there is no offense at the time of begging;
however, upon eating, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If a donor says, "Whatever you require, you may ask for as you please," or if one begs from the abodes of devas, nāgas, or yakṣas, there is no offense.
41. The precept on giving food to non-Buddhists oneself. This is studied in common with the Mahāyāna, though it may be granted according to the capacity of the recipient.
If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a male non-Buddhist or a female non-Buddhist, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Circumstance: The Buddha commanded Ānanda to divide the cakes among the assembly of monks. Having divided them, there was still a remainder, which he gave to a beggar.
There was a naked female heretic who was of upright and beautiful countenance; when Ānanda gave her the cake, it stuck to her.
It was said that there was a single cake which he gave to this woman; she gave it to another person, who in turn asked about what had been obtained. Immediately, suspicion and slander arose.
Furthermore, after a certain brahmin had finished eating here, he turned toward another country and encountered a man of profound faith who was an astrologer on the road.
He informed [the bhikṣu] that he had obtained food from a shaven-headed layman (*śramaṇoddeśa*). The physiognomist reported this to the bhikṣu, and upon hearing it, the Buddha established a precept.
Thereupon, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) all voiced complaints. The Buddha then permitted [the food] to be placed on the ground to be given, or for someone else to give it.
If one gives with one's own hand and the other accepts it, it is a *pāyattika*. If the other does not accept it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one employs a means to give but then changes one's mind and regrets it, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense in giving to parents, laborers, and the like; or if they forcibly seize it by power. The *Mūla-vinaya* states: [as above].
If one intends to eliminate that person’s wrong view by means of food, there is no offense.

The *Śāriputra Vinaya* states: There is no offense if the person is ill; if they are a relative; or if they seek to go forth [into homelessness] at which time one may give [to them] (referring to the four-month probationary period).
One should not give what has not been received; having first received it oneself, one may subsequently give it to another. This applies if it is for one's father, mother, or if they are imprisoned.
Those bound in fetters; those who urgently require food; pregnant women—give these a small or large amount. To animals, one mouthful should be given.
○ Forty-second: The precept against visiting other households without having informed [one's preceptor]. This is a shared rule for Mahayana practitioners.
If a bhikṣu, having previously accepted an invitation, visits other households before or after the meal without having informed another bhikṣu, except at the proper times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The proper times are: when one is ill, when making robes, and when robes are being offered; these are called the proper times.
There was a certain elder who prepared a meal and invited the Saṃgha. He waited for Pūrṇa (Bhadanta) to arrive;
however, at the time of the morning meal, Pūrṇa went to another house. He did not return until the mealtime was nearly over, so that the bhikṣus were unable to eat their fill.
Furthermore, a high minister sent sweet fruits to the monastery, also waiting for Pūrṇa to come before distributing them.
After he had finished his meal, he went to another house and did not return until it was past the proper time. Consequently, the community of monks was unable to eat the fresh fruit.

Therefore, a regulation was established: from then on, the community of monks did not dare to enter the city to accept invitations. The Buddha permitted them to enter the city after having entrusted their bowls to one another.

Furthermore, due to specific causes and conditions, one may enter the city without having formally entrusted one's robes to another during times of illness, when making robes, or when receiving robes as a gift.

Regarding "before the meal": this refers to the period from the appearance of the dawn light until the time for the midday meal. Regarding "after the meal": this refers to the period from the time for the midday meal until noon.
"Other monks" refers to those who dwell together within the same boundary (*sīmā*).

Having entrusted [the robes] and departed, if one returns midway, etc., one must entrust them again upon wishing to depart. If one enters another house without having entrusted them, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one has placed even one foot inside the doorway, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*.
For the other three groups [of monastics], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense if there is no monk present to whom one may entrust oneself;

or if one goes to a storehouse, to the edge of a village, or to the house of the person to whom one has entrusted oneself; or if one is held by force; or if there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states: "If one says to the donor, 'Even if I do not come, you should provide food for the Saṅgha so that it is not neglected,' there is no offense provided that the donor does not designate this person as the primary recipient."
43. The Precept on Insistently Sitting in a House Where Food is Being Served. This is studied by those of the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu sits insistently in a house where food is being served while there is wealth present, it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding Kālodayin: He went to the house of a laywoman observing the uposatha and sat down.
Her husband asked, "What do you require? He replied, "I require food. The husband then sent his wife out to give him food. Having finished eating, he did not leave.
The husband, filled with anger, went out and said, "Do as you please! The Buddha heard of this and established a precept accordingly.
Commentary: Regarding "a family that eats": men take women as their food, and women take men as their food; therefore, it is called a "family that eats. Regarding "possessing valuables":
[this refers to] carnelian, agate, pearl, amber, gold, and silver. (According to this precept, one incurs an offense specifically from a "family that eats," not from the mere possession of valuables.
The mention of "possessing valuables" is simply because the presence of such valuables indicates a place where husband and wife may engage in sexual desire.)
Regarding the offenses: for one who is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, or standing when one should be sitting, it is a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅).

For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika* (波逸提). For the other three assemblies (*saṃgha*), it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases: sitting within reach of hand from the door; being accompanied by two *bhikṣus*;
or being bound, etc. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: there is no offense if one has severed lustful desire.
If one sits in a house where a fast has been observed, or where there is another person of high respect seated, or if many people are coming and going from that house,
or if a woman has received the one-day precepts while the man has not, or if a man has received the one-day precepts while the woman has not—
sitting in such a household constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. However, if both have received them, it is not.
An offense.
○ Forty-fourth: The precept against sitting in a secluded place at a layperson’s home. This is the same as the Mahāyāna training rule. Whether it constitutes an offense or not is the same as above.
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place while there is wealth or valuables present within the layperson’s home, it is a pāyattika.
The case of Kālodayin: because he sat behind the door-panel and conversed with a laywoman who was observing the *upoṣadha* fast, this precept was established.
(45) The precept against sitting alone with a woman; it is shared by those training in the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in an open space, it is a pāyattika.
The origin [of this rule] also arose from a previous case; thus it was established.

Regarding the characteristics of the offense and non-offense, they are all the same as before. The *Śāriputra Vinaya* states: "To sit at a distance of one zhang [from a woman] constitutes a pāyattika."
If one sits at a distance of one *zhang* and five *chi*, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If the distance exceeds two *zhang*, there is no offense.

The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If one sits in private with a non-human female, a *paṇḍaka* female, or one who is not a fit object for sexual intercourse—such as those who are deaf or mentally infirm—one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) in all such cases."
46. The precept against causing another to not receive food. This is studied by those of the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu: "Venerable sir, come together with me to the village; I shall give you food."
That bhikṣu ultimately did not give food to this bhikṣu, but said to him: "Go away! I do not delight in sitting or speaking in one place with you;
I delight in sitting alone and speaking alone. For no reason other than this, he used such means to send him away.
This is a *pāyattika* offense. (The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Speaking" refers to reciting [the scriptures]; "sitting" refers to meditative reflection.)
The Case: Upananda had quarreled with another bhikṣu and harbored resentment in his heart.

On another occasion, when they were about to go on a journey to a place where there was no food and only a short time remained, he said to him: "You are a most wicked man; it is because of you that [we have come to this]."
"Furthermore, you have prevented me from eating. Go quickly! (and so forth). That bhikṣu left the city and arrived at Jetavana;

the time for the meal had already passed, and he was utterly exhausted by hunger. When the other bhikṣus heard of this, they censured him and reported the matter to the Buddha. Consequently, the following rule was established.

If, by means of a pretext, one sends [the person] away and abandons the place where they were seen or heard, or if one abandons the place where they were seen or heard oneself, it is a *pāyattika* offense when this is completed.

If one abandons the place where they were heard and goes to a place where they are seen, or abandons the place where they were seen and goes to a place where they are heard, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one sends them away to provide food, or if one is ill.
He lacks dignified deportment; people see him and are displeased, saying, "Go away! I shall send food to the saṃghārāma.
If he has broken the precepts, broken his views, or broken his deportment, and has been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) or expulsion (*pabbājanīyakamma*), he should be expelled.

However, if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacariya*), one may employ skillful means to have him leave; it is not for the sake of malice that he is sent away. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should act..."

If one causes annoyance to the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If a *bhikṣuṇī* causes annoyance to two assemblies, it is a *pāyattika*. If she causes annoyance to the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

The *Śāriputra Vinaya* states: "If one causes [a person] to turn back before they have entered the city gate, or even before they have entered the inner gate of a layperson’s house, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes them to turn back after they have entered the inner gate, it is a *pāyattika*."
*Pāyattika*. The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: "If one follows a physician's instruction and causes a patient to fast for the sake of their illness, there is no offense.
○ Forty-seventh: The precept against receiving medicine more than once. This is the same as in the Mahāyāna; if one requests it for the sake of the community, there is no offense.
If a monk accepts an invitation for medicinal requisites for four months, a healthy monk should accept it;

if he accepts beyond that—excepting invitations for regular supply, special invitations, invitations for a specific portion, or invitations for as long as life lasts—it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
Regarding Mahānāma of the Śākya clan: he provided medicine for the Saṅgha and, out of reverence for the elders, gave them the best quality.
He gave it whether requested or unrequested. The group of six (Ṣaḍvargika) monks went to his house and sought out rare medicines with difficulty.
He replied, "If I have some, I shall give it; if I do not have it, I shall go to the market and buy it to give you. The group of six then acted out of affection and spoke falsely.

He rebuked him. Because Mahānāma consequently ceased to provide medicine for the Saṃgha, [the Buddha] established a rule. Furthermore, based on these circumstances, he opened the allowance for regular invitations and so forth.

Regarding the commentary: "Four months" refers to the four months of the summer retreat. "Medicine prescribed by a physician for the sick" refers to those who are ill. "Regular invitations" refers to...
That person speaks as follows: "I shall always provide medicine. Regarding "further invitation" (*punar-yācanā*): after having finished [the distribution], one invites them again to give.
Regarding "invitation by division" (*vibhāga-yācanā*): one takes the medicine to a monastery (*saṃghārāma*) and distributes it. Regarding "invitation for as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīva-yācanā*):
that person says, "I shall provide medicine for as long as I live. There are four kinds of invitations; for example, there may be a limit regarding the night, but no limit regarding the medicine.
Regarding the observance of limits: there may be a limit for the night and a limit for the medicine, which should be received during the four months of summer;

or there may be no limit for the night but a limit for the medicine; or there may be no limit for the night and no limit for the medicine—in these cases, one should receive them according to the time of the offering.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: Whether it be four months of summer, four months of winter, or four months of spring, the invitation from a donor (*dānapati*) is not fixed;
it may be for four months, or for one month, or for half a month. Once the agreed period has expired, one must not seek further [invitations].
If one is invited for a meal before midday, one must not request a meal after midday; if invited for a meal after midday, one must not request a meal before midday.

The same applies to medicinal requisites and other items. However, if it is said, "I shall accept your offerings of the four requisites for as long as I live," at that time one may request them according to one's own wish.
[If one] receives [it] by passing it through [the mouth], for every swallow there is a *pāyattika* offense. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
The *Śāriputra Vinaya* (*Shisong lü*) states: "If one solicits and obtains [it], it is a *pāyattika*; if one solicits and does not obtain it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If one solicits bitter medicines such as *harītakī*, whether one obtains them or not, it is entirely a *dukkaṭa*. The *Vinayaviniscaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* (*Lüshe*) states: "[During] the four months..."

When the meal is finished, if one asks for coarse food after having been invited [to eat fine food], and seeks something better, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing); if one eats it, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

If one is invited to eat fine food but further requests coarse food, at the time of requesting it there is a *dukkaṭa*, but at the time of eating there is no offense. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-vinaya-vibhāṣā* (Shanjian lü) states:
"If a donor offers medicine, it should be used as medicine; it must not be used as food. If one asks for ghee when given oil, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (transgression)."
Appendix: The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: If a person offers medicine to the Saṃgha, the administrative bhikṣu should ask:
"Is it to be kept within the village, or is it to be placed inside the monastery? If they say it is to be kept within the village, [the bhikṣu] should say:

"When you need it, you must tell me that you require such-and-such medicine; prepare it for me so that there is no lack. If they say it is to be kept inside the monastery, he should perform a formal announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

The *karmavācanā*: A monk endowed with five qualities—one who is not swayed by favoritism, hatred, delusion, or fear, and who knows what is medicinal and what is not—should be appointed as the guardian of the Sangha’s medicines.
He should store the *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, and *bibhītaka* fruits in new vessels.
Pippalī, dried ginger, sugarcane syrup, and rock honey—if these are kept in a vessel that does not leak, they may be used to store ghee, oil, or honey.
One should seal the opening with a stopper and label it with the name of the medicine. If a sick bhikṣu requires them, one should joyfully give them to him.
If the patient knows for themselves that they require this medicine, they should take it themselves. If they do not know, they should ask a physician.
If there is no physician, they should ask their two teachers: "I have such-and-such an illness; what medicine should I take?
If the two teachers do not know, they should take the medicine and try it two or three times. If it does not cure them, they should take another medicine.
48. The Precept on Viewing Military Arrays. This is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu goes to view a military array, except when there is a specific reason or occasion, it is a pāyattika offense.
On one occasion, King Prasenajit personally led the six divisions of his army to suppress a rebellion. The group of six monks went to watch.
When the king saw them, he was displeased; consequently, he sent a package of stone honey as a greeting to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One rebuked them and established a precept.
Later, while the two ministers, Liśāta and Pūrṇa, were in the army, they longed with thirsting devotion to see the bhikṣu.
They dispatched a messenger to invite him, but the bhikṣu, being cautious and apprehensive, did not dare go; thus, this was excluded as a case of special circumstance.

If one goes and sees [the object], it is a *pāyattika*. If one does not see it, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If one intends to look but does not go, or encounters it on the road and does not avoid it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense in the following cases: when one is led away by force; or when all obstacles and difficulties prevent one from avoiding it. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If an army comes to the monastery, there is no offense if one does not intentionally look at them. If one intentionally looks at them, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*.
Even down to looking at people quarreling, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "When seeing an army... [text continues].
One should speak of their merits and faults. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "To go and watch an army of yakṣas is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Nidāna* states: "If there are those engaged in fighting, one should not go to watch them; if one sees a dispute, one must quickly abandon it and depart."
49. The precept concerning staying more than three nights among an army. This is common to the Mahāyāna. Alternatively, it is not an offense if one observes the capacity [of the disciple].
If a bhikṣu has a valid reason, he is permitted to stay among an army for two or three nights; should he exceed this, it is a pāyattika.

**缘起 (Nidāna):** Because the group of six monks stayed overnight in an army camp due to certain circumstances, householders criticized and disparaged them; therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule.

**相 (Lakṣaṇa):** During the third night, before the dawn light has appeared, one should leave the place where one can hear sounds and see forms. If one does not leave, and the dawn light appears, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one leaves the place where one can hear but not where one can see, or leaves the place where one can see but not where one can hear, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
A *duṣkṛta* offense; for a bhikṣuṇī, a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense in cases of various obstacles and difficulties. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "Even if there is a cause or condition, if the matter can be settled by letter, one should send a letter.
If it is necessary to go in person, only then should one go. Once the business is concluded, one must return immediately and not spend the night away. If the matter is not settled..."
One should stay for one night. If the matter is not settled after one night, one should stay for a second night. If it is still not settled, one should stay for a third night.
If it remains unsettled after exceeding three nights, it is a *pāyattika*. If the matter is settled immediately, to stay overnight when one should not is a *dukkaṭa*.
○ The fiftieth precept concerning observing military affairs. This is shared with the Mahāyāna.

If a bhikṣu stays within an army for two or three nights, and at any time observes military formations or combat, or observes the strength and power of the marching troops' elephants and horses, it is a pāyattika.
The occasion: Six groups of monks went to watch a military array and were struck by arrows. Their companions wrapped them in robes and carried them back.
When a lay devotee asked about this and learned the reason, he criticized and complained about it. Therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule.
The categories of transgression and non-transgression are the same as above. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "To watch birds or beasts fighting is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Fifty-one:
The Precept Against Drinking Alcohol. This is likewise prescribed in the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika offense. The occasion:
The Venerable Sāgata stayed as a guest in the house of a matted-hair brahmin and subdued the poisonous fire-dragon.
The ruler of Kauśāmbī conceived deep faith and went to pay homage to the World-Honored One; wishing to provide offerings for the Venerable, the group of six bhikṣus sought [alcohol] on his behalf.
The venerable one drank dark liquor until he was intoxicated and satiated; on the way back, he collapsed and vomited, while a flock of crows cawed in confusion.
The Buddha asked Ānanda about this, and upon learning of it, rebuked him, saying: "If you cannot subdue a small snake even now, how much less can you subdue a great dragon?
There are ten faults for those who drink alcohol: first, the complexion becomes ugly; second, strength diminishes; third, the eyesight..."
[The results are] obscure. Fourth, they manifest signs of anger and resentment. Fifth, they ruin their fields, livelihoods, and means of subsistence.
Sixth, they increase the occurrence of diseases. Seventh, they augment quarrels and litigation. Eighth, their ill repute spreads abroad. Ninth, their wisdom diminishes.
Tenth, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the three evil realms. From this day forward, take me as your teacher.
...up to and including not placing even the tip of a blade of grass or wood into wine and putting it into one's mouth.
[If a bhikṣuṇī does so,] it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if the wine is used as medicine or if the wine is applied to a wound. The *Śāriputra Vinaya* (*Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*) states: "Drinking sour wine, sweet wine, or if [it is] yeast..."
"Rice wine. Anything that can cause intoxication: for every swallow, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
If it merely has the appearance of wine, but lacks the fragrance and taste of wine and cannot intoxicate a person, there is no offense for one who drinks it. The *Mātṛkā* states:

"If one cooks fermented grain medicine, non-time-limited medicine, or seven-day medicine with wine, provided they no longer possess the nature of wine, they may be consumed. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
If food cooked with alcohol or medicine cooked with alcohol still possesses the aroma of alcohol, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If it lacks the aroma of alcohol, it may be eaten.
○ Fifty-second: The Precept Against Sporting in Water. This is studied in common by the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu plays and sports in water, it is a pāyattika. The occasion:
The seventeen groups of bhikṣus were playing in the water. King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā saw them from atop their palace.
The Queen sent a messenger to inform the World-Honored One, and thus this rule was established.
Commentary: Regarding those who play in the water: they go from this shore to the other shore; they may go with the current or against the current; they may dive here and emerge there;
they may draw patterns in the water with their hands; or they may splash one another with water.
If one plays in water, it is a *pāyattika*. If one plays with curd-milk, bitter wine, barley-juice, or the like in a vessel, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases: [omitted].
Crossing water while practicing the Way; pulling bamboo or wood, gathering stones or sand; searching for lost items; learning to swim, and so forth. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"To clench snow [or] dew on the tips of grass is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If there is water on a tray, or if there is water on a seat, to draw lines upon it with one's finger is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Samantapāsādikā* [states...].
It is said: "If one plays in water that is deep enough to submerge the tops of the feet, it is a *pāyattika*. If one rocks a boat or splashes water, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
○ The fifty-third precept on striking and poking is studied by those of the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu tickles another with his fingers, it is a pāyattika (meaning he pricks him so that his flesh itches, thereby inducing laughter). The occasion for this rule:
one member of the group of six bhikṣus tickled a member of the group of seventeen, which resulted in the latter’s death; therefore, the rule was established.
Excluding the fingers of the hands and feet, to strike or poke with a staff, a fan, a broom handle, or similar objects constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in cases where one touches someone while sleeping to wake them, or in all instances of accidental contact.
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: To strike or poke a *śrāmaṇera* or even an animal constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā* states: "If the body-faculty is impaired, [to cause it pain by] poking with a finger constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
(54) The precept against not accepting admonition is studied together with the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika.
The cause: because Chanda wished to violate the precepts and did not comply with the admonitions of the various bhikṣus, this rule was established.
Regarding the offense: for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if the person who comes to admonish is ignorant, or if the statement was made in jest or by mistake.

Appendix: The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states that one should not accept the admonitions of five types of persons: first, those who lack a sense of shame and remorse; second, those who have not studied extensively;
third, those who constantly seek out the faults of others; fourth, those who delight in strife and contention; and fifth, those who wish to discard their robes and return to lay life.

55. The Precept Against Intimidating Others. This is common to those training in the Mahāyāna. It is not an offense if one intimidates another by means of skillful observation or for the purpose of subduing them.
If a bhikṣu intimidates another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
The Circumstance: While the Buddha was walking up and down on his walking path, the bhikṣu Nāgapāla attended upon him.

At the first watch of the night, he requested that the Buddha return to his room, but the World-Honored One remained silent. He did the same at the middle and final watches of the night, yet he was instead seized and bound.
[He] made a terrifying sound like that of a non-human being. At dawn, the World-Honored One assembled the community, rebuked [the offender], and established the precept.
Commentary: Regarding "terrorizing": if one uses form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, or mental objects to terrify another person.

Regarding the offense: if the person before one sees, hears, or knows it, whether they are terrified or not, it is a *pāyattika*. If they do not see, hear, or know it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for the other three assemblies (*parṣad*), it is a *duṣkṛta*. One does not commit an offense if, in any case, one does not act with the intention of causing fear in others.
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If one causes [fear] by means of loathsome forms, sounds, and so forth..."

If one causes fear or distress, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling). If one causes fear or distress by means of desirable forms, sounds, and so forth, it is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

If one causes alarm or distress to others, it is in all cases an *dukkaṭa*. If one speaks of the three miserable realms (*apāya*) with the intention of transforming and guiding them, there is no offense even if they become afraid.
Regarding the six permutations concerning the perception of a monk as a monk: the first two constitute a *pāyattika*; the latter... [text ends]

Four minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*): [The permutations] regarding the actual absence of a cause for fear while perceiving it as such consist of six cases; two are grave, two are minor, and two are non-offenses. ○ Fifty-sixth:
The precept against bathing more than once every six days. This is studied in common with the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu bathes every half-month, a bhikṣu who is not ill should accept this; he must not exceed it, except during other times.

This is an offense of expiation (pāyattika). "Other times" refers to: the heat of summer, the time of illness, the time of manual labor, the time of wind and rain, and the time of traveling on a road. These are the [permitted] times.
There was a pond in the kingdom of Magadha. King Bimbisāra permitted the bhikṣus to bathe in it at all times.
Later, during the latter part of the night, the group of six bhikṣus entered the water to bathe. The king and his court ladies also arrived there and heard the sound of the bhikṣus bathing.
He remained still to wait for them. The group of six monks washed one another with various fine medicinal powders until the first light of dawn appeared;
the king was ultimately unable to bathe. All the ministers were filled with resentment and indignation, and thus [the rule] was established.
"Regarding 'sick,' it extends downward to having a body that is foul-smelling and filthy. Regarding 'one who acts,' it extends downward to sweeping the ground before one's house.
Regarding 'wind and rain,' it extends downward to even a single whirlwind or a single drop falling upon the body. Regarding 'a traveler,' it extends downward to half a yojana."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The time of heat" refers to when one is oppressed by heat and perspiration breaks out. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā-śāstra* states:
"At whatever place and at whatever time it is hot, one may take a bath two and a half months during that period."
Except at other times, if one bathes more than once, or if water is poured over half the body, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one employs the means but does not proceed, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one is compelled by force to bathe. The *Śāriputra Vinaya* states: "If [someone] arrived yesterday, today..."
Bathing on the same day [as the previous bath]. If one intends to depart the following day and bathes today, it is a *pāyattika*. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states:
"If one washes a teacher or a sick person, and their bodies are already moist, bathing for that purpose does not constitute an offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"In times other than those mentioned above, one should follow the bathing method of potters: first wash the two thighs and two feet, and afterwards wash the head and face."
Regarding the waist, back, arms, elbows, chest, and armpits:
as for the ritual of repentance and the establishment of the altar, one must bathe daily, even up to three times; following these Buddhist teachings constitutes no offense.
Furthermore, if there is hot water provided for the general community in a monastic forest (sōrin), this likewise constitutes no offense.
Appendix: One should not bathe together with laypeople; however, if they praise the Triple Gem, bathing is permitted.
○ Fifty-seven: The precept against lighting fires on open ground. This is the same as in the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, lights a fire in the open air for the purpose of warming his own body, or instructs another to light one,
except when there is a specific reason, it is a pāyattika offense.
Because the group of six monks were unable to warm themselves as they pleased in front of the senior monk, they went outside the room and lit a fire on the open ground to roast themselves.
At that time, there was a venomous snake within an empty tree; driven by the heat of the fire's fumes, it emerged from a hole in the tree.
The bhikṣus were all startled; they seized the burning wood and scattered it about, causing flying sparks to set the Buddha’s lecture hall on fire.

Therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule. Regarding the sick: if there is a need for warming the body by means of fire due to specific circumstances—such as boiling gruel, soup, or rice for a sick bhikṣu;
or if one is in a heated room (*jentāka*), a kitchen, or a bathhouse; or if one is fumigating alms bowls, dyeing robes, lighting lamps, or burning incense.
[The Buddha] said: "If one, being ill, lights a fire in an open space to warm oneself, or burns grass, wood, branches, leaves, and so forth, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one burns them until they are half-charred, or burns charcoal, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;

for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: 'If one lights a fire to warm oneself, and the flame reaches a height of four finger-widths, it is a *pāyattika*.'"
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If one is traveling on a road during intense cold, there is no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"When carrying a torch while walking, if one wishes to shake it off, one must not do so over ground that has not yet been burned; one should do so over ashes or on a tile.
If the torch should fall to the ground by itself, shaking it off directly upon it incurs no offense."
Appendix: The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states that there are five faults in sitting near a fire: first, it causes one to lose their complexion;
second, it causes a lack of strength; third, it causes the eyes to grow dim; fourth, it causes many people to gather and clamor; fifth, it leads to much talk of worldly matters.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are seven ways in which lighting a fire is unbeneficial: first, it ruins the eyes; second, it ruins the complexion; third, it causes the body to become weak; fourth...
1. Garments become soiled and ruined. 2. Beds and mats deteriorate. 3. One gives rise to causes and conditions for violating the precepts. 4. Worldly discourse increases. Appendix:
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "Therefore, if one burns forests or wildlands, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
58. The precept on hiding another’s belongings. This is studied by Mahāyāna practitioners as well.
If a bhikṣu hides the robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case of another bhikṣu—whether he hides it himself or instructs another to hide it—even down to doing so in jest, it is a pāyattika offense.
The Context: The group of seventeen monks placed their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases to one side and practiced walking meditation while waiting for the time of the meal to arrive.

The group of six monks waited until they had turned their backs, then took the items and hid them. When the time arrived and [the group of seventeen] went searching for them, [the group of six] stood before them and teased them.
Other bhikṣus observed this and censured them with disapproval. When the Buddha heard of it, he established a precept.

[The offense of] taking what belongs to another: for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta. There is no offense if one knows the object truly belongs to that person and takes it because its substance is entirely [one's own];
or if one takes it because it was blown away or soaked by wind and rain; or if one takes it because of a habit of careless storage despite being cautioned;

or if one takes it because they lent their own robe to the other and the other did not take care of it, fearing it might be lost; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya).
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is said: "To hide the belongings of the other four assemblies, or even the property of animals, constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī* to hide the property of the two assemblies [monks and nuns], it is a *pāyattika*; for all other cases, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
'If the owner finds it after it has been hidden, it is a *duṣkṛta*; if they do not find it, it is a *pāyattika*. If one hides an empty needle case, and it is found..."
Not permitted; all constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "To conceal extra robes or other items constitutes a *vinayātikrama* offense.
○ Fifty-ninth: The precept against wearing a robe that has been designated as a pure gift (*śuddhadeya*) without authorization. This is studied by those in the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī,
and later takes it back and wears it without informing the owner, it is a pāyattika.
The origin [of this rule] stems from the group of six [monks];

therefore, it was established as a precept. Regarding "giving a robe": this refers to a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*). There are two kinds of pure gifts: first, the true pure gift (*bhūta-viśuddhi-dāna*).

To say: "This is my extra robe (*atirekacīvara*). It has not yet been purified (*apariśuddha*). Now, for the sake of purification, I offer it to you, Venerable Sir, as a *tattvaviśuddhi* (true purification).
Second, the mutual *viśuddhiparivartana* (purification by exchange): To say: "This is my extra robe. It has not yet been purified. Now, for the sake of purification..."
When giving it to an elder, one should say to him: "Venerable sir, listen. You have this extra robe-cloth which has not yet been purified;
now give it to me for the sake of purification, and I shall accept it. Having accepted it, one asks: "To whom do you wish to give it? He replies:
[He] gives it to so-and-so. That person should say: "Venerable sir, you have this extra robe which has not yet been purified (*kathina*). Now give it to me for the sake of purification.
[The donor] then accepts it. Having accepted it, he gives it to so-and-so. This robe is the property of so-and-so;
for his sake, you should guard and maintain it, using it as you see fit.
Regarding this, it is a true pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*). One should inquire of the owner before taking and wearing it.
As for a pure gift passed on through succession, one may wear it according to one's inclination, whether or not the owner has been informed. For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika*;

for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The *Mūla-vinaya* states: "If one receives another's entrusted robe and subsequently, without asking the owner, takes it up and wears it oneself, it is a *pāyattika*."
If it is the property of a kinsman or friend, and that person feels joy in their heart when they hear of its use, there is no offense.
[Commentary: Examining the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, its underlying intent differs from that of the present *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

This [latter] establishes the precept for the sake of the donor, while that [former] prevents transgressions for the sake of the recipient of the deposit. Although these two do not correspond to one another, the principle should nonetheless be as follows:
This is the "Double Protection. Appendix:

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that one should not perform a formal act of purification (*pāriśuddhi*) for five types of persons: first, those who are not known; second, those with whom one is not yet intimately acquainted;
third, those with whom one has not yet become familiar; fourth, those who are neither relatives nor fellow-disciples; and fifth, those who do not belong to the same class.
(To be too old is an improper time; to have never gone forth is an improper class). Furthermore, there are two qualities for which one should not receive a pure gift (*pariśuddha-dāna*):
first, being unable to praise others; second, being unable to establish a good reputation for others. Furthermore, there are two other qualities:

first, being unable to accept another’s valuable possession as a pure gift and protect it as if it were one's own; second, being unable to give away one's own valuable possession as a pure gift to another.

One should not harbor resentment. Furthermore, there are two things [to consider]: first, not knowing whether that person is still in the world; second, not knowing whether that person is on the path.
If a bhikṣu is living alone and possesses extra robes (*atirekacīvara*), he should perform a "purification by remote designation" (*dūratovissajjana-pariśuddhi*).

If among his three robes (*tricīvara*) there is something that must be exchanged, he should bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, take hold of the robe, and generate this thought:
He speaks with his mouth: "I now relinquish this robe of mine, consisting of so many strips. Thus he says three times. Thereafter, he receives the extra robe, also according to the previous method.
He forms the thought and speaks with his mouth: "I receive this robe of mine, consisting of so many strips. Thus he says three times.
Having thus received it, the robe that was relinquished should be given as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*), again according to the previous method. [He] forms the thought...
One speaks aloud, saying: "I give this extra robe as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*) to [Name]. I shall take it from him for use.
If one does not wish to receive it through exchange, then upon obtaining the extra robe, one should immediately perform a pure gift in this manner. Regarding the method of individual pure gift:
when the eleventh day arrives, one should again follow the previous procedure, speaking aloud with the thought: "I take back this extra robe from [Name]."
Thereafter, one should again receive and maintain the pure gift according to the previous method.

If the pure gift is made in the presence of another person, one should perform a successive pure gift (*parivartaka-śuddhi*) according to the previous method, holding the robe and saying: "I offer this extra robe as a pure gift to you, Venerable Sir."
He should ask: "Venerable sir, this robe has been made a *viśuddhi-dāna* (pure gift) to me;
to whom shall I give it? He replies: "Give it as you wish among the five groups of monks. He then says: "I now give it to so-and-so.
Venerable sir, if you need it, take it from him and use it; cherish and protect it well. He [the recipient] then speaks of this matter to the one whose name was mentioned.
"Kauṇḍinya, a bhikṣu who fears violating the rule regarding extra robes (atirekacīvara) should not accept them. The Buddha said: "One should not speak thus to a bhikṣu by his specific name.
[This concludes] the precept against sixty types of robes that have not been discolored; this is likewise regulated in the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he should apply one of three kinds of discoloring agents; he may choose whichever color he prefers among them:
blue, black, or madder-brown. If he wears another new robe without having applied a discoloring agent, it is a pāyattika offense.
**缘起:** The group of six monks wore white garments while walking about. Laypeople criticized and disparaged them; therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule.
**Explanation:** Whether it be a new garment or one first obtained from another person, all such items are termed "new garments."
[The Buddha] said: "For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta. The *Śāriputra Vinaya* states:

"If one obtains a black garment (*nīla*), it should be purified with ochre (*sīrṣaka*) [note: 'nī' means black; 'qian' is pronounced as in *jiàn*; it is the name of a plant, also written as *qiàn*, meaning madder].

If one obtains an ochre garment, it should be purified with black and madder. If one obtains a madder garment, it should be purified with black and ochre. If one obtains yellow, red, or white garments, [they should likewise be purified]."
It should be purified by means of the three types: blue clay, madder, and [other] three kinds. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should mark it with three colors.
If one does not mark it, for every time it is worn, there is a *pāyattika* offense. If it is not worn, for every night it remains so, there is a *pāyattika* offense.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When performing the purification, the maximum size is four finger-widths; the minimum is like a pea. It may be one or three [marks]."

Whether there be five, seven, or nine [patches], they must not take the shape of a flower. If one obtains many small, miscellaneous new items that are joined together to patch a single area, one performs the ritual purification (*kappiya*) for that single area.
If they are patched individually and separately, one performs the purification for each one.
If making a new robe, one performs the purification at one corner; if patching with one strip or half a strip, one likewise performs the purification.
61. The precept against taking life. This is a natural transgression (prakṛti-sāvadya). In the Mahāyāna, it constitutes a grave offense.
If a bhikṣu intentionally kills the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
**Context:** Because Kāḷudāyin did not like seeing crows, he made a bamboo bow to shoot them; therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule.

**Explanation:** The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "As for 'animals,' this excludes dragons (*nāga*). All other animals are included [as such]. (Although dragons are indeed animals, they are capable of transformation.)"

Possessing supernatural powers, they protect the land and preserve the True Dharma; their functions are similar to those of the devas. Therefore, one who kills such a being commits a sthūlātyaya offense.

Killing oneself, inciting others to kill, or employing the means to kill—all these constitute a *pāyattika* offense. If one employs the means with the intent to kill but does not actually kill, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies [of the Saṃgha], it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense for accidental injury. The *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā* states: "If one intends to cut a vine but accidentally cuts a snake, there is no offense.
If one intends to cut a snake but accidentally cuts a vine, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one intends to kill this insect but mistakenly kills that insect [there is no offense]."
If one intends to strike an insect but strikes the ground, or intends to crush an insect but crushes the soil, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
The *Vinaya-vibhaṅga* states: If birds or sparrows nest and roost in the corridors of a monastery cell and cause a disturbance, one should have someone inspect them.

If there are no chicks or eggs in the nest, they should be immediately removed and discarded; if there are, one should wait until they have departed before removing them. If... [there are]... [chicks/eggs], [one must wait].
Regarding bee nests: those without larvae should be removed; those with larvae should be bound with thread, whereby they will not proliferate.
(62) The precept against drinking or using water containing insects is likewise regulated in the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu knows that water contains living beings and drinks or uses it, it is a pāyattika offense.
The origin of this rule stems from the group of six bhikṣus; therefore, it was established.

The six permutations—such as the perception of the characteristic, the perception of doubt, and so forth—should be understood accordingly. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika; for the other three assemblies, it is a dukkaṭa.
*Dūṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one does not know there are insects; or if there are coarse insects and one touches the water to make them go away;

or if one drinks water that has been strained. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one knowingly uses roasted flour, honey, sugar, oil, vinegar, gruel, milk, curd, cakes, fruit, or other such items while knowing they contain insects, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "There are five kinds of eyes."
One should not contemplate water with the following five types of eyes: first, an eye afflicted by sores; second, an eye with cataracts; third, a deranged eye;

fourth, an eye impaired by old age or disease; and fifth, a divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). For how long should one contemplate the water? It is said: for the duration it takes for a cart drawn by six oxen to turn around.

If one follows the current of a river, one may observe the water once for the absence of insects; within the distance of one *krośa*, the water may be used at will, provided that no other river flows into it in the interim.
However, for non-flowing water or rivers flowing against the current, one may use the water within the distance of one *vyāma* after observing it once.
There are five kinds of pure water: first, that purified by the Saṃgha; second, that purified by an individual...
1. Purification by straining; 2. purification by a cloth filter; 3. purification by a triple-layered filter; 4. purification by a spring; 5. purification by well water.

If one knows that the person [who drew the water] is one who observes the precepts and protects living beings, then even if one does not inspect it, there is no offense in using that water for rice-meat when it is obtained.
Once water has been inspected from sunrise until the appearance of the dawn light, it may be used accordingly throughout that period. [The Sangha...]

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states: "Regarding 'insects,' this does not refer to fish, turtles, and the like; rather, it refers to tiny creatures such as *jālīnaka* larvae and others, down to those with extremely subtle forms that can be seen by the eye.

One should not examine them with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), nor should one have someone with poor eyesight examine them—even one who can see the fine lines on the palm of the hand may be employed to inspect the water. However, one must not do so too hastily."

It has been too long—just as it takes an elephant to turn around once. If there are extremely minute insects in the water, one must not use it for washing hands or the face, nor for the great or small calls of nature.
If invited to a meal by a lay donor (dānapati), one should ask whether the water has been strained.

If they say it has not been strained, one should observe whether the person before one is trustworthy; if so, one should instruct them to strain the water. If they are not trustworthy, [one should not go].

Do not speak of it so as to cause harm to the insects; the bhikṣu should strain it himself for use. He should place the water containing insects into his own vessel and ask from where the water was taken.
According to the place from which it came, he should return and pour the water with the insects back into that source.

If the place where the water was first taken is far away, and there is a pool whose water has not dried up for seven days, he should place the water with the insects into it. If there is none [such], [he should dispose of it otherwise].
A pond. One should take water containing insects from a vessel and bring it to raise them. One must wait for a great rain and a sudden flood, then pour the insects into it, saying:

"Go now into the great ocean. While traveling on the road, if one knows that there are insects in well water, one must not carry it to fill a vessel, nor may one borrow the rope used for drawing water.
If there are insects in pond water or stagnant water, [one must likewise refrain from using it].
One may say, "Venerable sir, there are insects in this water; there are insects," thereby causing the person before one to feel doubt and displeasure.
If that person asks, "Is there no insect in this water? one should reply, "Venerable sir, look for yourself.
If the person is a kinsman or a fellow disciple, one should say, "There are insects in this water; you should strain it before using it."
Appendix: The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: "One should not travel even half a *yojana* without a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*).
If one lacks one, one should strain the water using the corner of the *saṃghāṭī*. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"It is also permitted to keep a water-strainer tube made of copper, iron, bamboo, wood, ceramic, or stone, with its mouth covered by fine cloth. The use of [strainers made of] dung is not permitted."

Regarding the cleaning of robes: the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states that one should tie the mouth of the water-strainer (*kuṇḍikā*) with silk and fasten its neck with a fine cord, then submerge it in water until the mouth is raised halfway out (if the mouth is fully submerged, water will not enter). Once it is full, draw it out and must still inspect it for insects.
However, as for the *chuo-ku* (mouth-broad) water jar (*kumbha*), regardless of its size, one should cover its mouth with silk and draw water from it as needed; this is extremely convenient.

(The *jun-chi* is also called *jun-chi*; here it is translated as "jar. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "The purification jar should be made of earthenware or porcelain, must have a capacity of two or three *sheng*, and should be kept in a clean place, grasped with clean hands.")

For the vessel used for touching [impure things], copper or iron may be employed; it is placed where one touches, to be grasped by hand as needed. The *Jizhong jingxun* states: "The water-strainer is an instrument for practicing compassion."
The conditions for benefiting sentient beings arise from this great practice; the ultimate Way is realized through this.
As the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: In the kingdom of Pārāśī, two bhikṣus were traveling together as companions to Śrāvastī to pay their respects to the World-Honored One.
On the way, they became exhausted with thirst and found no water. Upon reaching a well, one bhikṣu drew water.
He then drank the water. Another bhikṣu inspected the water; seeing insects in it, he did not drink. The bhikṣu who had drunk the water asked him, "Why do you not drink?
He replied, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not drink water containing insects. The other then urged him, saying:
"Elder, drink! Do not let yourself die of thirst so that you may not see the Buddha. He replied, "I would rather lose my life than violate the Buddha's precepts.
Thereupon, he died of thirst. The monk who had drunk the water gradually arrived at the place where the Buddha was.
The Buddha asked, "Where have you come from? He further asked, "Do you have any companions? He then related the matter in full. The Buddha said, "Foolish man, you..."
They did not see me, yet they thought they had seen me. That deceased bhikṣu had already previously seen me (the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"That upholder of the precepts died from not drinking [liquor] and was immediately reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Having attained a complete celestial body, he first went to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, heard the Dharma, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, and received the three refuges; therefore it is said that he had already previously seen me. The account is the same in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*).
If a bhikṣu is negligent and indolent, failing to restrain his sense faculties, even though he dwells in the same place as me...

He is far from me; though he sees me, I do not see him. If there is a bhikṣu on the other shore of the ocean who is able to be diligent and untiring, and who restrains his sense faculties, then although he is far from me, I always see him, and he is always near me.

(This explains distance and proximity in terms of the *dhātu*; if explained in terms of the *adhvan*, then a person who is heedless, even if born in an age of sages, is no different from the age of the Dharma’s decline, whereas one who is not heedless...)

Although you may be born in the final age, it shall not differ from the True Dharma. The Buddha-body is truly eternal; fundamentally, there is neither its appearance in the world nor its parinirvāṇa. I pray that noble and heroic persons will not give rise to the notion that this is the Age of Semblance Dharma or that the Dharma has been extinguished, thereby abandoning themselves.

You must vow to be diligent and untiring, to restrain all the sense faculties, and to strictly purify the Vinaya. Do not treat even minor offenses lightly. Always act as if you were personally receiving the compassionate countenance of the Buddha and directly hearing his clear instructions. By practicing without ceasing, you shall see that the single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly undispersed.
63. The Precept Against Intentionally Annoying Others. This is studied in common with the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu intentionally annoys another bhikṣu so that he is unhappy for even a moment, it is a pāyattika offense.
Context: The group of seventeen bhikṣus questioned the group of six bhikṣus: "How does one enter the first dhyāna, the second, the third, and the fourth dhyānas?
How does one enter emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness? How does one attain the four fruits? They replied:
"If it were as you have described, then you would have already committed a pārājika offense and would no longer be bhikṣus. At that time, ten...
The group of seven went to question the senior elder; knowing that he had caused them doubt and distress, they informed the Buddha, who then established the precept.
*Explanation:* "Doubt and distress" refers to [confusion] regarding birth, age, the reception of the precepts, or formal ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*).
Whether it be for the sake of an offense or for the sake of the Dharma, if one harbors doubt regarding the time of birth, they should be asked:
"How long has it been since you were born? If they reply, "For such a length of time," one should say: "You were not born for such a length of time;
you were born like other people, not at such a time. This applies equally to the Dharma and so forth.
Regarding the offense: if one intentionally causes doubt or distress by speaking clearly, it is a *pāyattika*;
if not clearly, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense in the following cases: [omitted].
The fact is indeed so. It is not an intentional act of causing vexation, nor even [the case of] speaking erroneously and so forth. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"Causing the other four assemblies to fall into doubt and regret constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If a nun causes two assemblies to fall into doubt and regret, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
Causing the other three assemblies to fall into doubt and regret constitutes a *duṣkṛta*."
64. The precept against concealing the gross offenses of others. This is a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and is likewise prohibited in the Mahāyāna;

it is precisely the precept against failing to instruct another to repent for their offense. Question: If one does not conceal another’s offense, would that not constitute speaking of the faults of the fourfold assembly?
Answer: It is merely prohibited that one may speak of these matters to outsiders; it is not prohibited to raise such faults according to the Dharma within the Saṃgha.

If one were to tolerate and indulge them out of leniency, allowing great evils to fester, this would cause their transgressions to deepen daily while simultaneously bringing disgrace upon the Dharma-gate.
Who with a compassionate heart could bear to sit idly by and watch this?
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it, he commits a pāyattika.
The circumstances were as follows: Upananda frequently committed offenses and told a bhikṣu who was his close friend about them, instructing him not to tell anyone.
Later, the two of them quarreled, and that bhikṣu immediately informed other bhikṣus of the offenses he had committed. The others...
The bhikṣu questioned him and learned the circumstances of the matter, then informed the Buddha, who established the precept.
*Commentary:* Regarding "grave offenses" (*sthūlātyaya*): these refer to the four *pārājika* and the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. *Exegesis:* Regarding "minor offenses":

if one knows [of an offense] while eating, and declares it after the meal; or even if one knows it during the first watch of the night, and declares it during the middle watch, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one knows [the offense] during the middle watch of the night, and desires to confess it during the latter watch but does not do so, and the dawn light appears, it is a *pāyattika*.

Concealing other offenses, concealing one's own grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), or concealing another person’s grave offense, all constitute *duṣkṛta*. If a *bhikṣuṇī* conceals a *parājika* offense committed by another *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pārājika*; if she conceals a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*;

for the other three groups of followers, it is *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases: [if the offender is] insane, deranged, afflicted by pain, the first offender, or if it is an offense that is not to be concealed.
As for this: previously one did not know; or there was no one with whom one could speak; or it would have endangered one's life or one's holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Upon seeing another's offense, one should stop after speaking to a single person. If one hears of it or suspects it, there is no need to speak."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not go and speak of this to just anyone; one should speak it to a virtuous bhikṣu.

If that offending bhikṣu is violent, or if, by relying on the power of a king, the power of a high minister, or the power of violent men, he creates the conditions for taking life and harms those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya), one should reflect thus:
'The karmic consequences of that offender's actions will surely manifest as retribution for himself. He himself...
It should be understood that this is like being caught in a fire: one should only save oneself; how could one attend to other matters? There is no fault.
An appendix to the third section states: "There are five internal qualities by which one should exhort another: [one must do so] at the proper time, not at an improper time."
It is truthful, not untruthful; beneficial, not detrimental; gentle, not harsh; and compassionate, not wrathful.
The fourth section states: The Buddha told Upāli: "One whose bodily deportment is impure, whose speech is impure, and whose livelihood is impure;
one who is of little learning and does not know the Sūtras, being of little learning..."
If one does not recite the Vinaya and lacks clarity in speech and argumentation—being like a white sheep—one should not censure the offenses of others.
If one is fully endowed with all the dharmas, one should censure the offenses of others at the proper time and in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, if this bhikṣu has both affection and respect for me, then he should censure the offense; or if he has affection but no respect, or if he has no respect but [has affection].
If there is affection, one should encourage [the person]. Or, even if there is no affection or reverence, if one can cause them to abandon evil and resort to the good, one should encourage them.

Or, if there is a bhikṣu whom they hold in high esteem and who is respected, trusted, and admired by them, and through whom one can cause them to abandon evil and practice the good, one should encourage them.
If none such exist, the Saṃgha should completely set them aside and expel them, saying: "Venerable one, wherever you go, there..."
I shall perform for you the formal act of censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), the act of calling to mind (*sativinaya*), and the act of self-accusation (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*).

I shall obstruct your rehabilitation from offense, obstruct the *poṣadha* ceremony, and obstruct the *pravāraṇā*. Just as a horse-tamer who finds a wicked horse difficult to train immediately restrains it with a bridle and drives it away, so too regarding such a bhikṣu, one should not first seek his permission;
this itself constitutes permission. (From the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*)
The *Gā* says: To expose another’s transgression using the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is a *duṣkṛta*. The same applies to the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*).
○ Sixty-five: Imparting the precepts improperly. This is a shared rule for Mahāyāna bhikṣus.

When one has reached twenty years of age, they should receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*). If a bhikṣu knows that a person is less than twenty years of age and yet confers the full ordination upon them, this person does not obtain the precepts.
That bhikṣu is to be rebuked for his folly; it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The Case: Seventeen groups of youths were former friends. The eldest was seventeen years old and the youngest was twelve.
They sought ordination together, and the bhikṣus conferred the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon them. However, they were unable to endure even a single meal.
At midnight, he suffered from remorse and cried out loudly in lamentation. The Buddha heard this and questioned Ānanda, who answered in full detail, whereupon the Buddha established this precept:

If a *upādhyāya* (preceptor), whether knowing or suspecting [the candidate’s faults], confers the full ordination (*upasampadā*), it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense once the third *karmavācanā* is completed. (2)

When the *karmavācanā* is completed, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses: one *duṣkṛta* when the *karmavācanā* is finished, two *duṣkṛta* when the *karmavācanā* is half-finished, and one *duṣkṛta* when the formal motion (*jñapti*) is finished.
From the time one undertakes the preliminary preparations up until the assembly of the Saṃgha, all constitute *duṣkṛta*.

If the Saṃgha knows or suspects [the offense], it is entirely *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *pāyattika*. There is no offense for one who did not previously know [of the situation] and has faith.

The words of the person receiving the precepts: if there are witnesses among bystanders, or if one trusts one’s parents, yet after having received the precepts one has doubts, it is permitted to count the months of the pregnancy as part of the years, or to count all [the months].
Fourteen *poṣadha* observances are taken as the number of years. (Every half-month a *poṣadha* is observed; in a year there are twenty-four such occasions.

During the bright fortnight and the major dark fortnight, the *poṣadha* is observed on the fifteenth day. If the dark fortnight is short, the *poṣadha* is observed on the fourteenth day. In a single year, there are only six occasions when the *poṣadha* is observed on the fourteenth day.)

Originally, there were eighteen occasions for the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day. Now, by employing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), all are calculated as *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day; thus, eighteen days are saved each year. Over ten years, this amounts to one hundred and eighty days.
If that person is nineteen years old, a total of three hundred and forty-two days are saved, which can be calculated as one additional year, thereby allowing them to be called "twenty years of age.
The *Upasampadā-kaṇḍa* states: "If one attains the state of an Arhat, they are then said to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*). The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If..."

At the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), if one’s age has not actually reached the required number but one conceives the thought that it has, and later a friend informs them that they are not yet full [of years], they should calculate the months of gestation and intercalary months.
If the total is sufficient, it is well; if it is not sufficient, they must revert to the status of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) and receive full ordination again.
Otherwise, they become one who dwells as a thief (*steyasaṃvāsika*). If one is nineteen years old but conceives the thought that they are twenty...

Having received full ordination (*upasampadā*), if after one year has passed a friend comes to see him and reports that he has not yet completed the required time, or if he himself remembers and realizes he has not completed it;
or if he was eighteen years old when he received full ordination and after two years have passed he likewise remembers and realizes this—these cases are all considered "properly received.
For the true teaching is difficult to encounter, and thus these instances are permitted by the Buddha.
66. The precept on instigating disputes. This is likewise regulated in the Mahāyāna.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that a dispute has already been settled according to the Dharma through confession, subsequently instigates it again, he commits a pāyattika offense.
The缘 (nidāna): The group of six [monks], knowing that a legal dispute had been settled according to the Dharma, spoke again as follows:
"You did not observe well; your observation was not established. You did not understand well; your understanding was not established. You did not settle well; your settlement was not established.
You caused disputes to arise where none existed before, and you failed to settle those disputes that already existed. Therefore, it was prescribed.
Commentary: "In accordance with the Dharma" means according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to what the Buddha has taught. There are four kinds of disputes:
disputes concerning speech (*vāda-vivāda*), disputes concerning accusations (*anuvāda-vivāda*), disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti-vivāda*), and disputes concerning legal matters (*kicca-vivāda*).
If one intentionally initiates speech that causes a dispute, it is a *pāyattika* offense if the words are clearly understood; it is a *dukkaṭa* (transgression) if they are not clearly understood.
Initiating other disputes, quarrels, or insults, as well as [instigating] a dispute that has already occurred, or causing others to dispute, is entirely a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*; for the other three assemblies, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense in cases such as when one has truly failed to observe properly.

The precept against not relinquishing wrong views: In the Mahāyāna, this constitutes a grave offense (pārājika), because it is a denigration of the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu should speak thus: "I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path," that bhikṣu should admonish him, saying:
