One must not sit with hands placed on the hips when entering the house of a layperson; this is how one should train (13).
Placing hands on the hips or resting elbows on the knees obstructs those sitting nearby. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One must not sit with the palms supporting the cheeks."
One must not walk into the house of a layperson while swaying the body; this is how one should train (the fourteenth).
"Swaying the body" means walking with the body twisting to the left and right. For a bhikṣuṇī who does so, it is a pāyattika offense.
There is no offense if she has such an illness, or if she is being struck by someone and twists her body to avoid the blow, or if there is a rogue elephant or lion.
He encounters those who touch him, or meets people carrying thorny branches; in such circumstances, he moves his body to avoid them.
Or, when crossing ditches, canals, or muddy water, he sways his body as he passes through. At times, when putting on his robes, he turns his body to check that they are properly aligned.
One should train oneself: "I shall not enter the house of a layperson while swaying the body and then sit down.
(15) One should train oneself: "I shall not enter the house of a layperson while dangling my arms. (16)
Hanging down the arms and then withdrawing them is also [permissible]. There is no offense if the companion walking alongside cannot keep up and one beckons with the hand;
the rest is as stated above. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one wishes to call someone, one must not raise both hands; one should beckon with only one hand."
One must not enter the house of a layperson with arms swinging about and sit down; this is how one should train (17).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not sit inside a house while moving one's hands or feet."
One should train oneself to enter the homes of laypeople with the body well-covered (18).
"Not well-covered" means being exposed in various parts of the body. There is no offense if one is bound, or if the wind blows the robe away from the body.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The *antarvāsa* (inner robe) should be made of a dense fabric; if it is thin, it should be made in two or three layers.
If the *antarvāsa* is thin, the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) should be made of a dense fabric.
If the *uttarāsaṅga* is thin, the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) should be made of a dense fabric. If the *saṃghāṭī* is thin, the *uttarāsaṅga*..."
The *saṃghāṭī* should be made of fine material. Question: It is currently handed down that the Buddha prescribed the three robes (*tricīvara*) all to be made of coarse hemp cloth;
why is this? Answer: Regarding the three robes of a *bhikṣu*, their purpose is to ward off the cold and shield against the heat. According to the Vinaya, ten types are fully enumerated, namely:
cotton cloth (*karpāsa*), *kṣauma* (linen) cloth, and so forth. How could it be that they are made only of coarse [material]?

Regarding the account of the coarse hempen cloth: it originated simply because when the World-Honored One first left the household life, having discarded his precious and fine garments, a tree deity offered him a single hempen robe.
This hempen robe was actually one left behind by a Pratyekabuddha a hundred years prior; it was extremely refined and certainly not coarse.
In later generations, as the story was passed down through successive generations, errors crept in and critical examination was lost, resulting in [the current misconception].
These are merely words. Although in this region there are currently separate garments that follow local custom, it is not necessarily required that they be double or triple-layered.
Furthermore, the claim that only hemp cloth is permitted while cotton cloth is forbidden is certainly not found in the Vinaya texts.
One should train oneself: "I shall sit well-covered in the houses of laypeople" (19).
One should train oneself: "I shall not walk into the houses of laypeople while looking left and right" (20).
There is no offense in the following cases: when looking up at the time; or when there is danger to life or danger to one's holy life (*brahmacarya*);

or when seeking a path of escape by looking around in every direction. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When walking, one must look attentively; one must not walk with the head lowered like a horse.
One should walk with a level gaze to guard against wild elephants, oxen, or horses, and should walk like a person carrying a palanquin. One must not [walk otherwise].
Regarding looking toward the east or west: if one wishes to look, one should turn the body toward the place being looked at. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:
"Not looking upward" means raising the eyes to look ahead at a distance of one *vyāma*. As for the measure of a *vyāma*, it is four cubits (*hasta*) in length.
One should not sit in the house of a layperson while looking left and right; this is how one should train (21).
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One should not sit down abruptly without being invited to do so; one should not sit down without having carefully observed the surroundings."
One should train oneself to enter the house of a layperson in silence (22).
"Not silent" means speaking loudly or calling out at a high pitch. There is no offense if the person is deaf and does not hear the sound.
One should train oneself to sit silently in the houses of laypeople (23).
One should train oneself not to enter the houses of laypeople while laughing or joking (24).
To smile with the teeth exposed. Exceptions where there is no offense include: when the lips are painful and one cannot cover the teeth; or when one smiles out of joy while contemplating the Dharma.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If there is something laughable, one must not laugh loudly with the gums bared and the teeth visible."
One should endure it. One should cultivate the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and death.
If [the urge] still does not cease, one should cover the mouth with the corner of one’s robe. The *Mātṛkā* states: "If one does not cover the mouth when yawning, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
One should not sit in the house of a layperson while laughing or joking; this is a training rule (25).
One should eat with mindfulness and attention; this is a training rule (26).
"Without paying attention" means discarding the soup and rice. "Not committing an offense" means that because the bowl is small, the rice falls onto the table. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"One who receives food with a single-minded focus holds the bowl with the left hand with single-minded focus, while supporting the rim with the right hand."
One should learn to receive food with a level bowl (27).
"Not leveling the bowl" means it is overflowing. There is no offense if, at times, because the bowl is small, the food falls back onto the table.
One should train oneself to receive soup in a level bowl (28).
Because the group of six received rice in such excess that there was no room to receive soup, it was therefore prescribed:
one should train oneself to eat soup and rice in equal measure (29).
Regarding "not waiting": the soup has not yet arrived while the rice is already finished; or the rice has not yet arrived while the soup is already finished.

There is no offense if, at that time, one specifically requires soup and does not require rice, or if one specifically requires rice and does not require soup; or if the time for eating is about to pass;
or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya) and one eats quickly.
One should eat in order; this is how one should train (30).

"Out of order" means taking food from various places within the bowl to eat. There is no offense in cases such as when the rice is hot and one scoops out a cool spot, or when the time for the meal is about to pass.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One must not select choice foods from within the bowl."
One must not pick at the food in the bowl while eating. This should be studied in detail (31).

[One should] place [the food] on the four sides and pick from the center down to the bottom of the bowl. There is no offense if one does so because the food is hot and wishes it to cool, or because the time for the meal is about to pass.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should not eat by picking up the bowl with bent fingers; one should not eat by sniffing the food."
If a bhikṣu who is not ill does not seek out soup or rice for himself, he should train himself thus (32).
This is because it is as if one were in a time of famine. There is no offense if he seeks it for himself when ill, or if he seeks it for another, or if another seeks it for him.
One must not cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more; one should train in this (33).
One must not look into the bowl of the person sitting beside oneself; one should train in this (34).

"Looking" means looking to see who has more and who has less. "Not transgressing" refers to when one's neighbor is blind; for their sake, one looks to see whether they have received food or not, whether it is pure or impure, and so forth.
One should train oneself (35): "While eating, one should maintain the mindfulness of keeping the bowl fastened.

To "not maintain the mindfulness of keeping the bowl fastened" means to look around to the left and right. There is no offense if, for instance, one looks toward a neighboring seat because of impaired vision, or if one observes the time of day and so forth.
One must not eat by forming large balls of rice; this is a training rule (thirty-sixth).
One must not allow the mouth to be filled [to capacity]. There is no offense if the time for the meal is about to pass, or if one eats quickly due to life-threatening dangers and the like.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not eat large mouthfuls; one must not eat small mouthfuls like a courtesan eating two or three grains at a time.
One should eat in a manner suited to the mouth.
One must not open the mouth wide and wait for the food. This is how one should train (37)."
No offense is incurred as described above.
One must not speak while eating rice; this is a training rule (38). There is no offense in the following cases:
when one is choking and asks for water, or when making noise while eating due to life-threatening danger. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Two..."
If the preceptor calls from above, one may respond if the mouthful has not yet been swallowed provided that the voice does not change; if this cannot be done, one must respond after swallowing.
If the person before you objects, one should reply: "There was food in my mouth, therefore I did not respond immediately. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"When receiving more food, it is permitted to say 'I need more' or 'I do not need more,' but one must not criticize or scold the food."
One must not form a ball of rice and throw it into the mouth from a distance; this is how one should train (39).
There is no offense if one is bound [in fetters].
One must train so as not to let food fall [on the ground] (40).
Half [of the food] enters the mouth; half remains in the hand. There is no offense in eating thin cakes, parched rice, melons, sugarcane, and the like.
One must not eat with cheeks full; this is how one should train. (41)
One should not intentionally fill the mouth so full that both cheeks bulge. There is no offense if the time for the meal is about to pass and so forth.
One must not chew food while making noise; this is how one should train. (42)
There is no offense in chewing dry cakes, scorched rice, fruits, melons, and the like. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When drinking congee, one must not make a sound;
when eating roots, stalks, and so forth, one must not make a loud noise. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"One must not swallow food whole, causing it to make a gurgling sound. However, there is no offense if one has a disease of the throat."
One must not take large mouthfuls of food. This is a training rule (43).
To "take [a mouthful]" means to open the mouth and call out from afar. There is no offense if one has a pain in the mouth, or if one is eating soup, curd, or gruel.
One must not lick food with the tongue; this is how one should train (44).
There are no offenses in cases where one is bound, or when there is grime on the hands. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not lick the hands while eating.
If ghee, oil, or other substances have adhered to the hands, one should gather them together by wiping them against the rim of the bowl, and only then take [the food]."
While eating, one must not count the fingers. However, if honey, salt, or similar substances are on the fingertips, it is permissible to count them; there is no offense.
One must not shake one's hand while eating; this is how one should train (45).
There is no offense if, for instance, there is grass or insects in the food, or if the hand is impure, and one shakes it off in order to remove them.
One must not eat with rice grains scattered in one's hands; this is how one should train (46).
"Scattered rice" refers to rice that has been dropped and discarded. There is no offense as previously explained. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
If food falls upon grass or leaves that have been received, it should be eaten. If there is soil upon it, one should blow the soil away and then eat. Or...
There are many indigenous people who obtain food by washing it;
one must not defile one's hands when holding a drinking vessel. This is a training rule (47).
If there is oily rice on the hand, there is no offense if one receives it upon grass, receives it upon leaves, or receives it after having washed the hands.
One must not discard bowl-washing water inside the residence of a layperson; this is how one should train (48).
There is no offense if one receives the water in a basin and discards it outside. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "If one asks the owner before discarding it, there is no offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One must not place leftover food into the water of the bowl. [The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*] says: "The Saṃgha..."
The *Ji-lü* (Mahīśāsaka-vinaya) states: When eating, one should take food according to the capacity of one’s stomach and must not accept more than necessary.

If a *karmadāna* (attendant) should suddenly give too much, before eating it, one should reduce the portion and give it to a neighboring seat-mate. If the neighbor does not take it, one should give it to a *śrāmaṇera* or a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*).
When washing the bowl, one must not let a single grain fall to the ground; if there are any [grains], they should be gathered together and placed [in a vessel].
If [the food] is on a board or on a leaf, or if it consists of fine grains or flour that cannot be gathered together,
there is no offense. *Zhòngzhì bīní shìyì jíyào*, Scroll Nine, Phonetics and Meanings.
*Ārīṭa* is not translated [into Chinese].
*Abhidharma* is sometimes called *Abhida-mo*. This is translated as "Incomparable Dharma" (*wubifa*) or "Dharma Corresponding to the Truth" (*duifa*);
it refers to the *Śāstra-piṭaka* (the Treatise Basket).
The *Kṣetra-sūtra* (契經) is precisely the *Sūtra-piṭaka* (修多羅藏). It is called "契" (*kṣetra*) because it accords with the capacities of sentient beings;
it is called "經" (*sūtra*) because it was proclaimed by the mouth of the Sage.
The character for "搏" (*bó*) is pronounced "博" (*bó*) and means to strike with the hand.
An army consists of twelve thousand five hundred men; "army" (shī) means a multitude.
*Nishīdana* is translated here as "sitting mat" (*zuòjù*) or "cloth for sitting" (*suízuò yī*).
*Nirvāṇaka* is also called *nivāsana* or *nivasana*; this translates as "skirt.
*Yī* (pronounced with the tone of *yí*) means "wound.
*Cuò* (with the phonetic *cái hé qiè*) refers to a "boil" or "pustule."
*Páibù* (俳步): both characters are pronounced *qiè*. It refers to various acrobatic performances.
*Qiān* (褰): the pronunciation is *qiān*. *Zhé* (襵):
the upper character is pronounced *zhé*; it refers to the pleats or folds of a garment. The lower character is pronounced *zòu*; it means to wrinkle or contract.
*Jiǎn* (跳-兆+專) is synonymous with *zuǎn*. Its pronunciation is *ruǎn*. It refers to the calf muscle.
*Saṃkakṣikā* was formerly called *saṃghaṭī*; this is translated as "arm-pit-covering garment. It is used to cover the right armpit and conceal the left shoulder.
*Chí* (尻) is pronounced with a level tone (*píngshēng*). It refers to the end of the spinal column.
*Yín* (齦) has the phonetic value of *yín*; it refers to the gums, the flesh at the base of the teeth.
When one "yawns" (*qiàn*), it refers to the act of stretching the face and limbs (*pínshēn*).
*Tuán* (搏): "tuán" in sound; to grasp and gather together with the hand.
*Yè* (噎): "yè" in sound; the throat is constricted so that the breath cannot pass.
*Chuò* (啜): *chāng yuè* in sound; identical to *chuài*.
The sound of "wa" is pronounced like "wa. It is the sound of drinking.
"Xi" (噏) is the same as "xi" (吸).
"Shi" (舐) is pronounced with the initial "shen" and the final "zhi" (神紙切); it means to take things with the tongue.
Gài (pronounced xì) or Gài (pronounced gài): to wipe and take up.
Shù (pronounced shù): to examine repeatedly.
*Zhòngzhì Píní Shìyì Jīyào*, Scroll Ten.
The Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of Ancient Wu compiled this commentary:
One must not void excrement, urine, mucus, or spit upon living grass or vegetables, except in cases of illness. This is a training rule (forty-nine).

For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a pāyattika offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if one voids excrement or urine in a place where there is no growing grass or vegetables, and it falls onto growing grass or vegetables;
or if it is blown by the wind or carried by birds and drops onto growing grass or vegetables. The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "There is no offense in a thicket of thorns.
If one is walking through a great forest where branches and leaves are densely interlaced, one should remain away from people."
If one is in a place where there is no open space amidst fields of living grass, one should carry dry leaves and perform the act of defecation upon them.
If such leaves cannot be obtained, there is no offense.
One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate in water, except when ill; this is a training rule (fifty).
The offense is as described above. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya* states: "If it is water that people do not use, or seawater, there is no offense.
Even if the water is fit for use, if it is in a remote place where no one uses it, there is no offense."
One must not stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill; this is a training rule (fifty-one).
There is no offense if one is bound, or if the feet are covered in mud or filth.
One must not preach the Dharma to a person who has their robe draped over one shoulder and lacks respect, except when they are ill; this is a training rule (52).
One must not preach the Dharma to a person whose robe is wrapped around their neck, except when they are ill; this is a training rule (53).
One should not preach the Dharma to those who have their heads covered, except in cases of illness; this is a training rule (54).
One should not preach the Dharma to those who have their heads wrapped, except in cases of illness; this is a training rule (55).
One should not preach the Dharma to one who has their hands on their hips, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (56).
One should not preach the Dharma to one wearing leather sandals, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (57).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If many people are wearing leather sandals and one cannot cause them to remove them, it is not an offense to preach the Dharma to those who are not wearing them.
One must not preach the Dharma to those wearing wooden clogs, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train (58)."
One must not preach the Dharma to those who are riding in vehicles, except in cases of illness; this is how one should train (the fifty-ninth precept). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
King Prasenajit was traveling in a carriage toward the Jeta Grove when he saw the Buddha. The group of six monks preached the Dharma for the king. Therefore, [the Buddha] established these rules:

[one must not preach] while the person is ahead and oneself is behind; while the person is on the path and oneself is off the path; while the person is seated and oneself is standing; while the person is...
Sitting on a high seat while the other is on a low seat; sitting while the other is lying down; covering the head; wrapping the head; hiding the elbows; placing hands on the hips;
tucking up one side of the robe; covering the right shoulder; wearing leather sandals; wearing wooden clogs; holding a staff; holding a parasol; holding a sword;
holding a shield, bow, or arrows—the origins of these cases are all the same, as is the case in the *Śīla-nidāna-sūtra*.
One must not stay overnight in a Buddhist stūpa, except for the purpose of guarding it; this is how one should train (60).
There is no offense in cases such as being captured or facing a threat to life. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:
"In all cases, such as incense altars, halls, flagpoles, and *caityas*, one should recite verses before stepping upon them. Otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
One must not conceal wealth or property within a Buddhist stūpa, except for the purpose of securing it; this is a training rule (61).
One must not enter a Buddhist stūpa wearing leather sandals; this is a training rule (62).
One must not enter a Buddhist stūpa holding leather sandals in one's hands; this is a training rule (63).
One must not circumambulate a Buddhist stūpa while wearing leather sandals; this is a training rule (64).
One should train oneself not to enter a Buddhist stūpa wearing shoes (pūvara).
(65) One should train oneself not to enter a Buddhist stūpa holding shoes in one's hands. (66)
There is no offense if one is seized by force and led into a stūpa.
One should train oneself not to sit or eat beneath a stūpa, nor to leave grass or food that defiles the ground. (67)
There is no offense if [the robe] is gathered and placed at one's feet, and carried out to be discarded when departing.
One must not carry a corpse past the interior of a stūpa; this is how one should train. (68)
There is no offense if one must travel by this path, or if one is led there by force.
One must not bury a corpse beneath a stūpa; this is how one should train. (69)
One must not burn a corpse beneath a stūpa; this is a training rule (70).
One must not burn a corpse facing a stūpa; this is a training rule (71).
One must not burn corpses within four paces of a Buddha-stūpa so that the stench enters it; this is a training to be observed (72).
One must not carry a corpse’s clothing or bed beneath a stūpa, except when they have been washed, dyed, or perfumed;
this is a training to be observed (73).
One should train oneself: "I shall not defecate or urinate beneath a stūpa" (74).
One should train oneself: "I shall not defecate or urinate facing a stūpa" (75).
One must not defecate or urinate on any side of a Buddha-stūpa so that a foul odor enters it; this is a training to be observed (76).
One must not carry an image of the Buddha to places for defecating or urinating; this is a training to be observed (77).
There is no offense if the path passes through the middle, or if one is held by force.
One must not chew a tooth-stick beneath a Buddhist stūpa; this is how one should train. (78)
One should train oneself not to chew tooth-sticks toward a Buddha stūpa (79).
One should train oneself not to chew tooth-sticks within four paces of a Buddha stūpa (80).
One should train oneself not to spit beneath a stūpa (81).
One should train oneself not to spit toward a stūpa (82).
One must not spit or expectorate on the four sides of a stūpa; this is a training to be observed (83).
One must not sit with legs extended toward a stūpa; this is a training to be observed (84).
There is no offense if there is a partition between them, or if one is held by force. The Fourth Division states:
"If the stūpas within the monastery grounds are full, it is permitted to sit with legs extended in the space between them."
One must not reside in an upper room while placing a Buddha-stūpa in a lower room; this is a training rule (85).
There is no offense in cases where life is at risk or where the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is threatened.
If another person is seated and one is standing, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train (86).

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: If a bhikṣu, on account of matters concerning the stūpa or the Saṃgha, goes before a king or a local lord, and that person says, "Bhikṣu, preach the Dharma to me," he must not tell him to stand up, for fear of causing suspicion. If there is someone nearby...
Regarding "one who is standing": this refers to preaching the Dharma to one who is standing while making a deliberate effort to do so. Even if the king permits it, there is no offense for the bhikṣu.
One must not preach the Dharma to one who is lying down while oneself is sitting, except in the case of illness; this is how one should train (87).
If another person is seated and one is not seated, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (88).
If another person is on a high seat and one is on a low seat, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (89).
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "In the past, there was a householder in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī whose wife became pregnant and longed for mangoes (*āmra-phala*).
At night, her husband entered the royal garden to steal some fruit but did not succeed.
When the first light of dawn appeared, he remained hidden in the tree. At that time, the king and a brahmin entered the garden wishing to eat mangoes. Brahma... [text continues]
The brahmin was below, while the king sat upon a high throne. As the brahmin preached the Dharma to the king, the fruit-thief thought to himself:
"I should have died, yet now I am free. There is no Dharma for me; there is no Dharma for the king;
and there is no Dharma for the brahmin either. For the sake of a woman, I stole the king’s fruit; yet the king remains arrogant, and the teacher sits below."
While he was listening to the Dharma from his high seat, the brahmin, out of greed for offerings and gain, descended from his own seat and preached the Dharma to the king.
"I have no connection with either the king or this brahmin; I am now liberated. Having said this, he immediately descended from the tree and spoke a verse to the king.
At that time, the person who had stolen the fruit was none other than the Tathāgata.
If another person is walking ahead and one is walking behind, one must not preach the Dharma to them. One should train oneself in this except in cases of illness (the ninety-first rule).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu has an eye ailment and another person holds a staff to lead him forward, there is no offense in preaching the Dharma for him."
If another person is on a high walking path and oneself is on a lower walking path, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
This is how one should train (91).
If others are on the path and one is not on the path, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except when they are ill; this is a training rule (92).
One should train oneself not to walk along a path while holding hands with others; this is a training rule (93).
There is no offense if one has impaired vision and requires assistance;
however, one must not climb a tree higher than a person’s height, except under specific circumstances. This is a training rule (94).
A certain bhikṣu entered the rains retreat upon a large tree. He voided excrement and urine from the tree down below.
A tree deity became resentful of this. The Buddha then established the rule that one must not enter the rains retreat upon a tree, nor may one void excrement or urine around a tree.
However, if there was already a place for such disposal, there is no offense in voiding excrement or urine there. Later, another bhikṣu encountered a fierce beast on his way.
When climbing a tree out of fear, one must not go too high, lest one be harmed by wild beasts;

therefore, there are specific causes and conditions for such actions (such as when śrāmaṇeras climb trees to gather twigs, flowers, or fruit, they commit no offense). The *An-gu-jian-du* (Kṣudraka-vastu) states: "If one wishes to take dry firewood from atop a tree..."
It is permitted to take [the bowl] by using a hook, by using a ladder, or by using a rope noose. If the entire tree is dry, it is permitted to climb it.
One must not travel with a bag containing the bowl slung over the shoulder by threading it onto the end of a staff; this is how one should train (95).
Bhadanta walked in this manner. When householders saw him, they thought he was an official and all stepped off the road to avoid him;

therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule. There is no offense in cases such as being seized by force. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: "One should not walk carrying things on one's back, except within a monastery.
For an elderly bhikṣu who requires a staff and a shoulder-sling (*kaṭhalla-kośa*), it is permitted to perform the formal ritual of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to provide them."
One should not preach the Dharma to a person who holds a staff without showing respect, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (96).
One should not preach the Dharma to a person who holds a sword, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (97).
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a spear, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (98).
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a sword, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (99).
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a parasol, except in the case of illness; this is a training rule (the hundredth).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu is on a dangerous and fearful road and a guard says, 'Venerable One, please preach the Dharma for me,' it is not an offense to preach for him."
The third formal inquiry:
"Venerable sirs, I have already recited the rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*). Now I ask the venerable sirs:
Are you pure in this matter? (This is asked three times. Venerable sirs, since there is silence, you are pure in this matter. Thus shall this be held."
Appendix: The Fourth Division states: "If the hairs in the nostrils are long, one may use tweezers to pull them out. If the nails are extremely long, like a grain of barley, they should be clipped;
one should not dye the nails with colored pigments. One should not use scissors to trim the beard and hair;
rather, the sideburns and hair should be shaved off entirely. If the hair is extremely long, it should be no longer than two finger-widths; [if it exceeds this], every two months..."
One should shave [the head]. One should not comb the beard or hair. One should not apply oil to the hair. One should not paint the eyes or the face.
If one suffers from eye pain, the application of medicine is permitted. One should not look at one's face in a mirror or in water. If the face has sores, the application of medicine is permitted.
One is permitted to stay alone in a room and look [at oneself] with water or a mirror. One should not wear earrings.
One should wear necklaces, armlets, anklets, rings, and finger-seals. One should not make a waistband of lead or tin.
One should not use five-colored thread to bind across the armpits or around the waist and arms. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"It is permitted to ride in a cart drawn by a bull with a dewlap, provided another person drives it; one must not drive it oneself. Combing or brushing the hair constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."
To leave a small amount of hair at the crown is a *duṣkṛta* offense. To let the hair grow long is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For an *āraṇyaka* bhikṣu, it is not an offense if the hair grows to two inches in length. If there is a sore on the head, one should trim it with scissors.
To rub the beard and hair with the hands is a *duṣkṛta* offense. When washing the feet, one must not converse with others. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There may be occasions when there is a matter regarding which I have neither previously prohibited nor permitted.
In such a case, if acting contrary to it results in impurity while following it results in purity, then this is pure and should be practiced.
If acting contrary to it results in purity while following it results in impurity, then this is impure and should not be practiced."
Seven. The section on the *Saiksa-dharmas* is concluded. ○ Eight.

The seven methods for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamatha-dharmas*). Three parts: first, the general heading; second, the detailed enumeration; third, the concluding inquiry. ○ First, the general heading:
These seven kinds of dharmas are studied by Mahayana bhiksus alike; they should skillfully harmonize those who are in conflict.
Because of disputes. Each of these origins is found within the third section, the *Khandhaka on the Settlement of Disputes*.
"Venerable sirs, these seven principles for settling disputes are recited every half-month from the midst of the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra.
If a dispute arises among the bhikṣus, it should be settled immediately."
Commentary: There are four kinds of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*). First, the dispute of speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*):

when bhikṣus dispute with one another, citing eighteen grounds for dispute, ranging from "dharma" and "adharma" to "what has been spoken" and "what has not been spoken. If they thus engage in mutual verbal contention, it eventually leads to physical fighting between them.
Second, the dispute of seeking [faults] (*anveṣaṇa-adhikaraṇa*): when a bhikṣu seeks out the offenses of another bhikṣu by means of the three...
Regarding the raising of a case: [the accused] has violated the precepts, violated the views, or violated the deportment; having seen, heard, or suspected such signs, one seeks out their offense.
As for the three types of disputes arising from offenses, there are seven kinds of offenses: first, a *pārājika*; second, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, a *pāyattika*; fourth, a *pratideśanīya*.
Five *sthūlātyaya*, six *duṣkṛta*, and seven *durbhāṣita*. Regarding the four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*): the first three disputes involve the underlying matter (*vastu*).

Among these, a dispute concerning speech (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*) is settled by two *vinayas*: namely, *sammukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of) and *yadbhūyaśo-vāda* (the majority decision), or it may be settled by only one *vinaya*, namely *sammukha-vinaya*.

A dispute concerning investigation (*anveṣaṇa-adhikaraṇa*) is settled by four *vinayas*: namely, *sammukha-vinaya*, *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement through recollection), *amūḍha-vinaya* (settlement for one no longer insane), and *pratijñā-kāraka-vinaya* (settlement by admission).

Either it is settled by means of *saṃmukha* (presence) and *amūḍha* (non-delusion), or it is settled by means of *saṃmukha* and *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (investigation of the basis of the offense); that is, the dispute regarding an offense is extinguished by three *vinayas*:
namely, *saṃmukha*, *pratijñākāraka* (adjudication by confession), or *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass). A dispute regarding a matter (*adhikaraṇa*) is extinguished by all *vinayas*.

According to the offenses committed, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "There are six roots of dispute: first, harboring resentment and refusing to speak; second, having an evil nature and desiring to harm others;
third, greed and jealousy; fourth, flattery and crookedness; fifth, lack of shame and lack of remorse; sixth, evil desires and false views."

Regarding the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties): the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that there are ten types of *adharmika* (unlawful) *pratijñā-kṣānti* (settlement by confession).

These include: confessing non-offense when one has committed an offense of the five categories; or confessing offense when one has not committed an offense of the five categories. There are ten types of *dharmika* (lawful) [settlement]: confessing offense when one has committed an offense of the five categories;
and confessing non-offense when one has not committed an offense of the five categories. This constitutes settlement in the presence of the parties.
Regarding disputes, there are two kinds of what is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*): if one who acts contrary to the Dharma commands another who acts contrary to the Dharma to be subdued;
or if one who acts contrary to the Dharma commands one who acts in accordance with the Dharma (*dharma*) to be subdued. There are two kinds of what is in accordance with the Dharma:

if one who acts in accordance with the Dharma commands another who acts in accordance with the Dharma to be subdued; or if one who acts in accordance with the Dharma commands one who acts contrary to the Dharma to be subdued.
Regarding the *tarjanīya* (reproof), the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection), there are three types of illegality:

if a bhikṣu has committed an offense that does not entail expulsion (*anavaśeṣa*), yet he himself declares that he has committed an offense entailing expulsion and requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha, if it is granted, it is illegal;

for he should instead be subject to formal suspension (*pravāsanīya*). Furthermore, if a bhikṣu who was insane or deluded regains his sanity and requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha, if it is granted...

It is contrary to the Dharma. Because the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who was not deluded) should be granted. Suppose there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense regarding which he has seen, heard, or suspected;
he himself says, "I have this offense," but later says, "I do not have this offense. He then requests the *smṛti-vinaya* (the discipline for recollection) from the Saṃgha.

If it is granted, it is contrary to the Dharma, because the *tattvānusaraṇa-vinaya* (the discipline for seeking the truth, i.e., the investigation of the characteristics of the offense) should be granted. There are three cases that are in accordance with the Dharma. Suppose there is a bhikṣu...
If one is falsely accused of a groundless charge, and someone constantly speaks of this matter, the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) should be granted.
If a bhikṣu has committed an offense and has already repented and removed it, yet someone still speaks of this matter, the *smṛtivinaya* should be granted.
If a bhikṣu has not yet committed an offense but is likely to do so in the future, and someone says he has committed it, the *smṛtivinaya* should be granted.

Regarding the *vinaya* of one not insane (*amūḍha-vinaya*), there are four kinds of what is contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*). Suppose there is a bhikṣu who is not insane, yet manifests the appearance of being insane.
When questioned, he replies: "I remember doing it intentionally while insane; another person instructed me to do it; I remember doing it in a dream;
I remember running here and there naked, standing, or voiding excrement. Such a person requests the *vinaya* of one not insane.
If a nun grants it, it is contrary to the Dharma. There are four cases where it is in accordance with the Dharma. Suppose there is a bhikṣu who is truly insane, deluded, and mentally inverted;
when questioned, he replies: "I do not remember; others did not instruct me; I do not remember acting in a dream;

I do not remember running or standing here and there naked, or urinating and defecating. If such a person requests the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one no longer insane), and it is granted, it is in accordance with the Dharma.

The *yathābhūta-vijñapti* (seeking according to reality) is for settling disputes. There are five types that are contrary to the Dharma (*adharma*). Suppose there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense belonging to one of the five categories of offenses (*pañcāpatti-skandha*).

If he first says he did not commit it and later says he did, yet he is granted the *yathābhūta-vijñapti*, this is contrary to the Dharma; for he should be disciplined according to what he actually committed. Thus, there are five types that are in accordance with the Dharma (*dharma*).
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense belonging to one of the five categories of offenses. If he first says he committed it and later says he did not, this is...
A person should grant the *yadbhūyaḥ-vinaya* (verdict according to the majority). The *Mūla-maudgalyāyanīya* states:

"If two bhikṣus have come into conflict and engage in various discordant words, mutually slandering and reviling one another, regarding these two persons, one should trust the one who maintains the precepts.
If both maintain the precepts, one should trust the one who is more learned (*bahuśruta*). If both are equally learned, one should trust the one who is younger."
Regarding desire: if both parties have few desires, one should place faith in those who possess the utmost fewness of desires.
It is impossible for a rift to arise between two who both possess the utmost fewness of desires. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If there are persons of great virtue and excellence..."
Those who wish to listen to the settlement of a matter by the Saṃgha may hear that settlement.

One should have a person within the assembly who possesses eloquence and the ability to speak, such that the details of the case become clear, explain it. If one settles a matter before ordinary laypeople, it is an offense of transgression against the Vinaya.
Bian asked: "In all matters of adjudicating cases, there are only four types of disputes.
In all four of these disputes, the faults of the bhikṣus are disclosed to outsiders, and each carries a grave prohibition.

Now, since it is not permitted to adjudicate cases before ordinary laypeople, for what reason are you alone, O Virtuous One, permitted to hear them? Even if they possess wisdom, they cannot avoid [the fault]."
If one who has not yet received full ordination adjudicates a legal matter before such a person, does this not violate the Vinaya? Answer:

Although the term "adjudicating legal matters" generally refers to all four types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), it mostly concerns matters within the category of disputes over the Dharma (*dhammādhikaraṇa*).

Within these, through the analytical discernment and subduing of what is lawful (*dhamma*) and what is unlawful (*adhamma*), and so forth, one can cause virtuous and eminent persons who hear them to increase their faith. Therefore, speaking in such a manner is permitted.

This does not refer to matters such as the formal act of penalizing a transgression (*karmavācanā*). Regarding the term "virtuous person" (*bhadanta*), it refers to those such as King Prasenajit and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada;
because their wisdom is profound and their faith is correct, they do not slander [the Dharma], and are thus called "virtuous."

Because they possess such heavy merit that they are able to protect the True Dharma, they are called "superior persons" (jinren). How could they be merely those of ordinary wealth and status? Appendix:
A bhikṣu who possesses ten qualities should be appointed to adjudicate matters of dispute. First, he must be fully endowed with the observance of the precepts.
2. Being well-versed in the teachings; 3. Having thoroughly mastered the recitation of both divisions of the Vinaya; 4. Extensively understanding their meaning; 5.
Being skillful in speech, with clear eloquence and the capacity for dialogue, enabling one to bring others to joy; 6. Being able to extinguish disputes when they arise;
7. Being without attachment; 8. Being without anger; 9. Being without fear; 10. Being without delusion. The Fourth Division states: "The Buddha..."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "One should know that a person who adjudicates legal cases possesses twenty-two qualities:
(1) they fully uphold the two hundred and fifty precepts; (2) they are widely learned and well-versed in the Abhidharma and Vinaya;

(3) they do not engage in disputes with others; (4) nor do they stubbornly adhere to their own views; (5) they reprove those who deserve reproach before proceeding; (6) they instruct those who deserve instruction."
Then, one should abide (7). After performing the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against one who deserves it, one should then abide (8).
One should not harbor affection (9), nor anger (10), nor fear (11), nor delusion (12). One should not accept food or drink from this group (13), nor accept food or drink from that group (14).
One should not accept robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, or needle-cases from this group (15), nor accept them from that group.
16. [Not sharing] robes, alms-bowls, sitting mats, or needle-cases; 17. Not providing for this group; 18. Nor providing for that group; 19.
Not entering a village together with this group; 20. Nor entering a village together with that group;
21. Not making a prior appointment or agreement; 22. Nor arriving there later or taking a seat later. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
A bhikṣu who is endowed with five qualities is able to extinguish disputes: he knows what is true and not untrue; he knows what is beneficial and not unbeneficial;
he finds companions and does not fail to find them; he finds impartial companions and does not fail to find them;
he finds the proper time and does not fail to find it. One who is endowed with these fourteen qualities is called the foremost upholder of the Vinaya.
First. Excluding the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, what are the fourteen? They are: knowing the offense; knowing the non-offense;
knowing the heavy; knowing the light; knowing concealment; knowing non-concealment; knowing what is curable; knowing what is incurable;

knowing the attainment of purification; knowing the non-attainment of purification; attaining the four meritorious qualities that abide in happiness in the present life—namely, the divine eye and the [divine ear].
The divine ear, the knowledge of past lives, and the exhaustion of outflows to attain the state beyond outflows—these are called the fourteen dharmas.

There are seven matters that are *tāḍāgha* (also written as *kālātha*); they resemble *tāḍāgha*. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The term *ta-ra* means 'ground' (*bhūmi*), and the term *tha-li* means 'abiding' (*sthiti*). It signifies the supreme mastery of wisdom."

One remains unshakable in the True Dharma, like a person standing on solid ground who cannot be overturned. What are the seven? There may be one who, due to madness, does not join this assembly nor that assembly;
such a person is called a *thalattha*. This is the first type of *thalattha*, which resembles a *thalattha* but is not actually a *thalattha*.
Such is the disease of mental distraction, dullness, and delusion. Because of this disease, one does not attach to this assembly, nor does one attach to that assembly.
Furthermore, some people, for the sake of profit, think: "If I attach to this assembly, I will lose that profit;
if I attach to that assembly, I will lose this profit. Thus, they do not attach to either. Furthermore, some people [do not attach] because they have obtained the profit of both assemblies.
He reflects thus: "In order to attain the benefit of both sides, I shall not be attached to this assembly, nor shall I be attached to that assembly.
This is called *na-tathā-tathā* (not so, not so). There are two kinds of *tathā* (so): first, guarding one's own mind.
Seeing the right and wrong of others, one should think: "The doer of karmic actions knows them for himself;

it is like being caught in a fire—one must only save oneself, so how can one concern oneself with the affairs of others? Second is waiting for the proper time: seeing others engaged in disputes and mutual accusations, one should think thus:
"This dispute and verbal contention shall be adjudicated when the time arrives; this is called the second *talaṭṭha*.

One partakes of the Dharma-food and flavor-food with this assembly, and likewise partakes of the Dharma-food and flavor-food with that assembly. Whether requested to adjudicate the matter or unrequested, one shall adjudicate it.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One who employs anger and resentment does not extinguish anger and resentment."

Only through the power of patience can it be extinguished. There are five circumstances in which a dispute is difficult to settle: not seeking resolution by the Saṃgha; not complying with the Buddha’s words;
not making a formal announcement (jñapti) according to the Dharma; the contentious minds of both assemblies do not cease; and one does not seek purification for the offense committed.
The five matters mentioned above are easily extinguished. When the bhikṣu Tālaṭa takes up a dispute, he should examine it by means of these five matters:
among them, who first came [to the order] with pure observance of the precepts? Who is learned, wise, and well-versed in the Āgamas?
Who acts in accordance with the Dharma toward their teacher? Who has faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha? Who does not disparage the Buddha’s precepts? Oṛṅ!

There are ten qualities of a *kula-bhikṣu* (a monk who serves as a mediator), for whom the Saṃgha should appoint [as a mediator]. As the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* states: "The term *ud-dhega* means 'disturbed,' while *kula* means 'level. One whose mind is impartial and free from duality is as level as a scale.
These ten qualities are: knowing the place where a dispute arises and passes; knowing the root of a dispute; being skilled in understanding disputes;

being able to analyze disputes; knowing the causes and conditions that give rise to a dispute; knowing the meaning of a dispute; being skilled in extinguishing disputes; ensuring that once a dispute has been extinguished, it does not arise again; and maintaining pure observance of the precepts.
The practice of the monk Tāḷiṭṭha, who is learned and possessed of great wisdom, consists of twenty-two qualities by which one should know him to be of keen faculties and erudite:
(1) he well understands the root from which things arise; (2) he skillfully distinguishes the characteristics of things; (3) he well understands the distinctions among things;
(4) he well understands the beginning and end of things; (5) he well understands the lightness and heaviness of things; (6) he well understands... [and so forth].

1. The matter of eradication; 2. Skillfully knowing that once eradicated, the matter does not arise again; 3. Skillfully knowing the person who performs the task and the person for whom the task is performed;
4. Possessing the power of authoritative instruction; 5. Being able to cause others to receive [the instruction]; 6.
Possessing the power of skillful means and gentle speech; 7. Also being able to cause others to receive [it]; 8. Possessing the power of self-subjugation; 9. Also being able to...
15. Causing others to receive [the teachings]. 16. Knowing shame and remorse. 17. Having no prideful mind.
18. Having no prideful speech. 19. Having no partiality or attachment in the actions of body, speech, and mind.
20. Not following the course of desire. 21. Not following the course of hatred. 22. Not following the course of fear. 23. Not following the course of delusion.

II. A detailed enumeration of the seven [methods]. First, the method for settling disputes through presence (*sammukhā-vinaya*), up to the seventh, the method for settling disputes by covering over with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*).
I. First, the method for settling disputes through presence.
One should grant the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence); one ought to grant the *saṃmukhavinaya*. Commentary:
One should not perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) in the absence of the person concerned. What constitutes "being present"? It is being present in regard to the Dharma and the Vinaya.

Regarding persons, the Saṃgha, and the boundary: what is "the presence of the Dharma"? It is that which consists of the Dharma held [by the assembly] to settle the dispute. What is "the presence of the Vinaya"?
It is that which consists of the Vinaya held [by the assembly] to settle the dispute. What is "the presence of the person"? It is the exchange of words and meanings [between the disputants].
What is "the presence of the Saṃgha"? It is when they assemble together in one place for a formal act (*karmavācanā*), and those who do not attend have given their authorization.
"Bestowal" refers to one who, being present, ought to be censured but is not censured. What is "presence within the boundary"?
It refers to one who, being within the boundary, establishes a restriction through a formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*).

Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses: if a matter of dispute has been settled and one initiates it again, it is a *pāyattika*. If one has already given their consent (*chanda*) and later regrets it, it is a *pāyattika*.
The same applies to the six subsequent methods of settling disputes through the *vinaya*.
Appendix: The *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā* states that there are ten types of *karmavācanā* (formal acts) performed without the assembly being present:

(1) the overturning of the bowl (*pātra-nyāsa*), (2) the relinquishing of the overturning of the bowl, (3) the householder’s family [being placed under restriction], (4) the relinquishing of the householder’s family [restriction], (5) the construction of a dwelling, (6) a novice monk who is insane, (7) not performing prostrations, (8) not speaking together, and (9) making offerings.

[Regarding the first,] the overturning of the bowl: this is a disciplinary measure against a layperson, which may only be performed through a formal act (*karmavācanā*) from a distance. [Regarding the second,] the relinquishing of the overturning of the bowl: since the person has already made three requests, one must allow them to remain within sight and hearing.

1. Regarding "out of earshot": this is for the sake of relinquishing [the formal act]. 2. Regarding "those belonging to a family under training" (*śaikṣa-kula*): because they protect and cherish the donors and lay believers, one also acts from afar. 3. Regarding "relinquishing a family under training": even if they request three times, one must have them remain in a place where they are within sight but out of earshot, so as to effect the relinquishment.

4. Regarding "building a hut": this refers to using abandoned monastic land; having performed the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to grant it to a layperson, one allows them to build a dwelling for the Saṃgha. Furthermore, after they have requested three times, one grants it to them while they remain in a place where they are within sight but out of earshot. 5. Regarding "a novice" (*śrāmaṇera*):

when a novice with wrong views is expelled, one also has him remain in a place where he is within sight but out of earshot, so as to carry out the expulsion. 6. Regarding "the insane": regarding the *karmavācanā* for insanity, since that person already suffers from a disease of madness...

Because they cannot be restrained or bound by means of formal legal procedures (*dharma*), (8) one does not prostrate; (9) one does not converse; and (10) one does not offer worship. This refers to cases where a bhikṣu commits various illegal acts that disturb the community of bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha performs these three types of *karmavācanā* (formal acts).

These may only be performed from a distance; it is not permissible to bring a great bhikṣu before them to subject him to punishment. Thus, it is clear that for these ten matters alone there is no need for the person to be present, whereas for all others, their presence is required.
II. The Method for Settling Disputes through Remembrance (*smṛti-vinaya*).
One should grant the *smṛti-vinaya*; indeed, one must grant the *smṛti-vinaya*. The Case:
The Venerable Ṭaṣama-māra did not commit a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), yet that person persistently questioned him about it. [In such a case,] one should grant [the *smṛti-vinaya*].
Regarding the *Smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection): he should make three requests within the Saṃgha, saying: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. I, [Name], have not committed a grave offense.
Yet, the bhikṣus say that I have committed a grave offense—a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *sthūlātyaya*.
They ask me, 'Do you recall committing a grave offense? I reply, 'I do not recall committing a grave offense.'"
"Having committed such a grave offense, may the elders not repeatedly interrogate me.
Yet, the bhikṣus continue to interrogate me without ceasing; I now do not recall it. I beg the Saṃgha for the *smṛtivinaya*.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the *smṛtivinaya* by performing the formal motion and threefold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)."
Explanation: What is the *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by recollection)? It means that regarding this offense of that bhikṣu, it should no longer be raised, nor should there be further recollection.
(Because the community of bhikṣus had repeatedly caused him to recall [the offense], now this *smṛti-vinaya* is enacted so that he shall not be questioned further.)
III. The Method for Settling Disputes through Non-Insanity.
One should grant the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of sanity); one ought to grant the *amūḷhavinaya*. The occasion:
Nanda was deranged and his mind was disturbed, whereby he committed many offenses. Later, he regained his senses. The bhikṣus...

If the interrogation does not cease, the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who was not insane) should be granted. He should request it three times; the Saṃgha should grant it through a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
[Commentary: What is the *amūḍha-vinaya*? It is that wherein the offense of that bhikṣu should no longer be raised, nor should he be subjected to the procedure of calling to mind (*smṛti-karman*).
4. The Method for Settling Disputes through Confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
One should administer the penalty of confession; one must administer the penalty of confession. Regarding this:
when the Blessed One was reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, there was one who had committed an offense who sat near the Buddha. The Buddha remained silent and did not [reprove him].

[The Buddha] spoke thus. Maudgalyāyana knew of this; he seized the [nun's] arm and dragged her out. The Buddha said, "You should not do so. Let her confess her guilt first, and only then impose the penalty.

If you claim that violating it is equivalent to having no violation, then it would likewise follow that upholding it is equivalent to having no upholding; why, then, do you abandon it?
This constitutes the offense of grasping. If you claim that the mind is devoid of acceptance and rejection, then you should not accept the concise while discarding the detailed.
If you claim that purity and defilement are equal, then hell and heaven must also be equal; foul abuse and beautiful praise must also be equal;
sandalwood and musk and excrement and filth must also be equal; nectar and pus and blood must also be equal; and celestial garments and swords and staves must also be equal.
[And so forth. Why do you not dwell perpetually in hell? Why are you not called a pig, a dog, a beast, a shaven slave, or a shaven thief?
Why do you not constantly smell excrement and filth? Why do you not consume pus and blood?
Why are you not beaten, struck with weapons, or have your body cut by knives and staves? If you have truly realized the nature of equality, you will naturally not destroy conventional truth.
You will surely experience happiness in the present life and skillfully transform sentient beings.
If you force yourself to accept such superior matters, it means Māra has entered your mind; this is not the True Path.
Since you have neither yet realized the nature of equality nor attained such superior states, to act solely according to your whims and inclinations, becoming indolent and lazy, and refusing to—

To study this dharma of precepts is to dwell as a thief; one is not a śramaṇa, lacks shame and remorse, is like a worm within a lion’s body, is the greatest of thieves, is a kinsman of Māra, and is the seed of hell.
Why do you not contemplate that because the Tathāgata has realized the equality of form, he is able to transform both the hells and the celestial palaces into purity?
The Tathāgata, having realized the equality of sounds, is able to transform the evil cries of celestial Māras into hymns of praise.
The Tathāgata, having realized the equality of fragrances, is able to transform the latrine of a phantom person into a fragrant palace.
The Tathāgata, having realized the equality of tastes, is able to transform food mixed with poisonous drugs into nectar (*amṛta*). The Tathāgata...
Because he has realized the equality of touch, he can transform the swords and arrows of Māra’s army into celestial flowers.

Because the Tathāgata has realized the equality of all phenomena (*dharma*), he is not turned by external things but constantly turns them; he is fully endowed with immeasurable and inconceivable wondrous powers of supernatural penetration (*ṛddhi*).
Because the Tathāgata has realized the equality of upholding and violating the precepts, his three karmas are without exception...
One who acts in accordance with wisdom can cause sentient beings who have broken the precepts to regain purity.

Since you falsely claim that the observance and violation of precepts are equal, why is it that your three karmas remain so defiled? Furthermore, why do you create obstacles for the Dharma of the precepts?
To deceive one's own mind in this way does nothing but bring harm upon oneself. Alas, how painful! Part Two: The Exposition of the Precepts of the Seven Buddhas is completed.
○ Part Three: Verses of Praise and Dedication (seven sections). First: Praising the Supreme Benefits of Guarding the Precepts; [continuing] up to: Seventh: Dedication toward the Buddha-way.
First: A person capable of guarding the precepts shall obtain three kinds of happiness: renown and material gain in this life, and rebirth in the heavens after death.
One should contemplate such a state: the wise person who diligently guards the precepts; for when the precepts are pure and wisdom is present, one attains the supreme path.
This is because guarding the precepts is not something that can be accomplished by those who are foolish. As for the three kinds of happiness, they are first set forth.
The present and future "flower rewards" (immediate karmic results) serve as an incentive; it does not mean that the original intent of guarding the precepts was actually to seek these.
In this context, "learning" refers to the training rules (*śikṣāpada*). Because of wisdom, the precepts become pure; because of the precepts, the nature of wisdom is revealed.
Thus, they mutually support one another to accomplish the two adornments of merit and wisdom, continuing until the attainment of Buddhahood—this is what it means to guard [the precepts].

Precepts are the actual fruit [of wisdom]. The former wisdom is the correct view resulting from hearing and reflection; the latter wisdom is the beginningless awakening (ādi-bodhi) that is untainted (anāsrava).
When this beginningless awakening accords with original awakening (mūla-bodhi), it is termed ultimate awakening (niṣṭhā-bodhi). Thus, one attains the foremost path.
II. Explaining that the paths of all Buddhas are identical:

Just as the Buddhas of the past, And those of the future, As well as the World-Honored Ones of the present, Who are able to overcome all sorrow, All together revere and honor the precepts; This is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
All forms of sorrow have the two obstacles—afflictive and cognitive—as their cause, and the two types of birth and death—fragmentary and transformational—as their fruit.

Only by revering these precepts can one overcome them; for each individual precept can remedy afflictions, and by penetrating the nature of the precepts, one can become free from the delusion regarding the cognitive obstacle.
III. Exhortation to Follow the Buddha’s Teaching:
If there are those who, for their own sake, Desire to seek the path of the Buddha, They should respect the True Dharma;
this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
"For oneself" means to distinguish [this practice] from seeking fame or profit. "Seeking the Buddha-way" distinguishes it from the paths of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

"True Dharma" (saddharma) refers to this *prātimokṣa*; it exists only when a Buddha appears in the world, unlike the meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samvara*), the path-concomitant restraints (*mārga-samvara*), or the worldly five constants and ten wholesome actions;
therefore, it is called the True Dharma. Furthermore, it is only when this precept exists that [the Sangha] exists.
The Sangha Jewel. Because there is the Sangha Jewel, it causes the Buddha-dharma not to perish; therefore, it is called the True Dharma (Saddharma).
Those who seek the path of the Buddha must surely respect this Dharma; how could one possibly treat it with negligence as a minor precept and slander the clear instructions of all Buddhas?
○ Fourth, the benefits of the Sūtra on the Precepts.
The Seven Buddhas, as World-Honored Ones, extinguished all fetters and afflictions;
by preaching this Sūtra on the Seven Precepts, all bonds were liberated, and they entered into Nirvāṇa, where all worldly play has forever ceased.
The Honored One, the Great Sage, has spoken; the Noble Ones praise the precepts. These are the practices of his disciples for entering the tranquility of nirvana.
It is said that the Seven Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, taught this in order to eliminate the various fetters and afflictions of sentient beings.
The Precept Sūtra universally enables all sentient beings to be liberated from all fetters and to enter nirvāṇa together,
extinguishing the various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of the three realms. Therefore, one should know that regarding these precepts spoken by the Great Sage and praised by the noble ones,
there is no disciple of the Buddha who does not practice them and thereby enter nirvāṇa.

V. A Fifth Reiteration of the Final Charge When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, He gave rise to great compassion And assembled the community of bhikṣus, giving them this instruction:
"Do not say that with my parinirvāṇa, Those who practice purity will be without protection."
I now proclaim the Sūtra of Precepts, And have likewise well-expounded the Vinaya.
Although I shall enter Parinirvāṇa, you should regard me as if I were still the World-Honored One. If this sūtra remains long in the world, The Buddha-dharma will flourish and blaze forth.
Because it blazes so brightly, one may enter Nirvāṇa; But if you do not uphold these precepts, [the Dharma will perish].
Just as at the time of sunset, when the world is shrouded in darkness, one should perform the Uposatha;
so too, as he approaches Nirvana, he bestows his final instructions, just as parents entrust their final testament to their children—far surpassing anything done on ordinary days.
The resolve to uproot suffering becomes even more urgent. The *Śīla-sūtra* refers to the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) of the five categories. *Vinaya* means the method for extinguishing offenses.
This is the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body abiding eternally in the world; therefore, it should be regarded as the World-Honored One himself.
When there are those who uphold the *karmavācanā* and those who practice according to what is taught, it is said that this sutra abides in the world, and it is called the Abiding of the True Dharma.
In this world, the three—teaching, practice, and fruit—are all fully complete; otherwise, the Wheel of Dharma would fall to the earth and the evil realms would be filled.
Therefore, it is likened to the time when the sun sets: in the darkness, the path cannot be seen.
6. The Exhortation to Protect and Maintain [the Precepts]:
One should protect and maintain these precepts Just as a yak loves its tail;
Sit together in harmony, as the Buddha has taught.
"Maoyin" (犛音茅) is the name of a species of ox. The yak cherishes its tail to the point of neglecting its own body;

this serves as a metaphor for those who uphold the precepts, who should protect the discipline even at the cost of their own lives. "As the Buddha has taught" means that it is recited according to the Dharma every half-month.
One does not commit the offenses of violating the Dharma, causing a schism in the assembly, and so forth.
○ Seventh, dedication toward the Buddha-way.
I have finished reciting the precepts; the Saṃgha has completed the Poṣadha ceremony. I have now recited the Sūtra of Precepts.
The various merits that have been described, I dedicate them all to every sentient being, That together we may attain the Buddha-way.
Question: This precept-text is established for the sake of the śrāvakas. Why then is it dedicated toward the Buddha-way?
If the fruit of the śrāvaka-dharma is identical to the Buddha-way, why does it say in the sūtras that while a śrāvaka maintains the precepts, a bodhisattva is said to break them?
If a śrāvaka breaks the precepts, can this be called a bodhisattva upholding the precepts? Answer: In various sūtras, it is only the śrāvaka’s mind that is censured, not the śrāvaka’s discipline.
This is because they desire only to save themselves and do not think of saving others, thereby falling into the pit of non-action (asaṃskṛta).

They are rebuked because they lack the function of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Furthermore, since Śrāvakas take the pursuit of personal tranquility as their goal, an offense committed with a mind of anger is light, whereas one committed with a mind of greed is grave.
For Bodhisattvas, whose primary aim is the liberation of sentient beings, an offense committed with a mind of anger is grave, whereas one committed with a mind of greed is light.
As for the title "Bhikṣu," it fundamentally applies to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; there are Śrāvaka Bhikṣus and... [Mahāyāna Bhikṣus].
Although the directions taken by Bodhisattvas and Bhikṣus differ, their essence as Bhikṣus is the same. Since their essence is the same, their precepts are likewise the same.
If one lacks these precepts, one is identical to a lay Bodhisattva; why then must one leave the household life to enter the homeless state?

Therefore, we know that the Bhikṣu precepts are to be observed universally by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna practitioners. This is analogous to the medicine for preventing hands from cracking: it depends entirely upon how it is employed.

From the root [precepts] arise the two hundred and fifty precepts of expedient outflows; each is established as an offense according to its own specific article and is termed a "root offense" (*mūlāpatti*).
It is not merely the four grave offenses that constitute the roots. If one commits an offense and does not confess it...

When one is about to commit an offense but the act has not yet been completed, it is called a "preparatory offense" (*prayoga-āpatti*). When the offense has been completed but is less grave than the fundamental offense, it is called an "outflowing offense" (*niḥsaraṇa-āpatti*).
Among the methods for treating offenses in the subsequent text, there is mention of a "consequential *sthūlātyaya*"; one should know that this refers precisely to this [consequential offense].

In the first two sections of the middle [part], the offenses are subsumed under the category of preparatory (*prayoga*) transgressions; this differs from the present case, which uses the two characters "from birth" (*congsheng*).

It should be understood that these are subsumed under the *niḥṣyanda* (outflow) offenses of the first two categories [of the Prātimokṣa].

Because they constitute offenses in their own right, they are termed "independent" (*mukhataḥ*). Since they are of the same class as the fundamental offenses of those two categories, they are so designated.

General Explanation of the Karmavācanā Method:
Now, *karmavācanā* is a term for performing formal acts (*karman*) to accomplish specific matters. All monastic affairs are accomplished by relying upon *karmavācanā*.
Therefore it is said: "Where there is the performance of *karmavācanā*, and where there are those who practice according to what has been taught, this is called the abiding of the True Dharma."
The World-Honored One further stated: "One who does not recite the *jñapti-karman* shall never be released from dependence (*niśraya*) for the rest of their life.

Thus, one knows that among the essential duties of a bhikṣu, nothing takes precedence over this. Yet, in the common traditions of later generations, it has been mistakenly held that the mere act of confessing an offense before another person suffices;
such an error is profound. Therefore, I have specifically clarified this meaning at the outset to provide a general outline of the fundamental principles. As for...
The one hundred and one matters concerning the Saṃgha are scattered throughout various sections;
there is no need for me to recount them again here. The fourth part states: "There are three types of *karmavācanā* that encompass all *karmas*. What are these three?
The *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. These three encompass all *karmas*."

The *jñapti-karman* is also called the *ekajñapti*. The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is termed the *ekajñapti-karman* in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, meaning one motion followed by one formal act (*karmavācanā*).
The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is termed the *trijñapti-karman* in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
This refers to the one motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). The *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā* states: "There are one hundred and one formal acts (*karman*):

twenty-four consisting of a single motion (*jñapti-karman*), forty-seven consisting of a motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), and thirty consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
The *Mūla-ekottara-karman* says: "The term 'one hundred and one' is merely an enumeration of the general number. Regarding this...
In the *Mahā-vinaya*, one may examine how many differences there are; these are then subsumed according to their categories, so that there is no contradiction or obstruction.

There are twenty-two *jñapti* (single-announcement) procedures, forty-seven *jñapti-dvitīya* (one-announcement followed by a second motion), and thirty-two *jñapti-caturtha* (one-announcement followed by three motions).
As for the *Pratimokṣa-sūtra* and the *Karmavācanā*, they clarify one hundred and thirty-four methods: thirty-nine *jñapti*, fifty-seven *jñapti-dvitīya*, and [thirty-nine] *jñapti-caturtha*.

There are thirty-eight [rules] for the four [categories], thirty-three for those requiring face-to-face confession (*pratideśanīya*), and fourteen for those involving mental recollection (*manasikāra*);
together there are one hundred and eighty-one rules. Although these detailed procedures and regulations are exhaustive, they cannot avoid the fault of legislating what was not originally legislated.
For this reason, Master Huaisu frequently raised objections, maintaining that it would be better simply to follow the original Vinaya.

The third section states: "There are four kinds of saṃghas: a saṃgha of four persons, a saṃgha of five persons, a saṃgha of ten persons, and a saṃgha of twenty persons. Among these, as for the saṃgha of four persons:

with the exception of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to criticism), the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the removal of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*), all other legal acts (*karmavācanā*) should be performed according to the Dharma.

As for the saṃgha of five persons: in the central lands, with the exception of the conferral of full ordination and the removal of offenses, all other legal acts should be performed according to the Dharma."

The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) should be performed. Regarding a community of ten monks (*daśavargīya-saṃgha*): with the exception of the rite for the removal of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*), all other legal *karmas* should be performed.
Regarding a community of twenty monks (*viṃśativargīya-saṃgha*): all *karmas* should be performed; how much more so when there are more than twenty.

One must not include bhikṣuṇīs and the like to complete the quorum. Nor may one include those who have been suspended (*utkṣiptaka*), those who have been expelled (*pravāsita*), or the very person against whom the *karman* is being performed.

The quorum is complete. One must not perform a *karmavācanā* that is both illegal (*adharma*) and contrary to the discipline (*avinaya*). These include: an illegal *karmavācanā* of a separate assembly (*bhinnasaṃgha*);
an illegal *karmavācanā* of a united assembly (*saṃhata-saṃgha*); a legal *karmavācanā* of a separate assembly; a legal-like *karmavācanā* of a separate assembly;

and a legal-like *karmavācanā* of a united assembly. Regarding the *karmavācanā* for not ceasing [reproach]: when those entitled to reproach do so and yet [the offender] does not cease, it is equivalent to a separate assembly. What is an illegal [act]?
Regarding the *vinayakarma*: it should consist of either one motion (*jñapti*) and one formal act (*karma*), or one motion and three formal acts.

To perform a motion without performing a formal act, or to perform a formal act without performing a motion, or to perform multiple motions, or to perform multiple formal acts—these are contrary to the Dharma.

To grant a formal accusation (*ukṣepaṇīyakarman*) to one who does not deserve it, or to grant it haphazardly—this is contrary to the Vinaya. What, then, is according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya?

Karmavācanā. One performs a formal motion (*jñapti*) according to the method for a formal motion; one performs a ritual act (*karma*) according to the method for a ritual act (this is "according to the Dharma").

One raises a charge against another according to the method for raising a charge (this is "according to the Vinaya"). What is an illegal *karma* performed by a separate assembly? Those who have not arrived do not grant their consent (*chanda*);

those present who ought to be censured are censured (this constitutes a "separate assembly"). They perform various kinds of *karmas*, making a formal motion regarding this matter, yet performing it for the sake of that other matter.
The *karmavācanā* (is illegal). What is an illegal *saṃgha-samagra-karman*? Those who have not arrived give their consent (*chanda*);
