[This method] is the most excellent, the most wonderful, and the most venerable. (The "Welcome" [invitation] applies exclusively to the Buddha’s own mouth; the three utterances and three refuges apply exclusively to the period before the four *karmavācanās* were established;

the eight rules apply exclusively to the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs; the self-vow applies exclusively to Mahākāśyapa alone; the realization of the Truths applies exclusively to the five bhikṣus; only this *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) bestows the precepts, serving as the framework for the Buddha's transformation of beings, ensuring that the True Dharma endures for a long time and that the fruits of the paths of the Three Vehicles remain unbroken.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one has previously received the full ordination—even if it was only for a brief moment—such a person should sit first."
First receive water; first receive food and drink. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:

"If a bhikṣu is actually one year of ordination (*lābha*) and falsely claims to be two years, yet receives offerings according to the sequence of two years, it constitutes a grave offense when calculated in terms of money. The *Nanhai Jiguishi* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) states:

"From the sixteenth day of the ninth month to the fifteenth day of the first month is the winter season" (formerly stated as: from the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month). From the first...

From the sixteenth day of the [twelfth] month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month constitutes the spring season (formerly stated as from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month).

From the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the sixth month constitutes the rainy season (formerly stated as from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month).

On the sixteenth day of the sixth month, for one day and one night, constitutes the period of conclusion (formerly stated as the sixteenth day of the fifth month; if one receives full ordination during this one day and one night, one may still undertake the subsequent *anvārambhaṇa* retreat; when the three months are completed, it is then calculated as such).

One summer retreat (*varṣā*). For example, among worldly people, one born on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month is also counted as being one year old; therefore, this [one summer] is taken as the completion of a year. If one receives the precepts on the seventeenth day of the fifth month, one is not permitted to undergo the subsequent summer retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*);

such a person is merely called a "Bhikṣu without a summer" (*avarṣika bhikṣu*). One must wait until the following year before undertaking either the preceding (*pūrvikā*) or subsequent summer retreat. Only when the three months are completed is one called a "Bhikṣu with one summer" (*ekavarṣika bhikṣu*). This is like a worldly person born on the first day of the year who is only designated as being one year old upon reaching the end of the year.

From the seventeenth day of the sixth month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month constitutes the long period (the old tradition states: from the seventeenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month).

This refers to the esoteric teachings of the Buddha, which differ from secular conventions. Whenever monastics from the Western Regions or the South Seas meet one another for the first time, they ask, "Virtuous One, how many years of *varṣa* (rainy-season retreats) have you completed?
The other replies, "So many. If they have completed the same number of years, he then asks, "In what season did you complete yours?"
If the time is the same, one asks for how many days [the shadow has been measured]. If the day is the same, one asks whether it was before or after the meal.

If both were before the meal, one then asks about the shadow. If there is a difference in the shadow, a distinction in size is established; if the shadows are the same, there is no difference in size.
Regarding seating order, one takes precedence based on who arrived first; thus, the administrative duties are assigned according to that prior appointment.

If, on the seventeenth day of the sixth month, one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) just as the dawn light appears, one becomes the senior most among those of the same *varṣa* (rainy-season retreat), because one could not have received it in the subsequent *varṣa*.

(The old tradition says "the seventeenth day of the fifth month"). If one receives the precepts at the very end of the night of the sixteenth day of the sixth month, then [one is also considered senior] among those of the same *varṣa*.
The middle [category] is the smallest, because they receive the later summer retreat (formerly called the sixteenth day of the fifth month).
Question: The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that even those who have received the full ordination for only a brief moment should sit first, and so forth;

the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* also contains precepts regarding sitting according to the Dharma. Now, between a bhikṣu and a bodhisattva, or among those who have received [the precepts], there may be cases where one has received them earlier.
Question: "Afterwards, by what sequence of precepts should one abide? Answer: The *Shiqian* (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning) states:

"Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles universally employ the *vinaya* discipline to encompass their respective stages. Each relies upon its own discipline to determine the order of their positions.

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva is in the Great Vehicle, they follow the Great; when in the Small Vehicle, they follow the Small. Thus, we know that within the assembly of the Small Vehicle, one still sits according to the positions of the Small Vehicle."
Within the assembly of Mahāyāna practitioners, one sits according to the stages and ranks of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states:
"If one first followed the Small Vehicle and later the Great Vehicle, everything is transformed into the inexhaustible precept-body (*anantarya-śīla*).

If one first received the Great [Vehicle] precepts and only later left the household life, desiring to be counted among the great *bhikṣus* without losing the Bodhisattva dharma, one should then receive the Vinaya discipline once more. However, regarding this...
Once one has attained the pure discipline (*śīla*) of body and speech that prevents wrongdoing, the unmanifested essence of the precepts (*avijñapti-śīla-bhāva*) no longer arises [as a new entity].
Therefore, in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the five categories and seven groups of offenses are all the disciplinary codes (*vinaya*) for renunciant bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, if one first follows the Small Vehicle and later the Great Vehicle, one may utilize the "small summer retreat" to fulfill the "great summer retreat. If one first receives the Great Vehicle and later receives the [monastic] discipline...
Regarding the ritual procedures (*vidhi*): in cases of minor matters, one follows the minor rules; in cases of major matters, one follows the major rules.
(Text) This is an immutable principle. The second division states: "If a bhikṣu transforms his female form, he shall enter the community of nuns using his original year of ordination."

If a nun transforms her male form, she is permitted to enter the community of bhikṣus; however, one who transforms into a person with both sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana) is subject to expulsion (*pravāsanīya*).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu transforms his female form, and if he previously committed an offense involving a bhikṣuṇī, he should confess it within the community of bhikṣuṇīs."
If one has previously committed an *asaṃvāsa* offense (an offense involving loss of communion), there is no need for further repentance. It is the same if a bhikṣuṇī’s sexual organs change.
If a śikṣamāṇā’s sexual organs change and she is twenty years of age, she should be granted the bhikṣuṇī precepts; if she is not yet twenty, she is a śrāmaṇera.
It is the same if a śrāmaṇerī’s sexual organs change. If a śrāmaṇera’s sexual organs change, he should either be granted [the status of] a two-year [probationary period].

Regarding the training in the precepts: one receives the two-year probationary discipline (*śikṣamāṇā*) among the community of nuns. Alternatively, if one is not yet of an age to receive the two-year discipline, one remains a *śrāmaṇerī*.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "If [the offense] reaches the third formal announcement, she is no longer a nun; she must be expelled. The *Dvitīya-bhāga* states:
"Those whose male organs have been severed by thieves and the like, or who have fallen off naturally, should not be expelled."
If one cuts it oneself, one should be expelled (parivāsa). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "To cut off the penis or half of it is a *duṣkṛta*;
to cut it off entirely is a *sthūlātyaya*; to remove one testicle is a *sthūlātyaya*; to remove both testicles, one should be expelled."
The *Vinayaviniścaya* states: When a bhikṣu practices, two kinds of afflictions may arise due to the loss of right mindfulness.
He may then recall a distant object from the past and give rise to defiled attachment, thereby committing various transgressions;

or he may give rise to defiled attachment toward a proximate object present before him and thus commit various offenses. Having understood the conditions that gave rise to these violations, he should [apply himself] to this very matter.
One should generate a mind of antidote to cause [the afflictions] to be eliminated.

If the conditions for defilement are so powerful that they cannot be dispelled, one should approach a venerable elder, one who is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, or a person of virtuous conduct, and request their instructions and admonitions to apply the mind toward their removal.

If they still do not cease, one should diligently engage day and night in recitation, hearing, and reflection, discerning the profound meaning and making offerings with utmost sincerity to the Triple Gem.
Regarding nurturing: one forgets one's own toil in places such as those for raising [others], providing service with all one's heart; or traveling to other regions; or reducing one’s own food;

or going to the charnel ground to dwell alone in an araṇya, practicing the contemplation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth; or practicing the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).

Alternatively, one may cultivate the perception of impermanence and the perception of death, hoping thereby to eliminate the afflictions. If they still do not cease, one should give rise to shame and remorse, reflecting:
"What I have done is wrong; my precepts are not pure, yet I continue to accept the fourfold requisites offered out of faith by other donors.
Furthermore, there are the Buddhas, those with the divine eye who are fellow practitioners of the holy life, and the various devas."
All shall behold me; therefore, you must not commit various sinful karmas, but should instead reproach yourselves as if extinguishing a fire on your own heads.
In this pure realm, I shall proclaim the removal of your sins; do not allow yourselves to fall into regret. If you perform the remedial practices as previously described, [the sins will be purified].
Your nature is prone to many afflictions that you have not yet been able to extinguish. You should carefully examine yourself;
perhaps you should relinquish the precepts and become a layperson, lest you incur sin by accepting the offerings of others.

When consuming such gifts, you further create numerous karmic actions of evil, which will certainly result in the ripening of bitter fruits in the future, as explained at length in the sūtras. You should therefore practice and maintain [the precepts] well.

Regarding the "ripening fruit" (*vipākaphala*), which refers to the retributive results within the three realms, it is collectively termed "ripening" (*vipāka*) based on three meanings: first, ripening at a different time;

that is, karma is created in this life and its fruit is experienced in a subsequent life. Second, ripening as a different nature; that is, while the causes may be either wholesome or unwholesome, the fruit... [is of a specific nature].
It is solely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Three [types of karma] ripen in different locations:
causes are created among human beings, yet the fruits are experienced within the six destinies (*ṣadgati*).

The second section of the *Nissaya-vastu* states:

At that time, because the preceptors of newly ordained bhikṣus had passed away and there was no one to instruct them, they did not maintain proper deportment, even behaving like the assemblies of Brahmins. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "I allow it."
There is an *ācārya*. As explained regarding the *upādhyāya*, one should make this request: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, [name], now seek the venerable sir to be my *niśraya* (preceptor). May the venerable sir grant me his *niśraya*; I shall dwell under the venerable sir’s *niśraya*.
Thus he should say three times. The other should reply: "So be it; I grant you my *niśraya*. Do not be negligent."
A newly ordained bhikṣu who delights in seclusion and tranquility is permitted to seek dependence (niśraya) elsewhere; he may go and return on the same day.
He should not send a messenger to receive or grant dependence. One must not grant dependence without having carefully examined the recipient.
In cases of illness or for those tending to the sick, one may remain without dependence. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One should request dependence..."
There are five qualities for remaining [in the community]: first, affection; second, respect; third, shame (*hrī*); fourth, dread of blame (*apatrāpya*); and fifth, delight in dwelling [there].

Furthermore, there are four kinds of teachers (*ācārya*): first, one who has neither food nor the Dharma—one should leave without asking permission; second, one who has food but no Dharma—one should leave after asking permission;
third, one who has no food but possesses the Dharma—even if it is difficult, one should not leave as long as life lasts; fourth...
If there is food and provisions available, even if one is driven away for the duration of one’s life, one should not leave.
If a disciple does not accept instruction, one should tell the person in charge of bedding to take away the bedding, and the person in charge of food to cut off the food.

If that person is violent, powerful, and capable of causing harm, the preceptor (upādhyāya) should flee, and the teacher on whom one relies (niśraya-ācārya) should take up his robes and bowl and depart beyond the boundary.

If one returns after staying abroad for one night, one immediately becomes separated from one's formal reliance (*niśraya*). If the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*) commits a transgression, the disciple should offer counsel;

however, one must not use harsh language, but should speak with gentle words according to the rules for instruction: "The teacher should not do such a thing. If the teacher follows this advice, it is well.
If, on the contrary, he responds with reproach, then that person—whether he be a preceptor or an ācārya—should be abandoned and one should depart from him. This applies to the ācārya as well.

One should take one's robes and bowl and go beyond the boundary to stay for one night, then return and rely upon another person as a preceptor. If that person has authority, one should go far away or rely upon a person of great virtue.
If the upādhyāya has passed away, has left the religious life, or has been subject to formal censure, one may go beyond the boundary to stay overnight.

If a disciple stays overnight outside the boundary, this is called "leaving the reliance" (*niśraya*). If the preceptor (*ācārya*) passes away, renounces the path, is suspended (*utkṣipta*), or stays overnight outside the boundary;

or if the disciple himself stays overnight outside the boundary; or if [the disciple] has completed five years and is well-versed in the Dharma and well-versed in the Vinaya—then he may leave the reliance.
This is called "abandoning the reliance. If a bhikṣu is not well-versed in the Dharma...
One who is well-versed in the Vinaya, yet cannot establish himself nor establish others, must remain in dependence for as long as he lives.

However, if one has reached ten years [of seniority], is well-versed in the Dharma, and is well-versed in the Vinaya, such that he can establish himself and also establish others—such a bhikṣu [is independent].
One may receive dependence from others. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "It is permitted not to receive dependence for up to six nights.
If a disciple wishes to move to another location, he must first inform his teacher two or three days in advance. The teacher should deliberate upon the destination;

only if there is someone there who can provide dependence should he permit him to go. Upon arriving at that place, he should first pay homage to the stūpas, then pay homage to the senior monks (*sthavira*), and finally request a room.
Thereafter, he seeks formal reliance (*niśraya*). The preceptor should ask: "Who are your two teachers? Where did you previously reside? Which sūtras do you recite?
If his answers are in accordance with the Dharma, one should grant him reliance. If they are not in accordance with the Dharma, one should say: "You do not know me, nor do I know you.
You should go to those who know you and seek reliance from them. If there is doubt, one should say: "Wait a moment. This person...
One should stay for a short time, observing him for up to six nights. If he is pleasing, one should grant him formal reliance (*niśraya*).

If he is not pleasing, one should speak to him as stated above. One should not rely upon the Saṃgha or dwell near a stūpa; rather, one should rely upon an elder (*sthavira*) who is a monk acting in accordance with the Dharma and capable of providing instruction.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one has accomplished five qualities and has completed five years [of seniority], yet has not received..."
Regarding dependence (*niśraya*): first, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what does not constitute an offense; third, knowing what is light; fourth, knowing what is heavy;

and fifth, reciting the *Prātimokṣa* training rules in detail. Even if one has received the precepts for many years, if one does not know these five things, one must remain dependent upon another for as long as one lives.
A *mahābhikṣu* should likewise receive dependence from a junior *bhikṣu*, and should also serve and provide offerings [to him].

When supporting a junior bhikṣu, one should omit only the ritual of prostrating at his feet. It is permitted to stay for five or six nights without a formal preceptor (*niśraya*) without committing an offense.
However, if there is a qualified preceptor available, staying even for a single night without relying upon him constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Furthermore, one must not take water used for washing the preceptor’s feet. In times of famine, however, one may stay daily in the presence of the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) with his permission. One should act accordingly.
One should come every day. If one is unable to do so, one may come every five days. If one cannot come every five days, one should come at the time of the *poṣadha*.
If one cannot come even at the *poṣadha*, one must come to see the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) by the time of the *pravāraṇā*, even if it means traveling up to two and a half *yojanas*.
The *Mūla-nidāna* states: "If one has not yet completed five years [of seniority], even if one has accomplished the five dharmas..."
One who has attained the ultimate good, is proficient in the Tripitaka, possesses the realization of the three vidyās, and has completely eliminated the three stains must also rely [on a teacher].
If one has completed five years of residence (pañca-varṣa), one is permitted to travel apart from one's reliance; however, wherever one goes, one must still rely [on a teacher].

If there is an intention to seek a teacher of reliance, one may remain for up to five nights; if there is no such intention, one night is not permitted. Regarding the food and drink used by the Saṃgha...
...and so forth. In all such cases, one is not permitted to receive [instruction]. This applies even within the first ten years of ordination. The *Ekottara-karman* states:

"If one has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) for sixty summers but is eighty years of age, and has never read or recited the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, nor understands its meaning, one must still rely upon an elder.
If no elder is available, a junior may also serve as such. Only..."
Except for prostrating, all other duties should be performed. Such a person is called a "senior or junior bhikṣu. The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states:

"If one departs briefly on some business with the intention of returning immediately, it is appropriate to rely upon one's former teacher; there is no need to undergo [the formal rite of] dependence again.

One should provide service and attend to both [the teacher and the student] regarding instruction and recitation. Even if both fall ill, if one has the capacity, one should care for both; if one lacks the strength, one should simply provide service [to the one who needs it]."

Regarding dependence: if there is no one to provide instruction and recitation, one may reside anywhere; however, if there is no one to rely upon as a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), it is not permissible to remain in residence.
At a certain monastery, there was a bhikṣu who had many disciples depending on him for reliance. When this teacher passed away, there was no one left for them to rely upon.

The Buddha commanded that they seek out another person of virtuous character, provide him with a fine dwelling, exempt him from administrative duties, and supply him with attendants and bedding. All...
[He] commanded that there be no deficiency. If there is no such person [to serve as a preceptor], one should not perform the second *poṣadha* in this same scripture.

Furthermore, regarding those who have entered the preceding *varṣā* (early rains retreat) and whose supporting teacher (*niśraya-ācārya*) dies, the Buddha commanded that they seek another supporting teacher just as before.

If none exists, they should seek a supporting teacher elsewhere and observe the subsequent *varṣā*. Furthermore, regarding those who have entered the subsequent *varṣā* (late rains retreat) and whose teacher subsequently passes away, the Buddha...
For a period of two months, they shall examine one another and dwell with vigilance.
Once the two months have passed, if there is a person to serve as a *niśraya* (preceptor), they shall provide support as before; if there is none, they must not exceed a second *poṣadha*.
They should seek a *niśraya-ācārya* from another location. If the original teacher has passed away, all cases are treated as previously described. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states:
The procedure for receiving dependence (*niśraya*) is concluded. Requesting the seven-day rule to go outside the boundary: when the seven days are completed, one returns to the monastery;
the dependence is not lost.
○ The Rules for the Teacher.
The second section states: "The Venerable Sañjīva was two years old. Taking a disciple who was one year old, he went to where the World-Honored One was.
Knowing [the situation], the World-Honored One asked intentionally: 'Who is this bhikṣu? He replied: 'He is my disciple. [The Buddha] asked:
'How many years old are you now? He replied: 'Two years. [The Buddha] asked again: 'How many years old is the disciple? He replied: 'One year. At that time...

The World-Honored One rebuked him in various ways: "What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, not conduct in accordance with the teachings, and something that should not have been done.
How could you, Upasena, teach others when you yourself have not yet weaned yourself from milk?
You ought to receive instruction from others; how can you instruct others? From now on, it is permitted for a wise bhikṣu of ten years' standing to bestow full ordination upon others."
Regarding the precepts and providing dependence to others, one should practice the duties of an *upādhyāya* (preceptor) and an *ācārya* (instructor).
If the Saṃgha intends to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a disciple— whether it be a censure, a suspension, a dependence, a prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople,

a formal charge for not seeing an offense, a formal charge for not confessing an offense, or a formal charge for not relinquishing a wrong view— the *upādhyāya* must investigate the matter therein according to the Dharma.
The principle is that the Saṃgha should not perform a *karmavācanā* (formal act) against a disciple; if it does, it must be performed in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, if the Saṃgha performs such a *karmavācanā* against a disciple, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) should manage the matter according to the Dharma, causing the disciple to comply with the Saṃgha, not to oppose them, and to seek the removal of the offense so that the Saṃgha may quickly grant the lifting of the *karmavācanā*. Furthermore, if a disciple commits an offense...
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) shall attend to them according to the Dharma.

Whether it be the *parivāsa* (probation), the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement after initial treatment), the *mānatva* (penance), or the *āvarhaṇa* (expiation of the offense), he shall grant each as is appropriate.
Furthermore, if a disciple falls ill, the preceptor shall look after him or have another person do so until he recovers. If he passes away, the disciple...

If one does not find pleasure in one’s dwelling place, one should move oneself or instruct another to move. If a disciple has any matter of doubt, it should be resolved according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, as taught by the Buddha.

(The *Karmavācanā* compiled by Tandi states: "Dharma" refers to the five kinds of practices of detachment: first, renunciation, which is not worldly; second, transcendence, which is not the grasping of dharmas;

third, desirelessness, which is not having desires; fourth, freedom from fetters, which is not having fetters; fifth, not approaching birth-and-death, which is not approaching. "Vinaya" refers to the five kinds of practices for deliverance: first, fewness of desires, which is not muchness of desires...)

2. Contentment, not lack of satiety; 3. Easy to protect, not difficult to protect; 4. Easy to sustain, not difficult to sustain; 5. Wisdom, not folly. What the Buddha has taught refers to five kinds of disciplinary instructions (*anuśāsana*): 1. Prohibiting that which is blameworthy; 2. Permitting that which is blameless; 3.

If there is a deficiency in the Dharma regarding what is prohibited or permitted, one should address it according to the Dharma; 4. For repeated transgressions, one should apply subduing measures and mindfulness; 5. Regarding true virtues, one should show affection and offer praise.
If wrong views arise, one should teach them to abandon those wrong views and abide in right view. One should protect them with two things: with the Dharma and with robes.
Regarding food: one should instruct [the disciple] to increase their virtue (*śīla*), increase their concentration (*samādhi*), and increase their wisdom (*prajñā*).

One should teach them learning and the recitation of the scriptures, and provide them with clothing, food, bedding, and medicine, arranging for these according to one's capacity. One should reprove the disciple with five matters:
"Go away! Do not enter my room; do not perform services for me; do not come to where I am" (the *ācārya* says: "Do not dwell under my guidance"); "I will not speak with you."

There are five matters for which one should be rebuked: lack of shame (*ahrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), not accepting instruction, engaging in improper conduct, and lacking respect.

Furthermore, there are another five matters: lack of shame, lack of dread of blame, being difficult to speak with, befriending those of bad character, and having a fondness for visiting the houses of courtesans, the houses of women, the houses of young maidens, the houses of eunuchs, and the dwellings of bhikṣuṇīs.
One should not visit monasteries, nunneries for *śikṣamāṇās*, or nunneries for *śrāmaṇerīs* with the intent of watching them catch turtles and tortoises;
such actions should be censured. One should not censure someone for as long as their life lasts, nor should one censure them throughout the entire *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).
One must not censure a sick person, nor should one censure someone in their absence, nor without having pointed out their transgression.
Having rebuked him, one should not immediately accept his offerings or service, nor should one grant him formal reliance (*niśraya*).
One may permit another person to receive them on his behalf with the intention that he may perform a Dharma-compliant confession and achieve reconciliation with his two teachers.
One should not entice away the disciples of others. Even if those two teachers have broken their precepts and so forth, one should maintain this intention:
"The reason I am enticing them away is because I wish to cause them to increase and benefit in the Dharma of the śramaṇa.

When a disciple repents according to the Dharma, the teacher should accept it. If a disciple takes leave of his two teachers to travel far away, the teachers should ask for what purpose and who will be his companions.
"Who is this? Where are they going? A certain unpleasant person blocked them, forbidding them from leaving. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: "One must not keep two śrāmaṇeras.
However, if one can teach them to uphold the precepts, increase their mental cultivation, increase their wisdom, and engage in study, recitation, and listening, then one may keep them.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One must not harbor the intention of ordaining others for the sake of providing for oneself. One should [ordain them]..."
He formed this thought: "I must cause that person, by means of my deliverance, to cultivate all wholesome dharmas and attain the fruit of the Path.
It is impossible for one who cannot subdue oneself to subdue others; it is impossible for one who cannot discipline oneself to discipline others;
it is impossible for one who cannot deliver oneself to deliver others; and it is impossible for one who is not yet liberated oneself to liberate others."

It is impossible. One who has accomplished ten qualities may be permitted to ordain others, grant them the going forth, and confer full ordination: first, upholding the precepts; second, being well-versed in the Abhidharma;
third, being well-versed in the Vinaya; fourth, training in the precepts; fifth, training in meditative concentration; sixth, training in wisdom;

seventh, being able to purify one's own offenses and being able to cause others to purify their offenses; eighth, being able to tend to the sick and being able to cause others to tend to the sick; ninth, [having] disciples...

Difficulties. Being able to deliver others from difficulties, or being able to cause others to deliver them from difficulties; having completed ten years—or at least ten full years—and knowing the Vinaya of both divisions (Dharmaguptaka and Mahīśāsaka), one may also ordain others.
The same applies to those who receive formal reliance (*niśraya*). However, it is not permitted to maintain a following of *śrāmaṇeras*.

If one keeps [a single disciple], it may extend up to three. If a Bhikṣu of great virtue is highly esteemed by many people, he should say to them, "I shall give [this person] to another," and further declare, "I know there are others;
however, I wish for this person to receive instruction in the recitation of the sūtras and the Dharma under a preceptor (ācārya) in order to increase their cultivation and study.
In this manner, he should give him to another so that he may receive personal instruction. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "When [the period of training] is complete..."

Only after completing ten years of summer retreats may one occupy the position of a teacher (*ācārya*). Furthermore, one must accomplish five qualities: first, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what is non-offensive;

third, knowing what is light; fourth, knowing what is grave; and fifth, being extensively able to explain and interpret the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, including the original formulation and subsequent modifications of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), as well as skillfully understanding the points of passage and obstruction when encountering difficult circumstances. One must constantly recite the core text of the precepts and be capable of resolving others' doubts.
[Query: Doubts. Regarding precepts, views, and extensive learning; benefiting both oneself and others;

and the conduct of dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*)—if one possesses such virtues without any transgression, they are called a Preceptor (*upādhyāya*), because as a "kinsman" (*upādhyāya*), they are able to teach the Dharma of renunciation (*nairyāṇika*).

Even if one has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), if they do not recognize the gravity or lightness of the various training rules (*śikṣāpada*), they must still live in dependence upon a person of eminent virtue, even if they have sixty years of seniority. If the teacher is junior...

Except for prostrating at his feet, one should perform all other [duties]. Such a person is called a "senior or junior bhikṣu" (vṛddhataraka-yavastaraka-bhikṣu), yet he is not permitted to grant others the going forth or the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

It would be better to be a butcher engaged in the work of killing than to grant the going forth and full ordination and then neglect them, disregarding the matter so that my True Dharma may quickly perish. One should rebuke him.

Not to reprove when one should reprove; to reprove when one should not reprove; not to forgive when one should forgive; and to forgive when one should not forgive—all these constitute an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).
If a person who has already received full ordination does not show respect and is incapable of being instructed, one should give him the six requisites and expel him.
If he is a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), one should give him the two robes, the upper and lower, and likewise expel him. If it concerns his parents...
If a small child, out of faith, offers something to a bhikṣu, it should be accepted. If the child asks for it back, it should be returned.

If the child offers a price, one may take whatever amount is given, however much or little it may be, and there is no offense. This refers to a case where such a small child was tied with a piece of saṃghāṭī cloth around the neck by a bhikṣu and supported at all times;
later, having grown up and desiring to repay his debt of gratitude, he brings an object to offer as a gift.
One should accept [the candidate] according to one's discretion. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When ordaining a person, one should first ask:

'For what purpose do you leave the household life? If they say it is for the sake of food and drink, they should not be ordained. If they say it is to seek the wholesome Dharma, out of weariness with birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction, they should be ordained.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "Whenever one wishes to grant another the going forth..."
First, one should provide the six necessary articles: the three robes, bedding, a bowl, a water filter, and a *nidāna*. The *Nidāna* states:
"When intending to ordain a *śrāmaṇera*, one should provide him with a bowl, a small bowl, and a copper cup, ensuring that nothing is lacking. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states:
"After having conferred the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon a great practitioner (i.e., a *bhikṣu*), for the duration of one year, one should instruct him in one..."
Once all the rites performed by the Great Path practitioners are completed, if there are others who subsequently seek to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), they should be granted it.

However, if the year has not yet been fulfilled, one must not grant it. After a *śrāmaṇera* has received the great precepts, he may further receive another *śrāmaṇera* as his dependent according to the rules of dependence;
likewise, after one year has passed, he may again receive one. He must not receive two persons as dependents at the same time. (From the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā*).
The Vinaya states: "Upādhyāya" (Preceptor) is translated in the Han language as "one who knows what is an offense and what is not an offense. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"In the dharma of receiving the precepts, one must first preach the Dharma for them, guiding and enlightening them so that they give rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings."

Once the higher mind (*adhi-citta*) has been attained, one then attains the higher precepts (*adhi-śīla*). (This should occur before ascending the altar. One must skillfully provide instruction so that the candidate fully understands;

how could it be permissible for the monastic assembly to have already gathered and the *karmavācanā* about to be performed, only then to recite the formal texts as a hollow ritual following ancient precedent? This merely causes the great assembly to sit for long periods in delay, leaving those receiving the ordination utterly bewildered and without understanding.
This is truly meaningless. The *Nanhai Jiguishi* states: "Whenever laypeople visit a *bhikṣu*, if they are solely reciting Buddhist scriptures and desire to enter the [monastic] order..."
Having shaved their hair and donned black robes, they are called "novices" (*śrāmaṇera*). Alternatively, those who seek secular texts without the intent to renounce the world are termed "students.
These two classes must both provide for their own sustenance; consuming from the permanent endowment (*sthavira*) is strictly prohibited by the holy teachings.

However, if one has rendered service to the community, it is appropriate to consume food in accordance with that merit. This may consist of ordinary provisions, or perhaps what was previously offered by a donor.
Even if one eats [the food] with a mind [of compassion], there is no fault. In the monasteries of the Western Regions, there are many students who come to the *bhikṣus* to study non-Buddhist texts.

There are two reasons for keeping them: first, to provide them with service and labor; second, to teach them to develop a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*). Since this involves both self-benefit and the benefit of others, it is not detrimental to maintain them.

This is especially true for those who practice the ascetic discipline of the "single bowl" (*dhūta-ekapiṇḍapātika*); in principle, they need not trouble themselves [with such tasks]. However, if there is even a small amount of service to be rendered, it is likewise [permissible].
This is essential. One should provide tooth-sticks and cause them to receive food, ensuring their needs are met at the proper time so as not to harm the path of compassion.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "Even those such as caṇḍālas and butchers, though they perform evil deeds, cannot destroy the True Dharma of the Tathāgata;
they do not necessarily fall into the three evil realms. [Yet] as teachers, they are unable to instruct [others]."
To scold one's disciples is to destroy the Buddha-dharma; such a person will inevitably fall into hell. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:
"It would be better to accept evil precepts and, within a single day, sever the life-faculties of immeasurable beings, than to harbor and maintain wicked disciples who cannot be disciplined.
Why is this? Such evil discipline brings calamity only upon oneself; harboring wicked disciples whom one cannot instruct [brings harm to others as well]."
[The Buddha] said: "It causes immeasurable sentient beings to commit evil; it enables them to slander immeasurable wholesome and sublime dharmas; it destroys the harmony of the Saṃgha;
and it causes many sentient beings to commit the five deeds of immediate retribution. For these reasons, it is more grievous than the transgressions of the evil vows."
The third section on the Dharma of a Disciple’s Service to the Teacher states:
Regarding the *upādhyāya*, one receives the precepts from him. Regarding those equal to the *upādhyāya*, they are those who are ten years senior to oneself.
Regarding the *ācārya*, there are five types: first, the *pravrajyā-ācārya*, upon whom one relies to obtain ordination; second...

1. The Preceptor for Ordination (*upādhyāya*): this is the one who performs the *karmavācanā* at the time of receiving the precepts. 2. The Preceptor for Instruction (*ācārya*): this is the one who instructs one in the proper deportment (*īryāpatha*).

3. The Preceptor for Receiving the Scriptures (*śāstr-ācārya*): this is the one from whom one receives the scriptures or explains their meaning, even down to a single four-line verse (*catuṣpāda-gāthā*).
4. The Preceptor for Dependence (*niśraya-ācārya*): this is the one upon whom one relies for dependence, even for as little as a single night. These are the [various] ācāryas.
[This refers to one who] has been [ordained] more than five years. The second section states:

If the Saṃgha intends to perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) against the preceptor, the disciple shall manage the matter according to the Dharma so that the Saṃgha does not proceed with it; if they do proceed, he shall ensure it is done lightly.

If the Saṃgha intends to issue a reprimand (*tarjanīya-karman*) or other such measures against the preceptor, the disciple shall manage the matter according to the Dharma so that the preceptor remains compliant with the Saṃgha, seeks the removal of the offense, and is quickly released.

Regarding the *karmavācanā*: if the preceptor commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, or if he is ill, or if he does not find the dwelling place pleasant, or if there is a matter of doubt, all these cases are as explained in the section on the preceptor’s rules.
If wrong views arise, one should exhort him to abandon them and protect him by means of two matters, also as explained in the section on the preceptor’s rules.
A disciple must not enter a village, nor enter another's home, without having informed the preceptor.
From other bhikṣus, or taking other bhikṣus as companions, he must not give [anything], nor receive [anything].
He must not assist in communal affairs, nor accept assistance from others in communal affairs. He must not shave another's hair, nor cause another to shave his hair.
He must not enter the bathhouse, nor rub another's body, nor have his own body rubbed by another.
One must not go to the dwellings during the day; one must not go among the burial mounds; one must not go outside the boundary; one must not travel to other regions.
At dawn, he should enter the teacher’s room to receive the scriptures and inquire about their meaning.

He should remove his urinal vessel and announce that the time has arrived. Having washed his hands with soap, ash, or water until they are clean, if there is any food available, he should fetch it for him.

If there is any gain or offering within the Saṃgha, one should take it on behalf [of the preceptor]. One should provide him with bathing powder and tooth-sticks, causing the teacher to wash his hands and rinse his mouth, and offer him suitable food.
If there is any gain or offering within the Saṃgha, one should announce: "I have received such and such items; this is the portion for the Upādhyāya.
One should then ask the teacher, "Do you wish to enter the village? If he says he will not enter, one should ask, "Where shall we obtain food?"
If it is said that something is to be taken from a certain place, one should go to take it as commanded.

If it is said to enter a village, one should wash one's hands and then slowly take the robes from the rack, ensuring they are not inverted or mixed up. First, take the *antarvāsa* (inner robe), spread it out, shake it, and inspect it; next, take the waistband.
The *saṃkakṣikā*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the *saṃghāṭī* should be spread out and shaken to inspect them, then handed to the teacher.
One should fold the *saṃghāṭī* and place it upon one's head or shoulder. Next, take the alms bowl and place it in its bag to carry away.

One should take the teacher’s undergarment, fold it, and lift it up; likewise, take the foot-washing items and the bedding to lift them up. When the teacher goes out, one should hold onto him as he walks along the path.
Wearing leather sandals, when leaving the room, one should look back and close the door. Then, using one's hand, one should push the door leaf to see if it is secure.
If it is not secure, one should close it again. If it is secure, one should take the cord from the hole in the door leaf and insert it inside.

One should place the door-bolt in a secluded spot and let the teacher go ahead. If one encounters an acquaintance on the road, one should engage in polite conversation with them, maintaining a virtuous mind as one proceeds.

At that time, one should avoid the path of human traffic. When wishing to enter a village, one should step slightly off the road, set the bowl aside on one side, spread out the *saṃghāṭī* robe and inspect it, and then present it to the teacher.
If there are guest houses, market stalls, or workshops outside the village, one should place the leather sandals for walking upon the path inside them.
One should then ask the teacher, "May I follow behind? If the teacher says, "So be it," then one should immediately...
One should follow accordingly. If the teacher says, "It is not necessary; I shall stay in such-and-such a place," one should stay in that place as instructed.

If the teacher enters a village and does not emerge at the proper time, one should form this thought: "He has entered the village to beg for alms; this portion is for the teacher, and this portion belongs to me."
Having left the village, he should return to take his leather sandals, step off the path, place his alms bowl on the ground, and fold his saṃghāṭī robe to place it upon his head or shoulder.
Upon reaching the place where his teacher stays to eat, he should sweep it clean, spread out a sitting mat, prepare a vessel for pure water, bathing utensils, and food containers.
He should further arrange a seat for bathing, a stone for washing the feet, and provide a towel for drying the feet. If [the teacher] is at a distance...
Seeing the teacher approaching, one should immediately rise to welcome him. Taking the alms bowl from his hand, place it in a suitable location.
Take the *saṃghāṭī* robe and spread it out to inspect it; do not allow it to be stained by grease or oil. If there is such staining, it should be removed. If it requires washing, wash it.
When the teacher has finished washing his feet, one should discard the water, take the foot-washing stone and the foot-wiping cloth, and return them to their original places.

Then, having washed one's own hands clean, one should offer pure water for the teacher to wash his hands. One should take whatever food one possesses and offer it to the teacher, saying, "This is my portion of food;
you may eat it. If the teacher requires it, he should take it. When the teacher is eating, one should stand in attendance and watch over him.
One should provide whatever is required. If the time for the meal is about to pass, one should eat immediately at that same time.
Once the teacher has finished eating, one should take the bowl from his hand and serve water for rinsing the mouth.

If one has finished eating oneself and there is leftover food, it should be given to a human or a non-human being, or placed on clean ground where there is no grass, or placed in clean water free of insects. Then, take the vessel used for holding the food, wash it thoroughly, and return it.
Return them to their original places. Take up the sitting mat, the foot-washing stool, the water vessel for rinsing, and the washbasin, and return them to their respective places.
Thoroughly sweep the area where you ate. Furthermore, when entering the teacher’s room, you should inspect it;

if there is dust or dirt, you should take out the rope-couches, floor mats, and so forth, noting their original locations, and place them outside to dry. When discarding the refuse from within the room, [sweep it clean].
One should look about. If there are needles, thread, knives, or even as little as one or two pills of medicine, one should take them and place them in a visible spot;
if there is anyone who recognizes them, they shall take them. Furthermore, one should sweep and wipe the area toward the ceiling, the pegs, and the clothing racks.

If there are damaged areas in the room, such as holes made by insects or rats, those that can be plastered should be plastered, those that can be pounded should be pounded, and those that can be leveled should be leveled.
He then leveled and smoothed it, making it as clean and pure as possible. If the seats originally arranged were not orderly, he should rearrange them so they are orderly;
if they were already orderly, he should leave them as they were. The robes worn and those not yet worn should each be placed in separate locations.

The bowl-bag and needle-case should be placed together in one spot. The leather sandal-bag and the oil-container should be placed together in another spot. If there is dust and dirt in the central courtyard, [he should clear it].
One should immediately sweep it clean. Having taken the water flask and washed it thoroughly, one should refill it with pure water and place it back in its original location.
Furthermore, one should provide the teacher with the water flask, the bathing flask, and the drinking vessel. If there is bathing taking place in the bathhouse, one should inquire [about the time].

If you wish to bathe, and if it is said that you shall bathe, you should first go to the bathhouse and inspect it. You should sprinkle [the floor], and then sprinkle it; you should sweep, and then sweep;
you should discard the used water, and then discard it; you should pour in fresh water, and then pour it in; you should split firewood, and then split it;
you should place it into the stove, and then place it in. You should provide the teacher with all the necessary bathing requisites. First, inform the Elder, and only then light the fire.
Once the fire has been lit, announce: "The time has come. If the teacher is ill, frail, or extremely old, you should support him by carrying him [into the bath].

You should rub and massage the teacher’s body. You should stand behind the teacher. If you wish to rub the body of another person, or if you are having your own body rubbed by another, you must inform the teacher so that he knows.
When it is time to bathe the teacher, bathe yourself first. If the teacher is ill, frail, or extremely old, you should support him as he exits the bathing chamber. Then...
Upon returning from the carriage, he goes back to his room. Arriving at the bathhouse, he inspects all the bathing requisites and returns them to their original places.
On that same day, he should inquire after his teacher three times—morning, midday, and evening—and must not be evasive or negligent regarding two types of laborious service for the teacher:
first, repairing the dwelling; second, mending and washing clothing. Whatever tasks are taught by the teacher according to the Dharma, he must perform them all with devotion.

When traveling or being dispatched to various regions to conduct affairs, one must not speak with boastfulness or exaggeration. If one has been rebuked, one should confess to the teacher in this manner:
baring the right shoulder, removing the leather sandals, kneeling on the right knee, and joining the palms, one should say these words: "Venerable Sir..."
I now repent and shall not do it again. If my repentance is accepted, that is well; if it is not accepted, I shall immediately humble myself and comply, seeking skillful means to resolve the offense.
If the teacher acts in five ways contrary to the Dharma, the disciple should repent and depart, saying:
"I act according to the Dharma, yet the teacher does not know this; I do not act contrary to the Dharma, yet he likewise does not know this. If...
"I have committed an offense, yet I abandoned [the teacher] and did not admonish him. If he committed one, I did not know it;
even when he confessed his offense, I did not know it. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:

"Furthermore, if there is a person who relies upon a preceptor, having shaved off their hair and beard within the Buddha-dharma and donned the dharma-robes, they go forth and practice with pure faith. That person, toward their preceptor, even until the end..."
Even by providing the four requisites for their livelihood, one cannot fully repay their kindness. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states:

"If they are one's parents or the two teachers—these four persons—even if they have broken the precepts, they should still be provided for and must not be treated with contempt. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
A person of wisdom, when approaching a place where a person of long-standing virtue resides, should avoid six positions before sitting down:
first, too far away; second, too close; third, upwind; fourth, on high ground; fifth, directly in front; and sixth, behind.

If a disciple follows his teacher and encounters a discourse on the Dharma along the way, if he remains until the appearance of dawn for the sake of greedily hearing the teaching, he does not incur the offense of being separated from the teacher. Why is this?
Therefore, because the mind has no fixed abiding.
Question: Among the five types of ācāryas, four kinds are definitely elders (sthavira), while those who merely teach reading may be juniors (navaka).
What should be the method for serving them? Answer: With the sole exception of prostration, everything else is exactly as when serving [an elder].

Regarding the Dharma for serving one's teacher: Question: It is said that a bhikṣu’s leftover food should be given to humans or non-humans, or placed on clean ground to be offered to birds and beasts, or placed in water to be offered to fish and insects. Why, then, is it now stated that it should be placed in water free of insects?
Answer: As stated in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, "insects" does not refer to species such as fish or turtles; rather, it refers to very small [creatures].
Regarding those such as the *diaoji* (crab-like creatures), it is primarily out of fear that their consumption of salty or greasy food might cause them harm to life.
○ The *Upādhyāya Dharmavibhāṣā* states: "There are three kinds of elders (*sthavira*): first, the elder by years, whose *śīla-kalpa* (monastic seniority) is highest; second, the elder by..."

Regarding the conventional *sthavira* (elder): even one who is only twenty years of age should be unanimously elected as the elder if he possesses great merit and great wisdom. Regarding the three types of *dharmatā-sthaviras*: the *arhat* is the [first] *sthavira*.
In the Sanskrit language, this is *sthavira*, which here is translated as "Elder" (*shangzuo*) and also as "Superior Person" (*shangshi*).

One who lacks the practice of benefiting both self and others is called an "Inferior Person" (*xiashi*). One who benefits only oneself is an "Intermediate Person" (*zhongshi*), while one who possesses both is a [Superior Person].
This is beneficial. Regarding those of superior capacity:
it is asked, if a novice bhikṣu has mastered the sūtras and śāstras but is not yet familiar with the Vinaya rules, he must remain in dependence for five summer retreats.
Even if one possesses great merit and great wisdom, why is he appointed as the *upādhyāya* (senior preceptor)? The answer is:

appointing him as the senior preceptor merely serves to have him propagate the sutras and expound the treatises, and to oversee the cultivation of meritorious deeds; it does not mean that [the disciple] is thereby released from the requirement of formal reliance (*niśraya*).
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "Those with less than one year of seniority up to nine years of seniority are called junior seats (*kaniṣṭha-āsana*).

Those with ten years of seniority up to nineteen years of seniority are called middle seats (*madhyama-āsana*). Those with twenty years of seniority up to forty-nine years of seniority are called senior seats (*sthavira-āsana*).

Those exceeding fifty years of seniority and above are called venerable elders (*vṛddha-sthavira*). The *Caturthabhāga-vinaya* states: "The Buddha told the bhikṣus: 'If a senior seat does not study the precepts...'"
Nor does he praise the precepts. If there are other bhikṣus who delight in training in the precepts and praise them, he is likewise unable to encourage or praise them at the proper time.
Such an elder should not be approached, nor should one study his teachings.
If one studies and practices that dharma, one will suffer for a long night. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: There are five factors by which the True Dharma perishes and disappears:
first, a lack of desire; second, dull faculties; third, although one recites the words and meanings, one cannot correctly receive them, nor can one enable others to understand them;
fourth, one cannot cause those who receive [the teaching] to possess respectful deportment; fifth, there is no one who preaches the Dharma.

They are unable to teach according to the Dharma; they engage in the five types of quarrels and mutual disputes; they do not dwell in forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*); nor do they cherish or respect forest hermitages.

If one acts contrary to these five factors, the True Dharma will not perish, vanish, or disappear. Furthermore, there are five other factors by which the True Dharma perishes, vanishes, and disappears:
not following the teaching of the Dharma, following the teaching of what is not the Dharma, not following the Dharma of patience, and following that which is not...
Regarding the Dharma of Patience: [If] one does not respect the elders, lacks dignified deportment, and the elders do not instruct them in the Dharma;

if one feels distress when the elders preach the Dharma, thereby preventing those of later generations from receiving instruction in the Tripiṭaka—once such a person has passed away, the bhikṣus will become negligent and practice what is non-Dharmic, losing all wholesome qualities.
Conversely, if these five conditions are reversed, the True Dharma will not perish, nor will it be lost.

It has vanished. Furthermore, there are seven factors that cause the True Dharma to perish and vanish: lack of faith, laziness, lack of shame, lack of remorse, forgetfulness, lack of concentration, and meager wisdom.
When the True Dharma perishes and the Semblance Dharma era begins, five kinds of unrighteousness exist in the world:
first, there are bhikṣus who, having attained a minor degree of *śamatha*, claim they have already attained the Noble Dharma; second, laypeople [claim to] be reborn in heaven; or...

First, there are those who have left the household life and yet fall into the evil realms. Second, there are those who abandon worldly occupations to leave the household life, but then break the precepts.
Third, there are those who break the precepts and receive much support, while those who uphold the precepts receive no support. Fourth, there is no one who does not suffer verbal abuse.
Even Arhats have been reviled. The Buddha told Upāli: "In the future there will be five terrors that do not exist now;
you should know this matter and seek their cessation through skillful means. What are the five?

There will be bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate ethical discipline, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom, yet they ordain others and grant them the precepts, being unable to cause those others to cultivate the body and ethical discipline."

The lack of cultivation of the mind and wisdom is called the first fear. To provide others with a place of reliance while not cultivating the mind and wisdom oneself, or to keep śrāmaṇeras without being able to cause them to cultivate the mind and wisdom, is the second and third fear.

To dwell in close proximity to lay attendants and śrāmaṇeras without cultivating the mind and wisdom oneself, and without knowing the three characteristics—digging the earth, cutting grass, and using water—is likewise a source of fear.

Irrigating [the fields] is the fourth fear. Not cultivating the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, yet reciting together the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—placing the beginning and end in the middle, and placing the middle in the beginning;
not knowing for oneself what is pure dharma (*śukladharma*) while seeing it, nor what constitutes an offense or a non-offense—this is the fifth fear.
There are further five fears that do not exist now but will exist in the future; these should be known.
Regarding this matter, one should seek skillful means to extinguish it. What are the five? In the future, there will be bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, precepts, mind, or wisdom;
they lack desire for practice and possess dull faculties. Although they recite the words and meanings of the teachings, they cannot attain right realization—this is the first fear.

Not cultivating the body, precepts, mind, or wisdom, they associate closely with bhikṣuṇīs and may commit a grave offense, thereby abandoning the precepts and returning to lay life—this is the second fear. Not cultivating...

Regarding bodily discipline, mental wisdom, and the profound sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata—such as those on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and the various profound and essential teachings on the twelve links of dependent origination—they are unable to believe in, delight in, or accept and uphold them. Even if they do accept them, they cannot master or penetrate them.

When these things are being taught, they lack a heart of compassion and a heart of affection; instead, they take pleasure in composing literary verses and embellishing phrases, delighting in worldly matters.

Regarding worldly conventions: when one speaks of mundane matters with a mind of faith and delight, or with a mind of attachment and pleasure according to what the world desires, this causes the profound sūtras taught by the Tathāgata—such as emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the twelve links of dependent origination, and other deep dharmas that lead to cessation—to be extinguished;

this is the third fear. Furthermore, failing to cultivate the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom, and abandoning the *āraṇya* (forest hermitage) for the sake of food and clothing [is likewise a cause for fear].
Whether staying in a secluded place, under a forest tree, or entering a village for the sake of food and clothing, one seeks much;
while seeking, one becomes agitated. This is the fourth and fifth fear (the fear of the Dharma-gate; since the blame lies with the elderly, it is recorded here as a warning).

The fourth section of the *Śrāmaṇerakārikā* states: "There are five qualities by which a bhikṣu should not be befriended: if he delights in quarreling; if he is overly preoccupied with worldly activities;
if he disputes with a preeminent bhikṣu within the Saṃgha; if he delights in wandering about incessantly; or if he is... [text fragment ends].
Regarding those who preach the Dharma to others and show people what is wholesome and unwholesome, there are furthermore five kinds of persons with whom one should not travel as companions:

those who prefer to walk too far ahead; those who prefer to walk too far behind; those who like to interrupt the flow of another's speech; and those who cannot distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome speech.
One does not praise good speech nor extol evil speech. When one obtains gain in accordance with the Dharma, one does not accept it for another's sake at an improper time.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, "A virtuous friend is half of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). The Buddha said, "Ānanda," [it is indeed so].
A virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the entirety of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "There are ten matters for which a bhikṣu is not loved by others.
What are the ten? Not associating [with others]; associating too frequently; associating for the sake of profit;

loving those who are not loved; not loving those who are loved; disliking truthful speech; interfering in the affairs of others; and desiring [to display] authority and virtue when one actually lacks them."
He treats others with contempt and delights in private conversations. He has many desires and cravings.

An *āraṇyaka* bhikṣu should not disparage a bhikṣu living in a village by saying, "You surely stay here because you relish the slight flavors on the tip of your tongue. Instead, he should praise him, saying:
"You dwell in the village, preaching the Dharma and teaching others; you act as a protector for the Dharma and provide shelter and protection for us. [This applies to] the bhikṣus in the village.
O Kāśyapa, you should not lightly disparage those who dwell in the forest (araṇya), saying: "You dwell in the forest only because you hope for fame and profit;
even deer and wild beasts dwell in the forest. You should instead praise them, saying: "From dawn until the end of the day, you count but your years and months [of practice].
You have distanced yourself from the village to contemplate in solitude; this is the supreme undertaking, and this is difficult to perform."
In such a place, one should be able to dwell there and bring the mind and its faculties to rest; one should not engage in discussion or contend with one another over victory and defeat.

Regarding the section on "Prostration according to the Dharma and Vinaya," it states: There are four types of those to whom one should prostrate. The first is the Tathāgata, to whom all humans and devas should pay their respects.
Therefore: (1) those who have gone forth do not pay homage to worldly people, for they are the ones who are respected by the laity;

(2) one should pay homage to those who received full ordination (*upasampadā*) before oneself, with the sole exception of the community of nuns, for their respect is likewise due; (3) those who have not yet received full ordination should pay homage to those who have received it.

There are ten types of persons who should not be prostrated to: those performing the *parivāsa* (probation) and other such penances; the four types of persons [undergoing discipline]; persons receiving training (*śikṣamāṇā*);

the three types of persons subject to suspension (*pratisaṃharaṇīya-karma*); all householders; and those who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*). Regarding the ritual of respectful salutation, there are two distinctions: the first consists of placing the five limbs upon the ground;

the second consists of grasping the calves and feet while saying "vandana" (this is a term for paying respect in the Western Regions [India], for which no translation has yet been found; it is likely equivalent to...).
*Vandanā* (sometimes called *vandana*; erroneously transcribed as *vaṃnam*), which is translated as "I prostrate.

If one performs a prostration knowing that another’s body has been defiled by impurity, or if one prostrates while one’s own body is defiled by impurity, in both cases one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*). There are two kinds of defilement by impurity: first, having finished eating but not yet rinsed the mouth;
second, having relieved oneself but not yet washed clean. When prostrating in the dark, one should not let [the head] touch the ground; one should say:
*Vandana* means to pay homage. The fourth *khaṇḍa* states: "There are ten occasions when a bhikṣu should not be saluted:

when he is performing the great needs (defecating), when he is performing the small needs (urinating), if he is naked, if he is shaving his head, if he is preaching the Dharma, if he is chewing a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), if he is rinsing his mouth, if he is drinking, if he is eating, or if he is consuming fruit.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "One should not [salute] while wearing..."
One should not perform a prostration while wearing only a single robe, nor should one accept a prostration while wearing only a single robe.

Regarding the method for filial piety toward one's parents, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Pindola Bharadvāja’s parents were impoverished; he wished to provide them with offerings of clothing, yet..."
"I venture to report this to the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If a person were to carry their father on the right shoulder and their mother on the left shoulder for a hundred years, even relieving themselves upon them and providing them with the most exquisite worldly food, clothing, and offerings, they still could not repay even a moment’s debt of gratitude.
From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to serve their parents with all their heart and for the rest of their lives."
If one does not make offerings, one incurs a grave offense. The *Mūla-nidāna* states:
"Parents perform difficult deeds for their children and shoulder manifold sufferings; even if [the child] has gone forth into homelessness, they must provide for their parents.
With the exception of robes and alms-bowls, all other things may be offered. If there are no other possessions, one may beg from donors at appropriate times. If one begs...
It is difficult to obtain; one should provide for them using the goods regularly acquired by the Saṃgha.

If there are no such goods, one should reduce by half one's own regular portion of food from the Saṃgha and use it to provide for them. This applies even to those who normally practice alms-gathering.
One should place within one's own stomach only as much food as is necessary for its filling; one should take half of that to provide for one’s parents.

Regarding the rules for the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one should not travel among people at all times; rather, one is permitted to observe the three-month summer retreat. One should inform the person upon whom one relies, saying:
"I shall observe the summer retreat (varṣā) here. Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], relying upon the village of [Name], the monastery of [Name], and the cell of [Name], shall observe the summer retreat during the first three months. This is for the purpose of repairing the dilapidated dwelling.
Thus it is said three times. The procedure for the later retreat is also the same. If there is no person upon whom to rely, one should perform the mental recitation.
Regarding the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat): if one comes solely for the purpose of entering the *varṣā*, the *varṣā* is thereby established.

Once the *varṣā* is completed, if a visiting monk (*āgantuka-bhikṣu*) arrives, he should neither move [to another place] nor depart. If he wishes to enter the *varṣā*, he should first go in person to inspect the dwellings and bedding.

Only after that should they receive [the assignment]. A formal act consisting of a motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) should be performed to appoint a person to distribute rooms and bedding.

That person should count the monks, count the rooms, and count the bedding—whether there is an abundance or a lack of merit—and so forth, until they have reached the presence of the Elder (*sthavira*).
Thus it was said: "Venerable Elder, please take these lodgings and bedding as you wish;

first give them to the Elder, and then pass them down in succession until the lowest seat. One should accept a lodging and maintain it according to one's ability, rather than dividing it among the entire assembly.
If one wishes to observe the rains retreat in such a place, one should first establish the boundaries. Thus it was said.
Upon departing, one should extinguish one's name [from the register]. One must not move the beds, mats, bedding, or furniture from this room to another room;

rather, one should consult the resident monks and only then move them. When leaving, they should be returned to their original places. If the dwelling is dilapidated or damaged, they may be moved to another room.
Once repairs have been made, they should be returned. The same applies to other monasteries. If there are no fixed bedding items, [the same rules apply].

This extends even to items such as staffs and fans; those not present in the dwelling should be assigned to them. If there are any remaining, they shall be distributed starting from the senior monk (*sthavira*).

There are both those who enter the *pūrvavārṣika* (early summer) retreat and those who enter the *paścimavārṣika* (late summer) retreat, and all must remain for three months. Those in the late summer retreat are also permitted to receive the invitation for self-examination (*pravāraṇā*).

One may accept the items obtained [as offerings]. One may accept bedding and furniture. One should not count a year toward the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) if three months have not yet been completed;
one should remain until the days are fulfilled. One should not observe the *varṣā* in the open air.
It is permitted to observe the *varṣā* under a tree, within a small hut, inside a mountain cave, or within the hollow of a tree. If various circumstances should arise during the *varṣā*...
On this account, listen: the rule for departing for seven days is permitted, provided one must return within those seven days.

If it is impossible to return after another seven days have passed, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) is permitted to receive the rule for staying beyond seven days—whether for half a month or one month.

If there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one should depart. If there is a matter concerning a schism in the Saṃgha, one should depart; or, if it is to stop a schism in the Saṃgha, one should depart.

One should go. If it is for the sake of reconciling that Saṃgha, one should go. Having received a seven-day leave to depart from the boundary, if there are obstacles and one does not return, the seniority (vassa) is not lost.

If, while at the previous place of retreat, one hears that great gains and offerings are being received at another location and immediately goes there, one does not obtain the seniority of the preceding year;
having violated the original commitment, one incurs an offense. Alternatively, one may go without cause, or having received a seven-day leave.
If the Dharma exceeds seven days, one violates the original commitment and incurs an offense. If one returns within seven days, there is no offense.
If, at the very end, one accepts an invitation for seven days to go outside the boundary, whether one returns or not, there is no offense. It is the same for the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*).

If one has accepted an invitation for the retreat and faces a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one should go and inform the donor and request to move elsewhere; if permission is granted, it is well. If...
[The Buddha] did not permit it; one should then depart. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states:

"If one is observing the rains retreat at this location, and hears that the Saṃgha at another location has obtained a large quantity of *varṣāśāṭī* robes, and goes there to stay, one immediately loses [the merit of] this location. After staying briefly there, if one returns to this location, one again loses [the merit of] that location.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one is traveling on the road and has not yet reached the place of residence, [one may observe] the rains retreat."

When the day arrives, one should enter the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) by the side of the road, or by a tree, or by a vehicle. When morning comes and it is light, one should proceed to one's dwelling place.
Upon reaching the final day of the *varṣā*, one should bare the right shoulder, kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and speak these words: "Venerable sir, please bear me in mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall observe the three-month *varṣā* retreat here at this monastery. Thus, [one should repeat] three times.

It is said that summer months are also called the rainy season; therefore, it is termed the "rainy-season retreat" (varṣā-vāsa). If a bhikṣu is traveling on the road and does not enter the retreat on the day of the earlier retreat (pūrvavarṣā), [he incurs an offense].
First, there is an offense of *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline): having arrived at the place of residence, one does not accept the later retreat during the later retreat period;

this constitutes a second offense of *vinayātikrama*. Such a person has broken the retreat and shall not receive the gift of robes. If the quarters were assigned during the spring or winter seasons, [the same applies].

When a senior elder (*sthavira*) arrives, one should occupy the quarters according to the established order. When a senior elder arrives during the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), one must not occupy the quarters according to that same order.
If one evicts another from their place during the rainy season retreat, it is an offense of *vinayātikrama*. One is not permitted to refuse to speak with them.

If one wishes to employ skillful means to have few affairs, one need not speak for half a month. Upon reaching the day of the *poṣadha*, one should speak together, exchange greetings, discuss matters, and offer blessings.
After the *poṣadha* day, one continues as before. The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states:

"It is permitted to dwell in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*) and to observe the rains retreat in a place where rain cannot reach one's robes or bowl. If there are no affairs, one should go forward [to the assembly]."

Regarding the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat): if there is a matter [that necessitates departure], one is permitted to enter the later *varṣā*. When wishing to enter the *varṣā*, one should first deliberate whether there are obstacles or no obstacles at this location.
There was a bhikṣu who entered the *varṣā*, but his coarse food was insufficient; the Buddha permitted that for this reason he might break the *varṣā* without fault.
The same applies to obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacarya*) or threats to life, and so forth. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Regarding the later *varṣā*..."
