[The] Seat. One should not take a room or bedding from the senior monk (*sthavira*) of the preceding *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat). If the preceding senior monk has two portions of bedding, he should give one portion to the subsequent [monk].
Regarding the seven-day rule (*saptāha-vidhi*), it must be received from among the five groups of monks; it may not be received through mental resolve (*manasikāra*).
This excludes those dwelling alone in an *araṇya* (wilderness hermitage). If one is on a boat, whether going upriver or downriver, one must not remain settled [in that state].
Regarding "dwelling": one who remains bound to a place without moving away attains the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat).

If one wishes to enter the *varṣā*, one should first deliberate upon whether the dwelling place is secure, whether there are good companions, and whether there are suitable conditions for seated meditation, preaching the Dharma, and medicinal food according to one's illness; only then should one enter the retreat.
If there is no circumstance authorized by the Buddha, one is not permitted to stay overnight outside the boundary for even a single night;

to undertake the "mute rule" (mūka-dharma) constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense, as it is the practice of non-Buddhists who do not engage in conversation. The *Mūla-karman* states: "There is a matter involving a specific cause."
The practice of observing [the *poṣadha*] for one day up to seven days may be announced to a single person. Beyond seven days up to forty days, one must request it within the *saṃgha*.
Beyond forty days, the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is lost; however, if there are difficult circumstances, it is not considered a loss of the summer retreat.
Question: During the final three-month *anvārambhaṇa* retreat, if the period is not yet complete, one is still not permitted to count toward the [seniority] year.

However, if one accepts a seven-day leave and does not return, it is called "not losing the year. Now, there are those who do not undertake the *anvārambhaṇa* or who arbitrarily break the retreat; may their years be counted?
If their years are not counted, will there not be confusion regarding the sequence of seniority in the precepts? Furthermore, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*:
Question: If one does not accept the *anvārambhaṇa* (the subsequent) retreat on the day of the *pūrvāvarṣā* (the preceding) retreat, there is one *vinayātikrama* offense.

Other schools do not establish this; from what source does it follow? Answer: Entering the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is a mandatory duty for a bhikṣu. If one violates the Vinaya regulations, one loses many benefits.
If there are unavoidable circumstances, the subsequent retreat is permitted. However, if there is no such reason, one must certainly accept the preceding retreat. (From the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*).
The establishment of this offense is intended to punish the transgression of showing contempt for the Dharma; in reality, it does not differ significantly from other schools.

However, what is meant by "losing a year" refers only to the fact that one cannot receive robe-offerings, cannot serve as a person who lays down the *kaṭhina* cloth, and—provided one has not yet reached ten years of seniority—cannot serve as a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), and so forth.
It does not mean that after having previously received the precepts, one is now further degraded and made to relinquish them.
This is a minor matter. This principle has already been clarified at the outset in the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas).

Regarding the ritual for the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination), there were monks who, having entered the summer retreat (*varṣā*) at separate residences, made a collective agreement that they would not speak with one another nor perform prostrations.

He inquired after their welfare. Those who had gone out for alms, whether earlier or later, each performed their respective duties. If they were holding their bowls together, they would signal their companions with their hands;

in this way, they dwelt in peace and comfort. When the rains retreat was concluded, they went to the Buddha’s dwelling. The Buddha greeted them with words of consolation, and they reported everything to him in detail.
The Buddha said, "You foolish people consider yourselves free from affliction, yet this is in fact an affliction.

You foolish people dwell together like enemies, just like white sheep. Through countless skillful means, I have instructed the bhikṣus to teach one another, to receive each other’s words, and to awaken one another in turn.
Yet you foolish people are identical to the non-Buddhists in your practice of silence."
[The Buddha spoke on] the Dharma. At that time, the group of six (ṣaḍvargika) monks brought charges against a pure monk. The Buddha said:

"If you wish to bring a charge against a monk who has committed an offense, you should first seek his permission. At that time, because the group of six resented the pure monk for having previously sought their permission, they again sought permission from the pure monk.
The Buddha said: "One may seek permission provided one possesses five qualities: knowing the proper time, and not [acting] at an improper time..."
According to reality, not with falsehood; for benefit, not for lack of benefit; with gentleness, not with harshness;
with a mind of loving-kindness, not with malice. Those six groups lacked these five qualities within themselves; those who possessed the remaining five qualities requested permission from them.

The group of six did not listen. The Buddha said: "From now on, when the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) has concluded, one should perform the *pravāraṇā*. One may permit the postponement of the *pravāraṇā*, but one should not seek permission [to do so].
Why? Because the *pravāraṇā* itself is the granting of permission. One should not perform the *pravāraṇā* all at once; one should permit the *pravāraṇā* to be performed one by one.

One should not perform the *pravāraṇā* according to one's own whim; one should perform the *pravāraṇā* in order, starting from the senior monk (*sthavira*). Permission is granted for the appointment of an official to oversee the *pravāraṇā*."

A person appointed to receive the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults) must possess five qualities: they must be free from partiality, anger, fear, and delusion; and they must know who has already performed their own *pravāraṇā* and who has not.

Such a person should be appointed through a formal motion (*jñapti*) and a second proclamation (*karmavācanā*). The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha appoint the monk so-and-so to act as the recipient of the *pravāraṇā*.
This is the motion. The formal ritual (*karman*) should be performed accordingly. One should not perform the *pravāraṇā* while remaining on one's seat.

The Elder shall rise from his seat and kneel with both knees on the ground; all the monks should likewise rise from their seats and kneel with both knees on the ground. Once the *pravāraṇā* is concluded, they may sit again.

One should perform the *pravāraṇā* clearly and at a measured pace, reciting it three times. With the upper robe draped over one shoulder, kneeling with the right knee on the ground, and joining the palms, one should speak these words:
"Venerable Sirs, today the community of monks performs the *pravāraṇā*. I, the bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *pravāraṇā*."
"If you see, hear, or suspect any offense, Venerable Elders, please speak to me out of compassion. If I see an offense, I shall confess it according to the Dharma.
Thus he should say three times. The one appointed to receive the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) should first announce this, and only then confer the invitation.

Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today the community of monks performs the *pravāraṇā*. If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: we shall perform the *pravāraṇā* in harmony.

This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). One should not perform the *pravāraṇā* in an illegal manner with a divided assembly, nor in an illegal manner with a united assembly, nor in a legal manner with a divided assembly.

One should perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) in accordance with the Dharma and in harmony. It is permitted to perform the *pravāraṇā* at the place where the *poṣadha* (confession of offenses) is held.

If one is traveling on a road and is able to perform the *pravāraṇā* in harmony, that is good. If it is not possible to do so in harmony, one may move to another location according to those who are close, friendly, and of like mind;

having established a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) there, one should perform the *pravāraṇā*. Then, one should dissolve the boundary and depart. If only a single bhikṣu remains, he should go [to the assembly] on the day of the *pravāraṇā*.
At the place where the *poṣadha* is recited, one should sweep and sprinkle the area, and so forth, until the *śalākā* (voting sticks) are prepared. One should wait for the visiting bhikṣus to arrive.
If there are five or more bhikṣus, one should appoint a person to administer the *pravāraṇā*. If there are four or fewer, they should perform the *pravāraṇā* among themselves.
They should say: "Today the Saṃgha performs the *pravāraṇā*; I, the bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *pravāraṇā* and am pure. This should be said three times. If there are none...
When someone arrives, one should mentally reflect and speak aloud in this same manner three times. If there is business to attend to, one should entrust the matter to another.
The one who receives the entrustment, if they also have business to attend to, should in turn entrust it to another. Once the business is concluded, one should go in person.

If there are the eight difficulties or other circumstances that prevent this, one should perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) in an abbreviated form—either by saying it twice, once, or by combining the three recitations with others, or combining the two recitations with others.
If they are to perform the *pravāraṇā* together, they may depart immediately, depending on the distance of their destination.

If there is bound to be a dispute during the *pravāraṇā* today, or if it might cause a schism in the Saṃgha, one should not perform the *pravāraṇā* that very day; rather, one should delay for a short time.

Regarding those who obstruct the *pravāraṇā* because their three modes of action (*trikarma*) are impure, it is as explained in the section on the *poṣadha*. The case of illness is also as in the *poṣadha*.

It is said: If there are bhikṣus who have attained the realization of superior fruits (*viśeṣa-phala*) and fear that by performing the *pravāraṇā* now they will not obtain such bliss, they should perform a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to extend the *pravāraṇā* until the completion of the fourth month.

Alternatively, if there are bhikṣus from other residences who are not in harmony and wish to come here for the *pravāraṇā*, it should be handled as explained in the section on the *poṣadha*. This is according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
The Vinaya states: When the eighth month arrives, if a guest still does not depart, one should not go [to the *pravāraṇā* ceremony] without performing the *pravāraṇā* oneself;

this is because one should not engage in quarrels or mutual recriminations. One should not perform the *karmavācanā* for the *pravāraṇā* in the presence of bhikṣuṇīs or those who have not received the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).
Once the *pravāraṇā* is concluded, one should not perform the *poṣadha*; the *pravāraṇā* itself is the *poṣadha*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
When the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) is concluded, one should go before the *sthavira* (senior monk) and announce: "The Saṃgha has unanimously completed the *pravāraṇā*.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If among those in the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), there is even one person who entered the retreat early, when the fifteenth day of the seventh month arrives, the entire assembly should together receive the *pravāraṇā* from that one person.
Once the *pravāraṇā* is finished, they remain seated until the fifteenth day of the eighth month. If...
In all cases of the later *anvāroka* (post-rainy season retreat), everyone should perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day of the eighth month.

If a bhikṣu is observing the retreat in a village and hears that on the day of the city’s *pravāraṇā* there will be various offerings and the Dharma will be preached throughout the night, and the community wishes to go [to the city], he should perform the *pravāraṇā* on the fourteenth day and may then depart.
He should appoint a person to preside over the *pravāraṇā*, whether it be one person or more.

2. One must not exceed [the number]. If two persons act as those who perform the *pravāraṇā*, one person shall receive the *pravāraṇā* from the *sthavira*, while the other should stand before the next seat in order.
Once the *sthavira* has spoken, the next person in order speaks.

In this manner, they proceed successively down until they reach their own seats, where they should receive the *pravāraṇā*. They must not wait until the *saṃgha* has finished its *pravāraṇā* before performing their own.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "It is permitted for eight senior monks (*sthavira*) to perform the *pravāraṇā* individually;

those of equal standing and below shall perform the *pravāraṇā* simultaneously. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "If there is anyone within the assembly who is not pure, one must refrain from performing the *pravāraṇā*.
One should perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of 'suspension of the *pravāraṇā*. One should investigate the person who is impure; if the offense is grave, they should be expelled."
For those who are light offenders, cause them to perform repentance and then conduct the *pravāraṇā*.

If such a person remains impure, even if they rely on their own cleverness and great wisdom, or rely on the power of their followers, kings, ministers, or officials, and cannot be expelled, one should wait until the subsequent *pravāraṇā*.
If they still do not leave when the time for the subsequent *pravāraṇā* arrives, the Saṃgha may go outside the boundary to perform the *pravāraṇā*, thereby attaining purity.

Purifying the Ears. The *Nanhai Jiguai Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) states: In Sanskrit it is called *pravāraṇā*, which is translated as "following one's will" (*suīyì*).
This refers to the meaning of allowing others to freely raise matters regarding the three types of conduct in order to confess faults and eliminate transgressions.

The older term "self-indulgence" (*zìzì*) is a literal translation of this meaning. It must be performed on the fourteenth day of the month; one should invite a master of the scriptures to ascend the seat and recite the sutras. Regarding...
At that time, the monastic community and the laity gathered like clouds; they lit lamps to continue the illumination and made offerings of incense and flowers.

At dawn, they all went out together to circumambulate the village and the city, each with a devout heart paying homage to the various *caityas*. Platforms, carts, and carriages bore the sacred images, while drums and music filled the sky; banners and canopies were draped and interlaced, fluttering and obscuring the sun.

Only at the hour of *yūzhōng* (the fifth watch) did they begin their return to the monastery, and it was not until noon that the great vegetarian feast (*mahā-bhakta*) was held. After noon, everyone...
Having assembled, they perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. First the bhikṣus, then the bhikṣuṇīs, followed by the three lower assemblies.
If the assembly is large and there is fear that it will take too long, many individuals should be appointed to receive the *pravāraṇā* in turns.

If one is accused of an offense by another, one should remove it according to the Dharma through confession. At this time, whether laypeople offer alms or the Saṃgha acts on its own behalf, whatever items are offered—

When about to arrive before the assembly, the one possessing the five virtues (who is free from attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, and who knows what may or may not be divided) should ask the senior monk (upādhyāya/senior elder): "Regarding this object..."
"May we take these items as the property for the Sangha’s *prātimokṣa* (distribution) ceremony? The elders replied, "Yes.

All clothing, knives, needles, awls, and the like were accepted and divided equally. Once the *prātimokṣa* ceremony was concluded, they were free to go their separate ways. Regarding those who speak of their offenses:
it is the desire to confess one's transgressions, to declare past faults, to reform the past and cultivate the future, and to offer sincere and earnest self-reproach every half-month.

Regarding the *poṣadha*: morning and evening, one should reflect upon the transgressions committed. If a violation of the first category of precepts (*āpatti*) has occurred, the matter cannot be remedied.
For violations of the second category, twenty persons are required. If one commits a minor offense, one should confess and repent before someone of equal standing;
by declaring one’s own faults, one hopes to achieve purification. Each must act according to their respective jurisdiction, and only then can the extinction of the offense be expected.
If one were to speak generally regarding the fault [of this practice], it is not permitted by the Vinaya.
Question: In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the persons appointed for the *pravāraṇā* do not exceed one or two; in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, many people are permitted to be appointed.

In both the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *pravāraṇā* is performed one by one in successive order. In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, with the exception of the eight persons beginning with the *sthavira*, the rest perform it according to their seniority.
This allows them to perform the *pravāraṇā* together. From what source does this derive? Answer: If those receiving the *pravāraṇā* are numerous, they cannot avoid clamor and confusion;

one should follow the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which requires that each person perform the *pravāraṇā* individually. However, if the assembly is so large that individual performance is difficult to manage, one should follow the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
Regarding the *kaṭhina* robe procedure:

After the community of bhikṣus had completed their summer retreat and performed the *pravāraṇā*, they went to see the World-Honored One. On the way, they encountered rain, and their robes were all soaked.
The *saṃghāṭī* robe was heavy, and [the monks] were utterly exhausted. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "When the summer retreat (*varṣā*) has concluded, there are four things that ought to be done:

the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*), the dissolution of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha-vimocana*), the establishment of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*)—if one wishes to re-establish it, whether making it larger or smaller, it is necessary first to dissolve it and then to establish it; however, if one does not re-establish it, then dissolution is not required—and the acceptance of the *guṇa-cīvara* (robe of merit)."
Having received the *kaṭhina* robe, one obtains five privileges: first, keeping extra robes; second, staying overnight apart from one's robes;
third, eating in a group apart from one’s own community; fourth, eating at successive meals; and fifth, entering a village before or after a meal without informing another monk.
How is the reception of the *kaṭhina* robe accomplished? If one obtains a new robe, a robe offered by a donor, or a rag-robe (*pāṃsukūla*), whether it be a new one or an old one...
Regarding robes: new items are made pure by marking them; if they have already been washed, they are made pure after being washed and marked.

They must not be obtained through wrong livelihood, nor obtained through flattery or crookedness, nor obtained through signs, nor obtained through provocation. They must not be kept overnight; they must not be subject to the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (shedyuo) unless they are subsequently purified.

They must be received on the same day they arrive, in accordance with the Dharma. A four-sided robe has a border; a five-strip robe has ten sections. Even if it exceeds this number of sections, it should still be accepted.
One should personally wash, dye, stretch, and roll it out; then cut it into ten sections and sew them together. One should receive it before the assembly of monks and announce as follows:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. Today the Saṃgha receives the *guṇavatī-cīvara*. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha, being in harmony, receive the *guṇavatī-cīvara*.
This is the announcement. Next, one should ask: "Who is able to hold the *guṇavatī*?"

Regarding the robe-cloth: if it is said that [a monk] is capable, he should be appointed by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so to hold the *guṇavat-cīvara* (robe of merit) for the Saṃgha. The formal motion (*jñapti*) is stated thus; the *karman* is performed accordingly.
Next, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is performed to entrust the robe to the holder: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. In this residence, there has been obtained robe-cloth that is to be distributed."

"Regarding this object: it shall be divided among the present Sangha. If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and listen. The Sangha shall bestow this robe upon a certain bhikṣu;
that bhikṣu shall take this robe and, for the sake of the Sangha, receive it as a *kaṭhina* robe and maintain it at this residence.

The formal motion (*jñapti*) is thus made. The ritual procedure (*karman*) is to be performed accordingly. The bhikṣu who holds the robe should rise, take hold of the robe, and follow the other bhikṣus.
When the hands reach the robe, it is called the "point of clear understanding. One should speak as follows: "This robe, the Sangha shall accept and make into a *kaṭhina* robe;
this robe, the Sangha now accepts and makes into a *kaṭhina* robe; this robe, the Sangha has finished accepting and making into a *kaṭhina* robe.
Having spoken thus three times, those bhikṣus should say: "The one who accepted it has accepted it well."
"Whatever merit and reputation there is herein belongs to me. The robe-holder should respond, "So be it. In this manner, the procedure continues in sequence down to the lowest seat.
If an uncompleted robe is obtained, it should be formally assigned (*karmavācanā*) within the Saṃgha, and a monk should be appointed to make it.
If it has been made and completed, it should be received according to the Dharma. When the four months of winter have ended, the Saṃgha should put forth the *kaṭhina* robe.

It should be put forth in this manner: the Saṃgha assembles in harmony; those who have not yet received full ordination are excluded; and for those who do not attend, their consent (*chanda*) must be declared.
"The Saṃgha is now in harmony. What shall we do? He replied, "We shall put forth the *kaṭhina* robe. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen.
Today the community of monks puts forth the *kaṭhina* robe. If the time for the Saṃgha has come, and if the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha, being in harmony, put forth the *kaṭhina* robe.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "If it is not put forth, and the period for the *kaṭhina* robe expires, there is an offense of *duṣkṛta* (transgression). [From the] *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*."
It is said: If one person acts alone, at the time of taking it up, he should say: "This *kaṭhina* robe has been cut;
I now accept it. Thus he should speak three times. At the time of cutting, he should say: "This *kaṭhina* robe, I shall accept.
At the time of sewing, washing, dyeing, marking, and purifying with a knife, he should also speak as above. Once it is finished, he should mentally reflect and speak aloud:
"I, bhikṣu [Name], accept this kaṭhina robe. Thus it is said three times. There are ten matters by which the kaṭhina is relinquished:
1. Relinquishing upon the completion of the robe: At the time of receiving it, one forms this thought: "Once I have finished making the robe, I shall relinquish it.

2. Relinquishing at the time of receiving: Originally one forms this thought: "Upon receiving the robe, I shall relinquish it. 3. Relinquishing when the time has elapsed: Originally one forms this thought: "At that time..."
1. Relinquishment by permission: One makes this thought: "When [the teacher] permits it, I shall relinquish it. 2. Relinquishment upon hearing: One makes this thought:

"Upon hearing that the two teachers have relinquished it, I shall relinquish it. 3. Relinquishment by sending: One makes this thought: "Once I have given this robe to another, I shall relinquish it. 4. Relinquishment by destruction:
Having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, one says of one's own accord in the interim: "I now relinquish it. 5. Relinquishment by loss: One makes this thought in the interim: [The robe is lost...]

8. Abandonment through ruin and disappearance: "I shall abandon it when it has fallen into decay and is no longer visible. This refers to the initial thought: "While I am staying here, I shall abandon it when I depart.
9. Abandonment through the passing of time: Not abandoning on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, but [abandoning] upon reaching the sixteenth day.

This is termed "renunciation" (*pratyākhyāna*). One incurs a *vyatikrama* offense. There are ten ways of renouncing [the robe]. By the fifteenth day of the twelfth month, one person shall announce the renunciation before the Saṃgha.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the washing, dyeing, beating, or sewing is not done according to the Dharma, or if it is too small..."

This is significant. If it is a garment of brocade or fine silk, or if one has accepted it before the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is concluded, or if one accepts it out of greed for gain and offerings, or if one intentionally relinquishes the five items, in all such cases the acceptance is not valid.
Acceptance lasts for thirty days, and relinquishment likewise lasts for thirty days.

If one enters the *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains) retreat, one accepts on the sixteenth day of the seventh month and relinquishes on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month. If [one enters] the seventh month...

It is received for seven days. It is relinquished on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month; or, if received on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it is relinquished on the fourteenth day of the twelfth month.
If it is the later retreat (paścimā vārṣikī), it is received on the sixteenth day of the eighth month and relinquished on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The five bhikṣus may not perform the kaṭhina ceremony."

Those who may wear the robe: (1) one who has not completed a year [of residence], (2) one who has broken the rains retreat (*varṣā*), (3) one who entered the later rains retreat, (4) one who has been expelled (*pravāsanīya*), and (5) one who is undergoing separate residence (*parivāsa*).
Question: The Buddha permitted the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe after the *pravāraṇā*; it must be relinquished by the fifteenth day of the twelfth month.

Now, regarding the making of the *kaṭhina* robe: it is worn at all times without restriction. Furthermore, as for the claim that "one piece of cloth serves as the three robes," is this correct or not?
Answer: It was originally because after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, the monks brought their robes to see the Buddha.
Exhausted by the dampness of the rain, one is then permitted to make a *kathina* robe, which yields five benefits.
This is strictly limited to the end of winter as its deadline; should one exceed this limit even slightly, one immediately incurs a transgression.

Furthermore, that which is chanted for acceptance among the Sangha and placed within a high offering chest is originally not an article to be worn. The five strips with ten partitions resemble an *antaravāsaka*.
[This is] indeed so. That the name "one *naḍa*" has been mis-transmitted through popular tradition is deeply erroneous and excessive. Question:
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* permits those who observe the later retreat (*paścimā vārṣikā*) to receive [the *kaṭhina* robe] on the sixteenth day of the eighth month;

yet the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* does not permit a monk observing the later retreat to make the *kaṭhina* robe. From which source is this derived? Answer: According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, even down to a single person...

Regarding the acceptance of the *pūrvavārṣika* (early summer) retreat: if the entire assembly accepts the *pūrvapravāraṇā* (early invitation) together with this person, they may then remain seated for the full three months.
It should be understood that although those who observe the *aparavārṣika* (late summer) retreat accept the *pūrvapravāraṇā* together with them, they have not yet completed the year;

therefore, they are not permitted to act as *cīvaradhara* (keepers of robes). If the entire assembly observes the *aparavārṣika* retreat, then [the end of the period is] the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
When the summer retreat is complete, the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is held; on the sixteenth day, the *kāṭhina* robe is then prepared.
What fault could there be in this? [End of] Volume Twelve of the *Zhòngzhì píní shìyì jíyào*, Explanatory Notes on Pronunciation and Meaning.
The character *cí* (辭) is read as *dàn* (誕). On the altar, it is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). It means "to release," "to deceive," "great," or "broad.
Since these meanings do not correspond [to the context], it is likely that the character *tàn* (憚) has been mispronounced.
The five strips each have ten partitions, with two partitions per strip; thus, the five strips together constitute ten partitions.
It is incorrect to say that each strip now has ten partitions; if that were the case, there would be fifty partitions across the five strips.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of Ancient Wu. Section:
The Methods for Administering Punishment.
Now, offenses arise from conditions; since that which arises from conditions lacks intrinsic nature, the path of antidote is produced and the seeds of offense are extinguished.

This is called "the intrinsic nature of offense is fundamentally empty. It does not mean negating the characteristics [of the offense] in order to seek its nature. Yet those who lack a sense of shame often use the "contemplation of the true reality of the mind" as a pretext, failing to contemplate the performance of remedial rites to eliminate their transgressions.

Alas! Even the characteristics of the offense itself—[are they not yet understood?]— (Note: The final phrase "罪相尚自不" appears to be an incomplete or truncated thought, likely intended to continue with a critique regarding the failure to perceive the very characteristics of one's own offenses.)
How much more so for one who has realized the true nature of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*)? Although sin arises from the mind, it must depend on objective conditions to constitute karma;

likewise, although sin is extinguished by means of the mind, how could one eliminate it without departing from objective conditions to grasp at emptiness? Moreover, objective conditions possess the function of supporting the underlying principle.
In principle, there is no capacity for things to stand alone; therefore, it is said that even if one repents without contemplating the mind, one can still resolve the flow of transgressions.

However, if one discusses the principle without making a formal disclosure (*vidūṣaṇā*), it will be difficult to clear the source of the transgression. It is my hope that each of you will harbor deep faith.

Do not harbor hesitation. Each of you should maintain a straightforward mind and refrain from following negligence. Originally, one establishes practice based on principle; subsequently, one returns to principle through practice.
In this way, may the pearl of precepts and the sun of wisdom shine together, and may the three wheels and seven branches be equally purified.
Thus, you shall perpetuate the lineage of the Buddha, glorify the wheel of the Sangha, forever close the gates to the evil realms, and swiftly lead others to Bodhi.
Daitō raised this path for discussion and asked: "The ancients spoke of three types of repentance methods, stating that one may omit the preceding ones but must not omit the succeeding ones.
This is because transgressions are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can dissolve; therefore, one must take contemplation according to principle as the primary focus.
Now, you alone support the ritual method (sahajapavidhi); is this not being mired in the minor teachings and failing to reach the Mahāyāna?"

Is this not the profound essence of the true nature (*dharmatā*)? Answer: "It is better to lack the preceding stages than to lack the succeeding ones" is said with reference to those who lack the necessary conditions.
This refers, for example, to one who wishes to emerge from an offense but cannot find twenty pure monks available.
Furthermore, this is to demonstrate that while each preceding stage does not necessarily include the subsequent ones, each subsequent stage must necessarily possess all those that precede it.

If one insists on practicing only the superficial form of the Dharma and refuses to carry out its actual application, this is merely out of concern for appearances, involving a deliberate concealment and suppression of the truth.
If one has not yet fully understood that the nature of transgression is fundamentally empty, how can one be called a "Wisdom Sun"?

Therefore, the present work alone upholds the practice of the Dharma (zuòfǎ), which is precisely the foundation for contemplation of principle (lǐguān). While the wise certainly realize that all phenomena are identical to principle, even the ignorant may enter into principle by means of phenomena.
Jingxi said: "Since it is called 'committing a grave offense,' it is not a matter of contemplating the mind alone. As for what is meant by "contemplating the mind":
In practicing ritual repentance, one must necessarily rely on the contemplation of the mind. Without the contemplation of the mind, grave offenses will not be extinguished;

only when ritual and principle are practiced in conjunction can the aforementioned purpose be accomplished. It is further said that the ritual precepts (*śīla*) are the foundation of the three contemplations;
thus it is stated: "When *śīla* is pure, samādhi manifests before one. If one lacks the ritual precepts, even mundane dhyāna is absent, let alone the three truths. Some have said:
"To ask why Mahāyāna practitioners need to uphold the precepts is erroneous. To say they do not 'uphold' them means that they maintain them without attachment.

If one were to call the failure to maintain them 'non-attachment,' that would actually be an attachment to transgression; how could such be called non-attachment? If there is no longer even the act of maintaining, where can there be the forgetting of maintenance?
(Text) Now, if one wishes to abolish the formal ritual procedures (*vidhi-karman*), then there will be neither *kāla-saṃvara* nor *vastu-saṃvara*. Since these two types of restraint...

[Text missing. Regarding the contemplation of principle, from where would it proceed? To rely on the so-called "ultimate reality" (*bhūtatathatā*) of the Mahāyāna merely results in the formation of a nihilistic view of emptiness (*durgṛhītaśūnyatā*).

This leads to self-delusion and the delusion of others; the error is no small matter. Reflect upon this, reflect upon it! The text is divided into six parts: first, the clarification of the four *pārājika* dharmas;
second, the clarification of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas; third, the clarification of the *sthūlātyaya* dharmas; fourth, the clarification of the minor [offenses].
I. Offenses. II. Explaining the various *karmavācanā* (formal procedures). III. Explaining the procedure for overturning the alms-bowl (*pātra*).
First, explaining the four *pārājika* (defeats) rules.
The second section states: The bhikṣu Nandika was led astray by Māra and committed an act of impurity beside a dead horse.
With a mind free from concealment, he should speak to the bhikṣus, saying, "Go and inform the World-Honored One.

If the Buddha permits the Saṃgha to grant him the *pārājika* precepts—meaning that although this person has already violated the *pārājika* precepts by committing a grave offense, because he has no intention of concealment and weeps, being unwilling to part with his saffron robes—the assembly of monks shall perform the formal procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) in harmony to grant him the *pārājika* precepts once again, whereby he may still dwell together with the bhikṣus.
He should request this three times, and the Saṃgha shall perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for him; once the precepts have been granted...
Having done so, you should practice in accordance with the Dharma. You must not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others. You must not provide formal reliance (*niśraya*) to others.

You must not keep novice monks (*śrāmaṇera*). You must not accept an appointment to instruct bhikṣuṇīs. You should not recite the precepts for the Saṃgha (this refers to lecturing on the Dharma of the precepts).
You should not remain within the Saṃgha to engage in questions and answers regarding the Vinaya. You should not accept an appointment from the Saṃgha to serve as an administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*).
When acting as a messenger on matters of legal adjudication, one should not enter a village too early nor return at sunset.
One should associate with bhikṣus; one must not associate with non-Buddhists or laypeople. One should comply with the dharma of the bhikṣus; one must not speak of other mundane matters.
One must not recite the Vinaya in the midst of the assembly—unless there is no one else capable of reciting it (this refers to the fortnightly recitation of the precepts). One must not [further...]
One who has committed an offense shall not perform a *karmavācanā* (formal act) that is not authorized by the Saṃgha, nor shall he perform a *karmavācanā*.

He shall not receive from a pure (*pariśuddha*) bhikṣu the spreading of a seat, water for washing the feet, the wiping of leather sandals, the rubbing and massaging of the body, prostrations, welcoming, inquiries after his well-being, or the holding of his robes and bowl.

He shall not be appointed to raise up a pure bhikṣu, nor shall he be subjected to the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) or the *pratijñākāraka* (settlement by confession). He should not testify to what is correct.

Regarding human affairs: one must not obstruct a pure bhikṣu from reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*) or performing the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*). One must not engage in disputes with a pure bhikṣu.
At the time of the recitation of the precepts or the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), whether he comes or does not come, the community of monks incurs no offense.
If he commits the *pārājika* offense again, he should be expelled. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "Until all afflictions (*kleśa*) have been completely exhausted..."
One should always practice accordingly; failing to do so incurs an offense (referring to the period prior to realizing the fruit, i.e., before attaining the stage of Arhat).
Once the realization of the fruit has been attained, one should no longer [be subject to] such practice. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"One who trains for the *pārājika* offense should sit below all bhikṣus and above all śrāmaṇeras; they must not share the same room with a bhikṣu."
If they stay for more than three nights, one may not again stay with a śrāmaṇera for more than three nights.
If the bhikṣu’s food is impure, his [the śrāmaṇera’s] is also impure; if his food is impure, the bhikṣu’s is also impure. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
Regarding the training rules for a śrāmaṇera under instruction, all the precepts established by the Buddha must be received and practiced. He may perform the poṣadha together with the bhikṣus.

Regarding the *pravāraṇā* (self-criticism) *karmavācanā*: one must not perform the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā* *karmavācanā* with an incomplete quorum. This means that for a *poṣadha* *karmavācanā*, there must be four bhikṣus who are pure (*viśuddha*).

If there are only three pure bhikṣus and one who is a trainee (*śaikṣa*), it is not permissible to perform the *poṣadha* *karmavācanā*; one may only perform a *poṣadha* in the presence of another (*pratyekamukha*). The same applies to the *pravāraṇā*, which requires five persons.
No other *karmas* whatsoever may be performed. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "Once this bhikṣu has obtained the *karmavācanā*, he is called..."
For one who maintains pure precepts, though this single body cannot transcend birth and death, nor can it attain untainted merit, yet it serves as a barrier against entry into hell.
It is like a tree leaf that, once fallen, returns to grow upon the tree.
This is impossible. Question:

For one who is still in training (*śaikṣa*), the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* permits the attainment of the fruit and allows for the relinquishing of the practices; yet the *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states that such a person cannot attain the fruit.
How are these two accounts to be reconciled? Answer: The *Mūla* refers to the manifestation [of the fruit] in response to a specific challenge; therefore, it speaks of attaining the fruit.
This can be expected. The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* points to the general path of the Buddha-dharma; therefore, once the fruit of realization is attained, it is impossible to regress.

Just as fallen leaves have no principle of regrowth, how could those who commit transgressions not feel trepidation? Since ritual practice leads to the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*), those who repent must exert themselves with great diligence.

The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "The characteristics of sexual misconduct and false speech are easily manifested; however, the two precepts regarding killing and stealing have characteristics that are difficult to discern.

Because they are subtle, one acquires [the offense] through subtlety, and one understands them from subtlety. Therefore, do not speak to a person who harbors doubts, saying: 'You have committed a *pārājika* offense.
You should instead direct them to go and ask their teacher, their fellow students, or their disciples. If they perceive signs of an offense..."
Have him sit in meditation in a single room so that he may observe himself. If his precepts are free from blemish, his mind will enter meditative concentration;
if he has violated the precepts, his mind will remain unsettled. Thereafter, resolve the matter according to what is appropriate.
Question: If one commits an act of unchastity (*abrahmacarya*) and does not conceal it at all, one may receive the *pārājika* precepts;

I do not yet understand whether this also applies to committing the other three grave offenses (*tīni garukāpattīni*). Answer: This is difficult to explain. Nevertheless, please allow me to attempt an explanation.

Take, for instance, the precept against stealing (*adattādāna*); it constitutes a grave offense through five conditions: first, it must be another’s property; second, the perception that it is another’s property; third, taking it with the intent to steal; fourth...
It is worth exactly five *kārsāpaṇas*. Regarding the fifth [offense], "leaving the original place": suppose a bhikṣu happens to see an object and gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment;
with the intent to steal, he lifts it and moves it from its original place. At that moment, a grave offense has already been committed.

If he subsequently reflects and repents, returning the item without taking it and without any intention to conceal his fault, and urgently seeks to undergo the training (*śikṣamāṇā*), how could he not be absolved? However, if he has already taken the object and only later...
To confess [one's transgression] and then recklessly grant [the precepts] to others—how could this not invite blame? Furthermore, regarding the precept against killing:

if one intends to kill person A but mistakenly kills person B, although the precept itself has not been lost, secular law already renders such a person unacceptable. How much more so when one fulfills that murderous intent;
even if the act is not concealed, how could such a person ever be granted the training? However, according to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Śuddha-karmāvaraṇa-vinodana-sūtra*:
Yet, even there, it has never been the case that a single thread of connection has not been maintained. Next is the precept against great falsehood (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*).
If one commits a great falsehood for the sake of gain and support, one necessarily cannot be without a mind of concealment; thus, in principle, such an act is not permitted.
However, if one utters a great falsehood because of a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and thereby escapes [death], one must immediately confess and seek forgiveness.
Furthermore, how could it ever be possible to completely eliminate [disputes]? You should know that one must be well-able to extinguish contention;
only a person who is free from attachment, free from aversion, free from fear, and free from delusion can be entrusted with such a task.

The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra states: "If there is a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, is complete in dignified deportment, and protects and maintains the True Dharma, and upon seeing one who destroys the Dharma, is able to expel them, reprimand them, and discipline them—know that such a person shall obtain immeasurable merit beyond calculation.
However, if a virtuous bhikṣu, upon seeing one who destroys the Dharma, neglects to expel, reprimand, or bring them before the assembly..."

Know that such a person is an enemy within the Buddha-dharma. Even if they have committed the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes, and know for certain that they have committed such serious matters, their mind from the outset is devoid of fear or shame;
they are unwilling to confess and reveal their transgressions regarding the Buddha’s True Dharma.
They never possess a mind that protects or cherishes [the Dharma], but instead disparage and treat it with contempt, speaking many words of fault.
Such persons as these are also said to be heading toward the path of the icchantika. Furthermore, those who say that there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Saṅgha—such persons as these...

It is also called "the path leading toward the icchantika" (Sanskrit: *icchantika*; translated here as "one with excessive greed," because they deeply delight in birth and death; or *an-icchantika*, translated as "one without desire," because they do not delight in nirvāṇa;
or *atyantika*, translated as "extremely evil," because they have completely severed their roots of goodness).
Question: According to the Vinaya, a bhikṣu commits a *pārājika* offense; once it has been severed like a withered tree, it does not grow back.

For one who has committed an offense of the second category (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), he must undergo *parivāsa* (probation) and *mānāpya* (rehabilitation), and furthermore, he must be cleared of the offense before a community of twenty monks. This applies even down to an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
Furthermore, one must necessarily perform face-to-face confession before others to achieve purification. Why, then, does the *Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa Sūtra* state:

"If one has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution, or violated the four parājikas or eight parājikas, by reciting this mantra, all such offenses shall be entirely extinguished without leaving so much as a hair's breadth;
not only will the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas no longer regard these as transgressions, they will even regard them as merit?"

[The Buddha] gave it to him. [This continues] until he attained the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). If one observes it in this way, regardless of whether a transgression is great or small, it is sufficient merely to maintain the mantra;
there has never been a scriptural rule for confessing [the offense] to another person. How can the meaning of the Sūtras and Vinayas be reconciled with this? Answer:
The subtle and wondrous phrases of the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-tejorāśi* are called the "Mantra-Mind" (*dhāraṇī-citta*) and are also called the "Mind-Mantra. This is precisely the secret exposition.
In the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi*, observe what is taught in its explicit exposition: at the very beginning, it commands that one answer questions with a straightforward mind.

Because the mind and speech are direct, there will forever be no trace of deviousness. If, regardless of whether an offense is great or small, one is unwilling to confess and reveal it to others, one has already violated the Single Path of the Tathāgata;
how could such a person be fit for the unsurpassed mantra-mind? This is what the Sūtra reveals.
Because of the secret seal and divine efficacy, it is said that there are no sins that are not extinguished. This is true not only for this sutra;

generally speaking, all the *Uṣṇīṣavijaya*, *Mahākaruṇā*, and *Vaipulya* dhāraṇīs, as well as the sutras concerning the thirty-five Buddhas, the fifty-three Buddhas, and the names of the five thousand five hundred Buddhas, all share this meaning.
It is precisely because the afflictions, karma, and obscurations of sentient beings are so deep that [they do not realize this].

Knowing that those who commit offenses are difficult to discipline, difficult to subdue, difficult to uproot, and difficult to eliminate, the Vinaya establishes strict rules for expulsion and exclusion, while the Sūtras and Dhāraṇīs open the path for self-renewal.
Through this process of alternating suppression and integration, these two systems act as mutual complements:

they ensure that those who have not yet committed offenses do not dare to do so intentionally, and that those who have already committed offenses are able to extinguish them. This may truly be called a heart of ultimate compassion.
These are supreme and wondrous skillful means. Were there no Vinaya regulations, the Sangha Jewel would not be honored in its maintenance;

were there no sutras and mantras, sentient beings burdened by karmic obstacles would fall forever. Through the four *siddhāntas*, they are skillfully applied, all emerging from a single voice; how could one allow for arbitrary partiality or disparagement?
△ Second, the exposition of the *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Monastic Offenses).
The third section states: "If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceals it, one shall be given the penance for concealment (*parivāsa*) in accordance with the number of days it was concealed.
He should, within the assembly, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the monks, join his palms, kneel on his right knee, and declare: 'Venerable sirs...'"
Venerable Saṃgha, listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and concealed it.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], having committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, now request from the Saṃgha the *parivāsa* ritual according to the number of days it was concealed. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the *parivāsa* ritual according to the number of days it was concealed.
Thus he requests three times. The Saṃgha should then perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the fourth proclamation (*karma*).

He shall be granted [the penance]: if he concealed it for one day, he shall perform the *parivāsa* (probation) for one day; if he concealed it for two days, he shall perform the *parivāsa* for two days; and so on, up to five days, ten days, half a month, or one month, or six months.

(The same applies to one year and so forth). While practicing *parivāsa* (concealment), if one commits another grave offense (*pārājika*), one should request the *mūlāpakarṣa-parivāsa* (renewed probation from the beginning);

this is performed by a formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). (That is to say, while properly practicing *parivāsa*, if one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, then all previously practiced disciplinary methods are nullified; one must again request the Saṃgha to undergo renewed punishment from the original day, proceeding as before. When the *parivāsa* is completed, one should request the *ṣaḍrātra-mānatva* (six-night penance);
this is performed by a formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations. Having performed it, next...

One should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) to expiate the offense. Regarding the commission of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that was not concealed:

one should request the six-night *mānatva* penance; once it has been performed, one is exonerated from the offense. If one commits a further offense while performing the *mānatva*, one should request the *mānatva-mūlāpakarṣa* (the reduction of the *mānatva* to its original state, which carries the same meaning as the *mūlāpakarṣa* for concealment);
once it has been performed, one is exonerated from the offense. If one has committed numerous *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, or if they were concealed...
If one conceals [the offense] for one night, or even up to ten nights, it is permitted to undergo the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* procedure for many offenses together.

One is granted the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act of motion and three proclamations) for the concealment of ten nights, followed by the *mānatva* (probation) for purification from the offense. If two offenses have been committed and both were concealed;
or if one remembers one but not the other; or if there is doubt regarding one but none regarding the other; or if one recognizes one but not the other—[the same procedure applies].

If one says [something] once but does not say it once again, one should grant the *parivāsa* (probation) according to what was remembered, recognized, and stated—provided there is no longer any doubt regarding that which was recognized.
If, after having been granted the *parivāsa*, one later remembers, recognizes, and states [the offense], one should again grant the *parivāsa* according to the offense committed.
This applies whether the concealment lasted for two months, or if one remembers one month but does not remember another month, and so forth. If one commits two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses...

Regarding the offense: having left the monastic order, and after having left the monastic order, returning to receive the full precepts—whether both [the offense and the leaving] were concealed, whether it was concealed first and confessed later, or confessed first and concealed later—in accordance with the number of days it was concealed, the *parivāsa* (probation) *karmavācanā* shall be granted.
Alternatively, if one confesses both the earlier and later offenses simultaneously, one is immediately granted *mānāpya*. Once the *mānāpya* has been performed, one is cleared of the offense.

There are likewise four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding whether one or more offenses were concealed, or whether one or more were not concealed; these are treated in the same manner. There are likewise four permutations for each case where one remembers [an offense] or does not remember [an offense].
It is the same when requesting the period of concealment (*praticchādana*), whether one mentions [the offense] or does not mention it. When performing the period of concealment...

When the *mānatva* penance is completed, there are likewise twenty phrases for each case. When a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) returns to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*), there are likewise one hundred phrases.
For those who are insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain, there are likewise one hundred phrases for each.
When the Saṃgha performs the formal act of suspension for not seeing an offense, for not repenting, or for not relinquishing an evil view, there are likewise one hundred phrases for each.
It is also like this:
diagrams consisting of various fourfold sets, twentyfold sets, or even hundredfold sets—
covering one offense while not covering another— are constructed as fourfold set diagrams.
A fourfold chart on remembering one offense while not remembering another;
a fourfold chart on doubting one offense while not doubting another;
and a fourfold chart on recognizing one offense while not recognizing another.
Regarding the diagram on the right with five sections, each containing four phrases—totaling twenty phrases—it concerns the period for requesting *paryuṣaṇā* (concealment).

It begins from the commission of an offense and concludes with the act of leaving the monastic order (*pravrajyā-tyāga*) while requesting concealment. Furthermore, there is the case of leaving the monastic order while practicing concealment.

There are twenty phrases each for those who leave the monastic life after completing the *parivāsa* (concealment penance), those who leave during the *mānatva* (probation), and those who leave after completing the *mānatva*.
Together with the preceding cases, these constitute one hundred phrases regarding leaving the monastic life.
By analogy, the seven matters concerning becoming a *śrāmaṇera* (novice) and so forth also each have one hundred phrases. These are illustrated in the chart below.
The "Diagram of One Hundred Phrases" and the "Diagram of Seven Hundred Phrases" for those who have left the monastic path are as follows: for instance,
regarding the single phrase "becoming a śrāmaṇera," the upper portion contains five periods, and within each of these periods, the lower portion contains one covering.
Regarding the four sets of four propositions for each of the [five] non-concealments, there are five such sets of four propositions in a single session, totaling twenty propositions.
Since there are twenty propositions for each of the five sessions, they collectively constitute one hundred propositions.

These represent the various distinctions when one who has forfeited full ordination returns as a *śrāmaṇera* to receive full ordination again; all of these should be applied according to what is appropriate in each case.

And he bestows upon them various *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedures). Regarding the three types of illnesses, such as insanity and so forth, there are approximately one hundred cases each concerning the restoration of the original mind.

Regarding the three types of formal accusations, such as for not seeing one's offenses and so forth, there are likewise approximately one hundred cases each concerning the petition for release from suspension.
Together, these constitute seven hundred cases.
If one ceases the practice of the *parivāsa* (probation), or ceases it while undergoing the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction of the period),
or ceases it after completing the *parivāsa*, or ceases it while undergoing the *mānatva* (penance), or ceases it after completing the *mānatva*, and subsequently receives the precepts again.
Each should be granted according to their respective circumstances. The five phrases regarding those who become *śrāmaṇeras* are likewise.

The diagram for the five phrases concerning one who has left the path (*pravrajyā*) and again receives full ordination (*upasampadā*)—that is, one who becomes a *śrāmaṇera* and again receives full ordination—is also the same as these five phrases. [The same applies to those who are] insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
One regains one's original mind; each of these also consists of these same five phrases.

Not being accused of an offense, not being accused for failing to repent, and not being accused for not relinquishing wrong views—each of these also consists of these same five phrases, resulting in a total of forty phrases.

There is the case of one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense—namely, having committed a *pārājika*-like offense (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) or concealed it—or having committed a *pāyattika* down to a *durbhāṣita* (wrongly spoken) offense and concealed it.
Such a person should perform a confession for a *duṣkṛta* (misdeed) and is then immediately granted *mānatva*.

If there is one who has committed a *pāyattika* offense—meaning one who conceals offenses such as those involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) and so forth—they must first perform a confession for the *duṣkṛta* and subsequently perform a confession according to the Dharma. If they have committed...

Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense: if one conceals it with the intention of concealment for a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, one should first perform a confession for the *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) and then grant the *paryuṣitaka* (concealment) *karman*.

If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense but does not remember the number of times it was committed, nor the number of days, or if one remembers the number of times but does not remember the number of days, in all such cases, one should grant the *paryuṣitaka* from the time of purification.
If one remembers the number of days but does not remember the number of times it was committed, one should calculate [the days].
The same applies to the day [of concealment], as well as to cases of doubt or lack of doubt regarding concealment.

If, while performing the *mānatva*, one commits a further offense and conceals it, one should again grant *mānatva*, followed by the *pārivāsika* (or *mūlāpakarṣa*), and then the restoration from the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*).

Regarding the concealment of one's own offenses up to the restoration from the offense, one should not perform the formal act of concealment (*jñapti*) for one another; rather, one should undergo the *mūlāpakarṣa*.
Regarding the *mānatva* [probation]: according to the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, twenty people are required to absolve one of the offense.

For a bhikṣu practicing the *paryuṣitaparivāsa* (the practice of concealment), there are eight matters that cause the loss of a night, for which he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense (as explained below; if in these eight instances one fails to announce what should be announced, then that day does not count toward the practice of the *parivāsa*.

After confessing the *duṣkṛta* offenses, one must further supplement the practice by performing it for one more day). The first is failing to announce when going to another monastery. The second is failing to announce when visiting bhikṣus arrive. The third is... [text fragment]

1. To go outside on account of business without informing [the community]. 2. To remain within the monastery grounds for four days without informing [the community]. 3. To depart from the monastery without informing [the community]. 4.

To stay within the monastery for more than four days without informing [the community], except when accompanied by a practitioner (*yogācāra*). 5. To leave without sending a messenger to inform [the community] when ill. 6. For two or three people to sleep in the same room together. 7. To reside in a place where no *bhikṣu* is present. 8.

Not to inform [the community] at the time of the fortnightly *poṣadha* recitation. One should inform [the community] with full decorum as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. I, the *bhikṣu* named [so-and-so]..."

I, the bhikṣu [Name], having committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, concealed it. I, the bhikṣu [Name], for as many days as I have concealed it, request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of the period of concealment (*parivāsa*).
The Saṃgha has already granted me the formal act of the period of concealment for as many days as I have concealed it.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], have already completed [X] days and have not yet completed [Y] days; I inform the Venerable Ones so that they may know: I am practicing the period of concealment. If I practice...
Regarding the *mānatva* [penance]: one should always remain overnight within the Saṃgha and make this declaration every day.
On the day of the *poṣadha*, that person—being gentle, pliant, and possessing great shame and remorse—should go before a pure bhikṣu and say:
"Venerable Elder, today I have abandoned the instruction and failed to perform it; should I wish to perform it, I shall go before a pure bhikṣu."
He spoke, saying: "I shall do today exactly as instructed. The *Mūla-ekottara-karman* states:

When one is undergoing *pārivāsika* (i.e., *parivāsa*, or separate residence) or practicing *mānatva*, if one hears that there is a bhikṣu who is quarrelsome, a disputatious person, or one of those who are shameless and indolent, and that he intends to come here, one should abandon [the matter] before the bhikṣus.
Regarding the procedure for its practice: once that person has departed, they should return to a pure bhikṣu and receive the procedure from him.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa wishes to travel far, he should complete the relinquishment before departing and say to a single dharma-abiding bhikṣu:"
"Venerable sir, listen. I now relinquish the practice of *parivāsa*. I shall perform it again later. Thus one should say three times.
If one does not relinquish it and departs, and should see a bhikṣu on the road, one must then declare: "Venerable sir, I, the bhikṣu [Name], am practicing *parivāsa*.
So many days have already passed; so many days remain. Venerable sir, please bear this in mind. If one relinquishes the *parivāsa*, upon arriving...
In other cases, one should request that the Sangha allow that monk to undergo *parivāsa* (probation) once again; the Sangha should grant permission for this.
There was a monk who, while undergoing *parivāsa*, or while undergoing *mānatva* (penance), or while undergoing *ābṛhaṇa* (rehabilitation), passed away. The monks informed the Buddha:
"Did he pass away while possessing the full precepts, or did he pass away having broken the precepts? The Buddha said: "He possessed the full precepts in all instances."

The *Vinayasamgraha* states: There are six types of persons who, having committed an offense subject to formal instruction (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), may purify themselves by confessing their offense before a single bhikṣu;
they are then said to be purified. First, one who upholds the Sūtra Piṭaka; second, one who thoroughly upholds the Vinaya Piṭaka;
third, one who thoroughly upholds the Mātṛkā Piṭaka; fourth, one who is by nature extremely modest, such that upon confessing their offense, they feel shame and...

Death. Fifth, the most senior elder among the assembly. Sixth, a person of great merit. When these six types of people are seen by others to be subject to punishment, slander and criticism immediately arise.

If they can decisively sever their intention regarding the offense committed, vowing never to do it again, and if they feel deep shame and remorse with a mind free from deceit, then [the offense] shall be extinguished.
This applies even if they have committed an offense that is not shared with the community (*asādhāraṇa-saṃghāvaśeṣa*).

When the faculties (indriya) are transformed, the transgressions also perish accordingly. (Among the thirteen matters for bhikṣus: first, playing with one's own genitals; second, touching a woman; third, coarse speech;

fourth, deception regarding the body; fifth, building a dwelling without a patron; sixth, building a dwelling with a patron—these are all not shared with bhikṣuṇīs. Among the seventeen matters for bhikṣuṇīs, there are likewise ten matters that do not coincide with those of the bhikṣus; therefore, they are called "unshared" [asaṃvāsa]). The *Śāriputra Vinaya-mātṛkā* states:
"If an Elder commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and undergoes the mānatva penance, it causes people to lose faith; he should attain a single-minded state."
He gave rise to the thought: "From this day forward, I shall not do it again. He immediately attained purification. It is the same for a virtuous and learned person.
It is also the same for one who would rather violate the precepts than perform *mānāpya*. It is also the same for a sick bhikṣu who lacks the strength to perform *mānāpya*.
There was a bhikṣu who committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; as the assembly did not number twenty, he wished to go elsewhere.
While on his way to a place to perform repentance, he encountered bandits who took his life. Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who had committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;

as the community was not pure, he wished to go elsewhere to perform repentance. On the road, he encountered bandits who took his life. This person, with single-minded devotion, gave rise to the thought of performing repentance according to the Dharma;
he immediately attained purity and did not fall into the evil realms. The Commentary states: There are generally six kinds of methods for repentance. (First, the *pārivāsika*...)

(1) Sitting; (2) two persons of great virtue; (3) shame; (4) physical weakness; (5) the assembly being incomplete; and (6) the assembly being impure). One must not apply these [grounds for suspension] recklessly, nor harbor any侥幸心理 (chance-seeking presumptuousness).

To do so would be self-deception in the Tang dynasty, and even one’s sins would not be removed. One must extensively consult those who clearly understand the Vinaya; only they can resolve such matters.

Question: Regarding the six types of persons mentioned in the *Vinayaviniścaya*, who are the eyes of gods and humans and the leaders within the Saṃgha—should one not regard their *duṣkṛta* offenses as equivalent to the four *pārājika* offenses?
If such gross offenses are now pardoned in this manner, would there then be no restrictions regarding the remaining rules of training (*śikṣāpada*)?
Answer: Since they have already become leaders within the Saṃgha, it is natural that they will not fail in their observance of both light and heavy precepts.

This is because the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśa-vāsanā*) are powerful; perhaps one has inadvertently contravened the pure dharmas, and confessing such acts would, conversely, provoke widespread doubt.

One must vow to oneself that there shall never again be any deception. These methods of repentance (*pāpadeśanā*) are fundamentally not for those who seek to deceive themselves through mere expediency;
how could one ever hastily claim to be free from obstacles?
△ The *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of "stealing a sandwich" (*sandhi-thulan-tsha*).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "From a *pārājika* offense arises a grave *thulan-tsha*. One should confess and eliminate it before the entire *saṃgha*. (Regarding sexual misconduct:

the two bodies have touched one another but have not entered. Regarding theft: having selected five *kārsāpaṇas*, they have not yet been moved from their original location. Regarding killing: the person has been injured but has not died. Regarding lying: one falsely claims to have attained realization.)

It is not manifest. From a *pārājika* offense arises a minor *sthūlātyaya*: in the case of sexual misconduct, it is when two bodies face one another but have not yet made contact; in the case of theft, it is when one has touched another's property of value but has not yet taken possession of it.

Or, having selected light objects but not yet removed them from their place; or killing where the preparatory effort for harm has been initiated but the person has not yet been injured; or lying where it has not yet been uttered and one desists—these arise from *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses as grave *sthūlātyaya* (heavy *sthūlātyaya*) offenses.

[Examples include: masturbation where the semen has not yet been emitted and one desists; touching a woman’s body where one is clothed while the other is unclothed; coarse speech or demanding service where the words are not fully articulated; matchmaking where the proposal is not accepted; speaking and then going to report it back after the message was received; building large or small dwellings where the construction is not completed; slandering out of anger where the words are not fully articulated;

causing a schism in the Saṃgha, being an associate in a schism, reviling the Saṃgha, or refusing admonition—all these reach the point of the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) before they are abandoned, and all are grave preparatory offenses (*sthūlātyaya*). All [of these].
One should go outside the boundary and confess before four bhikṣus to eliminate it. Minor *sthūlātyaya* offenses arising from *saṃghāvaśeṣa* are eliminated by confessing before one bhikṣu.

(These include: grasping the penis with the hand but not manipulating it; both parties being clothed yet touching one another; speaking coarse words or soliciting offerings and stopping before the words are uttered; acting as a matchmaker by going to deliver a message but not returning to report the result;

planning a large or small dwelling but not constructing it; becoming angry and slandering someone but stopping before the words are uttered; attempting to cause a schism in the Saṃgha up to the point of being "wicked-natured"; and abandoning the proposal at the time of the initial motion—all these are termed minor preparatory offenses.)

This refers to the offense arising from the act itself; it is also called *upāya-sthūlātyaya* (the grave offense of the preliminary means) and is also called the *hetu-sthūlātyaya* (the grave offense of the cause).
The *Caturvargika-karman* states: "There are three distinctions among independent *sthūlātyaya* offenses:

those such as being the leader who breaks the wheel of the Dharma (*cakrabheda*), stealing four *kārsāpaṇa*, or killing a deity and the like, are classified as high-grade. Those such as being the leader who disrupts the ritual (*karman*), an associate who breaks the wheel of the Dharma, or stealing three or two [kārsāpaṇa], are [classified differently]."

Possessing [a coin] of such value and so forth is termed a medium offense. If one breaks the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), shaves the hair, goes naked, keeps human skin, uses a stone bowl, eats raw flesh or blood, wears the garments of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), or steals a single coin and so forth, these are termed minor offenses.
One should understand that, according to the rules for *sthūlātyaya* (grave offenses) arising from such acts, there are three methods of confession.

This independent offense is also called a *svabhāva-sthūlātyaya* (offense of intrinsic nature) and is also called a *phala-sthūlātyaya* (resultant offense); that is to say, it is a *niṣyanda-pāpa* (outflowing offense).
Question: Since schism in the Saṃgha is a heinous crime (*ānantarya-karma*) and a grave difficulty, how can it be expiated through the confession of a *sthūlātyaya* offense? Answer:

The leader who breaks the Wheel of Dharma commits an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), whereas his companions do not. As for the breaking of the Saṃgha through formal acts (*karmabheda*), neither the leader nor the companions are said to commit an immediate transgression.
Furthermore, although the leader who breaks the Wheel of Dharma commits an immediate transgression, he does not lose his bhikṣu precepts;
therefore, it is merely termed a *sthūlātyaya* offense and is not called a *pārājika*. If the Saṃgha wheel has not yet been broken, [the offense remains as such].

One may perform repentance; however, if the precepts have been broken to the point of constituting a grave offense (ānantarya), one cannot merely perform ritual repentance (*dharmakṣamaṇa*), but must instead perform the "repentance of non-arising" (*anutpādakṣamaṇa*).
As for those who have broken the wheel of the Dharma (*dharmacakra*) or those who have disrupted the *karmavācanā* ceremony, these are all generally subject to repentance.
Nevertheless, if one has renounced the precepts and subsequently returns to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), this will result in a grave impediment (*saṃkleśa*).
△ Fourth, the rules for dealing with minor offenses. The treatment of *naiḥsargika* offenses has already been explained in the section on the thirty matters.
Here, we shall simply provide a general explanation for the various offenses, such as *pāyattika* and *dukkaṭa*.

The third section states: If a bhikṣu has committed an offense and wishes to confess it before another bhikṣu—referring to minor offenses such as *pāyattika* or *duṣkṛta*—he should go to a pure bhikṣu, bare his right shoulder;
if the other is a senior (*sthavira*), he should prostrate at his feet (this practice is omitted if the other is junior).

He should then kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, state the name of the offense and its category, and speak these words: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind."
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense. I now confess it before the Elder; I shall not dare to conceal it.
Through confession there is peace and happiness; without confession there is no peace and happiness. Remembering my transgression, I disclose it; knowing it, I do not conceal it.
"Elder, please bear in mind my pure body of precepts; I have fulfilled the pure Uposatha. Thus he should say three times.
The other should say to him: "Reprove your own mind; you should give rise to a sense of weary detachment. He should reply, "So be it.

If one wishes to confess before two bhikṣus (referring to those cases among the *pāyattika* offenses where the matter is somewhat grave and requires confession before two persons for the mind to become settled—this may also apply to a residence where there are only three persons including oneself), one should go there.
In the presence of those two pure bhikṣus, he should bare one shoulder and confess his offense as if it were mere dust. The one receiving the confession should first ask the second bhikṣu:
"If the Elder permits me to receive the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so, I shall accept it."

He should say: "So be it. If one wishes to confess before three bhikṣus, it is also like this (for those offenses among the *pāyattika* that are heavy by nature, the mind only finds peace through repentance before three persons;
or if at that residence there are four people including oneself, he should direct his words to two others before accepting the confession).

If one wishes to confess within the *saṃgha* (from four bhikṣus up to an indefinite number are all called the *saṃgha*; this refers to the confession of the middle and upper grades of *sthūlātyaya* offenses, as well as the relinquishing of robes within the *saṃgha*, which constitutes confession within the *saṃgha*).
One should go before the Saṃgha, baring one shoulder, removing one’s shoes, prostrating at the feet of the monks, kneeling with palms joined, and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense. I now beg the Saṃgha for confession. This should be said three times.
