The one receiving the confession should first make a formal announcement and then accept the confession: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen. That bhikṣu [Name]..."
"Venerable Saṃgha, I, [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense. I now repent before the Saṃgha. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen:

I accept the repentance of the bhikṣu [Name]. This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, one accepts the repentance. The other should perform the confession as previously described. One should say to him:
'Reprove your own mind and give rise to a sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*. He should reply: 'So be it. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states:
When a senior monk (*sthavira*) has committed an offense against a junior monk (*navaka*), he should manifest four dharmas in their presence to confess it: first, baring the right shoulder;
second, removing his leather sandals; third, joining his palms; and fourth, declaring the offense he has committed.

When a junior monk seeks to repent an offense before a senior monk, he should manifest five dharmas in their presence, adding the third [dharma] of kneeling on the right knee. (These senior and junior monks are not restricted by the nine-year or twenty-year [seniority] limits.)

This is an external treatise. However, one who has first received the precepts and has reached even a brief moment [of practice] is immediately called an *upādhyāya* (Elder). Furthermore, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, an Elder shall repent before a Junior; however, with the exception of prostrating at the feet, one must also kneel in the *hu-gui* posture.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states that one should perform *kṣamāpana* (repentance/confession) when endowed with five qualities:
first, having faith; second, exerting diligence; third, giving rise to reverence; fourth, uttering pleasant words; and fifth, associating with virtuous friends. (10)

The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "If one is captured by bandits or is ill, although it is a corresponding offense (*saṃprayukta-āpatti*), it is permitted to perform confession through mental reflection and verbal expression.

Subsequently, one must confess before a pure bhikṣu. Furthermore, one is permitted to accept the confession of another. Regarding 'corresponding offenses,' this refers to cases where one has committed the same offense as another.

In ordinary times, one may not confess toward a fellow offender, nor may a fellow offender accept another's confession. However, because one is currently in a state of distress, those who are not ill and have not been captured by bandits are first [instructed] to act [as follows]."

The thought arose: "I shall now repent of this transgression before a pure bhikṣu later. Having formed this intention, he was immediately able to receive the repentance of that sick man who had been captured by bandits, ensuring that after death he would not fall into the lower realms.
△ Fifth, the exposition of various *karmavācanā* procedures.
The third section states: There were two bhikṣus who delighted in quarreling and would revile one another, their mouths spewing swords and blades as they sought each other's faults.
They also incited others to engage in strife. The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform a formal reprimand (*pratikarṣaṇīya-karma*) through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

[The Buddha] said: "Grind [the offense]. Once the assembly of monks has been convened, perform the formal act of *ukkhepanīya* (suspension). Having performed the *ukkhepanīya*, perform the act of *sativinaya* (reprimand for lack of mindfulness).
Having performed the *sativinaya*, assign the penalty. Listen, virtuous Sangha:

this bhikṣu so-and-so delights in quarreling and mutual abuse, uttering words like swords and spears, seeking out the faults of one another. After they have thus quarreled among themselves, if there are other bhikṣus who quarrel..."
Go there and exhort them, saying: "Exert yourselves! Do not be like others. You possess great learning and wisdom, and your wealth is superior;
you have many friends and associates. We shall act as your allies so that where the Saṃgha has no dispute, a dispute may arise, and where a dispute already exists, it is not resolved.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of forbearance, grant its consent. For...
"Monks such as we have performed the *karma* of censure (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*). If hereafter they should again engage in strife or mutual abuse, the Saṃgha shall further increase their punishment.
Thus is the motion (*jñapti*). The formal act (*karman*) is to be performed accordingly. If they comply with the Saṃgha, do not oppose it, and seek the lifting of the *karman*, it should be lifted.

They must request it three times within the assembly, and the *karman* consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) shall be performed for them. [If they do not comply,] they shall be expelled."
Bhikṣus, one should not allow a person who has not been summoned to enter the boundary.

However, it is permitted to send a reliable messenger into the Saṃgha to announce a confession (referring to one who has defiled a family or engaged in evil conduct). One should grant him reliance (*niśraya*), the training in the Vinaya, and wisdom that accords with the Saṃgha;
he must not dare to disobey as he seeks the *karmavācanā* for his release. He should be released. There are ten qualities by which a bhikṣu should be granted [these things].
1. To perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of prohibiting [a monk] from going to the homes of laypeople (*avadātavasana*), such as by speaking ill of or reviling them.
2–4. To employ means that cause the decline or ruin of lay families, or to act in ways that are unbeneficial or provide no stable support for them.

5. To incite quarrels and discord among laypeople. 6–8. To slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha in the presence of laypeople. 9. To address laypeople with insults regarding their low birth or base status. [The Saṅgha] grants permission according to the Dharma.
(10) A layperson who is insincere. There are five qualities by which a bhikṣu should not have this *karmavācanā* performed for him:

he does not show respect toward his parents, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas; and he does not firmly uphold what ought to be upheld (in such cases, other methods such as censure or subjugation should be employed).
If, however, he shows respect toward his parents, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, and firmly upholds what ought to be upheld without abandoning it—as [is required]—...
If this bhikṣu has committed one of the ten previous offenses, he should be subjected to the formal act of *karmavācanā* for suspension from entering the homes of laypeople (*gṛhastha*).

Once this has been performed, another bhikṣu should be appointed to go to the home of a layperson on behalf of this bhikṣu to perform his confession. There are eight qualities by which such a person should be appointed:

first, he must be learned; second, he must be able to speak well; third, he must understand the matter himself; fourth, he must be able to discern the intentions of others; fifth, he must be able to receive the words of others; sixth, he must be able...
He should remember and uphold [the precepts]. Seventh, he must be free from deficiencies. Eighth, he must understand the meaning of words regarding both the wholesome and the unwholesome.

When these eight qualities are present, one should perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation) to appoint him to go to the house of a layperson (*gṛhapati*) and speak thus:
"Householder, repent! The Saṃgha has already imposed a penalty upon this bhikṣu. If he accepts the repentance, it is well; if he does not accept it, you should place this bhikṣu under your care."
If one sees with the eyes but does not hear with the ears, one should instruct them to perform repentance according to the Dharma. When they return and say, "Householder, I have repented;
that bhikṣu previously committed an offense, but it has now been repented and the offense is removed," if he accepts the repentance, it is well.

If he does not accept [the charge], the offending bhikṣu should go in person to confess. Having confessed, he should comply with the Saṃgha and not dare to oppose it, requesting the lifting of the *karman*.

[The Saṃgha] shall grant the lifting. If one has committed an offense but says "I do not see it," or if one has an offense but does not confess it, or if one does not abandon an evil view—all such cases constitute grounds for formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-karman*).
If the *tarjanīya-karman* (reprimand) or the *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment) has been performed...

The *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence); the *apravāraṇā-śrāvaka-kula-karman* (act of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople); the *adarśana-utksepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense); the *apratikarmāṇa-utksepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension for not making amends);
the *apratinihsṛṣṭe-pāpake-dṛṣṭike-utksepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views); the *yathā-cchanna-divasa-karman* (act according to the number of days of concealment);

the *mūla-parivāsa-karman* (act of initial penance); and the *ṣaḍ-rātra-mānatva-karman* (act of six-night probation). Once such *karman* as these have been performed, there are five matters that [the monk] must not do.
One should perform five things: first, bestowing the full precepts upon others; second, receiving others as one's *niśraya* (dependence); third, maintaining *śrāmaṇeras*;

fourth, being appointed by the *saṃgha* to instruct *bhikṣuṇīs*; and fifth, if appointed by the *saṃgha*, one must not fail to provide instruction. Furthermore, there are five things one should not do: first, reciting the *Prātimokṣa* precepts;

second, answering questions from the *saṃgha* regarding the meaning of the *Vinaya*; third, performing formal acts (*karmavācanā*) as appointed by the *saṃgha*; and fourth, selecting [candidates] within the *saṃgha*.
Those who have gathered wisdom should collectively deliberate upon various cases and precedents. Five monks shall be appointed as messengers. Furthermore, one should not go out early or return late;
one should not associate with non-Buddhists; one should not speak in a discordant manner; one should not commit further offenses;

one should not harbor resentment toward the *karmavācanā* or the person performing the *karmavācanā*; and one should not accept the offerings, prostrations, and other honors from virtuous bhikṣus. Not...
One should praise virtuous bhikṣus; one should not obstruct the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇa*. One should not dispute with virtuous bhikṣus.
One should sit in a lower position than the great bhikṣus and walk behind them.

One should sweep and sprinkle for pure bhikṣus, spread out seats, and even carry their robes and bowls, rub their bodies, and so forth, according to the rules for serving a teacher. One should see pure bhikṣus three times each day.
A pure bhikṣu, when the uposatha day arrives, should sweep and sprinkle the area, and so forth, until the *śalākā* (voting sticks) are prepared.

Once the uposatha is concluded, these items should be collected and stored away. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are five matters for which the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure)—also known as the *kukkucca-karman*—is to be performed.

The first is the habitual practice of the eight matters, namely: dwelling in physical intimacy, dwelling in verbal intimacy, dwelling in both physical and verbal intimacy, and dwelling in physical... [text truncated].

Regarding those who dwell in close association (*upaniśraya*): they sit together on the same bed, sleep together on the same bed, eat from the same vessel, mutually exchange clothing, and go out and come in together.
Regarding verbal close association: they engage in speech with minds that are mutually defiled. Regarding physical and verbal close association: they sit together on the same bed.

...up to the point where, while speaking, they act toward one another in turn, mutually defiling their minds, speech, and bodies (there are six for the body and two for the mouth, totaling eight matters).
Second, repeatedly committing offenses; third, not ceasing despite being admonished three times. Third, entering a village too early and leaving too late in the darkness;

associating with evil friends and evil companions; and traveling to improper places. Fourth, engaging in disputes and mutual accusations, not ceasing despite being admonished three times (when five factors are accomplished, disputes arise again: first, self-exaltation; second...).

Coarse and wicked nature; third, meaningless speech; fourth, speaking at improper times; fifth, not associating with virtuous people. Fifth, showing disrespect toward juniors; third, refusing to desist despite being admonished;

if one undergoes the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) yet does not act accordingly; or if one repeatedly commits minor offenses and continues to offend even after verbal admonition—these all warrant the *asaṃbhāṣanīya-karman* (the act of not speaking together), which is what is known as the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence). [Also those who] defile others' households and engage in evil conduct... with...

Regarding the *nāśana-karman* (act of banishment): if a monk disturbs laypeople and causes them displeasure, the *anumodana-karman* (act of inspiring joy) is to be conferred upon him—this is what is known as the *pratisedha-gṛhastha-kula-karman* (the act of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople).

If he does not acknowledge his offense, acts contrary to the Dharma (i.e., fails to repent), or does not relinquish his evil views, the *utksepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension) is to be conferred upon him.
A monk undergoing the *parivāsa* (probationary period) must practice seven matters in accordance with the rules. What are the seven? [The first is] the matter of a monk... [and so forth].

Matters concerning bhikṣuṇīs; matters concerning their retinues; matters concerning entering villages; matters concerning undergoing various hardships; matters concerning receiving prostrations (i.e., being appointed by the Saṃgha);
and matters concerning kings. What are the matters concerning bhikṣus? [A bhikṣuṇī] must not receive prostrations from a bhikṣu;

must not speak of a bhikṣu’s faults; must not engage in debate with a bhikṣu; must not speak of a śrāmaṇera’s faults; and must not bestow rewards or punishments upon a śrāmaṇera (referring to commendation or reprimand). Not...
One may converse with śrāmaṇeras, but one must not employ them as servants. When the assembly gathers, one must not act as the Dharma-preacher for the assembly, except in a separate location.
These are called the duties of a bhikṣu. What are the duties of a bhikṣuṇī?
One must not receive prostrations from bhikṣuṇīs, nor speak of their offenses, nor converse with them, nor speak of śikṣamāṇās.

Regarding the offenses of a *śrāmaṇerī*: one must not bestow blessings upon her as a punishment; one must not engage her in conversation; one must not obstruct the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā* of the *bhikṣuṇīs*;

one must not obstruct the *bhikṣuṇīs* at the gate of the monastery (due to the incident where the *bhikṣuṇīs* struck Venerable Kāpiḷa, the Buddha commanded that when monks see *bhikṣuṇīs* entering the monastery, they should stop them at the gate;

if they have urgent business, they may enter only after having announced it; however, monks currently undergoing the *parivāsa* probation and other such penances are not permitted to obstruct *bhikṣuṇīs*); and one must not go to instruct or admonish her.

Nun. If she has already received [the offense], she must not go [to teach]—that is to say, even if she was previously appointed [to teach], as long as her offense has not been cleared, she may not go to instruct.

This is called a matter concerning bhikṣuṇīs. What are matters concerning relatives? She must not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; she must not receive formal reliance (*niśraya*) from others;
nor may she keep śrāmaṇeras. She must not accept provisions from bhikṣus; she must not bestow scriptures upon others; nor may she receive them from others.

Regarding the Sūtras: one should recite the sūtras one has previously memorized in a low voice. If there is a disciple who has been one's own preceptor, one should instruct him to rely upon another and sever ties with that family;
this is called "matters concerning kinsmen. What are the matters concerning entering a village? One must not enter too early or leave too late.
One must not walk ahead of or behind others as a śramaṇa enters [the village] (referring to those in *parivāsa* and so forth; bhikṣus should sit in a position lower than all pure bhikṣus).
One must walk behind. If one walks separately in front or separately behind, this constitutes a refusal to follow the practice of the Dharma.
One must not go to the homes of acquaintances or donors. One must not reside in a monastery where there are no bhikṣus. When sitting or eating, one must remain below the bhikṣus.

One must not have others bring food for oneself, nor must one bring food for others (except when it is one’s turn by rotation to serve as the attendant, in which case bringing food for others does not constitute an offense). This is called entering.
Matters concerning the community (*saṃgha*). What are the tasks involving the endurance of communal hardships?

Rising at dawn, one should sweep the stūpa courtyard and the monastic quarters, wash the places where the monks relieve themselves, and perform all such duties as these according to one’s physical strength.

One must not give one’s consent (*chanda*), nor accept the consent of others—except when it is one’s turn in the rotation to transmit consent on behalf of another, which does not constitute an offense. These are called the tasks involving the endurance of communal hardships. What are the matters concerning receiving prostrations?
One must not accept any prostrations. One must not accept [prostrations] during a *jñapti-karman*, a *jñapti-ekavācika-karman*, or a *jñapti-trivācika-karman*.
These are called matters concerning prostration. What are matters concerning kings? One must not rely on the power and influence of kings, great ministers, householders, or violent men.

One must not harbor resentment toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, or the person performing the *karman*. One should only reproach oneself and must not blame others. These are called matters concerning kings.
Regarding the matters: when a bhikṣu undergoes the *parivāsa* and *mānatva* penances, performing these seven matters is called "conforming conduct" (*anuloma-carita*).
Not performing them is called "non-conforming conduct. One who has undergone the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) should conform to five matters:

matters concerning bhikṣus, matters concerning bhikṣuṇīs, matters concerning their retinues, matters concerning formal acts (*karman*)—that is, the matter of receiving prostrations—and matters concerning kings (excluding only the matter of entering a village).

[Having performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the imposition of the *yadbhūyaḥ-karma* (the act of majority), one should say: "Venerable sir, do not commit this offense again. Should you commit it, the Saṃgha will treat you even more severely.

These five matters should be practiced in accordance with each one. Having practiced them and having thus been subdued and humbled in mind, the Saṃgha should perform the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (the act of reconciliation) for him.
For one who has performed the *an-ālāpya-karman* (the act of non-conversation), he likewise must practice the aforementioned five matters in accordance with them. [One should] perform...

Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, one must further practice five duties in accordance with the rules. Even if he has been a dependent for a hundred years, one should drive him away if he upholds the precepts [but fails in these duties].

At the very least, this applies to a monk who has known the two sections of the Vinaya for ten years. Every morning at dawn, one should inquire after his well-being, provide him with the vessels for excrement and urine, and the spittoon, and then lift them and place them in their usual locations.
One should provide him with a tooth-stick, sweep the floor, welcome him when he brings food, wash his robes, and fumigate his bowl.
All [necessities] should be provided, with the sole exception of prostrations and massage. However, in the event of illness, one may permit massage (2).
One should instruct them in both divisions of the Vinaya; if they are unable to do so, one should at least instruct them in the five categories of offenses (3).

One should instruct them in the thorough knowledge of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) (4). One should instruct them in the thorough knowledge of the characteristics of transgressions and non-transgressions, as well as in proper dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
Instruction: One should prohibit what is not in accordance with proper decorum (five). Once [the training] has been completed, it is termed "abandoned.

Those who perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of banishment should also practice the aforementioned five matters accordingly. Once the formal act is concluded, they should be settled and made to dwell on the outskirts of the monastery.
Having performed each of the five matters in accordance with the Dharma, one should grant the *niḥsargika* (relinquishment).
One who performs the *pramodana-karman* (act of reconciliation) should likewise perform the aforementioned five matters in accordance with the Dharma.

Once the *karman* has been performed, he should be sent to the household of the layperson whom he offended to confess his fault, causing that person to rejoice. If that person rejoices, it is termed "relinquishment" (*niḥsarga*). One who performs the *utkṣepaṇa-karman* (act of suspension) should also...

One should practice in accordance with the five preceding matters. Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, [the vessel] should be placed outside the monastery, with its opening facing toward the *araṇya* (forest hermitage).
If anyone comes to enter the stūpa courtyard or the monastic quarters and sweeps the ground, the bhikṣu should sweep away their tracks.
If anyone comes to replenish the water at the foot-washing place or the water at the places for defecation and urination, he should pour it out again. If...
A practicing disciple or a dependent disciple must not address their teacher as "Upādhyāya" or "Ācārya. They should not speak to them;

rather, other people should speak on their behalf to ensure they act in accordance with the Dharma. They should abandon evil and heterodox views. One should not converse with a bhikṣu who holds such evil and heterodox views.
One should not dwell with them. One should not share the Dharma-meal with them. One should not share in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha with them.
One should not share in the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or the *karmavācanā* with them. One may speak to non-Buddhists; if they wish to sit, one may let them sit.

However, one must not speak to those who have been formally suspended (*ukkhittaka*) to have them sit. If they are ill, one should not attend to their medical needs. One may, however, speak to their donors or relatives.
The village people said: "The person who was nominated has fallen ill. You should go to see him. If he passes away, you must not provide offerings of flowers and incense for his corpse;
you must not prepare food, drink, or non-timely beverages to offer to the Sangha on his behalf;
you must not distribute his robes and bowl; and you must not cremate his body. Take the bed upon which he lay, place the corpse upon it, tie his robes and bowl around his neck, and drag the bed out."
He spoke these words: "The affairs of the Sangha are pure; the affairs of the Sangha are pure. One should not give rise to ill will toward wicked and heterodox bhikṣus. Why is this?
Even toward one who has been reduced to a charred wick, one should not give rise to ill will. One should reflect thus: 'May future generations not practice such false views.
If a herdsman, a wood-gatherer, or someone carrying robes and bowls comes to offer them, they may be accepted. Thus it was said.

He acts as the donor. If the person who has been subject to suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) complies with the five requirements, attains right view, and becomes gentle and pliant in mind, they may be granted release (*osāraṇā*).

There are three matters by which one may be subject to suspension: impurity of morality (*sīlavipatti*), impurity of view (*diṭṭhivipatti*), and impurity of livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*). One may be subject to suspension for three reasons: on account of what was seen, heard, or suspected. [Impurity of view includes:

claiming that sexual misconduct does not obstruct the path; claiming that killing bears no karmic retribution; or holding to the views of nihilism (*uccheda*) or eternalism (*sassata*), or calculating the world to be finite or infinite, and so forth. [Impurity of livelihood] consists of three causes and conditions by which one may be subject to suspension: what was seen, heard, or...
Doubt. Furthermore, a bhikṣu who accomplishes five qualities may expose the faults of others: [the fault] is real and not false; it is at the proper time and not an improper time;
it is beneficial and not unbeneficial; it is spoken with gentle words and not with harshness; it is done with a mind of loving-kindness and not with malice.

Moreover, he accomplishes another five qualities to be able to expose the faults of others: his bodily action is pure, his verbal action is pure, his livelihood is right, and he is learned in the Dharma.
Abhidharma. One who is well-versed in the Vinaya. Furthermore, there are five ways of accusing another: there is accusing after having reviled; there is reviling after having accused;
there is reviling while simultaneously accusing; there is reviling without accusing; and there is accusing without reviling.

Among these, [cases where] one first reviles and later accuses, or accuses and later reviles, as well as those who revile while simultaneously accusing—these the Saṃgha should not accept. Accusing without...

Regarding those who revile: one should examine them. If one possesses five qualities, one should not accuse another: being swayed by affection, swayed by hatred, swayed by fear, swayed by delusion, or for the sake of profit.
If one accuses another while possessing these five things, at the breaking up of the body after death, one will fall into an evil destination and enter hell.
If one possesses five qualities, one should accuse another: not being swayed by affection, not being swayed by hatred, not being swayed by fear, and not being swayed by delusion.

Not for the sake of profit. If one accomplishes these five qualities, one may perform an act of suspension against another; at the breaking up of the body after death, one will be reborn in a good destination and be praised by those who practice the holy life.
If a bhikṣu has been suspended and goes to another community of monks, he should speak as follows:
"Elder, I have been subject to a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*). My conduct has been compliant with the Dharma and my mind is supple;
please grant me release. The Saṃgha should ask: "On account of what matter were you suspended? If he replies, "I was suspended without cause," they should say to him:

"We share with you both the food of the Dharma and the food of taste. If he says, "I was suspended for a cause," they should say to him: "Return to your original place within the Saṃgha and relinquish [the offense]. If he...

If one stays in an empty monastery, or if [the community] has become non-existent, or if one has left the path, or if one has gone elsewhere such that there is no longer any Saṃgha, one should be asked:

"For what matter were you subject to suspension? If he replies, "I was suspended for this matter," and his mind has become supple and he has practiced the Dharma of repentance for his transgression, then the *samanvāhāra* (reinstatement) should be granted.
The *Mūla-nidāna* states: "If monks are fighting... If it is manifest...

Regarding the two types of teachers: they should be admonished. If one has completed ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*) and yet remains without a formal reliance (*niśraya*), the bhikṣus should admonish him (which constitutes a *tarjanīya-karman*).
If he does not desist, they should perform the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* against him (which is the *niśraya-karman*;

it compels him to rely upon one who upholds the Vinaya, and others shall no longer converse with him). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "Once the *avamanyanā-karman* has been performed (which is the *prasādaniya-karman*...)"

A single bhikṣu should be sent to the householder’s residence to confess the offense. If the householder, wishing to cause harm, refuses to accept the confession after three attempts and dismisses that bhikṣu, the Saṃgha incurs no fault even if he remains by force.
If a bhikṣu engages in playful joking and idle conversation with a bhikṣuṇī, thereby disturbing the other bhikṣus, an act of *aprasāda* (uncleanliness) should be performed against him.

[This concerns] the *karma* (specifically that subsumed under the *tarjanīya-karman*). The *Vinayavastu* states: "If a monk has been expelled from a community by a single location, he may not perform confession in another location;
however, it is permitted to perform confession in another location provided that the monastery [in question] is empty."
△ Sixth, the explanation of the *pātra-pratigrahaṇa* (the rite of overturning the bowl).
The fourth section states: There are ten conditions under which the *pātra-pratigrahaṇa-karman* should be performed against a lay household: they revile and slander bhikṣus;
they act to the detriment of bhikṣus; they act to their disadvantage; they employ means to deprive them of a dwelling place; and they incite strife among bhikṣus.
“Kauṭhila, you have spoken ill of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha before the bhikṣus; you have slandered a bhikṣu with groundless and impure charges, and you have violated a bhikṣuṇī.
Since one or another of these offenses has occurred, the *pātra-nikubjana* (turning-over of the bowl) karmavācanā must be performed.

Once it has been performed, a person endowed with the eight qualities (as described in the *karmavācanā* for prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople) should be appointed to go to that household and say: ‘Now, the Saṅgha is performing [the rite] for you.’”
The bowl is turned upside down (*pātra-nyāsa*), and they do not associate with one another.

For such reasons, if that person repents according to the Dharma and accords with the Saṃgha, and does not dare to act in opposition, requesting the lifting of the bowl-turning, the Saṃgha should lift it for them.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It was the custom in Śrāvastī for the householder Upāli to regularly invite the monks for a meal. When the bhikṣus arrived, he interrogated them..."
When questioned on their meaning, those who were able to explain them rejoiced greatly and personally served them various kinds of food;
those who could not answer were reviled, and servants were sent to give them coarse food. All the bhikṣus were unwilling to go there.

The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform the *pātra-āvṛti* (covering of the bowl) karmavācanā against that upāsaka. There are eight matters for which the Saṃgha should perform the *pātra-āvṛti* against an upāsaka. What are they?
These are the eight: to slander a bhikṣu in his presence; to revile a bhikṣu in his presence; to scold and abuse a bhikṣu in his presence;

to cut off a bhikṣu’s gains and offerings; to take no pleasure in working together with a bhikṣu; to revile the Buddha; to revile the Dharma; and to revile the Saṅgha. These are called the eight matters.
At that time, Dharmapāla would always eat after having fed the bhikṣus, and on that day he waited for the bhikṣus.

He did not come back. He went to ask the Buddha, who said, "Because you treated a bhikṣu with contempt, the Saṃgha, wishing to benefit you, has performed the *pātra-āvarta* (inverted bowl) karmavācanā against you.
At that time, not far from the Buddha, there was an arhat. The Buddha said to Fayu:
"You may go and ask: 'What is called salt? How many kinds of salt are there? Then he went and asked. The Arhat replied: 'I know you are the lay follower Dharmika;
you have treated the bhikṣus with contempt. The Saṃgha has already performed the *pātra-āvartana* (bowl-turning) karmavācanā against you.
Are you not satisfied? You dwell here happily, yet you come again to trouble me. Salt is indeed salt. Thus [he spoke] regarding the Dharma."

Having heard this in advance, Fayü’s mind was filled with bewilderment. He returned to where the Buddha was, and the Buddha asked, "Did you grasp the full meaning when you asked about the significance of salt?
Fayü replied, "This bhikṣu has heard little and has not yet studied under a teacher; he simply said 'salt' because that was what he asked about.
At that time, not far from the Buddha, there was another Dharma-master bhikṣu named Pūrṇa. The Buddha said to Fayü, "Go to him."
Question: He then went and asked. The Dharma Master replied: "The meaning of 'salt' has two aspects: flavor-nature (*rasa-svabhāva*) and substance-nature (*svabhāva*).

As for flavor, it is like the water of the ocean, which has the single taste of saltiness. As for substance, there are black salt, red salt, *siṃhala* (Sindh) salt, *vimardaka* salt, and *pailava* salt."
*Kacalavaṇa*, *sītavaṇa*, and *pippalivaṇa*. Briefly stated, there are two kinds: that which is raw and that which is boiled; these are called "salt.

Having heard this, Dharmapāla was delighted and came to address the Buddha, saying: "This bhikṣu has skillfully understood and distinguished the meaning of salt, both in its broad and concise forms, and is able to answer according to both direct and inverse order.
The Buddha said: "This is but an ordinary person who, within my Dharma, has not yet attained the flavor of the Dharma. Previously...
"A bhikṣu" refers to an Arhat. Yet you, out of arrogance, failed to distinguish the true from the false, performing what was not beneficial for a long night.
Regarding this matter, you have now expressed fear and remorse. The Buddha has ordered you to bathe, change your clothes, and proceed with your retinue to the midst of the Saṃgha.

There, you must three times request the lifting of the *pātra-āvṛti* (the bowl-covering) through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*). The Saṃgha shall then direct you to remain within the boundary (*sīmā*) where you are visible to the eye but not audible to the ear.
One should dwell where it is heard. The formal act (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) for the revocation [of the *pātra-nyāma*] is performed.

Once the Saṃgha has performed the *pātra-nyāma* (the bowl-covering) ritual against someone, no one—from monks down to lay followers (*upāsikā*)—should go to that person's place. One should take a robe and tie it upon the lintel of their door, and proclaim in the street:
"So-and-so has had the *pātra-nyāma* ritual performed against them. If any visiting monks arrive, they should be informed that the *pātra-nyāma* has been enacted.

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act): one must not perform it haphazardly. If the person says, "It would be well if the śramaṇas did not enter my house," such a person should not be dealt with [in this manner].

However, if they possess a sense of shame and remorse, one should perform the act for them. If, having recognized their own faults, they act in accordance [with the Dharma] and their mind becomes supple, they should be released.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu should not issue a formal announcement (*jñapti*) on account of a trivial matter."

The robe-makers performed the *pātra-cchādana-karman* (the formal act of covering the bowl). A lay follower (*upāsaka*) likewise should not, on account of some minor matter, fail to show respect and faith toward a monk.
Even if a monk has accomplished eight qualities, a lay follower should still not cease to show respect and faith. [However, there are cases where one should not:
disparaging the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and the precepts; wishing harm upon other lay followers; bringing a bad reputation to a lay follower; wishing to...
If one seizes the dwelling place of an upāsaka, treats what is unlawful as lawful, and deceives the upāsaka;
or if an upāsaka becomes angry with a bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should not go to his house. If the entire village is angry with the bhikṣus, the bhikṣus should not reside in that village.
*Chongzhi vinīti shi yi ji yao*, Scroll Thirteen: Phonetic Explanations.
*Jiu*: Pronounced as *jiǔ*. To supervise; to reprimand; to urge; also, to examine.
Essential Collection of the Principles and Meanings of the Vinaya, Volume Fourteen.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of Ancient Wu. Section:
The Dharma of Robes.
Regarding the acceptance of *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) garments, there are ten types:

those chewed by cattle, those gnawed by rats, those burned by fire, those stained by menstrual blood, those worn by a woman after childbirth, those from within a shrine, those scattered about by birds, wind, or rain, those from a cemetery, and those obtained through a vow.

One should not accept robes offered by a king; nor robes for traveling to and from [funerals] (referring to those used for funeral processions). One should not take the robes of a dead person from within a moat or ditch.
One should not take discarded robes (*pāṃsukūla*) found on walls, fences, or in ditches (for these may have been washed and dried by householders).

One should not take the robes of a dead person from a place where legal cases are adjudicated (where officials command *caṇḍālas* to discard corpses, and they say, "If you want to take the robes, leave the corpse behind"). One should not take [robes that are] not yet...
Regarding the robes of the deceased: one should not beat a corpse’s robe that has not yet decayed in order to cause it to fall apart.

One should not take robes from a large heap (as these belong to the householder who removed them). A *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) has no owner; it belongs to whoever first takes it. If several people take it together, they should divide it.

One should not take robes used for adorning or making offerings to a stūpa. It is permitted to cut the robe with a knife. If one obtains a robe that has not yet been washed, it is permitted to wash it oneself.

Washing. One may employ another to wash [robes]. It is permitted to keep washing implements, such as a washing board and scissors. [Robes] should have five strips; six strips are not permitted. Seven strips are permitted;
eight strips are not permitted, nor up to nineteen strips. Twenty strips are not permitted.
If the number of strips exceeds this, one should not keep them. It is permitted to make an *antarvāsa* from cloth four cubits long and two cubits wide. Wide...
One should make an *uttarāsaṅga* three cubits in length and five cubits in width. As for the *saṃghāṭī*, "width" refers to the vertical measurement and "length" refers to the horizontal measurement.
Question: Regarding the three robes of a bhikṣu, all schools take the standard measure to be three spans vertically and five spans horizontally.
If one now makes robes that exceed these measurements, is there also an offense? Furthermore, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the *saṃghāṭī* does not exceed nineteen strips.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* does not exceed fifteen strips; only the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* permits up to twenty-five strips.

Nowadays, all refer to the twenty-five-strip robe as the "uppermost upper robe" (*uttarāsaṅga*). Is this also definitively so? Answer: Three or five cubits (*hasta*) is the limit that must not be exceeded.
Thus, the *Vinayasamgraha* states: "Beyond this, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This is the case for robes manufactured at present.
While vertically there may not necessarily be more than three [folds], horizontally there are never fewer than five. It is erroneously said that when folding, one should take square sections;
however, one should know that if one receives, maintains, or wears [the robe] in such a manner, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense) at every step.

Furthermore, when robes are made in the Western lands—whether from discarded rags (*pāṃśukūla*) or garments offered by donors—the number of strips and partitions may be reduced, provided that the resulting dimensions are sufficiently broad and long.
If one were to categorize them into miscellaneous fragments, the divisions would become numerous; it is not only the *Mahāsāṃghika* and *Dharmaguptaka* that do not value many categories.
Even the *Mūlasarvāstivāda* merely speaks of "the first three," "the middle three," and "the last three," never referring to them as superior, middling, or inferior.
Moreover, the Brahmajāla Sūtra mentions only the nine-strip, seven-strip, and five-strip *kāṣāya*.
When the Buddha entrusted the robe to Kāśyapa for transmission to Maitreya, it was likewise only this thirteen-strip golden-threaded *kāṣāya*. Yet now, you alone esteem the twenty-five-strip robe;
to thus waste labor and squander the fundamental resources is truly laughable.
When making new robes, one layer of *antarvāsa*, one layer of *uttarāsaṅga*, and two layers of *saṃghāṭī* are prescribed.

If they are old robes, two layers of *antarvāsa*, two layers of *uttarāsaṅga*, and four layers of *saṃghāṭī* are permitted. If they are *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe) garments, the number of layers may be as many as desired.
When obtaining a seamless robe (*khaṇḍa-cīvara*), if its width and length are sufficient, it should be cut and pieced; otherwise, it is deficient.
It is permitted to apply patches. One should not enter a village without wearing the cut-and-sewn robes (khaṇḍa-cīvara).

One should not enter a village with the robes worn backward; however, it is permitted to wear them backward outside the village. One should not wear only a single robe, except when at the place for defecating or urinating.
One should not wear garments embroidered with patterns, nor garments made of grass, bark, leaves, jeweled necklaces, or skins.
There were garments made of vulture feathers, human hair, horse tails, and yak tails. When these garments became worn out, it was permitted to repair them;

it was permitted to patch them with layers of cloth, to bind the edges with thread, and to mend them by cutting patches square or round according to the size of the holes. At that time, a householder came bringing a garment.
He says, "I give this to such-and-such a bhikṣu. The bhikṣu says, "I do not need it," and immediately takes the robe, places it before the bhikṣu, and departs.

It is permitted to hold and record it for the sake of the donor. If [the bhikṣu] needs it at a later time, he is permitted to accept and keep it. As for robes of great value, they may be spread upon the ground.

One should not walk upon it. One should not use expensive cloth to make a floor-covering; however, it is permitted to use it as a bedding mat, a sitting mat, a pillow, or an upper garment for covering.
It should not be used to make a canopy (a curtain set up around the four sides of a room), nor should it be used to make a portico (a curtain set up before the eaves).
It is permitted to keep a sash of the color of the *kāṣāya*, three finger-widths wide, wrapped three times around the waist. If the sash is fine and soft, [it may be] counted...
Knots should be cut off quickly; one should wear toggle-fasteners, but they must not be made of precious materials.

For those suffering from cold, it is permitted to wear double-layered *chū* garments (the term "double" refers to two layers; "chū" refers to inner stuffing such as cotton wool; this is used interchangeably with "zhù"). In countries of cold snow, it is permitted to make socks and to wear hats.

For those whose bodies have sores or who suffer from body odor, it is permitted to make towels for wiping the body. For facial perspiration, it is permitted to make towels for wiping the face. For those suffering from tears, it is permitted...
One should prepare a purification cloth (*praṣṭhara*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*) not required at the proper time should be given to the Saṃgha;

if the robes required at the proper time are too many, one should reduce them by half and give them to the Saṃgha. To maintain only the three robes (*tricīvara*), a water flask, and an alms bowl constitutes having few desires and few affairs.

One should make a waistband (*kāyabandhana*); its maximum width is four finger-breadths, and its minimum is like a barley grain (*yava*). As for the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭi*), it should have one strip long and one short. This applies from the seven-strip robe up to the ten-strip robe.
The three-strip robe consists of two long strips and one short strip; the fifteen-strip robe consists of three long strips and one short strip.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One should cherish and protect one's robes as one does one's own skin. Those that require washing, dyeing, or mending should be attended to according to the need.
There are nine types of *saṃghāṭī*, ranging from nine strips to twenty-five strips. The first three types consist of two long strips and one short strip; the next three...
There are three types. The first has three long sides and one short side; the second type has four long sides and one short side—these are what should be made and what should be worn.

Beyond these measurements, it becomes a "torn robe" (*pāṃsukūla*). The superior size is three cubits in height and five cubits in width; the inferior size is two and a half cubits in height and four and a half cubits in width;
those between the two are called the medium size. This applies equally to the *uttarāsaṅga* and the *antarvāsaka*, just as with the *saṃghāṭī*.

The measurement [of the *antarvāsa*]. Furthermore, there are two types of *antarvāsas*: one measuring two units in height and five in width; the other measuring two in height and four in width. The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states:

"A cloth-strip (*kaṭhina*) is placed on the shoulder, and a button-knot (*granthi*) is attached to the chest. There are three varieties of leaf-patterns (*patra-lakṣaṇa*): the large is four finger-widths wide, resembling the outspread feet of a crow;
the small is two finger-widths wide, resembling the surface of a thumb. That which falls between these is called the medium; it should not be worn.
Regarding the three robes and the shaving of the head: one should maintain a separate set of garments for shaving. Alternatively, one may shave while covering the body with a *saṃkakṣikā*.
One should store these garments in a bag; those used regularly should be placed on top, and those not used regularly below.

A mosquito net should measure twelve cubits in circumference, with a canopy fixed above it measuring four cubits in length and two cubits in width; it should be suspended from straps adjusted according to the height of the person.
Letting them hang down so as to overlap forms a door. When it is hot, one should shake the fan. If mosquitoes enter from the bottom, one should press them down with a woolen rug or mat.
The *saṃghāṭī* is the principal among robes; it should not be worn for use in various activities or when entering a village.

When begging for alms, when eating as one pleases, when entering the assembly to eat, when paying homage to the *caityas*, when listening to the Buddha’s Dharma, and when prostrating to the two teachers and fellow practitioners of the holy life, one may wear the *saṃghāṭī*.

However, the *uttarāsaṅga* should be worn only in clean places and during activities such as eating. As for the *antarvāsaka*, it may be worn at any time and in any place according to one's convenience.
According to the *Mūlakalpa*, one should not take items abandoned by merchants who have been plundered by bandits;
however, if the merchant leader gives permission, they may be taken. The same applies to the clothing found in cemeteries or at shrines belonging to others.
It is permitted for bhikṣus to possess thirteen types of requisite robes: first, the *saṃghāṭī*; second, the *uttarāsaṅga*; third, the *antarvāsaka*...
*Vaśa*. (1) Four *niṣīdana* mats; (2) a lower garment (*saṃkakṣikā*); (3) an additional lower garment; (4) an upper robe (*saṅghāṭī*); (5) an additional upper robe;
(6) a face-cleansing cloth; (7) a body-cleansing cloth; (8) a wound-covering cloth; (9) a hair-cutting cloth; (10) a cloth for medicinal expenses.
For each individual garment, one should fold it separately according to its name and maintain it as such. One should speak thus:
Addressing a single bhikṣu: "Venerable one, please attend to me. This saṃghāṭī robe, now completed as a finished garment, I now formally accept and maintain as my personal possession.

Thus he should say three times. The formal acceptance of other robes should be performed according to this same procedure. Regarding a robe purchased with medicinal funds, one must add the phrase "for the purpose of treating illness.
Furthermore, if there are any other robes, they should be offered to the two teachers (the preceptor and the instructor).
Regarding the formal assignment (*viniyoga*): one should distinguish and hold it by addressing a single bhikṣu, speaking as follows: "Venerable sir, please attend to me.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], possess this extra robe (*atirekacīvara*) which has not yet been formally assigned; it is appropriate that it be so assigned.
I now perform the formal assignment before you, venerable sir, designating Master [Name] as the trustee. I now hold it [in trust]. This is to be recited three times.
If a robe is about to tear, one should sew it together with long thread. If a hole is seen, it should be patched.
If the interior has rotted, one should fold it double-layered;

however, if it is completely ruined and beyond repair, it should be made into a lamp wick, or chopped up and mixed with mud to fill the holes in pillars, or used as plaster for walls. When using it in this manner:
This enables the field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) offered by the donor to increase spontaneously. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"If the three robes are torn, regardless of the size of the holes, as long as the seams remain unbroken, they still constitute being in possession (*parigraha*).
If the robes have long since lost their color, the status of being in possession is not lost; however, if they are later dyed with a superior color, they no longer constitute being in possession."

Question: Regarding the three robes currently handed down by tradition, it is said that if they are torn, one is not permitted to mend them oneself. Furthermore, when a bhikṣu passes away, his robes are hung upon a tree;
why is this? Answer: This is permitted by the Vinaya and may therefore be followed. To institute what is not prescribed by the rules is called "unlawful" (adharma).
That one is not permitted to mend torn robes oneself appears in the *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions); this book contains many errors.
This has already been discussed at the beginning of the scroll. It is a clear provision of the Vinaya that a bhikṣu’s three robes must be given to the attendant who cares for him during his illness;
how can this be resisted? Even if one wishes to avoid the calamity of the golden crested [dragon], one must have the Dragon King come to beg for them;
or if one wishes to tie them around a child's neck, one must likewise have the parents request them. If they are hung high on the tip of a tree, they will be empty and of no use.
This is beneficial, yet it is not recorded in the Vinaya and is truly laughable. To recklessly waste items offered for almsgiving—how could this not be a transgression?
The *Mātṛkā* states: "One must not keep rag-robes that have been defiled by impurities. If one obtains a rag-robe..."
One should wash, treat, and make them clean; having properly sewn and dyed them, one should accept and maintain them.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The three robes should neither be too few nor too many. To keep fewer than required is an *duṣkṛta* offense; to keep more is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. This applies unless they are *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) garments."
If it is a layperson's robe (*gṛhapati-cīvara*), one should cut it into pieces, treat them properly, and sew them so they are even and regular, adding separate borders.

If the cloth is too small and one cannot obtain enough for the cut-and-sewn style, one should apply patches (*pratyaṃśuka*) upon the garment—whether five, seven, nine, or even up to fifteen. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"To wear the robes of a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. However, if one does not know it is the robe of a non-Buddhist, there is no offense."

Whatever the Buddha has permitted should all be destroyed. If one knows it to be the robe of an outsider, one should pull out the threads and lay them on the ground, causing people to tread upon them so that they are quickly worn away.
The left strips and fringes should fray to the left; the right strips and fringes should fray to the right; and the central strips and fringes [should likewise fray].
The two-sided mosquito net should be made according to the size of the bed. The meditation belt should not exceed eight finger-widths in width, nor should it be less than five finger-widths.
One should maintain the three robes: the undergarment, the upper robe, and the rain-bathing robe.
A cloth for covering sores; a mosquito net; a cloth for spreading on the walking path; a cloth for warding off fleas; a single-layered spreader cloth;
a sitting mat; a thigh-protector cloth; an arm-protector cloth; a head-covering cloth; a body-wiping towel; a hand-and-face-wiping towel; a needle and thread pouch; and a bowl bag.
Sandal-bag, water-strainer, and such robes or robe-like items—all these should be accepted and maintained.

For those suffering from cold in the head, it is permitted to cover it with a cloth; it is also permitted to make a cap, but one should stop when it is warm enough. Sandals should not have deep heels;
they are permitted to reach up to the ankles. Upon obtaining a new robe, one should first wash it, stretch it out, and measure it, and only then cut it.
Sew and dye them, and maintain them according to the Dharma. They must not be used to wrap other objects; guard them with care as one would one’s own thin skin.

The *Śariputrābhidharma-vinaya* states: "The three robes are maintained [as *parihārika*]; they do not require the ritual of *śuddhi-vyākaraṇa* (declaration of purity). The rain-cloak is maintained for four months; once the four months have passed, it requires *śuddhi-vyākaraṇa*.
The sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) is maintained; it does not require *śuddhi-vyākaraṇa*. The wound-covering cloth (*gaṇḍū-praticchādana*) does not require *śuddhi-vyākaraṇa*. [End of] Wound.

Once cured, one must perform the *suci-kamma* (declaration of purity). Regarding bedding and sitting mats (*śayanāsana*), once accepted and possessed, they need not be declared pure. Regarding miscellaneous small garments, once accepted and possessed, they need not be declared pure.

Regarding hand-towels, once accepted and possessed, they need not be declared pure. If one has previously accepted and possessed the three robes (*tricīvara*) and, having relinquished them, accepts new ones, one must declare this to a bhikṣu through body or speech.
If there is no bhikṣu present, one should hold the robe with one's hand and declare it oneself. If [the hand]...

One must not hold it; it does not constitute a formal declaration. One should state its name. The three robes that have been relinquished may be made into small scraps of cloth and should be declared as pure (*śuddha*).

As for the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), one should accept and keep only one; two are not permitted. Bedding and furniture may be kept in whatever quantity one desires. The sore-covering robe (*gaṇḍūṣa-cīvara*)— [End of fragment]

One may keep one [robe], but not more than that. One may keep two hand-towels. As for miscellaneous small garments, however many one possesses, it is said that they may be kept as one’s own property without violation.
Beds, mattresses, mats, and rugs all belong to the category of room-furniture; they need not be formally dedicated (*śuddhi*). The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states:
"Whenever wearing robes, one should abandon three types of mentalities: first, the mentality of fond attachment and adornment; second, the mentality of treating them with contempt; third..."

One should not harbor these three types of thoughts: a mind that falsely seeks reputation, a mind that deceitfully wears tattered robes desiring others to perceive one as virtuous and disciplined, or any such mental state.
Rather, one should seek only dyed garments, obtaining whatever is sufficient for the body, in accordance with the Great Master’s teaching.

As one advances in the cultivation of wholesome qualities, five kinds of mental states should be generated: first, knowing the proper measure—using things with due consideration so as not to cause damage; second, knowing the intervals [between uses].
One must not wear a single garment too frequently; it will become foul-smelling and quickly deteriorate. Third, one should know how to reflect:

contemplate that the source [of these requisites] was obtained with extreme difficulty, cultivate a mind of gratitude, and when using them, do not engage in unrighteous acts. Fourth, know the proper time: use them in accordance with the seasons, whether cold or hot, and according to the appropriate measure.

Fifth, know the proper number: the thirteen types of monastic requisites are sufficient to sustain the body; to accumulate and store excessive clothing fosters greed and causes one to neglect their practice.
The fourth section on the rules for the bowl (*pātra*) states: When a bhikṣu enters the midst of the Saṃgha to eat and lacks a bowl, it is permitted for a neighboring seat-mate to lend one.
Or, if one borrows one from within the Saṃgha, one must not fail to wash the bowl before using it for food. One must not keep wooden bowls; that is the practice of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
One should not keep a stone bowl; this is the Dharma-bowl of the Tathāgata. One should not keep bowls made of gold, silver, or lapis lazuli;
these are the ways of laypeople. It is permitted for a bhikṣu to make an iron bowl. It is permitted to keep all kinds of tools.
It is permitted to fumigate the bowl, but no substances whatsoever should be placed inside it. One should not set the bowl aside without having washed it. It is permitted to make a bowl.
[The bowl] is placed in a bag; it is worn across the shoulder with a strap, and the bowl is held under the arm with its opening facing outward.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It is not permitted to place a partition inside the bowl. However, if a partition is made with a cake or rice, there is no offense. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One should protect the bowl as one protects one's own eyes;
it should be mended where it needs mending and fumigated where it needs fumigation. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The bowl is..."
The insignia of the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, must not be used to contain impure substances. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:

"After midday, one should not use the alms bowl for drinking; however, it is permitted to make drinking vessels from copper, iron, or clay. It is also permitted to make separate vessels for sipping rice gruel."
Regarding the *Bhaiṣajyavastu* (Section on Medicines), it says:

If a *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicine for the proper time) is mixed with a *kālika-bhaiṣajya* or a *vikālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicine for the improper time), it should be accepted and treated as a *kālika-bhaiṣajya*.

If a *vikālika-bhaiṣajya* is mixed with a *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* (seven-day medicine) or other types, it should be accepted and treated as a *vikālika-bhaiṣajya*. If a *saptāhika-bhaiṣajya* is mixed...
Medicine for as long as life lasts (*yāvajjīvikam bhaiṣajyam*) may be accepted and used as seven-day medicine (*saptāhikam bhaiṣajyam*).

If it is medicine for as long as life lasts mixed with other medicines for as long as life lasts, it may be accepted and used as medicine for as long as life lasts. One must not cook it oneself and then consume it.

One must not eat food that has been stored overnight within the boundary (*sīmā*) or food that was cooked there. One should construct a clean kitchen (*kalpiya-śālā*) in a quiet place in a peripheral room. [Thus spoke] the householder Maṇḍa.

Various kinds of food and drink were prepared and offered along the road for the Buddha and the Saṅgha. As they traveled through the wilderness, there was leftover food. A person was sent to take it all and give it to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha permitted them to accept it as a meal provided by a donor (*dānapati*).

He instructed that a lay attendant (*kappiya-kāraka*) should take charge of it; the bhikṣus themselves should not receive it directly. If anything is required, one may request it at will. There are eight types [of such provisions].
There are fruit juices: pear juice, *jambū* juice, jujube juice, sugarcane juice, *śīrṣaka* fruit juice, *śāluka* juice, *bhallāśa* juice, and grape juice.
If they do not cause intoxication, they may be drunk at improper times; if they cause intoxication, they must not be drunk.
Furthermore, one should not keep juice received on this day until the next day. One should not eat impure fruit;

rather, one should apply the five methods of purification: purification by fire, purification by knife, purification by a wound, purification by being pecked by a bird, and purification by being unfit for planting.
If food is purified by a knife, purified by a wound, or purified by a bird, one should eat it after removing the seeds. If it is purified by fire, it is not fit for sowing; it may be eaten entirely.
If the Saṃgha acquires a fruit orchard, it should be accepted. One should instruct the monastery attendants or the upāsakas to tend to it; if they wish to receive a share, they may do so.
One should calculate the food and provide its value as payment. A *śrāmaṇera* may also manage the food; provided the fruit is not damaged, there is no offense.

If seeds are produced from excrement, there is no offense. When a bhikṣu plants vegetables or fruit, whether he sows the seeds himself or transplants them himself, it is permitted for him to eat them later.

Regarding butter jars and oil jars, covering them is permitted. If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person), one should hold the lid and suspend it over the top; one must not [leave them uncovered].

[If] one touches it with the hand [thinking], "This is the monastery's ghee; it is not among the seven-day medicines that may be consumed," one should not eat it. One should not consume impure vegetables. One should not perform the purification (*parikarma*) oneself.

One should not take hold of them with one's own hands and have another person perform the purification. One should place them on the ground and have a *kappiyakāraka* (a person authorized to handle pure things) perform the purification. Once the purification has been performed...
One should eat what is received; one must not intentionally touch that pure food so as to cause it to become impure. To touch it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;

if one does not touch it, there is no transgression. If a layperson brings food to entrust to a bhikṣu, whether the bhikṣu later eats it himself, takes it back home, or gives it to another bhikṣu, receiving it is permitted.
If a sick bhikṣu requires gruel, he may have a *śrāmaṇera* or a lay attendant (*upāsaka*) add water and rice.

Boil it until it bubbles. Wash your hands and receive it; thereafter, boil it yourself until it is cooked. One must not let the gruel remain overnight within the boundary (*sīmā*), nor may one boil it within the boundary.

If one boils the gruel again, boiling it oneself is permitted (if a pure kitchen boundary has been established, then the two faults of keeping it overnight and boiling it within the boundary do not apply).

If one intends to receive clarified butter (*ghṛta*) but mistakenly receives oil, or intends to receive oil but mistakenly receives clarified butter, and so forth, none of these constitute a valid reception. This is during times when grain is expensive.

Listen to the eight matters concerning bhikṣus: (1) eating and staying overnight together within the same boundary; (2) cooking within the boundary; (3) cooking for oneself; (4) taking food for oneself;
(5) receiving food early in the morning and, having already finished a full meal, eating again without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (remaining-food) rite;
(6) likewise bringing remaining food from the place where one ate; (7) likewise eating things such as walnuts and fruits; (8) edible things found in water.
It is also thus (8). If grain becomes cheap again, it is not permitted [to consume it as stored], provided it is unfit for food.
However, if a bhikṣu has a cause for illness, he may consume it for as long as his life lasts. The *Nikāya-grahaṇa-vinaya* states: A bhikṣuṇī may give food to a bhikṣu;
a bhikṣuṇī’s stored food, when given to a bhikṣu, constitutes pure food. A bhikṣu may also give food to a bhikṣuṇī; a bhikṣu’s stored food, when given to a bhikṣuṇī, [constitutes pure food].

Regarding purification (*pariśuddhi*): The fourth fascicle states that as for food and drink offered to a stūpa, whether it be a *śrāmaṇera*, an *upāsaka*, or the person who manages the construction, they should eat it [only after it has been purified].
Food offered to a stūpa must possess the three virtues and six flavors. If it consists of seasonal fruits or vegetables, these must all undergo purification (*kappiya*).

Nowadays, however, people offer plain white tofu, flour, meat, and uncut vegetables along with grains and fruits; this is truly shameful. It is not permitted for *bhikṣus* to eat items offered to a stūpa—not only those belonging to the Esoteric Section (*guhyatantra*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: [The character *liǎo* (卄/秝)].
Whether raw or cooked, whether leaves or bark, none of these may be eaten. If one requires them to apply to a wound, it is permitted to use them;
however, having applied them, one must not remain within the assembly but should stay in a secluded place. Once cured, one should bathe thoroughly and return to the community.
During illness, if one does not recover by taking [the medicine], it is permitted to take it. Having taken it, one must not lie upon the beds or mats of the Sangha for seven days. Above.

One must not stay in the monks' latrine, nor enter the monks' bathhouse, heated room, lecture hall, or dining hall. One must not accept invitations for meals in the monastic community, nor attend any Dharma teachings or *poṣadha* ceremonies.
One should not circumambulate a stūpa; however, if the stūpa is located in the open air, one may perform a distant prostration from downwind.
On the eighth day, having bathed, washed one's clothes, and performed incense fumigation, one may join the assembly. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "There is none..."

Regarding the practice of fasting: to do so [without cause] constitutes a transgression of the Dharma (*vaidharmya-apatti*). [Question: "As for Fu Dashi (Bodhisattva Fu), whom the world calls an emanation of Maitreya, he frequently engaged in various ascetic practices such as total fasting.

Furthermore, Bodhisattva Zhiji maintained the 'water fast' (*shuizhai*) by reducing his food intake. If later generations imitate these, is it not sinful? [Answer: "When Bodhisattva Fu practiced asceticism and total fasting, it was because he wished to take upon himself the suffering of sentient beings. When Bodhisattva Zhiji practiced the water fast and reduced his food, it was because he wished to subdue the habitual tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśa-vāsanā*).

Moreover, within the Secret Mantra (*Guhyamantra*) sections, there are various ritual procedures; none of these involve fasting for no purpose. Therefore, there is no sin. However, if one resorts to practices such as the water fast or total fasting merely to seek fame and profit, this is categorized as 'wrong livelihood' (*mithyājīva*), and the sin is even more grave."

The *Nidāna* states: "One should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle what is permissible) distribute the fruit to the Saṃgha. If there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one should have a *śrāmaṇera* do so.
If there is no *śrāmaṇera*, having first performed the *kappiya*-procedure oneself, the bhikṣu may accept it and consume it himself. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
Regarding eating raw [food]: it is permitted to cook it further. If one eats it raw, it is permitted to cook it after it has been purified by fire.

What is meant by "purified by fire"? It is when it has even once been touched by fire. The *Vinayavastu* states: "The consumption of rock honey is permitted at five times: first, upon returning from a long journey;

second, during illness; third, when food is scarce; fourth, when no other food is available; and fifth, at a place where water is being distributed. If one does not drink the water, it is not permitted to eat it.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should not reach up to touch fruit on a tree.
When carrying food or drink by boat or carriage, if there is no pure person (*pariśuddha*) to drive or guide it, it is permitted for a bhikṣu to drive or guide it himself.

While the Saṃgha was transporting rice by carriage, a certain brāhmaṇa threw a handful of impure rice into the cart. The Buddha said: 'If it can be distinguished [from the pure rice], it should be removed.'"
If they cannot be distinguished individually, take a handful and go away. There are five methods of purification for eating roots:
peeling, cutting, breaking, washing, and fire-purification. There are three methods of purification for eating stalks and leaves: knife-purification, washing, and fire-purification.

Within a single vessel or a single heap, if one part is pure, it is called "pure in its entirety. If there are grains among the rice, it is permitted to keep a pestle and mortar and have a lay attendant (karmadāna) thresh them.

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "If seasonal medicines (*kālika-bhaiṣajya*) and the like are used to assist in the preparation of seven-day medicines (*saptāhika-bhaiṣajya*), and they are consumed as seven-day medicines, there is no fault.
Or, if seven-day medicines and the like are used to assist in the preparation of lifetime medicines (*yāvajjīvika-bhaiṣajya*)," [there is likewise no fault].
There is no fault in taking medicinal substances as lifelong medicine. Alternatively, one may use seven-day medicines and the like to supplement time-medicine and take them as time-medicine;
this is because they are predominant in their potency and mutually assist one another in their formation.

Regarding the method for receiving food, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "If one wishes to accept an invitation, one should go to the place where the Saṃgha takes its small or large meals and remain within sight.

When the donor announces that the time has arrived, the *upādhyāya* (senior monk) should go at the head, proceeding in a formation like a flight of geese. However, if there are matters concerning the Three Jewels [to attend to], one should not go."

Regarding the matter of attending to the sick: one should first inform the *upādhyāya* or *sthavira* before departing. If there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one may go without asking permission.
Upon arriving at that place where food is served, one should not stay crowded together in a disorderly manner; rather, one should sit according to seniority.

The *sthaviras*, *madhyamas*, and *navakas* should look out for one another. If anyone sits improperly or fails to properly cover their body, one should snap one's fingers to alert them, or otherwise send someone [to correct them].
One should speak so as to make [the others] understand; one should not crave honor. Therefore, one arrives later so as to cause the bhikṣus to rise.
If a donor offers fruit to the elder (upādhyāya), he should ask: "Is the fruit pure? If it is not yet pure, he should tell them to make it pure. If it is already pure, [he should accept it].

One should ask, "For whom was this sent? If it is said, "For the Elder," one may take it as one pleases. If it is said, "For the Saṃgha," one should tell them to distribute it so that it reaches everyone.
The same applies to the soup. If there is a bhikṣu who cannot eat, it is permitted for a neighboring seat-mate to request food on his behalf.

If there is no such person, the neighbor should give him half of their own portion. One must not eat what has been obtained before the formal announcement has been made; one should wait for that announcement.
One should speak of obtaining [the food] equally, and then eat. One should not eat with elbows propped on the sides of the bowl, obstructing one's neighbor.
One should not cough or spit loudly; rather, one should discard saliva slowly. Any waste from what has been eaten should be gathered at the edge of one's feet and discarded when departing.
After eating, one should recite a great *dakṣiṇā* (blessing) for the donor, even if it is only a single verse. Other bhikṣus... [should not...]
One should depart first. However, if it is for the sake of the Three Jewels or for attending to the sick, one should inform [the preceptor] before departing.
If a *dānapati* wishes to hear various teachings, one should explain them to them as appropriate. The fourth section states: "Two people should not eat from the same bowl.
One must not eat while leaning back against a pillow or a desk (leaning the body against the desk as if half-lying down). For elderly or infirm *bhikṣus*, this is permitted."
The bowl should be placed at the corner of the bed or set upon a water flask. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It is not permitted to eat from the same vessel.
If one has no bowl, one should use a hook-bowl (*gōu-bō*) or a ceramic bowl (*jián-tí*). If even these are unavailable, place the food on a leaf atop a vessel.

They should take food from one another; they must not reach for food simultaneously. With the exception of the five types of primary foods (*bhojana*) and the five types of mixed primary foods, there is no fault in eating other items such as cakes, fruits, and vegetables together.
When not ill, one is not permitted to eat while sitting at a table. The elder (*upādhyāya* or *sthavira*) should eat slowly;
he must not finish eating quickly and remain watching, causing the juniors to eat in haste and fail to be satisfied. (From the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*).
The Vinaya states: One must not eat while wearing only a single lower garment (*antarvāsaka*). Those who are aged or infirm should wear a soft and smooth *saṃkakṣikā*.

Those who are gravely ill may eat as they please while wearing only a single garment in a secluded place. When setting aside food, one should offer it universally to all sentient beings rather than restricting it to a single class.
Rice should be moistened with water, and cakes must be broken into small pieces and scattered upon the ground according to one's inclination.

One should eat; one should not refuse. When the meal is finished, one should preach the Dharma for them. Alternatively, the senior monk (*sthavira*), the next-ranking monk, or whoever is capable, should be invited in advance.
While the verse on giving (*dāna-gāthā*) is being recited, one must not consume food; there is no fault in eating after the verse has been completed. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"When a layperson invites the Saṃgha to a meal, those who have not been invited should not go."
If there is a matter of necessity, one may go for the sake of food. When a guest bhikṣu arrives, he should ask the host, "May I enter?
If the host does not permit it, he should say, "Give us our share of the food; we shall eat together with you on equal terms.
If that is still not possible, each should take his portion in his bowl and go outside to eat together. If even that is not possible, and there is [a place] within the monastery...
Regarding food: one should bring it and give it to them. One should not eat from the same vessel as a layperson (*avadātavasana*).

If one goes to the home of a relative and they say, "We are not strangers, nor are we impure; why do you not eat with us? one is permitted to eat together while maintaining mindfulness directed toward the Buddha.
"However, do not let your hands touch one another.

Regarding the third section on the method of attending to the sick, it says: The Buddha was inspecting the various rooms and saw a bhikṣu who was ill and lying on a large [bed], with no one to look after him.
He passed urine. The Buddha asked, "Why is there no one to attend to you? He replied, "When I was not ill, I did not look after others' illnesses;
therefore, now that I am ill, there is no one to attend to me. The Buddha said, "Because you did not attend to and provide for the sick, you have gained no benefit and obtained nothing.
If you all do not look after one another, who then shall look after those who are ill? The Buddha then assisted the sick man.
The bhikṣu arose, wiped away the bodily impurities, and having wiped them, washed himself. He further washed the bhikṣu’s robes and dried them in the sun.
He discarded the old, worn-out bedding grass, swept the dwelling place, and sprinkled it until it was clean. He spread new grass and laid out a cloth;
once he had settled the sick bhikṣu back in his bed, he covered him with another cloth and departed. After the meal, he informed [the Buddha] of these circumstances.
"O monks, you should attend to the sick; you should not neglect them. You should act as caregivers; you should not fail to do so.
Whoever wishes to make offerings to me should make offerings to the sick. I permit the preceptor, or even the disciples, to look after them.
If there is no one at all to care for them, the Sangha should assign a caregiver. If they are unwilling, they should be appointed in turn."
If they refuse to comply with the sequence of duties, they should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If there is no bhikṣu present, a bhikṣuṇī, or even an upāsaka and so forth, should attend to the patient. A bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇerī, or upāsikā must not touch a bhikṣu.
