There are five circumstances in which it is difficult to care for a patient: (1) desiring to eat what is not permitted to be eaten; (2) [the rest of the list follows].

(2) Willingness to take medicine. (3) The caregiver possesses a sincere heart but does not speak according to reality. (4) One fails to act when one ought to act, and fails to remain still when one ought to remain still.
(5) When the body suffers pain, one cannot endure it; or, when the body is slightly capable of enduring it, one fails to perform what should be done and instead relies on others to do it.
Furthermore, one is unable to sit in stillness to pacify the inner mind. Those who act contrary to the above matters find [the practice] easy.
Observe. There are five qualities by which one is able to tend to the sick: First, knowing what the patient may eat and what they may not eat, and being able to provide what is permissible to eat.
Second, not loathing or despising the patient’s excrement, urine, saliva, or vomit. Third, possessing a heart of compassion and mercy, rather than tending to them for the sake of food or clothing.
Fourth, being able to manage their medicine and care until they recover, or even if they die. Fifth, being able to preach the Dharma to the patient, causing them to...
He rejoiced. It is permitted for one who tends to the sick to accept or decline an invitation, and to eat the remains of food left by the sick.
The fourth section states: "It is permitted to give the sick person food at their own discretion and medicine appropriate to their illness, and to provide excellent care for the patient.
A sick bhikṣu should not reside in an upper story or a large room. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "In the south, there were two bhikṣus..."
They came together to see the Buddha. One bhikṣu was ill, so another bhikṣu waited for two or three days and said, "I wish to go on ahead to pay my respects to the World-Honored One;
you may come after you have recovered. The other replied, "Wait until I have recovered, and we shall go together. He answered:
"I have not seen the Buddha for a long time; my longing is like that of one who thirsts. I could not bear to wait any longer, so I went at once to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha, knowing [the situation], asked him intentionally: "From where have you come? The bhikṣu reported the preceding circumstances in detail. The Buddha said: "This is an evil matter."
If a bhikṣu is negligent, indolent, and lacks diligence, and is unable to restrain his sense faculties, he will race after the six desires;

though he may dwell near me, he does not see me, and I do not see him. If a bhikṣu can restrain his sense faculties, is not negligent in mind, and remains focused on the Path, though he may be far from me, he sees me, and I also see him. Thus it is said.
Why is this? Because it accords with the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata; because it destroys all evils; because it abandons desire; and because it cultivates tranquility.
You have likewise left the household life to practice the holy life (brahmacarya). If you do not look after one another, who will? You should go back and look after the sick bhikṣu.
If a bhikṣu travels with merchants and falls ill in the wilderness... [the merchants] likewise... [should look after him].
A companion should carry his robes and bowl for him, attending closely to support and guide him; he should not remain far behind.

If he is unable to walk, he should borrow a vehicle from a merchant, or perhaps pay with the value of grain or fodder. He must not ride in a cart drawn by a cow or a mare; he should ride in a cart drawn by a bull or on a pack horse.
If he is critically ill and lacks the capacity to distinguish [what is appropriate], there is no offense in simply mounting whatever he can reach. However, if he mounts what is unsuitable...
It is permissible. One should leave behind one, two, or three capable persons to look after things; go to a village to seek a vehicle to come and welcome [the returning party];
and leave behind provisions so that those staying behind do not lack for food. If it is in the wilderness and no one is willing to stay, one must not simply abandon them and depart.

One should construct a hut, spread out a bed of grass, maintain a fire, fetch water and fuel, and leave behind all types of medicine: medicinal foods taken at the proper time (*kālabhojana*), medicines taken at night, and medicines taken for seven days (*saptāhika*).
Regarding the medicine for longevity: speak to the sick person, saying, "Venerable one, remain at ease. Once I have reached the neighboring village, I shall seek a vehicle to come and receive you.
Upon reaching the village, do not circumambulate the stūpa; instead, inquire after the health of the two teachers and should speak thus to the bhikṣus in the village.
If there is a sick bhikṣu in the wilderness, you should go together to welcome him. Even if he says, "There are many tigers and wolves in that place;
I fear they will devour me," one must still go to see him despite hearing these words. If he has already died, one should honor his remains.
If he is alive, one should bring him to a village and say to the resident bhikṣus, "Venerable sirs, this is a sick bhikṣu from such-and-such a place in the wilderness; I [have brought him here]."
Having completed the forest offering, he has now come here; let the Elder look after him next. If he does not look after him, there is an offense of *vinaya*-transgression.
If no bhikṣu is available, he should say to the upāsaka, "O Long-lived One, there is a sick bhikṣu in the wilderness; lend a vehicle to go and fetch him.
He should then escort him as far as the donor’s house and place him in a separate screened area. If there are many people, two or three should be taken.
The one capable of nursing should attend to the patient. If the patient says that many people are required, those who wish to stay should all remain together.
They should jointly exhort and solicit for food before and after meals, and even for life-long medicine, providing these supplies so that there is no lack.

If a visiting bhikṣu arrives, one must not immediately tell him to nurse the patient; rather, one should take over the carrying of his robes and bowl, and so on, until the meal is finished and he has rested.
Regarding speech: "Venerable sir, this sick bhikṣu has been looked after by me for a long time; it is now your turn, Venerable sir, to look after him.
If he passes away, you should make offerings to his relics. If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī are traveling together with merchants and the bhikṣuṇī falls ill, the bhikṣu must not abandon her and depart.
He should say, "Go, go, sister," and provide her with appropriate care, as explained in the Vinaya.
Except for embracing and grasping. If it is necessary to massage or apply oil to the body, one should employ a woman to do so.

If there is no permanent resident [monk], and the deceased has robes and a bowl, one should hire someone to perform the cremation; if there are none, one should depart after leaving them behind. If there are laypeople who feel resentment or disapproval, [one must act accordingly].
One should form the perception that it is the ground and carry it to a distant place. If a venerable bhikṣu is ill, he should be placed in a well-lit room;
his disciples should constantly attend to him on all sides, sweep and sprinkle the room, burn incense, and prepare a seat.

If a bhikṣu comes to inquire after his illness, [the attendants] should provide him with food before or after the meal, as well as non-timely liquids. If there are matters to be discussed, the patient should respond. [End of section on] Illness.

If one lacks sufficient manpower, an attendant should respond. If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) comes to inquire after him, one should say, "Welcome, long-lived one," and ask him to sit down while preaching the Dharma for him.
You will gain great merit; as the World-Honored One has said, "Caring for a sick bhikṣu who observes the precepts is no different from caring for me.
If there is an offering, he should accept it and recite a prayer of blessing (*svastyayana*). If the patient suffers from diarrhea...
One should not allow a sick person to remain for a long time; they should be sent away quickly. If the patient is unable to go out, one should keep three vessels:
one to give to the patient, one to carry [the excrement] out, and one to wash and oil with oil and dry in the sun, using them in rotation.
One person should stay by the door so that no one enters suddenly; another person should stay by the patient’s side to attend to them from time to time.
This is the teaching on proper conduct. If a bhikṣu of little merit falls ill, he should not be placed in an exposed location where his foul odors would permeate the outside.
Nor should he be placed in a secluded or cramped spot where, at the time of death, people might not know of him; rather, he should be settled among the community.
If the patient has a teacher or a disciple, they should attend to him. If there is no one, the Saṃgha should appoint one, two, or three persons to care for the sick. If the patient has...

Regarding the cost of medicine: it should be provided. If there is none, the Sangha should provide it. If the Sangha has none, and that patient possesses expensive robes or bowls, they should be exchanged for lighter ones to provide the supply.
If the patient is stingy, one should inform the Sangha, saying: "The sick bhikṣu so-and-so does not understand impermanence;
he is miserly regarding his robes and bowls and refuses to exchange them. Once informed, one should speak to him with gentle words.
The Dharma should be explained so that they gain understanding; only then should one trade [for medicine]. If nothing more can be obtained, one should beg for it and give it.

If that is not possible, one should take the finest portion from the Sangha’s meal and give it. If even that is unavailable, the caregiver should go begging with two bowls and give the superior portion.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "One must not have an ignorant person care for the sick; there must certainly be..."
Regarding external conditions: one must personally go outside and instruct those who are unskilled in nursing so that they do not cause the patient harm through improper means.
One should prevent them from falling into water or fire, consuming poisons, handling knives or axes, falling from cliffs or ditches, climbing high trees, or eating forbidden foods;
all such things should be prohibited. Without consulting a physician, one should not hastily give anything to the patient.

Regarding the administration of medicine: if there is a patient or an attendant, there is no offense even if they remain lying down in the light of a lamp. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (*Shisong lü*) states:
"A junior bhikṣu attending to a patient may sit together with that patient. The *Vinayasamgraha* states:
"If a patient is poor and lacks the funds for medicine, the preceptor, spiritual friends, and others should provide it for them; or one may seek it from a donor, or use the property of the Saṃgha."
If there are items—whether items belonging to a stūpa or decorative articles such as banners and parasols—one may sell them according to their value to provide for the cost of medicine.

If the illness is later cured, the price should be repaid; however, if one lacks the means, there is no fault in not returning it, for [the patient] is like a son of the Great Master, and these are the father’s property.
As for the attendant bhikṣu who provides for the sick person, with the exception of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), he should perform all other duties.
Question: The various Vinayas provide provisional allowances for those who are ill, as well as rules for tending to the sick, all of which have fixed procedures.

However, the *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "With the exception of natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), all others should be performed. Does this mean that there is no transgression whatsoever regarding any of the prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)? Answer:

When one is in a position to observe the precepts but fails to guard them strictly, the offense of violating a light precept will certainly be incurred. However, when faced with difficult circumstances...

Lacking skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), those afflicted by illness and suffering will surely fall into peril. Therefore it is said: "Apart from natural transgressions (prakṛti-sāvadya), all else should be performed.
This is a statement concerning the ultimate limit under specific circumstances; it is not a teaching that permits one to abandon all restraint at will.

The fourth section on dwellings states: "Whatever is required according to the rules for constructing a dwelling is permitted to be given. It is permitted to construct a hall for the *poṣadha* ceremony;

it is permitted to construct long beds; it is permitted to construct a hall for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). For those who are aged, ill, or physically debilitated, it is permitted to use ropes to bind [the bed]."

[The Buddha said: "If one walks while holding onto a rope, or walks while grasping a rope, the hands will become chafed. It is permitted to make a loop, or a bamboo tube, through which a cord is passed;
one may grasp the tube with the hand and perform *caṅkrama* (walking meditation). If one becomes exhausted from walking, it is permitted to place beds at both ends [of the corridor].

One should not make images of dragons or snakes near the door. It is permitted to make images of grapevines or lotus flowers. It is permitted to make leaf-patterns above the door, but it is not permitted to make images of soldiers."

Regarding horse-shaped [images]: one should not spend the remainder of one’s life managing a single room. If one constructs an exceptionally grand and fine building, such as a multi-storied hall, it is permitted to manage its construction for twelve years, provided it is completed within six years;
for other buildings, the duration should be adjusted according to their size and scale. One should not accept a room for administrative duties from the Saṃgha at all times;
rather, it is permitted after the end of the three-month summer retreat, to be assigned according to the seniority of the *upādhyāya*. It is not [permitted] otherwise.
One should take up residence in a work-dwelling (karmadāna-śālā) in various places, but one should stay in a single location for ninety days.
A person engaged in construction work should not reside in a place where many people live, nor should they engage in only minor maintenance tasks.

If a bhikṣu engaged in construction work passes away while residing in such a work-dwelling, this dwelling belongs to the Saṃgha. The bhikṣu engaged in construction work should send someone to inform the Saṃgha and request [the dwelling].

If the occupant of a room has already passed away, that room belongs to the Saṃgha. If the person who commissioned its construction passes away, that room is given to the administrator (vaiyāvṛtyakara).
If the bhikṣu administrator departs before the rooms have been distributed, he should entrust someone to take charge of them;

he should also indicate the location of the rooms so that they may be used for constructing a bathhouse and bathing. One bhikṣu builds the room and another covers it; the one who built it first should [hand it over].
First, regarding the resident monks: two monks may jointly construct a dwelling; it is permitted for them to work on it alternately.

If the senior monk (*sthavira*) is already there, he shall receive the room assigned for the summer retreat (*varṣā*) and must not receive another room. If a monastery building is in ruins, a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*) may say, "If you give this to me, I shall repair it.
It is permitted to give it to him through a formal motion and second (the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). Rāhula was at Nālandā.

He was dwelling in a forest grove. A householder conceived the intention to build a dwelling and offer it to him. At that time, Rāhula was traveling through the human world, so the householder instead offered the dwelling to the Saṃgha.
When Rāhula returned, he informed the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha ordered him to go to the householder’s residence and ask:
"Have you seen anything in me that is censurable or contrary to the dharma of a śramaṇa? Or have you heard such things spoken?"
"If one acts thus with the body? The householder replied, "No. He reported this back to the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If there is someone who, with a joyful heart, builds a dwelling and gives it to one person, or to many people, or to the Saṃgha, and then subsequently gives it to another person—whether to many people, to the Saṃgha, to those of the same school, or to a different school—it is in all such cases called [a gift]."

It is an illegal gift, an illegal acceptance, and an illegal residence. If there is someone who delights in building a dwelling and gives it to one person, or to many people, or to the Saṃgha, or to both divisions of the Saṃgha, all such cases are called legal gifts, legal acceptances, and legal residences.
For a novice śrāmaṇera, it is permitted to install partitions within the room, permitted to construct an inner chamber, and permitted to make a door.
Walls. One may construct half-walls; it is permitted to construct paths using stone, brick, or wood. It is permitted to construct channels and ponds, using stone, brick, or wood to line their edges.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When establishing a monastery (*saṃghārāma*), one should first select an excellent site for measurement.
The location for the stupa should be in the east or the north. The grounds of the Saṃgha and the grounds of the Buddha must not encroach upon one another, nor should they be allowed to...
Water from the area of the *saṃgha* flows into the area of the Buddha; water from the area of the Buddha may likewise flow into the area of the *saṃgha*.

A stūpa should be constructed in a high and prominent location. One must not wash, dye, or sun clothes within the stūpa courtyard, nor wear leather sandals, cover the head, cover the shoulders, or spit on the ground there.
Flowers from the stūpa garden should be used to make offerings to the stūpa. If a donor says, "These flowers are for the Buddha," then they should be offered as fruit.
If giving it to the Sangha, one should follow the instructions of the donor. If there are many flowers, one may give them to a florist and say:

"Make garlands from this much flower and give them to me; for the remainder, give me such-and-such a price. If one receives the price, it may be used to light lamps, purchase incense, or make offerings to the Buddha, or to repair a stūpa.
If the price is excessive, it may be placed among the Buddha's inexhaustible assets (*akṣaya-nīvi*). Flowers from a stūpa pond are treated in the same manner.
It is so. One must not wash clothes, bathe, wash hands or face, or wash the alms bowl within the pond of a stūpa. However, it may be used at will at the lower outlet where the water flows out.
A latrine house must not be situated in the east or the north; there should be a partition installed in the middle so that the two [sides] cannot see each other.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "A latrine should be constructed in the northwest corner behind the monastery. Within the monastery, there are four..."

Beneath each corner pillar, a spittoon should be placed. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one obtains fragrant incense, it should be smeared upon the interior walls, beds, and floors of the dwelling;
flower garlands should be offered to the Saṃgha and fixed to the wall with pins. If a dwelling receives such incense, the donor gains merit. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"In all dwellings, it is permitted to apply plaster to the interior and exterior surfaces as well as the ceiling. The Saṃgha should maintain [these facilities]."
Axes, chisels, knives, saws, hoes, spades, ladders, stools, mud-plastering tools—these are the various implements for building houses.

Regarding the fourth section on the rules for bedding (*śayanāsana*), it says: "It is permitted to make mattresses. Whether of wool or cotton, one should make a stuffing. If the mattress becomes soiled with grease and grime, one should make a coverlet."
One may cover [the bedding] with felt and use it as a pillow; it may be square, round, or triangular. One must not privately use the communal bedding for sleeping.
It is permitted to make a mark [on it]. One must not place a communal mark on one's private property.
It is permitted to dye one's private property to create a mark, such as a mark resembling water sprinkled on the ground or a wheel-shaped mark. One must not move these marks from within the room.
One should place bedding and mats in another location. Two people should not sleep on the same bed, except in the case of the sick.
Two people should not lie upon the same blankets or bedding. Even if there is only one mat and one blanket, it is permitted for each to wear a separate undergarment beneath them.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "Exquisite beds, seats, and large couches should be accepted by the Saṃgha; they are not [for] individuals."
It is permitted. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "It is allowed to use any one of the ten types of robes to make a bedding mat (*śayanāsana*).
One may stuff it with wool, camel hair, cotton, or even soft grass; its maximum thickness is permitted to reach eight finger-breadths."
The third section on the Rules for Utensils states:
"It is permitted to possess large cauldrons, copper pots, iron pots, earthenware pots, copper jars, iron jars, and ceramic jars."
A griddle for frying pancakes, copper bowls, and cups—these are permitted to be used as clothes racks. Lighting lamps is permitted; it is permitted to use iron to construct lamp stands.
For elderly or infirm bhikṣus, it is permitted to keep urinals and spittoons. One should not pick lice from one's person and discard them on the ground in a place where many people reside;
however, it is permitted to make a louse-case. It is permitted to make a razor and to keep a hair-receptacle. One may also pluck out nasal hairs.
Tweezers and nail clippers may be used; they should be kept in a case and provided with a lid. They must not be made of precious materials, nor should one carry a large, fine circular cover.

One should not hold a large, royal circular fan. However, if one obtains such items already finished, it is permitted to accept them for the sake of the stūpa, though they should not be kept for personal use.
It is permitted to keep a whisk. It is permitted to accept various vessels made by potters.
There are three kinds of items that should not be kept: earthenware stools, earthenware bushels, and earthenware pecks. It is permitted to make a tongue-scraper, a toothpick, and an ear-spoon.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "It is not permitted to privately keep a copper bowl; if one receives it as an offering from a pure person (*śuci-pudgala*) and uses it, there is no offense.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "One should keep three kinds of bags: first, a bowl bag; second, a medicine..."

Bags. There are three types of miscellaneous bags; they should be placed in their proper order, with lengths corresponding to one another. They must be made wide and provided with straps, and a lining of felt should be placed inside.
He bound it with thread so that it would not shrink or curl up. Lay devotees of pure faith offered various food vessels;
the Buddha permitted the community to accept them. Having accepted them, they were placed in the storehouse, yet the monks continued to eat from their alms bowls.

The donors remarked with dissatisfaction, "They receive only the merit of giving, but not the merit of making use. The Buddha said, "One should indeed make use of them. There are two kinds of fans: one made of bamboo...
It is made [of bamboo]. There are two types of fans made from leaves and decorated with colors; these may be accepted by the *saṃgha*. There are five kinds of *vījana* (whisks):
first, made by twisting wool; second, made from hemp; third, made from finely torn cotton cloth; fourth, made from old, worn-out materials;

fifth, made from the tips of tree branches. If one uses precious materials, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense. There are two causes and conditions under which the use of a palanquin is permitted: first, ...
There are two types of people who require a well-rope: first, those who are aged, infirm, and weak; second, those who are afflicted by illness and lack strength.

The rope for the long [rope] is one hundred and fifty cubits (*hasta*), while that for the short is ten cubits; those between these two lengths are called "medium. It is permitted for the Saṃgha to keep razors as well as various other necessary items. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"In cold weather, it is permitted to construct a fire-pit outside the building to burn [fuel]; once the smoke has cleared, [the fire] should be maintained."
[They] enter. [One may] make [a vessel] out of copper, iron, clay, or stone. It is permitted to keep three needles; it is permitted to keep a bushel-measure and a scale.
It is not permitted to keep fields, houses, or shops. If there is an offering, it is permitted for the Saṃgha to accept it, provided a *karmadāna* (pure person) is made aware of it.
It is not permitted to keep many small copper vessels; it is not permitted to keep large copper vessels. If one keeps [a vessel] larger than one *sheng*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The *Vinaya-viniścaya* states: "A monk should possess a small knife and a small seal. There are three types of knives: the superior is six finger-widths long and one finger-width wide;
the inferior is four finger-widths long; those between these two are called medium. Their shape is like a curved chicken feather or a curved crow wing.
There are four types of seals: white copper, red copper, brass, and wood; none of these should be made of precious materials."

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: One should fashion a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*). At the top of the staff, one should attach a ring shaped like the rim of a bowl, fitted with small rings that produce a sound when shaken to serve as a warning signal.
One should not strike dogs with the staff; rather, one should raise it to frighten them away. [End of passage on] Dogs.

If one is terrified by fierce anger, one should take a handful of rice, throw it on the ground, and command the creature to eat; this may be repeated two or three times. When no one is around to ask questions, one must immediately depart.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "One should make a rattling staff to drive away venomous insects. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states:
"In places that are terrifying at night, it is permitted to shake the *khakkhara* (monastic staff) to make a sound, causing all evil and venomous insects to go far away."

Question: Now, according to the *Dedeng Jing* (Sutra on the Ladder to Attaining the Way), the staff is fashioned such that its majestic deportment is so dignified that it is extremely difficult to maintain.
This is entirely different from the intent of the Vinaya. Why is this? Answer: In the Vinaya, the significance of the *khakkhara* (staff) lies primarily in its practical utility.

In the ritual prescriptions of the sutras, the significance lies primarily in its symbolic representation of the Dharma. While the symbolic representation may represent one distinct approach, its practical utility is likewise of great benefit.
Furthermore, the practice of people today possessing *śikya* (strainers) and *kalaśa* (water-pots) originates from the Guhyatantra (Esoteric Section) and has no connection with the Vinaya school.

Yet, those same scriptures also state that one may keep a staff for the sake of the elderly or the infirm; while this accords with the Vinaya, it cannot avoid the contradiction between its own preceding and succeeding statements.
One should understand that since the name of the translator is lost, it is appropriate to set it aside under the principle of "leaving a doubt unresolved."

○ Regarding the monastic regulations of the *Saṃghāṭī-vinaya*, it is said that Daṇḍaka (i.e., Dhanika) thought to himself: "I have built a single hut; the Elder has taken possession of it in turn and driven me out.
A second and a third time, he likewise drove me out. He then continued building until he completed a house with fired tiles. The World-Honored One then issued a decree.
It collapsed. Later, he took timber from the royal forest to build a house, but was again rebuked by the World-Honored One: "In vain you toil for yourself; what is the use of such busywork?
From this day forward, cease these arduous tasks and live in accordance with the community of monks, passing your time according to their shared joys and sorrows.

Thereupon, Daṭṭhāna abandoned his worldly affairs and practiced with sincerity day and night, devoting himself exclusively to the cultivation of the path. He attained the various dhyānas and achieved the Way.
Having attained the fruit and given rise to the six supernormal powers, he realized and witnessed this for himself. Deeply rejoicing and finding solace, he spoke these verses:
"If you wish to attain the bliss of tranquility, you should practice the Dharma of a śramaṇa. To rest is to sustain body and life, like a snake entering a mouse hole.

If you wish to attain the bliss of tranquility, you should practice the Dharma of a śramaṇa. Clothing and food sustain body and life; whether coarse or fine, accept whatever is obtained from the community. If you wish to attain...
To extinguish suffering, one should practice the Dharma of the śramaṇa; be entirely content with what one has and single-mindedly cultivate the path to nirvāṇa.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu who knows the monastic quarters should make this vow: 'May those bhikṣus who have not yet arrived come;
may those who have already arrived be provided with clothing, food, bedding, and medicinal requisites so that they lack for nothing. One who can make such a vow [is a member of] the Saṃgha."
One should give according to their wishes. If they require food, one should freely provide them with excellent food. If they require housing or bedding, one should freely provide all of these.
Without having informed the Saṃgha, one may use nineteen coins to provide for guests; if more are required, one should inform the Saṃgha before giving.
One who serves as the *karmadāna* (steward) should know the time limits, know when to announce [the time], and know when to strike [the gong].
Regarding the *gandi* (wooden gong): one should know how to sweep and plaster the lecture hall and the dining area; know how to arrange the beds and stools in continuous succession;
know how to instruct on the purification of fruits and vegetables; know how to inspect for insects in the fermented grain wine (*kaṣāya*); know how to serve water at the time of eating;

and snap the fingers when the assembly breaks into idle chatter. The third section states: "If the *saṃgha* present obtains a large quantity of divisible clothing or goods, it is permitted to establish a storehouse."
[The procedure for] the storehouse: a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation). [The procedure for] appointing a person to guard the goods: a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

If a bhikṣu is unwilling to serve as the guardian of goods, he should be provided with abundant merit in the form of gruel. If he still refuses, he should be given two shares of all the robes and food he receives.
If he still refuses, he should be dealt with according to the Dharma. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "If external offerings enter..."

The *kośastha* (storehouse manager) bhikṣu may receive two portions. If there is a *dhūta* bhikṣu who, although residing within the monastery, does not dwell in the communal quarters and does not eat from the community store, but for whom a donor has personally built a dwelling, the Saṃgha shall not appoint him as a *karmadāna* (steward) or assign him administrative duties.
If a bhikṣu is capable of benefiting the Saṃgha through recitation, instruction, and preaching the Dharma, and thereby gains offerings, the Saṃgha [shall not interfere].
When one has recovered from illness and is capable of attending to monastic affairs, and possesses a dwelling, robes, and a bowl, one should first give the best of these to him.

Regarding food, drink, fruits, and wood, he may be given an additional portion. If someone comes to the monastery, whether they be noble or lowly, or even a bandit, everyone should be received with greetings and inquiries after their welfare.
If someone calls for what they require, one may give it from one's own property; however, regarding the property of the Sangha, one must first inform the Sangha and seek their consensus.
If it is appropriate, one may give. If a person of forceful character or evil intent comes to beg, the guardian of the property may, for the sake of protecting the residence, give as he sees fit;
once given, the Sangha may not reprimand him. The *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: "There are four kinds of adjudicators:

those who have little learning and lack a sense of shame; those who have much learning but lack a sense of shame; those who have little learning but possess a sense of shame; and those who have much learning and possess a sense of shame."

Regarding *hrī* (shame/modesty): among these, those who lack modesty despite being of little learning, as well as those who lack modesty despite being of great learning, when they speak or adjudicate matters within the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should reprimand them with various forms of stern and urgent censure so that those lacking modesty will not do so again.

If there are those who possess modesty but are of little learning, when they speak or adjudicate matters within the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should assist and provide instruction so that those possessing modesty may [flourish].

Furthermore, regarding those who speak and adjudicate matters within the Saṃgha: if there is one who possesses a sense of shame and is learned, and they speak and adjudicate matters within the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha, having heard their speech, should praise them, saying "Excellent!
so that those with a sense of shame [will likewise act] later when speaking and adjudicating matters within the Saṃgha.
The third section states: When a visiting bhikṣu wishes to enter a monastery, he arrives at the gate holding...
If there is a lock and key, one should open it. If it cannot be opened, one should knock gently. If they do not hear, one should knock loudly.
If it still does not open, one should go to the base of the fence or wall, climb over, and enter to open the door. One should not circumambulate the stūpa to the left;
rather, one should ask, "Is there a room for me of such-and-such an age? and further ask, "Is anyone currently living in this room?"

"Are there bedding materials? Is there a blanket? Are there utensils? Is there clothing? Is there an abundance of merit? If he says, "There is," and you wish to take [these things], you should say, "I shall take them.
You should go to the room, open the door, and if there are snakes or insects, you should drive them out.
You should sweep and sprinkle it clean, then spread out the beds and bedding again. You should prepare a vessel of pure water, a washing vessel, and drinking water.
Regarding the water vessels: one should ask, "Where are the places for the large and small excretions? Where is the pure ground (*śucibhūmi*)? Where is the impure ground (*aśucibhūmi*)?
Which is the stūpa of the Buddha? Which is the stūpa of the śrāvakas? Which is the room of the first elder, and so on, up to the room of the fourth elder?
One should pay homage to them in their proper order. One should also ask, "Where is the place for the monks' main meal? Where is the place for the light meal? Where is the assembly at night?"
The place of residence; the place for the recitation of the precepts. What is "food assigned by the Saṃgha"? Food sent by a *dānapati*; food on the eighth day of the month;
food on the fifteenth day of the month; food on the first day of the month; food invited by a *dānapati*. Next, where does one go?

Which *dānapati* has had their bowl overturned (*pātra-āvartana*) by the Saṃgha? Which house is a "family under training" (*śikṣādattaka*)? Where are the dogs fierce? Where are there good people? Where is...
When an old bhikṣu hears that a guest bhikṣu has arrived, he should go outside to welcome him, take his robes and bowl, and provide a seat for him.
He should provide water and utensils for washing the feet and offer drinking water. He should ask, "Venerable sir, how many years of seniority do you have?
If he replies, "I have so many years," he should say, "This is your room; these are your rope bed, wooden bed, mattress, pillow, woolen rug, and blanket."
This is the ground-covering. This is the spittoon. This is the urinal. This is the place for defecation and urination.
This is the pure ground. Furthermore, such-and-such a place is good; such-and-such a place is bad. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When a visiting bhikṣu arrives..."
One should pay homage to the four senior elders (*sthavira*). If one is able to see them at that time, one should pay homage; if one is unable to see them at that time, one should desist.

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When the drum is beaten, the conch is blown, and the three proclamations announce that the time has arrived, one should have a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) or a garden-keeper [perform the duty]."
A wooden *kīṭaka* (wooden gong) should be used. If there is no *śrāmaṇera*, a *bhikṣu* may also strike it.
If a *bhikṣu* has set aside a robe and twelve years have passed without its return, the Saṃgha shall assemble and appraise it; it shall then be used for the sake of the *cāturdisa-saṃgha*.

If that *bhikṣu* returns later, he must compensate with property belonging to the *cāturdisa-saṃgha*. It is well if he does not accept the compensation. If there is grain or rice, it should be given as a gift to the *cāturdisa-saṃgha*.
Regarding "the Sangha": when acting on behalf of the Sangha of the four directions, it is permitted to eat at will.

With the exception of the stupas of Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas, the surplus property of other stupas is permitted for use by the Sangha of the four directions. If that [other] stupa later requires its use, one should take property from the Sangha of the four directions and return it to them.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "A bhikṣu should assist in construction, but he should not work throughout the entire day. Regarding this—
During the cold winter season, one should work in the afternoon; during the hot summer season, one should work in the forenoon. One must calculate the time of day and cease work early.
If the supervisor knows that those people are working in the morning, he should provide them with light food.
If they are working in the afternoon, he should provide them with non-timely beverages and oil for anointing their hands and feet; otherwise, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
What constitutes one load for a layperson should be divided between two bhikṣus. The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states:

"The Saṃgha must not establish unlawful regulations (that which is not ordained by the Buddha is termed 'unlawful,' such as the Yuan dynasty’s adaptation of the Baizhang Qinggui). Those engaged in construction work should consume the monastery's provisions.

One should fashion an image of a bodhisattva; with the exception of anklets and earrings, all other ornaments are permitted to be fashioned.

If it is for an Arhat, the four wheels are installed; for the other three fruits, one wheel is successively reduced.
If it is for an ordinary lay bhikṣu who is merely virtuous, there are no wheels or hubs above, which is called a *piṇḍaka-stūpa* (flat-topped stūpa). The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-vaibhaṣika* states:
"When constructing a stūpa, a small one may be made large, but a large one should not be reduced to a small one. If there is a layperson capable of making a large one [it should be done]."
Excellent. If one is unable to accomplish it oneself, the bhikṣu should exhort others to provide assistance in its construction. If it is old and dilapidated, it should be renovated.
If the clay image of the Buddha is damaged or deficient, one should either enlarge it or create another that is similar according to one’s preference.
As for painted images that are not distinct, they should be wiped away and repainted anew. As for other Buddhist scriptures on leaves or paper, they should be polished...
[The text] is destroyed. One should wipe out what is old and may write anew.

Those who have mastered the entire Sūtra-piṭaka, the entire Vinaya-piṭaka, and those who hold the entire Abhidharma-piṭaka should not be appointed as administrators of monastic affairs. For the sake of the Saṃgha, one should accept fields;
the fruits harvested therefrom should be utilized. In accordance with royal law, one should determine the shares for the cultivators. In all cases...
A monk supervising construction must first inform the senior monks of the monastery before lending anything to others; he may do so only after providing a written contract or clear guarantees.

One must not privately use it. Even if the entire community of monks assembles, one may not lend it to others, nor sell it, nor privately use it.

If the *dānapati* says, "This is an excellent garden and field; why do you know [this]? one should reply: "Although this garden and field..."
"Very well. If wicked people wish to encroach upon it, you may transfer it as you see fit, donor.

If someone comes and requests a vacant plot of land belonging to the Sangha to build a dwelling for them, you should first grant it to them with a stipulation as to how long they have to complete the work. If they say, 'I will finish it within this much time,' you should say to them:
'If you do not complete it within that time, I shall give it to another. If two people both request it, [and] one person..."
One person says, "I shall build a single-story pavilion for the Saṃgha. Another says, "I shall build a two-story pavilion. The Saṃgha should grant it to the one who builds the two-story pavilion.
This continues in this manner up to seven stories. If they all say they will build a seven-story pavilion, it should be granted to the one capable of completing it.
If they are all equally capable of completing it, it should be granted to the one with the largest retinue. If one has not previously made such a commitment, one may give it to another.

This is a violation of the Vinaya according to the rules of the elder bhikṣus: one must not personally occupy a fine room or excellent bedding, mats, and pillows, while leaving those that are worn out, tattered, or soiled for guests.
Instead, one should maintain and repair the fine items to wait upon guests. As stated in the *Nanhai Jiguishi*:

The robes of the bhikṣus are mostly provided from the permanent endowments of the Saṃgha, whether from the surplus of fields and gardens or the proceeds from fruit trees, which are distributed annually to serve as the value for clothing.
For the donors originally relinquished their villages specifically to provide for and sustain the community of monks;
how could it be tolerated that they were given only food while being forced to remain with bare bodies? The remainder of the offerings should be used [for robes].
"The robes are not damaged; this is the general consensus among the monastic community in the Western Regions (India).

Furthermore, in the monasteries (*do-ch'ang*) of the Divine Land (China), there may be places where robes are provided by the institution itself, which is also permissible. As for food, it is common to both the clergy and the laity; this depends on the original intention of the donor.

Even if one were to consume it [privately], in principle it would not be a transgression. Whatever is donated to the monastic community—whether fields, houses, or miscellaneous items—all such things belong to the assembly."
Regarding the clothing and food of the Sangha: this indeed truly eliminates the worry of transgression.

If one’s original intention is to create a state of inexhaustibility and non-obstruction, then although the gift is given to the Sangha, the sentiment extends universally to all beings; thus, those who consume it are entirely without fault.
This is solely due to what was originally intended by the donor. As for the Sangha cultivating fields, they must do so together with pure persons (śuddhakarman).
Regarding the distribution of shares: the Saṃgha merely provided oxen and land, yet they were entirely ignorant of all other matters. Some, being greedy, did not divide the shares;

instead, they employed their own slaves and personally supervised the farming operations. Bhikṣus who protected the precepts would not eat their food, for since the Saṃgha managed these affairs themselves, they sustained their bodies through wrong livelihoods.
They drove laborers and plowed the fields, which was nothing short of an act of anger and a destruction of the seeds [of the Saṃgha].
The ground is frequently infested with insects and ants that cause injury; one’s daily food intake cannot exceed one *sheng*. Who, then, could endure this a hundred times over?
For this reason, men of upright integrity loathe its complexity; they take up their staffs and alms bowls and abandon it to gallop toward the distance.
Sitting alone in the quiet forests and wilds, they joyfully keep company with birds and deer. They sever the clamor of fame and profit, cultivating the tranquil extinction of *nirvāṇa*. If...
To seek profit for various secular households is permitted by this Vinaya; however, to till the soil and harm living beings is not allowed by the teachings of our school.
To damage insects and obstruct one’s spiritual practice—how could it possibly exceed this?
*Chóngzhì píní shìyì jíyào*, Scroll Fourteen: Phonetic Explanations.
*Chóu*: Pronounced *dào*; also pronounced *táo*. It means a canopy or curtain.
The character 縋 (zuì) is pronounced zhù;
it refers to a cord or strap. It is pronounced dì;
it means to suspend something by means of a rope. The character 緇 (zī) is pronounced mí tú; its translation is not recorded.
[The character] 䴵 should be written as 蕤 (ruí, with the phonetic component 追 *zhuī*). Regarding "great *kṣiṇā*":
it is sometimes called *dàxùn* (達儭) or *tánxiè* (檀噺). This refers to the dharma of requiting gifts, which is precisely the ritual of incantation and aspiration (*pariṇāmanā*).
*Gūpātra* likely refers to the *anupātra* (the next-smallest bowl) or the *kṣudrapātra* (small bowl).
*Vasī* (pronounced "zi") means a female ox.
*Dha* (pronounced "tuó") means a stallion.
*Jāva* (闍維) is also called *ya-xun* (耶旬) or *chabi* (荼毘). The *Xiyu ji* (Record of the Western Regions) states that *nirvāṇa* (涅疊槃那) is translated here as "incineration" (*fenshao*).
The character *hua* (鏵) has the phonetic value of *hua*.

*Qiāo* (pronounced *qiāo*, with the initial *q* and rhyme *yáo*) refers to the ten types of clothing, which are varieties of woven fabrics from the Western Regions. There are ten kinds in total, such as hemp cloth, cotton cloth, and so forth.
*Tiáo* (pronounced *tiáo*, with the initial *t* and rhyme *diào*; alternatively pronounced *dú* with the initial *d* and rhyme *diào*).
*Zuǎn*: pronounced *zhuàn*.
*Xiāo*: pronounced *xiāo*. It refers to the upturned tail feathers of a bird. *Pàn*:
pronounced *pàn* (with the *pu* and *huàn* initials). It refers to the threads at the bottom of a garment.
*Nien* (撚): pronounced *niǎn* (with the initial *tǐn*). It means to pinch or press an object with the fingers.
*Qiánzhui* (犍椎) refers to items such as bells, drums, fish-shaped gongs, and stone chimes; these are struck to assemble the congregation.
*Kǔjiǔ* (苦酒) is vinegar.
It is called *stūpa*, or alternatively *futu*, *toupó*, *sitoupo*, or *tabo*;
today it is abbreviated as "ta" (tower). It is translated as "square mound," also as "round tomb," and also as "lofty and prominent.
In meaning, it is translated as "sacred temple. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra, Latter Part* states: "The Buddha’s stūpa has thirteen tiers and is topped with the mark of a wheel. [A pratyekabuddha...]"

The *stūpa* has eleven tiers; the *arhat* has four tiers; the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) has no further tiers, because he has not yet been liberated from the suffering of the various existences within the three realms.
"Lan" (婪) is pronounced "lan" (嵐); it also means greed.
*Xiè* (pronounced *xiè*): to bind;
to fasten. Compiled by the Śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu of Ancient Wu, from the *Chóngzhì Píní Shìyì Jíyào*, Volume Fifteen.
The third section of the *Āraṇyaka-dharma* states:
At dawn, wash the hands. Take the robes and shake them out; place the *saṃghāṭī* on the head or upon the shoulders.
Wash the bowl and place it in its net bag. Take the leather sandals, the staff for walking in the open air, and the key; exit the room, close the door, and push [it shut].
Check whether it is secure. If it is not secure, you should install a bolt. If it is secure, you should pull the cord inside and look around in all four directions.
If no one sees you, you should hide the door-hook. If someone sees you, you should place it in a concealed spot or take it away with you.
While traveling on the road, one should constantly contemplate wholesome dharmas. If one encounters people, one should first greet them, saying, "Welcome.

If one wishes to enter a village, one should set the bowl down securely on the ground, put on the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), and entrust one's leather sandals, staff, and umbrella to someone at the edge of the village.

Upon entering the village, one should observe the characteristics of the alleys, the characteristics of empty spaces, the characteristics of the marketplace, the characteristics of the gates, and the characteristics of refuse heaps. When entering the dwellings of laypeople...
In a house, one should observe the characteristics of the first gate, up to the characteristics of the seventh gate.

If one wishes to adjust one's robes, one should face a wall, holding the staff with the right hand and the bowl with the left hand. One should not stand in the middle of the path, nor should one stand in a secluded place.
One should not go out to meet food. If called, one should go. If one receives rice, dry rice, or the like, one should not place it all together in one spot. If...
This is one alms-bowl; it should be separated [from others] by means of an object, such as a tree leaf, bark, a metal ring, a secondary bowl, or a small bowl.

Powdered grain should be wrapped in a hand-towel. One should not beg from prominent families, nor should one beg insistently or demand that it be obtained. If one knows it will be obtained, one should wait.
Once the begging is finished, one should leave the village, step off the path, set the bowl on the ground, fold the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and place it upon one’s head or shoulder.
While walking, one should constantly contemplate wholesome dharmas. Upon seeing people, one should first greet them with "Welcome," and proceed to the usual place for eating.
In that place, one should sweep and sprinkle water; prepare vessels for water, vessels for leftover food, a seat, a foot-washing stone, a vessel for water, and a towel for wiping the feet.
If other forest-dwelling bhikṣus arrive, one should rise to meet them from afar, take their bowls for them, provide them with a seat, and provide them with water-vessels and so forth.
Once they have washed their hands with soap powder, one should set aside a portion of the leftover food, keeping it clean and pure. If bandits should come, one should give it to them.
Next, he should offer water to that forest-dwelling bhikṣu; next, he should offer him food. While he eats, he should watch over him and provide whatever is required:
salt, vinegar, vegetables, water, fans, and so forth. If the time for the meal is about to pass, they should eat together.

After he has finished eating, he should take the bowl for him, give him water to wash his hands, and if there is any leftover food, he should give it to humans or non-humans. He should then wash the vessel containing the remains.
He should return vessels, beds, seats, and other items to their original places. He should sweep and sprinkle the dining area.
If bandits arrive, he should say: "This is water; this is for washing the feet; this is food. It has been set aside specifically for you; it is clean. If you wish to eat, then eat.
An araṇya bhikṣu should be well-acquainted with the divisions of the night, well-acquainted with the cardinal directions, and well-acquainted with the stars. He should not...
One should spread out fine bedding and sleep peacefully. During the first and last watches of the night, one should remain alert in mind and engage in contemplation.
When a bhikṣu eats, whether it be a human or a non-human, one should give him food, even if it is but a single morsel. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"The sons of the Śākya, having gone forth into homelessness, become attached to wealth, profit, and various articles for sustaining life; they are unable to perceive the Truths. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "I wish..."

During these three months of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), he remained in silent seclusion so that the bhikṣus would not see him, except for one who was invited to provide him with food, and except on the days of the *poṣadha*.
At that time, the bhikṣus respectfully received the Buddha’s instruction and collectively established a regulation:

"One must not see the World-Honored One at will. Should anyone violate this regulation, they shall be made to perform the confession for the offense of transgression (*pāyantika*). At that time, there was a bhikṣu...
The novice named Cūḍapanthaka was observing the *pūrvavāsa* (early retreat) in Rājagṛha, while the Blessed One was observing the *paścimavāsa* (later retreat).

When Cūḍapanthaka had completed the three months, finished his *pravāraṇā*, and concluded his robe-making, he took up his robes and bowl, practiced the *dhūta* austerities, and together with his disciples—dignified and composed—he went to where the Buddha was staying.
He gently knocked on the door-panel, and the Buddha opened it for him.

The gatekeeper opened the door. Cūḍapanthaka entered, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat down. The Buddha asked him in greeting, “Cūḍapanthaka, why is it that you yourself are so majestic and are surrounded by such majesty?
Cūḍapanthaka replied, “Venerable Sir, if anyone comes wishing to go forth, I tell them:
‘Good son, you should dwell in an araṇya; you should live on alms; you should possess only the three robes; [you should wear] rag-robes; [you should dwell] under trees...’”
Sit down. I shall praise such matters as these for you. If you say you are able [to practice them], I will ordain you as a renunciant;

if you say you are unable, let you go as you please. If there are those who wish to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), or seek a preceptor (*niśraya*), or seek instruction in recitation, [I shall provide it].
Or, practicing proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), with tranquil mindfulness and reflection, he replied as before to all who came seeking him.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, his own body became dignified and handsome, and his disciples were likewise so. The Buddha said, "Excellent, Little Army (*Cūḍapanthaka*)!
You are able to vow to deliver immeasurable devas and humans, to benefit boundless classes of sentient beings, and to cause those who come seeking the Dharma to attain peace and happiness."
"Kṣudraka, you should know this: if one can praise the virtues of the dhūta practices, one praises my own person;
if one reviles the virtues of the dhūta practices, one reviles my own person. Why is this? Because throughout the long night, I have extolled such means of deliverance.
Yet, you must not contravene the regulations of the Saṃgha. Kṣudraka said to the Buddha, "I truly did not..."

[The monks] asked, "Venerable Sir, what regulations has the Saṃgha established for this place? The Buddha told them the reason and said, "Whether you are guests or hosts, the Saṃgha's regulations must be observed.
However, for forest-dwelling bhikṣus, there shall be an exemption from these regulations for their benefit.
If you wish to see me, come at any time as you please. Having heard this, Cūḍapanthaka rejoiced and practiced accordingly; he prostrated to the Buddha and departed.
[The Buddha] dismissed them. The six bhikṣus then went to Kṣudraka and interrogated him regarding his transgression. Kṣudraka related the Buddha’s words to them in full.
At that time, those who had renounced the world from the Śākya clan each thought to themselves: "When Kṣudraka came, we were able to attend upon him and converse with him intimately;
yet we, though remaining here, have not been able to do so because of our great greed, for which the Buddha has expelled him."
"We, we ought to regard our long robes, alms bowls, and other belongings as a disease, as an abscess, as an arrow; they should be held [only] for the sake of discarding them.
Thereupon, they took all their possessions to Ānanda. Ānanda informed the Buddha, and the Buddha directed Ānanda to accept them and place them in a large room.
He then told the bhikṣus: "If there is anything lacking, take and use it as you wish. [The Śākya] bhikṣus...

Having discarded his robes and belongings, he immediately went to where the Buddha was. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, whereby five hundred members of the Śākya clan, while still on their seats, personally realized full perfection.
They shattered the shell of ignorance, severed the delusions of the three realms, and became Arhats.

Having accomplished the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, they attained true knowledge that "birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, and what was to be done has been accomplished."

His task is accomplished; he shall not undergo further existence. His mind is free from obstruction, like a hand waving through space. Whether cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, neither love nor hatred arises.
He views gold and earth as equal and without distinction. Regarding all fame and profit, there is nothing he does not relinquish.
Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas pay him homage. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāliparipṛcchā* states: "One who is not a foolish person is fit to dwell in an araṇya."
Even if one is not widely learned, but clearly understands the characteristics of the precepts, one may likewise dwell in an araṇya. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"When a person comes to an aranyaka bhikṣu, he should first engage them in conversation; he should maintain right mindfulness with a pleasant countenance and a cheerful expression, and must not hang his head.
He should say, 'Welcome. He should keep fire, as well as a fire-drill, food, eating utensils, water, and a water vessel."
Vessels: water for washing the feet, water vessels, pure water jars, and constant-use water jars should always be kept full of water.
One should know the directions, know the days, know the divisions of time, and know the constellations. One should recite the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; one should understand them.

One should know the four dhyānas and the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]. If these have not yet been attained, one should know how to study and recite them. One should not keep sun-crystals or moon-crystals.
One should not dwell in a desolate mountain wilderness that is a place of fear. The *Vinayavastu* states:
"If a bhikṣu is alone in a solitary place, he may mentally recite the *Poṣadha*, perform the *Pravāraṇā*, accept robes, receive the seven-day rite, and receive seven-day medicines."
[He gave] a single invitation and pure gifts of clothing and requisites. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, regarding the verse spoken by the World-Honored One when he left the assembly to travel alone:

"If one finds a good companion through careful examination, one may dwell and travel together with them with vigor and strength; though wandering among the various assemblies, the mind remains ever joyful."
If one does not find a virtuous companion, one should dwell alone with courage and vigor, abandoning towns, kingdoms, and villages, remaining untroubled like a wild elephant in the forest.
As the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said in verse: "One's food need not exceed a single *śoṇa* of rice;
for sleep, a single small bed suffices; two woolen rugs are enough to cover the body; everything beyond that is merely a thing of folly."
In the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the Bhikṣu Vatsīputra addressed Ānanda with this verse: "Dwell in tranquility beneath the empty tree;
Direct your mind toward the Dharma of Nirvāṇa. Practice dhyāna without negligence; What is the use of speaking much?"
The third section of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"When the Saṃgha is split and there is an unlawful concordance, one should not sit in a place where evil arises through body and speech;
when there is lawful concordance and the matter has been resolved, one should sit in a seat leaving a single space vacant. The fourth section states: [as above].

When discussing the Dharma or legal matters, those who are three years junior [to their seniors] are permitted to sit together on wooden benches; those who are two years junior are permitted to sit together on small rope-seated stools.

When a bhikṣu enters the midst of the Saṃgha, there are five rules he must observe: (1) he should maintain a mind of loving-kindness; (2) he should humble himself as if he were a cloth for wiping dust;
(3) he should be well-attentive to his sitting and rising; (4) upon seeing a senior elder, he should not remain seated comfortably; (5) upon seeing a junior... [he should rise].
(3) One should not rise from one's seat. (4) One should not engage in miscellaneous worldly talk;
whether preaching the Dharma oneself or requesting another to preach it, if one sees something improper within the Sangha that one cannot mentally endure, one should remain silent. Why is this?
5. Fearing that the Saṃgha might become divided, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "When entering the midst of the Saṃgha, one should employ five methods:
first, a humble mind; second, a heart of loving-kindness; third, reverence; fourth, knowing the proper order of seating; and fifth, not discussing other matters.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "A junior bhikṣu should address an elder as 'Venerable One' (*bhadanta*), and an elder should address a junior [as 'Venerable Brother']."
Regarding the term *āyuṣmat* [for "venerable"]: Section Three of the *Dharmavastu* on the Method for Distributing Property states:
"If the *saṃgha* present obtains a large quantity of divisible clothing and goods, it is permitted to appoint one person to distribute them. This is announced (*jñapti*)."

2. *Karma* (Formal Act): When a robe or other divisible property is obtained while a single monk is residing [there], and if four or more guest monks arrive, one should entrust the robe to a single monk and have him perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) to divide it.

If there are two or three monks, they should divide it together by means of three verbal declarations to one another. If there is only one monk, he should mentally reflect and say aloud: "This is my portion."
There is a dwelling place; there is a bhikṣu; there is the perception that there is a bhikṣu; one desires to form a separate faction, yet it is not accomplished:
a duṣkṛta offense. There is a bhikṣu, but one has doubt [regarding his status]; it is not accomplished: a duṣkṛta offense. There is no bhikṣu, but one has the perception that there is a bhikṣu;

it is not accomplished, yet there is no offense. There is no bhikṣu, but one has both the perception that there is a bhikṣu and doubt; in both cases it is accomplished: a duṣkṛta offense. There is no bhikṣu, but one has the perception that there is no bhikṣu; it is accomplished.
[The same applies to] the distribution [of property]. There is no offense. Whether the acceptance of robes is accomplished or not, and whether there is an offense or no offense, it is likewise.
When a monk with many acquaintances dies, there are many monasteries, gardens, fields, fruit trees, separate rooms, and various items, such as bronze jars, bronze basins, and axes.

Regarding items such as chisels, lamp-stands, heavy objects, beds, mats, and pillows—since there are often many people who guard the monastery (saṃghārāma)—as well as carts, water-jars, staffs, fans, tools, robes, bowls, sitting-mats, and needle-cases:
[if one does not know] what to do with them, the Buddha said: "If you have many acquaintances [who can look after them], [you may leave them]."

There is no individual ownership; everything belongs to the Saṃgha. If there are robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, or needle cases, the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the local community present) should divide them.

All other items belong to the *cāturdisa-saṃgha* (the universal Saṃgha of the four quarters) and should not be divided. Even if the two divisions of the Saṃgha obtain a large quantity of divisible clothing and requisites, they should be divided into two portions.
Even if there are only śrāmaṇerīs, they should likewise be divided into two portions. Even if there are only śrāmaṇeras, they should likewise be divided into two.
[It shall be] divided. If there are no śrāmaṇerīs, the bhikṣu-saṃgha should divide it. If there are no śrāmaṇeras, the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha should divide it.

If a bhikṣu passes away in a place where no other bhikṣus reside, the upāsakas or the park-keepers of that place should take charge of it and record it, awaiting the arrival of members of the five classes of renunciants to give it to them. If none come, they should send it to the nearest [monastery].
While staying in a monastery, the extra robes (atireka-cīvara) relinquished by the bhikṣus should be offered to the Saṃgha or to a Buddha-stūpa;
they should not be given to laypeople or to non-Buddhists. A bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa or mānatva should also be given a share.
If one has been subject to a formal act of censure (tajjanīya-karman) or other such procedures, it may be placed on the ground for them or given to them through another person. If...
If there are those who act as messengers for laypeople, one should calculate the amount of their labor and provide them with food or wages.

When a sick bhikṣu dies, his robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case should be granted to the caregiver through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. Furthermore, if there are many who possess three sets of robes (*tricīvara*), [the same procedure applies].
One should give [the deceased] what they habitually possessed. One must observe this patient-care attendant:
if they have been an excellent caregiver, give them the superior set of three robes; if mediocre, the mediocre set of three robes; if inferior, the inferior set of three robes.
If a monk who was in debt passes away, it is permitted to use his extra robes to repay the debt; or, if there are no extra robes, sell the three robes to repay it, provided there is a surplus.
[To] the attendant of the sick person. The attendant of the sick person should ask the sick bhikṣu: "Which are the three robes? Which are the extra robes?
To whom do you owe [robes]? Who owes you [robes]? To whom should you give them? If he does not ask, he should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
There is a bhikṣu who, having entered the summer retreat in one place, stays in another place for a greater number of days.
Regarding the taking of the *varṣā* (rainy-season) goods (this refers to having a valid reason for departing after having accepted the "seven-day rule" and going to reside elsewhere):

if the [benefits] of both places are equal, it is permitted to take half from each (this means that because of a valid reason, even if one cannot return to the original *varṣā* residence within forty days, it is not called a breach of the summer retreat).

One should not, having already received a share of the robes while observing the *varṣā* at this place, receive a share of the robes again at another place. If one departs before the distribution of robes has taken place during the summer *varṣā*, one should make an entrustment (*anuśāsana*).

If one person takes a portion, the Saṃgha should give it back to him. Whether he did not entrust [his belongings], or entrusted them carelessly, or whether the one who received the entrustment forgot, in all such cases it is not the fault of the Saṃgha.
When a bhikṣu dies and leaves many robes and articles, the present Saṃgha should divide them; they should not be kept beyond the end of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).
Even if a donor intends to give them for a stūpa, or for the performance of assemblies and the like, the present Saṃgha may receive a great deal of them.
One should not retain the distribution of robes and clothing; these are non-seasonal robes and must be distributed.

If a bhikṣu residing at a certain place acquires a large quantity of robes and clothing from the summer retreat, that bhikṣu should form this thought: "This is my property, whether it has been formally accepted or not.
If other bhikṣus arrive, he should not distribute a share to them. If a large quantity of robes and clothing is acquired and subsequently the Saṃgha is split...
It shall be divided into two portions. If [the robe] has not yet been obtained and the Saṃgha is split, one should ask the donor; according to what he says, it should be given to him.
If the donor says he does not know, or says "give it to both," it should be made into two portions.
When the bhikṣus obtain the divisible clothing and requisites, if a bhikṣu goes from this faction to that faction, he should not be given a share. If there is a bhikṣu...

He set out for that community, but died before he arrived; his robes and bowl were given to the community where he intended to go. After the bhikṣu had been subject to the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), he passed away;
his robes and bowl were given to the community of monks who had jointly performed the formal act of suspension.

Question: In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*’s rules for the treatment of offenses, it is stated that if a person subject to suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) passes away, their robes and bowl should not be divided but should be discarded.
Now, however, you say that when a suspended bhikṣu dies, his robes and bowl are to be given to the monks who participated in the formal act of suspension (*karmavācanā*).

From what source does this derive? Answer: The *Mahāsāṃghika* refers specifically to one who has not renounced their evil views. Here, the reference applies generally to all cases of being charged with an offense.
If the two groups do not contradict one another, both may be followed.

If there is a monk who has divided [the community] into two factions, and a donor invites them to a meal at a single location while also bestowing robes and thread, they should accept according to what the donor provides.
If monks have obtained robes for the *anvāraṇyaka* (summer retreat) and have divided into two factions, they should calculate the number of persons in each group.
[The portion] should be divided. If the robe for the *varṣā* (rainy season) has not yet been obtained and the Saṃgha is split, it should also be divided according to the number of people present.
Whether the summer robe has been obtained or not, if one goes to another faction, [the robe] must be shared with them. Generally, there are eight kinds of gifts of robes:

those given to the community of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*), those given to the community of nuns (*bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha*), those given to both communities (*ubhaya-saṃgha*), those given to the Saṃgha of the four directions (*cāturdisa-saṃgha*), or those given to a specific boundary (*sīmā*).

Regarding internal monks: whether they are monks who have performed the *karmavācanā* together, or those to whom [the gift] is given by mentioning their names, or if it is given to a single person, in all cases it should be assigned according to the portion bestowed.
The fourth section states: "The property of the Sangha of the four quarters should not be divided; it should not be taken into one's own possession."
One should not engage in buying or selling. Nor is it for the Saṃgha to sell; nor may it be sold by many people, nor even by a single person.

Whether it is an item that has been personally acquired, or a share, or something bought or sold—if one does so, the personal acquisition is invalid, the sharing is invalid, and the buying or selling is invalid. One commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
What constitutes property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions? It includes monasteries, monastery property, dwellings, and rooms.
Abandoned objects: basins, jars, cauldrons and pots, axes, chisels, lampstands, various miscellaneous heavy items, rope beds, wooden beds, and bedding.

Wood and bamboo are not permitted to be divided; however, it is permitted to divide fruits and flowers. If flowers are offered to the Buddha, or if one constructs a private dwelling on land belonging to the Saṃgha, and an elder or visiting bhikṣu arrives, one must rise and yield the way.
There is no rational basis for incorporating Saṃgha property into one's own possession.

There are five ways of distributing rice gruel for the Saṃgha that lead one to hell as swiftly as a shot arrow: acting out of attachment, acting out of aversion, acting out of fear, acting out of... [ignorance].

Ignorance. Not knowing whether [the portion] has been divided or not. There are five factors for dividing rice porridge: freedom from lust, hatred, fear, and ignorance; and knowing whether it has been divided or not.
This applies even to the appointment of a *śrāmaṇera* or a messenger; it is likewise so. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If one observes the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) in another location, one should not receive a share of the robes here. It must be a retreat observed in this very place that entitles one to a share of the robes here."

Excluding those facing life-threatening danger or obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), there are five circumstances in which one should not give the *varṣā-cīvara* (the robe for the rainy season retreat).

First, one who has been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepaniya-kamma*). Regarding this, if they hold any of the three types of views and do not relinquish them, and the formal act of censure for not relinquishing such views has been performed—excluding only this case of censure for not relinquishing evil views—then all other cases, such as censure for not acknowledging an offense, censure for not confessing, or acts of reprimand (*tajjanīya-kamma*), may have the robe placed on the ground for them or given to them by another person.
Second, one who has abandoned the religious life (*pravrajyā*). This includes cases where they rely on the power of a king or the power of a high minister.
1. If a group of bandits comes seeking [the robes] with the intent to cause harm, one should give them away. 2. Regarding the three types of impermanence:

if the robes for the rainy season retreat have already been collected but not yet distributed, and at the point of death one entrusts them to a certain person, they should be given to that person after death.
3. Breaking the rainy season retreat: neither entering the retreat early nor entering it late. 4. When departing, failing to entrust the distribution of the robes. If a bhikṣu...
Even if one is not currently in residence during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), if a donor has prepared an offering for that person's sake, one should receive a share.

If the donor wishes to give it to other monks as well, it should be given according to the donor’s intention. There are four kinds of things that, by the donor’s word, should belong to the *saṃgha* present before them.
What are the four? "I give clothing," "the value of clothing," "goods," and "the value of goods. Furthermore, there are ten ways in which [property] is acquired. One should...
They belong to the present Saṃgha. What are the ten? They are: food at the proper time; medicine for the night (i.e., non-time gruel); seven-day medicine; and lifetime medicine.
Regarding the belongings of a deceased bhikṣu: [these include] gifts for the monastery, for a great assembly, untimely robes, miscellaneous items, and invitations to meals.

According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, when a śrāmaṇera passes away, his belongings belong to his preceptor (*upādhyāya*). However, it is also stated that when a śrāmaṇera’s life has ended, his property is to be divided among the monks present.
Question: Regarding the property of a deceased śrāmaṇera, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* present two conflicting statements. Which of these should be followed? Answer:
If the deceased śrāmaṇera was originally nurtured by his upādhyāya, then one should follow the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
If the deceased śrāmaṇera had long shared in the same offerings as the saṃgha, then one should follow the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. These are merely citing one corner [of the case] each.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "When giving to a śrāmaṇera under training, one should divide [the property] equally with the great bhikṣus. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:

"If a bhikṣu borrows property belonging to a stūpa or property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters and uses it, after his death, the value of his robes and bowl must be calculated and repaid;
the remainder shall be divided by the Saṃgha. If a bhikṣu’s robes and bowl are borrowed for use by a stūpa or used by the Saṃgha of the four quarters, after his death..."
If the value of items belonging to the *stūpa* or the *saṃgha* is calculated, they must be returned; those belonging to the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the present community) should be divided.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "If the *saṃgha* receives cakes, even if they are as small as a tree leaf, they shall be distributed among the assembly.

If they receive clothing, even if it is as meager as enough to serve as a wick for a lamp, the assembly shall likewise share it. If they obtain high-quality woolen cloth (*kambala*), it should be sold for coins or cowries, and then..."
[The text] is divided as follows. The *Nidāna* states: "If a bhikṣu dies in a bhikṣuṇī monastery, his robes and bowl should be returned to the bhikṣus.
If a bhikṣuṇī dies in a bhikṣu monastery, her robes and bowl are returned to the bhikṣuṇīs. If there are no bhikṣus present at that location, the bhikṣuṇīs shall receive them;
if there is no community of bhikṣuṇīs present, the bhikṣus shall take them. There are four kinds of items that must not be divided. First, [the four...]"
