First, property belonging to the Saṃgha; second, property belonging to a stūpa; third, medicine for the sick belonging to the community; fourth, assets belonging to the monastery.
When a great assembly is convened and much precious wealth is obtained, those entitled to receive it shall divide it equally according to the law in accordance with their respective order.
If the number of members is large, one share should be given to a thousand people, who shall then divide it among themselves; or perhaps to a hundred, or thirty.
From one person up to ten people constitute one portion; let them take their own respective shares.

Within a group of ten, if even one person dies after the distribution of robes has already been completed, that deceased person’s share should enter the Saṃgha. If it has not yet been distributed, the remaining nine persons shall receive it together.
This principle applies to larger numbers as well. The *Mūlakacāra* states: "One should not take property from this location and give it to another residence."
One should enjoy [the items] according to their designated place. If one gives them privately, one must fully compensate for their value.
If one does not return them, one incurs a grave offense against the Dharma. The Saṃgha should not accept the three robes of a sick bhikṣu;

even if it accepts them, they should not be distributed. Upon seeing that they are deficient, they should be returned. Regarding the property given to the two assemblies of monks and nuns, one should inquire of the donor and act according to their words.
Regarding the distribution of goods benefiting the two assemblies, they should be divided equally among them. To male and female śrāmaṇeras, one-third [of the portion] should be given;

to śikṣamāṇās and those seeking ordination, one-half [of the portion] should be given. As for food and gifts received through invitation, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs should calculate the number of persons and distribute the gifts accordingly;
it should not be divided into equal halves. Furthermore, when a Dharma assembly is held, the gifts obtained therein should likewise be distributed.

Nuns: If a donor’s original intention was solely to provide for those residing at this specific monastery and does not extend to others, then if anyone comes to eat there, they must be compensated by calculating the value of the items provided. The *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states:

"If those observing the rains retreat have a reason to travel and depart after having entrusted their portion to others, one should take that portion. If it has not been entrusted, then one should not take it. If...
If the person entrusted with the items does not take them, one should repay the value using one's own property according to the amount.

When a bhikṣu has passed away, if another bhikṣu arrives during any of the five designated times, he should be given a share: first, at the time of striking the *gaṇḍī*; second, at the time of reciting the *Triskandhaka* Sūtra on Impermanence;

third, at the time of paying homage to the *caitya*; fourth, at the time of casting the counting sticks (*śalākā*); and fifth, at the time of making the formal motion (*jñapti*). If the assembly is not in harmony...
If there is no person authorized to preside over the assembly, one should perform the ritual of the "first and last" (ādyantavidhi).

This means taking a small amount of the deceased's property—such as two coins or similar—and distributing it individually to the foremost elder (*sthavira*) at the head of the assembly and to the lowest-ranking monk; this serves as a formal record of the distribution.
Thereafter, the *saṃgha* present before them shall divide [the property] equally as usual; no further formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is required.

If someone arrives after the initial and final rituals have been completed, they should not be given a share. If [the property] was present during the first four periods but absent during the last two, one should still give them a share.
If it was made for oneself and is currently within the boundary (*sīmā*), all those who are entitled to receive it should accept the benefit. If it was not made...
Regarding the rule that "the white [property] is not subject to division at the beginning or end": this applies only to the Śrāvaka disciples of the Blessed One.
All those currently in Jambudvīpa, or residing elsewhere, have an equal share in it. However, all the sūtras and śāstras should not be divided;

they shall be stored in the scriptural treasury (sūtra-piṭaka) and read collectively by the Saṃgha of the four directions. Other books may be sold, and the proceeds should be divided among those present. As for all promissory notes...
If the object pledged can be recovered early, it may be divided immediately. If it has not been recovered, it shall be stored in the monastic treasury;
at a later time, it may be used for the benefit of the Saṃgha of the four quarters.
If a bhikṣu is ill and says, "After my death, you may take this object and give it to that person," this is a worldly custom and does not constitute a valid entrustment. This object should...
As for those who were face-to-face with the deceased, it is well to give [the items] to them. The corpse should be cremated as an offering;

only after the recitation of the scriptures is finished should the goods be divided. If the deceased had entrusted property to others, that property shall be divided by the assembly at the location where it is held.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "When a bhikṣu is alive, all his sūtras and vinaya texts should be assigned to those capable of reciting them."
Regarding the reciter: if there is no one available for the distribution, the *saṃgha* present should give [the property] to the one capable of reciting;

it should not be divided or sold. Question: Regarding the Sūtras, Vinaya, Abhidharma, the *Vinayavibhaṅga*, and the *Mātṛkā* of a deceased bhikṣu, two different traditions exist. Which of these should be followed?

Answer: The purpose of the sutras and treatises lies in their circulation, reading, and recitation. However, with the exception of selling them by dividing them up, other matters may be adjusted according to the circumstances.

Regarding the second section on the Dharma of preaching the Dharma, it says: "One may listen to the explanation of the meaning without reciting the full text of the words and phrases. Two bhikṣus should not occupy the same high seat together."
While seated, one should preach the Dharma. One should not arrange high seats close together to preach the meaning while seeking out each other's faults.
One should not press or constrain one another. One should not chant in unison. One should not preach the Dharma with a singing voice that exceeds the proper measure.
There are five faults in preaching the Dharma with a singing voice: first, one develops attachment oneself, becoming fond of musical sounds; second, those who hear it develop attachment.
Third, those who hear it practice and study it. Fourth, elders feel resentment and give rise to arrogance.
Fifth, in places of quietude, one’s recollection of sounds causes distraction to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The fourth section states:

"If a bhikṣu speaks words that merely resemble the [true] text but violate the Dharma and the Vinaya, this bhikṣu causes many people to fail to obtain benefit, creates various karmas of suffering, and thereby extinguishes the True Dharma."

If a monk conforms to the words and phrases [of the scriptures] and does not violate the Dharma and Vinaya, he benefits many people, prevents them from performing deeds that lead to suffering, and ensures that the True Dharma endures for a long time.
Conversely, if a monk prescribes what has not been prescribed or abolishes what has been prescribed, [he harms the Sangha].
In this way, they gradually cause the precepts to be ruined, depriving many people of benefit and creating manifold karmas of suffering, thereby extinguishing the True Dharma.

If a bhikṣu does not establish what was not established, and does not abolish what was established, then in this way they gradually cause the precepts to be fulfilled, benefiting many people, refraining from creating karmas of suffering, and causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time. Therefore, you all—
That which was prescribed should not be prescribed; that which was prescribed should not be abolished. One should study and train according to the precepts established by the Buddha. Question:
Now, observing the *Wubai wen jing* (Sūtra of Five Hundred Questions) and various Vinaya texts of the different schools, there are many contradictions.
Furthermore, observing the *Baizhang Qinggui*, it also differs greatly from the Vinaya. If later generations were to follow these [latter works], would they not destroy the True Dharma? Answer:
The destruction of the True Dharma is entirely due to the lack of clarity regarding the study of the Vinaya.

The *Five Hundred Questions Sutra* (*Wubai wen jing*) is clearly recognizable as having been interpolated and expanded by later generations through forced associations. Even the *Baizhang Qinggui* has long since lost the original intent of Master Huaihui;
it is entirely a fabrication and embellishment by secular monk-officials and abbots of the Yuan dynasty, whose literary composition is incoherent.
Those people who practice [the teachings] today do so all because they are unacquainted with the study of the Vinaya.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are four kinds of detailed expositions. What are the four? If a bhikṣu speaks thus:
'O Venerable Elders, I heard and received this from the Buddha at such-and-such a city; this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha.'"
Regarding the Teaching: if one hears such a statement, one should not immediately give rise to suspicion, nor should one condemn it.

One should first carefully determine the words and phrases, then investigate the Sūtras and Vinaya, and examine the legal codes. If [the statement] is inconsistent with them and contradicts the Dharma, [it should be rejected].
One should say to that bhikṣu: "What you have spoken was not spoken by the Buddha; or perhaps the Elder did not carefully grasp the Buddha’s teaching. Why is this?
When I investigate the Dharma and Vinaya, it does not correspond with them. Elder, you need not recite or practice this."
Furthermore, do not teach other bhikṣus; you should now abandon it. However, if upon investigation it is found to be consistent with the Dharma and Vinaya, you should say:

"Venerable sir, what you have spoken was spoken by the Buddha; you have truly grasped the Buddha’s word. Why is this? Because upon my investigation, it is consistent with the Dharma and Vinaya and does not contradict them.
Venerable sir, you should maintain and recite it well, and teach it to other bhikṣus so that it is not lost."

This is the first detailed explanation. Furthermore, if one says, "I heard this Dharma and so forth from the Elder in the harmonious Saṃgha of such-and-such a village or city," one should likewise investigate and examine it. If it is inconsistent [with the teachings], one should say:
"This was not spoken by the Buddha; that Saṃgha and that Elder did not carefully grasp the Buddha’s words. The same applies to the Venerable One, and so on.
Now, one should discard it. If it is consistent [with the Dharma], one should say: "This was spoken by the Buddha;
the elders and senior monks of that Saṃgha have also carefully received the Buddha’s words. One should ensure they do not forget them. This is the second detailed explanation.
Third, if someone says they heard it from many bhikṣus who know the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātikā, one should likewise respond as above. Fourth, [if they say they heard it from]...
If one says that [the Dharma] was heard from a single bhikṣu who knows the Vinaya-mātṛkā, it should also be understood in this way.

The *Mūla-vinaya* states: "In the place of the Elder, a lion-throne should be placed. If it is a fixed location, a brick path should be made; if the location is not fixed, a wooden ladder should be provided.
A spittoon should be installed for the Dharma Master to discard his spittle. [Failure to do so] incurs the fault of being stingy with the Dharma, which brings about five [retributions].
There are five faults: first, one will be born blind; second, one will lack wisdom; third, one will be far removed from the Buddha-dharma; fourth, there will be enemies within one's home;
and fifth, one will not enter the ranks of the noble ones, falling into hell at the end of life. The *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* states:
"Beneath the lion throne, one should provide a footstool, or support the feet with stones. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "There are five types of persons for whom one should not preach the Dharma."
Regarding the Vinaya Piṭaka: it refers to those who, being ignorant by nature, persistently pose heterodox questions;
or ask without seeking to resolve doubts; or ask for the sake of mockery; or ask to harass others; or ask to seek out faults.

One should proclaim the noble words [of the Dharma] and must not seek profit as a means of livelihood. If one speaks what is not the Dharma, the Elder should restrain them. Furthermore, one should preach the Dharma.
A person should not take on many disciples as attendants. There is no offense for those who follow him of their own accord.
If a Dharma teacher preaches to others without being invited to do so, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*vayatikrama*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"When listening to the Dharma, if a senior elder (*sthavira*) arrives, one should not have a junior monk (*navaka*) rise. If two teachers arrive, one should rise of one's own accord out of respect."
One must not cause others to arise [in anger]. There are five types of persons for whom one should not preach the Vinaya: those who ask with a testing intent; those who ask without doubt;
those who do not ask out of remorse for an offense committed; those who ask with a view to refutation; and those who ask without accepting the words [of the teaching].

On the six monthly days of the *poṣadha*, healthy bhikṣus should assemble together in one place to expound the Dharma. If a non-Buddhist master of debate should come there harboring a mind of envy, [one should respond appropriately].
If you wish to refute those who preach the Dharma, you should do so by challenging them with reasoned inquiry and subduing them through the Dharma; do not resort to anger or harsh speech.
The one preaching the Dharma should teach with a single-minded focus, giving rise to a mind of compassion and the intent to benefit others. Their speech should be pure, clear, and adorned;

it should proceed in orderly succession with inexhaustible eloquence, in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. One should speak for the sake of the Dharma, and not for the sake of profit.
Regarding the *Vinaya-vastu*: "When preaching the Dharma or listening to the Dharma, if a senior monk (*upādhyāya*) arrives, one should not rise;
nor should the senior monk compel a junior monk to rise. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "On the eighth and fourteenth days of the month, the Dharma is preached."
On the fifteenth day, during the *poṣadha*, one should not preach the Dharma using a melodic or chanting voice.
If laypeople scatter flowers and they fall upon the head or the robes of a *bhikṣu*, he should brush them away. If they fall upon a high seat, there is no fault.
The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states: "A *bhikṣu* preaching the Dharma should deliberate upon the assembly and determine what teaching should be given so that it may be understood and accepted. If...
If one should hear profound teachings, one must explain the profound; if one should hear shallow teachings, one must explain the shallow.
To fail to benefit the person before one is called "evil exposition. Furthermore, one should eliminate greed, non-attachment, non-malice, and non-delusion.
One should not harbor a mind of self-deprecation, nor a mind that disparages the great assembly.

One should establish such minds as a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of sympathetic joy, a mind of altruism, a mind of endurance, an unshakable mind, and a mind free from delusion; with these established, one should preach the Dharma.

Furthermore, one should not preach the Dharma due to other incidental conditions, but should preach it intentionally, for the Dharma is weighty and difficult to hear; this Dharma is a treasure and a medicine, capable of bringing benefit.
It benefits others. For this reason, it is said that even a single four-line verse, if it can cause another to understand it as it truly is, will bring benefit and peace for a long night.
Thus, I shall cite essential words and sublime phrases from the sūtras to directly reveal their meaning.

The *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya-mūla* states: "There are five kinds of benefits for one who is learned (*bahuśruta*): first, skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kuśala*); second, skillfulness regarding the sense bases (*āyatana-kuśala*);

third, skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu-kuśala*); fourth, skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kuśala*); and fifth, [skillfulness] regarding the instructions and admonitions required for that purpose."
Regarding the instruction: one should not seek [this] from others. The *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states that two instances permit the use of a melodic chant (*gāndhārī*):
first, praising the virtues of the Great Master; second, reciting the *Triśaraṇa-gamana-sūtra*. Those who do not understand melodic chanting should practice it in a secluded place.
One should not recite the sūtras or the Dharma by singing or drawing out the voice. At night, one may recite the sūtras with a lamp lit. During the summer months, [this prevents] damage...
One should construct a lamp-stand. Only those who possess clear wisdom, extensive learning, and a powerful memory, and who are capable of refuting non-Buddhists, may study external texts.
During the first part of the day and after midday, one may read Buddhist scriptures; when evening arrives, one should open the external treatises.
The same applies during the three watches of the night. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "One should not intermingle the speech of non-Buddhists [with Buddhist teachings]."
[They] intermingle the Buddhist sūtras [with secular works], allowing them to be understood according to the local vernaculars and dialects, and thus recite and study the Buddhist sūtras.
Question: Furthermore, if one introduces the classics of Laozi, Zhuangzi, and Confucius into the sūtras and śāstras to explain their meanings and principles, is this considered a transgression?
Answer: Their eyes of the Teaching have not yet opened; they merely wish to embellish the phrasing and extensively cite texts [from secular sources].
[End of] discourse. This is called "intermingling. If one attains the Dharma-seal of the true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), one can both discern and encompass:

discerning with clear boundaries and distinctions, neither being overly rigid nor being indiscriminate; and encompassing such that even coarse words and subtle speech are all the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).

Furthermore, whether by drawing from collateral sources or using indirect analogies to cause others to attain understanding, it all accords with the four *saṃgraha-vastus* (four means of integration) and contains no contradiction or obstruction.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: If a junior monk wishes to teach the Dharma to a senior monk, he should sit on a higher seat out of respect for the Dharma.
If a senior monk wishes to receive the Dharma from a junior monk, he should sit on a lower seat out of respect for the Dharma.

Furthermore, it is permitted for a junior monk to teach the Dharma to a senior monk while sitting on a seat of equal height, out of deference to the senior monk. There are five benefits to chanting (*bhāṣya*).
The body does not grow weary; one does not forget what has been memorized; the mind is not exhausted; the voice does not falter; and speech is easy to understand.
Furthermore, when the devas hear the chanting, their hearts are filled with joy. To recite Buddhist sūtras using the phonetics of non-Buddhist texts constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If a bhikṣu has no place to receive instruction for recitation, he may even learn it from a śrāmaṇera..."
The Māṇavas receive the Dharma simply by seeking an auspicious time and having a person of great virtue as a companion and witness;

they may also receive the Dharma from a layperson, provided they do not address them as *ācārya*. In this manner, the Dharma may be received through successive transmission, provided one takes care to ensure that one’s dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) is not lost.
Question: It is traditionally said that for a layperson (*avadātavasana*) to preach the Dharma while a bhikṣu listens is a sign of the decline of the Buddha-dharma.

How can it be permitted to receive the Dharma from a layperson? Answer: Whenever the householder Anāthapiṇḍada would teach the sūtras to newly ordained bhikṣus in the Jetavana, he would invariably first prostrate at their feet before preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, the layman Vimalakīrti occasionally [preached] by refuting the partial and disparaging [the narrow].
This is trivial. It would cause all the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas to lose their proper decorum; yet they never dared to presume the status of teacher for themselves.
These were all the fragrant precedents of the Buddha’s lifetime—how could they be called signs of decline?

If one were to call a layperson (śrāvaka) a "teacher" and a bhikṣu, in turn, perform acts of reverence toward him, or if one were to receive instruction from such a person in non-Buddhist studies, these would all constitute violations of the Dharma.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The study of writing is permitted, but it is not permitted to do so out of a desire for excellence to the point of neglecting one's religious duties.

However, for the purpose of subduing non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the reading of non-Buddhist texts is permitted, provided that one does not develop views based on those texts. It is permitted to recite the sūtras according to the local dialects of the country, but one must not deviate from or lose the intent of the Buddha.
It is not permitted to render the Buddha’s words into the language of non-Buddhist texts; one who violates this incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense. The *Vinayaviniscaya-saṃgraha* states:
The Dharma may be received during all four modes of deportment. One who receives the Dharma should maintain three modes of deportment;

out of reverence for the Dharma, one should not receive it while lying down. According to the rule for disciples, whether old or young, upon arriving before the teacher, they should join their palms and bow low.

When he asks after your well-being regarding the four great elements, you should give rise to reverence and respect. With a straightforward mind free from guile, request the resolution of your doubts.
Receive the teaching with single-minded attention so as not to forget it. If you have no further questions, receive the Dharma as usual, prostrate at the teacher’s feet, and withdraw.

The teacher, in turn, should respect the student; without treating them with contempt, he should teach with an open mind, without stinginess regarding the Dharma, and should skillfully guide and respond.
Possessing patience and compassion, one should ensure that those who receive the teachings do not experience weariness or distress. One should constantly attend to them and instruct them frequently.
Those who are dull-witted by nature should also be taught with particular care. If one imparts the Dharma using the melodic intonation of chanting, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

One should not praise the recitation of non-Buddhist scriptures; however, if it is for the purpose of subduing followers of other paths and one knows oneself to be capable, one may do so three times each day.

When the time is divided into two parts for excellence, one should study the Buddha-dharma during the first and middle watches of the day; when it is divided into one part for inferiority, one should practice external texts toward evening.
One should not calculate months and years to establish these three divisions.
The third section of the *Zuochanfa* (Method of Seated Meditation) states: "If a bhikṣu falls asleep, his fellow practitioners should wake him. They should use a meditation staff (*dhyāna-yaṣṭi*).
If he continues to sleep, they should rub his eyes, wash his face with water, pinch his ears or nose, or rub his forehead."

Having put on his robes, he rubbed his body with his hands. If he arose and went outside to look toward the four directions or gaze up at the stars, or reached a place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) to practice *caṅkrama*, he restrained his sense faculties so that his mind would not become distracted. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
When taking up the meditation staff (*dhyāna-daṇḍa*), one should generate a mind of reverence. One who is sleeping is not to be trusted; one who is striking [with the staff] may be trusted.

There are five conditions for using the meditation staff to strike another: first, out of compassion; second, without causing him distress; third, when he is asleep; fourth, when his head is leaning against a wall;

and fifth, when his legs are stretched out. It is permitted to use a meditation weight (*dhyāna-pīṭhaka*); one should make a hole in it, pass a cord through the hole, and attach a knot at the end of the cord.
The cord is hung over the ear. When it is four finger-widths from the forehead, one places the meditation weight (*dhyāna-śilā*). If the meditation weight falls once, one stretches out the legs once;
if it falls twice, one stretches them out twice; if it falls three times, one should rise and walk. Regarding the two periods for listening to the Dharma: the night period and the day period.
Regarding the seven-day period and the period of constant sitting meditation, the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "During the time of sitting meditation, one should not calculate the duration."
They should be driven away. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: There was a king in the north who sent two boys to King Prasenajit;
one was named Taṃsuka and the other was named Palaka. One held the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), and the other held false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).
This was known far and wide. Later, through the skillful means of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, they were taken under his care and made to sweep the grounds of the monastery at night.
Having witnessed the miraculous transformations of an Arhat and seeing the various devas listening to the Dharma, he conceived a mind of right view.

He went to the Buddha to hear the Dharma, left the household life, and realized the fruit [of Arhatship]. King Prasenajit felt disdain and shame; the Buddha then ordered him to serve water while the bhikṣus were eating at the house of the elder, so as to manifest his superior virtue.
The king then sighed in admiration and submission. When the bhikṣu asked about the causes from his past lives, the Buddha said: "In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were two men..."
Taking ordination as his companion, he traveled to a borderland country. Without a teacher to instruct him, he practiced meditative concentration on his own;

yet, though he had actually realized nothing, he developed a mind of self-conceit, believing he had attained realization. At the time of his death, he slandered the True Dharma and gave rise to wrong views, saying:
"The Buddha Kāśyapa deceived the world; he claimed to have severed all afflictions and attained arhatship, yet I am unable to sever even a single affliction."

[They were] all [exhausted]. How could there be any other person who attained arhatship? Because they slandered the noble Dharma and gave rise to wrong views, they fell into the evil destinies for a long time.
Furthermore, throughout many lifetimes, they constantly dwelt in the borderlands, giving rise to minds of wrong view.

However, because they had studied, recited, and upheld the principles of the aggregates, bases, elements, and dependent origination, as well as being thoroughly skilled in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), by virtue of this—
By the power of karma, one may leave the household life within my Dharma and attain the Way, practicing concentration without a teacher; such is the fault.
Therefore, one should not practice concentration on one's own initiative without a teacher. The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"If one can properly maintain *śamatha*, then for twenty years, thirty years, or even eighty or a hundred years, afflictions will not arise. This is so.

This gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*). [Note: *Śamatha* is translated here as "cessation. If it is *tattva-śamatha* or similar forms, these are concentrations (*samādhi*) accompanied by wisdom (*prajñā*), and thus the fault of overweening pride does not arise.

If one practices only mundane concentration (*vastu-samādhi*), which merely stills coarse and floating discursive thoughts—even if one successively suppresses and eliminates lower defilements until reaching the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and identifies this as *nirvāṇa*, it remains nothing but overweening pride.]

Regarding the miscellaneous rules, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: The six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) are: first, the recollection of knowing the number of days and months; second, the recollection of knowing the place where one eats;

third, the recollection of knowing the time of receiving the precepts and the number of summer retreats (*varṣā*) passed; fourth, the recollection of the robes and the alms bowl, including their acceptance, maintenance, and those to whom they have been purified and given away (*viśuddhi-dāna*); fifth, the recollection of food.
Common and distinct [categories]. Regarding the six recollections, the body may be strong or weak. The *Caturthabhāga* states that there are five faults in not chewing a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*):

first, the breath is foul; second, one cannot distinguish flavors; third, internal heat increases; fourth, it does not stimulate the appetite; and fifth, the eyesight becomes dim. The five benefits of chewing a tooth-stick are the opposite of these and should be understood accordingly.
As for the tooth-stick, the maximum length is one span (*vitasti*), and the minimum is four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). It should not [exceed these limits].
Regarding those who chew [tooth-sticks]: one should not chew the bark alone; rather, one should chew them in a secluded place. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If tooth-sticks are difficult to obtain, one should cut off the portion used for chewing and discard it. After washing it, the remainder may be used again the following day. As for the length of the tooth-stick:
the maximum is sixteen finger-widths (*aṅgula*), and the minimum is four finger-widths or more. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas) says:

In the morning, one should chew a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) and rinse the mouth thoroughly before performing acts of reverence. To fail to chew a tooth-stick, to relieve oneself without washing, or to eat with impure hands—these are considered contemptible.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that one should sweep the ground with the wind; there are five ways of sweeping the ground that do not yield great merit:
if one does not know how to sweep against the wind, how to sweep with the wind, or if one sweeps without eradicating the tracks [of dust].
Having removed the filth, one should no longer sweep with a broom over the original spot. There are five dharmas by which one attains great merit; the opposite of these may be understood accordingly.
If the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) is downwind, one should say to him: "Please move aside slightly; I wish to sweep the ground. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:
Every morning, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada would sweep the grounds of the monastery. On one occasion, due to other business, he was unable to enter the monastery.
Seeing that the ground was not clean, the World-Honored One took up a broom himself and wished to sweep it.

At that time, Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas all joined him in sweeping, after which they entered the dining hall and sat down. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "There are five benefits to sweeping the ground. First, one's own mind..."
1. One’s own mind becomes pure; 2. one causes the minds of others to become pure; 3. the devas rejoice; 4. one plants the karma for physical beauty; 5.
at the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens. Later, when Anāthapiṇḍada entered the grove, he heard that the Buddha and his great disciples had personally swept the forest.
Fearing to tread upon it with his feet, he was ashamed and hesitant to proceed. The Buddha instructed him to recite the Dharma as he walked forward, out of respect for the Buddha.
Because they revere the Dharma, all Arhats hold the Dharma in high esteem. The fourth *fen* (division) states: "There are five benefits to walking meditation (*caṅkrama*):
one is capable of traveling long distances, able to engage in reflection, has little illness, digests food and drink well, and attains long-lasting stability in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

One should not sleep during the day. However, if one is elderly, ill, or has traveled a great distance, it is permitted to enter a room, close the door, and sleep. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Upon arriving..."

Before entering the latrine, one should cough or snap one's fingers to inform those within—whether human or non-human—who are there. Those inside the latrine should likewise snap their fingers or cough.
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "If one has not washed and purified oneself, one should not circumambulate a stupa, practice walking meditation, or pay homage to the Buddha."

When reading scriptures, performing prostrations to others, receiving prostrations from others, eating, entering the assembly, or sitting upon a monastic bed or seat, because the body is impure and not in accordance with the Dharma, the devas are displeased;
consequently, all the dhāraṇī mantras one maintains will lack efficacy. This applies even when performing vegetarian offerings or copying sutras.
If one creates an image [without proper ritual], the merit obtained will be meager. The *Ekottara-karman* states:
When it is time for defecation, one should take a water flask toward the latrine, set aside one's robes to one side, and carry fifteen lumps of earth.

These should be placed outside the latrine (each lump being about the size of half a peach, placed upon a mound or a wooden board near a flowing stream; the vessel containing the ash and earth should be one cubit long and one span wide). Furthermore, one should carry three additional lumps of earth, along with a cloth for wiping the body.
Holding the water flask, one enters the latrine and bolts the door crosswise. Having finished the evacuation, one cleanses with a wooden stick (*śalākā*) and wipes it clean.

Next, taking three lumps of earth, one washes [the organ] three times with the left hand. Then, tucking the flask under the left armpit, one pushes the bolt aside with the right hand and returns to the washing area carrying the flask in the right hand.
Squatting down, the flask is placed on the left thigh and pressed there with the elbow. One then takes...
Take seven portions of earth. Wash the left hand with each portion individually; wash both hands together with the remaining seven portions.
Use the final portion to wash the water vessel (*kuṇḍikā*), and then rinse the feet. Take the robe and depart. Once arrived in the dwelling, rinse the mouth with pure water.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one has hemorrhoids in the lower part of the body and cannot wash, one should wipe with a soft material. If...
One should not chew a tooth-stick on a latrine; nor should one do so while covering the head, or while covering the right shoulder. One should instead bare the right shoulder.
The *Sūtra of Good Observance* states: When approaching death or when falling asleep, one should first recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the precepts, and the devas.
Reflecting on impermanence. Regarding each of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), one asks:

Having thoroughly examined the *Vinaya-saṃgraha-yukti*, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka*, and even the *Mahāsāṃghika*, *Mūlasarvāstivāda*, *Pañcavargika*, *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā*, *Samantapāsādikā*, *Vinayamātṛkā*, and so forth, I have only seen the extensive elucidation of the rules of discipline (*śīla-dharma*); I do not see that there exists anything separate [from these].
Verses and Dhāraṇīs. In the present age, those who study the Vinaya take verses and dhāraṇīs as their primary concern. What is the meaning of this? Answer:
The Dharma-gates are immeasurable, and although each possesses its own great merit, those of initial capacity turning toward the Path must enter deeply through a single gate.

Since one has already joined the ranks of the bhikṣus, one should know that the study of the Vinaya comes first. Furthermore, when seeking to clarify the fundamental principles of the Vinaya, there are only two [approaches].
The matter is most urgent. First, one must thoroughly recite the precepts and fully comprehend what constitutes observance, violation, allowance, and prohibition.

Second, one must maintain dignified deportment and single-mindedly cultivate the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness. This requires that, throughout the two periods of six hours each day, one always remains with a unified mind, maintaining mindfulness without confusion;
only then can one integrate all elements into a single whole, sever delusions, and realize the truth. If one's efforts are scattered across many different threads, then...
In the end, it will be difficult to enter the Way. The present *Pranidhāna-gāthā* originally derives from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

As for the various *mantras*, they all belong to the Vajra Family (*Vajrakula*). Although the Dharma gates are inconceivable, in terms of cultivation and realization, each has its own fundamental school.

If one practices single-mindedly and without interruption according to one's own school, then *samādhi* will be easily accomplished. To gather many flowers without a thread to bind them together is of no avail.
If it is blown upon by the wind, it will surely scatter; if it is gathered in, it is entirely complete. Whether it be a single verse, or even a single word, all constitute seeds of the Way.

To discriminate among them is to render them entirely non-existent. Whether in accordance with the Vinaya or not, whether manifest or hidden, whether "honey-like" (mystical) or not, they merely become scattered merits.
This is why the True Dharma gradually declines and why the final age cannot be revitalized. There is...
For those of resolute character, it is better to specialize in the precepts and fulfill the fundamental duties of a bhikṣu.
Those of sharp faculties can indeed attain the ultimate realization through the precepts alone, fully encompassing the divine efficacy of both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings.

Even those of duller faculties can take the precepts as a staircase to gradually ascend to the inner sanctum of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings. In this way, one’s learning will have a true source and will not be subject to [the faults of] superficiality.
This is merely the lamentation of one who lost his sheep on a forked path.

Part Three. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Follow your own mental inclinations and maintain your dignified deportment; this is my instruction. What does it mean to follow one's own mental inclinations?
It means observing the body internally—this is the application of mindfulness to the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna)—and applying oneself with diligence to maintain it so that mindfulness is not scattered.

He brings order to, and subdues, the greed, envy, and worldly afflictions of the world. He contemplates the body externally, the body internally, and both internally and externally; he does the same for sensations (*vedanā*), the mind (*citta*, i.e., *manas*), and phenomena (*dharma*).
In this way, the bhikṣu attains right mindfulness and right awareness. How does he maintain his deportment? Whether going out or coming in...

Whether bending or stretching, looking down or up, holding the robes and bowl, drinking, eating, taking medicine, voiding or discharging excrement, sleeping or waking, coming or going, sitting or standing, speaking or remaining silent—one should always maintain this single-mindedness. This is called a bhikṣu’s mastery of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).

(During the two periods of six hours [day and night], within the four modes of deportment, one practices the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness with a single mind; this is the fundamental principle of the study of the Vinaya.)
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: There are five benefits of leaving the household life. First, one gains benefit for oneself alone, which is not shared with others.
Second, while previously knowing oneself to be a lowly person driven by others, after having left the household life, one receives the respect, praise, and prostrations of others.
Third, one shall attain the peace and security of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. Fourth, at the end of one's life, one shall be reborn in...
In the heavens. Fifth, one is constantly praised by all Buddhas, the assemblies of śrāvakas, and all superior human beings.
*The Sūtra on the Lightness and Heaviness of the Offenses of Violating the Precepts*, translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha. At that time, the Venerable...
At the hour of *prahāṇa*, Mahāmaudgalyāyana arose from his meditative concentration and went to where the Buddha was.

He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, there is a doubt in my mind that I now wish to inquire about."
"I only pray that you will grant me permission. The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana, "Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you.

Maudgalyāyana then addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī lacks a sense of shame and dread of blame, and treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, they may commit offenses such as those of the *śaikṣa* rules, or likewise offenses of *prādeśanika*, *pāyattika*, *sthūlātyaya*, or *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
“Śiṣya, one who commits a pārājika offense incurs how many unwholesome transgressions? I pray that you will explain this.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana, “Listen attentively, listen attentively! I shall now explain it for you.

If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, being shameless and devoid of remorse, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt and violates the śaikṣa precepts, they will fall into hell for a lifespan equal to five hundred years of the Cāturmahārājika devas. Compared to human reckoning...”
The interval is nine hundred thousand years (it should be stated as nine million years; perhaps ten characters are missing above the "thousand").

Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, if one lacks shame and remorse, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and commits a *pātideśanīya* offense, it is equivalent to the lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which is one thousand years.
He falls into hell. By human reckoning, this is three hundred and sixty million years (*tri-koṭi-ṣaṣṭi-lakṣa-varṣa*).

Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, if one is shameless and lacks a sense of propriety, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and commits a *pāyattika* offense, he will fall into hell for a lifespan of two thousand years as measured by the Yāma devas.
By human reckoning, this is fourteen hundred and forty million years (*caturdaśa-koṭi-catvāriṃśat-lakṣa-varṣa*). (One should say [the latter] as stated.)
(144 million years). Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, if one lacks shame and remorse, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and commits a sthūlātyaya offense.

Just as a lifespan in Tuṣita Heaven is four thousand years, when one falls into hell, by human reckoning it is fifty billion and sixty thousand years (it should be stated as five hundred and seventy-six million years).
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, if one lacks shame and remorse and treats the Buddha’s words with contempt...

One commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. For example, if one were to fall into hell with a lifespan of eight thousand years as a Paranirmitavaśavartin (i.e., Nirmāṇarati) deva, it would equal two hundred thirty-four billion four hundred million years by human reckoning (which should be stated as three hundred twenty-three million four hundred thousand years).

Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana, if one lacks shame and remorse, treats the Buddha’s words with contempt, and commits a *pārājika* offense, they will fall into hell for a duration equal to sixteen thousand years as measured by the lifespan of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods.

By human reckoning, this amounts to nine hundred twenty-one billion and sixty thousand years (*it should be stated as nine million two hundred ten thousand six hundred million years*). When the Venerable Maudgalyāyana heard what the Buddha had said, he rejoiced.
"Rejoicing, they practiced accordingly.

[The interlocutor] asked: "If this question is authentic, how can the remaining five hundred questions be considered spurious? [The Master] replied: "It is by relying on the authentic that the spurious may be attached to it.
Therefore, last year we drew lots to reach a decision, and the lot drawn was one containing both the authentic and the spurious."
○ Regarding the Verse Summary of the Precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa-saṃgraha-gāthā*):
According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, at the time of the council (*saṃgīti*), the verse summary was recited first, followed by the main body of the Vinaya text.

Within the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, there are likewise verse summaries; this is likely for the sake of facilitating memorization for beginners. Now, as for the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*... [text continues]
This verse does not exist [in the original]. Even if one were to draw it from another school by way of analogy, the sequence would not correspond.

Yet, if one were to retain the old version as it is, there is concern that beginners might find it difficult to memorize. Therefore, I have ventured to provide an example in verse form, so that beginners may first recite this.
Thus, the essential framework of the precepts of the Five Categories has been summarized. Written with reverence by the Śramaṇa Zhixu: sexual misconduct; stealing five coins or more;

intentionally taking the life of a human being; speaking false testimony out of ignorance; and [the prohibition against] false claims of spiritual attainment, excluding those who suffer from overweening pride (adhimāna).
These are the four *pārājika* offenses; one who commits them cannot be saved.

They are: intentional emission of semen, physical contact with a woman, lewd speech, solicitation for sexual intercourse, acting as a matchmaker, a dwelling exceeding the prescribed size, and a large dwelling without authorization.
Groundless defamation based on a fragment; causing a schism in the Saṃgha and its faction; being expelled yet resenting the Saṃgha; having a wicked nature and refusing to accept admonition.

For the first nine of these, the offense is incurred immediately; for the latter four, it occurs after three admonitions. These are the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, which require confession before a community of twenty monks.
There are two indeterminate rules (*aniyata-dharma*). There are thirty rules involving forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*):
[the rules concerning] extra robes, staying apart from one’s robes overnight, keeping [an extra robe] for more than one month, and receiving [robes] from a nun who is not a relative.

As well as having [a robe] washed, dyed, or beaten; begging from one who is not a relative; accepting an invitation to a meal beyond the limit; requesting a higher price for [materials] to have them made together;
and asking for a robe more than six times—these are the first ten rules. Making bedding out of silk-cotton; using dull black [wool] that is not mixed with other colors.
Not keeping [the bowl] for less than six years; not patching the sitting mat; carrying wool on a long journey; having it washed, dyed, or carded by a layperson;
accepting gold and silver; buying and selling; trading as twenty items; seeking a better long bowl; having a robe woven by one who is not a relative.

Consenting to seek fine cloth directly; giving a robe and later becoming angry and seizing it back; medicinal remnants kept beyond seven days; requesting the use of rain-cloths before the designated time;

keeping emergency gift-clothes (*ātyayika-cīvara*) beyond the permitted period; being separated from one’s robes for more than six nights during the month; and diverting property belonging to the Saṃgha into one’s own possession—these constitute the thirty rules.
Relinquishing an object to the Saṃgha; the confession for a *pāyattika* offense.
The ninety *pātayantika* rules: false speech, disparaging speech, divisive speech, staying in the same room with a woman, and staying three nights with one who has not received the precepts.
Reciting together [the precepts], confessing the aforementioned offenses, and proclaiming superhuman attainments; preaching the Dharma to women, digging the earth—these are the first ten.
Destroying the villages of spirits, causing distress, reviling, and spreading out monastic bedding in the open, as well as failing to put it away within the room.
20. Forcibly seizing a place for lodging; dragging another out of a monastic cell; sitting on a bed with detachable legs on a loft; pouring water with insects onto mud or grass;
covering a room [with thatch] beyond three sections. 21. Going oneself to instruct nuns; being appointed by the Saṃgha to teach until sunset.
Slandering those who instruct nuns; giving robes to one who is not a relative; making robes; sitting in a secluded place; making appointments; traveling together; riding in a boat;
obtaining food through the praise of a nun; traveling with a woman; the thirty [offenses]; receiving more than one meal's offering; passing it on; and eating in a separate group.

Receiving invitations for more than three bowls; failing to perform the *kṛta-śeṣa* rite (the ritual of leaving food remaining); thereby causing others to commit an offense; giving food at an improper time or that which has been stored overnight;
soliciting fine food without it being offered; the fortieth rule is concluded. Eating with non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*); visiting other households without informing [one's preceptor].
To sit forcibly in a family’s dining room; to sit in a secluded place; to be alone with a woman in an open space; to cause others to be unable to eat;

to accept an invitation for food and medicine beyond the permitted limit; to observe an army for more than three nights; and while staying there, to observe military affairs—this is called the fiftieth [offense].
Drinking alcohol; playing in water; tickling while refusing admonition; bathing after frightening others; lighting a fire on open ground;
playing by hiding another’s clothing; wearing clothes without asking the owner; and not discoloring new robes. This concludes the sixty rules.
1. Intentionally killing the life of an animal; 2. Drinking water containing living organisms; 3. Annoying others or concealing their offenses; 4. Bestowing the precepts improperly; 5.

Initiating a dispute that has already been settled; 6. Traveling together with a group of thieves; 7. Not relinquishing an evil view despite being admonished; 8. Providing support to those who share in the same [evil] activities.
Keeping a *śrāmaṇera* who has been expelled; the seventy *pāyattika* rules. Refusing counsel and lightly reviling the precepts;

being ignorant and violating the *karmavācanā*; not giving consent and later regretting it; eavesdropping in private and striking out of anger; physical assault, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and slander—the eighty *pāyattika* rules.
Entering a royal palace to seize treasures; entering a village at an improper time; high beds stuffed with cotton; needles made of bone, ivory, or horn;
sitting mats, patches for sores, and rain-bathing robes exceeding the prescribed size, or equaling the size of the Buddha’s robe—these ninety *pāyattika* rules are concluded.
Purification through confession according to the Dharma; not confessing a downfall leads to doubt;

accepting food from a nun who is not a relative; failing to stop a nun from soliciting on one's behalf; and accepting food from a family under suspicion—these four are the rules for expiation (*pratideśanīya*).
The various rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*) to be practiced: first, the manner of entering the homes of laypeople while wearing robes; receiving food; the methods for defecating and urinating;
preaching the Dharma; showing reverence to stupas; walking hand-in-hand; climbing trees; and carrying a staff with a sling—these are the rules one should train in.

The presence before one's eyes, recollection, being undeluded, and speaking for oneself; the search for the offense, the majority decision, and the "covering over with grass"—these seven methods for settling disputes are the categories of offenses that a bhikṣu should know.
As it is said, those who practice in this manner are praised by all the Buddhas.
*Chóngzhì píní shìyì jíyào*, Scroll Fifteen: Phonetic Explanations. *Bèi*:
pronounced *bài*.
Also called *bainì* or *fànbèi*; this translates as "praise" (*zàn tàn*).

Skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*) consists of cultivating the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness based upon the five aggregates, fully possessing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and even entering the three gates of liberation.

Skillfulness regarding the bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*) consists of thoroughly knowing the six sense faculties and the six sense objects; that is, understanding how all phenomena are subsumed within the twelve internal and external bases.
Furthermore, one understands impermanence, selflessness, and so forth.

Through skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*), one thoroughly knows the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*). While there are differences in how they are categorized—whether as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), or the eighteen elements—the principle of impermanence and selflessness is non-dual.
Moreover, one knows the six elements within the body, namely: earth, water, fire, [wind, space, and consciousness].
Wind, space, and consciousness are likewise both impermanent and without self.
Being skillful in dependent origination, he thoroughly understands the dharma of the forward and reverse progression of the twelve links of dependent origination.

Skillful in the possible and the impossible, he knows that it is possible for one who performs good to ascend, and impossible for one who performs evil to ascend. It is possible for one who performs evil to descend, and impossible for one who performs good to descend.
It is possible that one who commits evil will fall downward; it is possible that one who commits evil will ascend upward—this is impossible.
One should thoroughly understand these laws of correct cause and effect.
Yāma is translated here as "Time" (kāla) and also as "Sublime Virtue" (sukha).
Tuṣita is translated as "Sublime Fulfillment" (sukhapratiṣṭhita) and also as "Contentment" (saṃtuṣṭi).

Those precepts held in common with the bhikṣus are also as previously explained; only regarding the precepts not held in common, they follow...
This compilation of texts is intended to be concise; no further detailed explanations will be provided.
The Eight *Pārājika* Dharmas: 1. The precept against sexual misconduct. 2. The precept against stealing. 3. The precept against killing. 4.
The precept against great falsehoods. These are identical to those for *bhikṣus*. 5. The precept against physical contact with a male body.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, makes physical contact with a man who has a defiled mind—
from below the armpits to above the knees— whether by grasping, rubbing, pulling, pushing, stroking upward, stroking downward, lifting up, lowering down, clutching, or pressing,
this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion. This is the offense of bodily contact.
Furthermore,
the householder Mṛgāra and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā were mutually infatuated with one another. On another occasion,
when the householder invited the bhikṣuṇīs for a meal, Thullanandā, knowing that he had invited the Saṃgha for her own sake, remained at the monastery.
She did not go. The householder surveyed the assembly of nuns and asked, "Where is Thullanandā?
Why has she not come? They replied, "She is in the monastery; she has not come. The householder finished his meal quickly and went immediately to the monastery.
Seeing the householder approaching from afar, Thullanandā lay down upon her bed. The householder asked, "What ailment do you suffer from? She replied:
There was no suffering or distress. That which I desired, he did not desire; yet he said, "I desire it;

it is not that I do not desire it," and immediately came forward to embrace and lie with her, rubbing his mouth against hers and kissing her. A novice nun guarding the dwelling saw this and told the other nuns.

The nuns expressed their disapproval and reprimanded him, then informed the bhikṣus, who in turn informed the World-Honored One. The Sangha was assembled, and after rebuking him, the precept was established.
A man; with the perception of a man; she rubs her body (against his) and makes physical contact, experiencing the pleasure of touch:
*pārājika*. If there is doubt regarding a man: *sthūlātyaya*. This applies likewise even to grasping or pressing. If she touches a man’s garment or ornaments with her body...
If a man, with a mind of lustful attachment, touches a nun’s body with his own clothing, ornaments, or accessories, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If he, with a mind of lustful attachment, touches her clothing, ornaments, or accessories with his own body, clothing, ornaments, or accessories, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If he, with a mind of lustful attachment, engages in physical contact but does not experience the pleasure of the touch, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. This applies equally even to grasping or pressing. If...
If a male deva, a male asura, or even a male animal capable of transforming its form touches the body [of a bhikṣu], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If they are incapable of transforming their form, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If a woman touches the body, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*) touches the body, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If, with a lustful mind, one touches robes, bowls, and so forth, or even touches one's own body, in all such cases [it is likewise].
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense if, when taking or giving, one touches it by mistake; or if one touches it while rescuing or releasing something;
or if there is no intention at all; or if it was before the precept was first established; or if one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
○ The sixth: the precept against the eight matters.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, knowing that a man has a defiled mind, consents to him taking her hand, taking hold of her robe, entering a secluded place, standing together, speaking together, walking together, or leaning their bodies against one another, or making a mutual appointment—this bhikṣuṇī commits a *pārājika* offense.
One may not dwell together with those who are *mleccha*.

Because of committing these eight offenses, and because they also arise from the person before one, it is thus prescribed: from grasping the hand up to physical contact, each constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
committing the eighth offense constitutes a *pārājika*. This applies to sons of devas, sons of nāgas, and even animals capable of transforming their shapes.
In these cases, one commits seven offenses, each being a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). Upon committing the eighth offense, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If the animal is unable to transform its form, or if the woman has a defiled mind, committing the eighth offense constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases:
If there is taking or giving, and the hands touch; or if there is rescuing or releasing, and one grasps the robe;
or if there is giving, prostrating, confessing, receiving the Dharma, entering a secluded place to stand together, speak together, or walk together;
or if one is struck by someone; or if a thief comes, an elephant comes, a wild beast comes, or a thorn comes—one turns the body to avoid them.
If one happens to lean against another by mistake; or if someone comes to request instruction, to listen to the Dharma, or to accept an invitation; or if someone arrives at the monastery;
or if one meets with another at a place where it is improper to commit evil deeds.
○ The seventh precept concerning concealing another’s grave offense:
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a pārājika offense, yet she does not disclose it herself nor inform others.

If she does not inform the assembly, and at a later time that bhikṣuṇī should pass away, or be censured by the assembly, or cease her religious practice, or join the ranks of non-Buddhists, and subsequently says: "I previously knew that such and such an offense existed."
This bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion because she concealed a grave offense.

Sister Sthūlanandā’s younger sister, named Ciñcānandā, committed a pārājika offense. Fearing that her younger sister would incur an ill reputation, the elder sister remained silent and did not report it.
Later, when Ciñcā left the monastic order, the other nuns said to her, "We saw your younger sister..."
“Do you abandon the path? She replied, “I already knew that he had such-and-such matters. The nuns rebuked her, saying, “Why did you conceal another’s grave offense?
She informed the bhikṣus, who in turn informed the World-Honored One, who then established the precept:

if one knows [of the offense] before the meal and speaks of it after the meal, or even if one knows during the middle watch of the night and speaks of it during the last watch, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense); if one knows during the last watch and does not speak of it... [the offense is as follows].
If one speaks [of the offense] until the appearance of the dawn light, it is a *pārājika*. Excluding the eight *pārājikas*, if one conceals other offenses:
for concealing a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) committed by oneself, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; for concealing the offense of another person, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if one does not know, if there is no one toward whom one may speak, or if at the time of speaking there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*). (From the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*).

The Vinaya states: If the Saṃgha has performed an act of suspension against this nun—such as for "not seeing" [an offense]—and she is at that time insane, deranged, or her mind impaired by illness, she commits no offense if she does not disclose the other's transgression.

If the Saṃgha subsequently lifts the suspension, or if her pain ceases and she regains her original state of mind, and she then conceals the other's offense until the end of the night (meaning until the appearance of the dawn-light), it is a *pārājika*.
○ The eighth [offense] regarding the failure to relinquish [a position] after being formally charged and having been admonished three times:
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that a bhikṣu has been formally charged by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and as taught by the Buddha,

yet he does not comply and does not repent while the Saṃgha has not yet granted him restoration to communal residence, and she nevertheless complies [with his conduct], the other bhikṣuṇīs shall say to her:
"Sister, this bhikṣu has been formally accused by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions.
He does not comply and does not repent; the Saṃgha has not yet granted him restoration of communal residence. You must not comply with him.
When that bhikṣuṇī thus admonishes the other bhikṣuṇī, if she persists in her position and does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī should be admonished a second and a third time.
She is to be admonished three times so that she may relinquish this matter. If, after being admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī is defeated (pārājika) and shall not dwell in communion; she has committed an offense involving formal accusation.
The Venerable Chandi was censured by the Saṃgha, yet he attended upon the bhikṣuṇī Wei-ci, coming and going to serve her.

When the other bhikṣuṇīs admonished him, he replied, "This is my brother; if I do not provide for him now, when shall I ever have the chance? Despite this, he continued to comply with her and did not desist.
The bhikṣuṇīs, feeling resentment and reproaching him, informed the bhikṣus, who in turn reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha then ordered the community of bhikṣuṇīs to issue a formal reprimand.

The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) was established as this precept. There are two kinds of compliance: first, regarding the Dharma; second, regarding robes and food.
If [the offense] is committed after the third *karman* is concluded, it is a *pārājika*. If one abandons [the intention] after the second *karman* is concluded, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one abandons [the action] after the *karmavācanā* (formal act) is completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses. If one abandons it after the *jñapti* (motion) is completed, there is one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one instructs another, saying "Do not abandon it," there is a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If one does not reprove or admonish [the offender], there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There is no offense in cases such as an illegal *karmavācanā* performed by a separate assembly (*bhinnasaṃgha*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The bhikṣuṇīs should say to this expelled bhikṣu: 'You..."

One should humble oneself and submit to the great *saṃgha*. If one does not humble oneself and submit, the *bhikṣuṇī* *saṃgha* shall perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of "not prostrating," "not conversing," and "not making offerings.

If the *bhikṣuṇī* *saṃgha* has not yet performed the formal act of "not prostrating," then teaching the Dharma, receiving the Dharma, giving things, or receiving things—each such act constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. If the formal act has already been performed...
After the grinding, for each instance, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. The nuns should first admonish her with gentle words;

if she relinquishes [the offense], they should instruct her to perform many *duṣkṛta* and many *sthūlātyaya* confessions. If she does not relinquish it, they shall perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) against her.
○ Seventeen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas. In the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya there are nineteen; in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya there are twenty.
First, acting as a matchmaker; second, groundless defamation; third, defamation based on partial evidence—all are treated identically to those for bhikṣus.

If a bhikṣuṇī goes before an official and says that a layman, or a layman’s son, or a slave, or a hired laborer [was assaulted] by day or by night, for even the duration of a single thought-moment, or a finger-snap, or a brief interval, this bhikṣuṇī commits an offense of the first category, which is a saṃghāvaśeṣa requiring formal relinquishment.

(Regarding "offense of the first category": it is an offense committed upon the very first act. Regarding "requiring formal relinquishment": it is that which must be relinquished so as not to constitute a further offense.)
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a householder who built a vihāra and offered it to the bhikṣuṇīs. At another time, the bhikṣuṇīs abandoned the vihāra and departed.
When the householder passed away, his son began to plow the land of this vihāra.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to him, "This is the property of the Saṃgha; do not plow it. The householder’s son replied, "That is true. While my father was alive, he built this..."

He gave it to the bhikṣuṇīs. The bhikṣuṇīs abandoned it and departed. [The householder thought: "My father has passed away; I am now free. Why leave this place empty? Is it not useless for both sides?
The bhikṣuṇīs then went to the magistrate and reported the matter. The magistrate summoned the householder’s son and adjudicated according to the law.
He was fined, and his former wealth and goods were all confiscated by the state. When the Buddha heard of this, he established a precept. At that time...
The junior queen of King Prasenajit built a vihāra and offered it to the bhikṣuṇīs. After the bhikṣuṇīs had accepted it and were residing there, they later traveled abroad.
The king’s junior queen then transferred the gift to her daughter, a brahmin woman. When the bhikṣuṇīs returned to the vihāra, they told the brahmin woman to leave.
She replied, "This is truly your vihāra; the donor built it for you. You went away on your travels, so I have taken it."
"Give it to me; I cannot leave now. The nun became angry and dragged her out by force. She then went to the magistrate and spoke to him.
The magistrate summoned the nun, but she did not dare go. The Buddha said, "When summoned, you should go. The nun then went to the magistrate's office.
He replied, "All these grounds belong to the royal house; the affairs belong to the householder; the rooms belong to the donor;
and the same applies to the beds, seats, and bedding. To maintain and repair the rooms so that the Saṃgha may dwell therein brings great merit.
Why is this? Because by giving to me, they enable me to dwell in peace. The judge then gave the monastery to the female ascetic (brahmacāriṇī).
The Record. The Buddha told the bhikṣu: "This nun spoke improperly, and the official also adjudicated improperly. Why is this?

The former gift was lawful (because it accorded with her original intention); the latter gift was unlawful (because it contravened her original intention). Regarding 'litigation': going before an official to dispute right and wrong together.
Regarding 'a slave': one either purchased or born into the household. Regarding 'a hired laborer': one employed for work by means of wealth. [End of] the woman.
A "Brahmin" refers to one who has gone forth outside of this Dharma. If a judicial official records the matter in writing, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If he speaks of it verbally but does not record the name, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. For monks and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one is summoned;
or if one wishes to make a representation; or if one is taken away by force; or if one is...
[They] were bound and taken away. If there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), although one may speak [of it], one does not report it to the authorities.
The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya* states: "If a nun is insulted or oppressed by others, she should inform her parents. If she has no parents, she should inform her kinsmen.
If she has no kinsmen, she should inform the bhikṣus, and so on, up to the upāsikās. If the bhikṣus and..."

If a nun possesses power and influence, one must not fail to support her; [otherwise,] it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. When speaking, one should say, "She has slighted me," and one should speak for the purpose of admonishing her;
one should not speak otherwise.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing beforehand that a woman is a thief whose crime deserves death and who is known to the public,
ordains her as a nun and grants her the precepts without having questioned the king or his ministers, nor having inquired into her lineage, this bhikṣuṇī commits an offense involving the first rule,
which must be relinquished— a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (five).
There was a female thief who stole the wealth of a Licchavi woman and fled. The Licchavis dispatched men to search for and kill her.
The female thief then went to the city of Rājagṛha and entered the order as a nun within the Nigrodha Park.

When the Licchavis informed King Bimbisāra that she had gone forth, he sent a messenger to tell the Licchavis. The Licchavis then expressed their reproach and resentment; therefore, [the Buddha] established this rule at that time concerning the nuns.

If one does not know whether a person is a thief or not a thief, or whether they deserve death or do not deserve death, the Buddha said: "There is no offense for one who does not know. As for a 'thief':
if one steals five coins or more than five coins, and the three *karmavācanās* have been completed, the *upādhyāyinī* commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
There is no offense if one was unaware; or if the king, a minister, or a member of a noble clan granted permission for her to go forth;
or if she was released from confinement to allow her to go forth; or if she was rescued and set free. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"If the preceptress (*upādhyāyinī*) knew [of the impediment], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if the teacher (*ācāryā*) knew, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if the Saṃgha knew, it is a *duṣkṛta*."

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has been formally accused by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions, yet she does not comply, has not confessed her offense,
and the Saṃgha has not yet performed the *sāṃvāsika-karman* (act of restoration) for her— out of favoritism, she does not inquire of the Saṃgha.
If a bhikṣuṇī, without being instructed by the Saṃgha, goes outside the boundary to perform a *karmavācanā* for the absolution of an offense,
she commits an initial offense entailing relinquishment, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (6).

The nun Wei-ci was accused by the Saṃgha. Stūlanandā, without having informed the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha and without the Saṃgha having issued a formal injunction, went outside the boundary on her own authority and performed the *karmavācanā* for the removal of her offense.
Therefore, it was established as a rule: if the three *karmavācanās* are completed, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

After two *karmavācanās* are completed, there are three *sthūlātyaya*s; after one *karmavācanā* is completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya*s; after the formal motion (*jñapti*) is completed, there is one *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) to assemble the Saṃgha, it is a *duṣkṛta*; for a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases:

when the Saṃgha has been formally informed; when the Saṃgha has issued a command; when one is able to humble oneself and repent for the offense; or when the Saṃgha, out of anger, does not grant absolution from the offense. He...

If one releases [the formal act] with his consent, there is no offense. If, after the formal act (*karmavācanā*) has been performed for him, he moves away, dies, travels far, or renounces the path, and another person releases [the act] on his behalf, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī crosses a body of water alone, enters a village alone, stays overnight alone, or walks behind alone, she commits an offense of the first category, a saṃghāvaśeṣa that must be relinquished (70;
some other schools divide this into four separate precepts).
There was a nun who, crossing a river alone, lifted her robe high; a bandit saw her and became lustful, seizing her and molesting her.
The lay devotees (gṛhapati) were disgusted by this, saying it was just like a courtesan.

Furthermore, there were disciples of Cāmandikā who, having some minor business, entered a village of their own kinsmen not far from the monastery while traveling alone and stayed overnight there alone. The lay devotees suspected them of intending to have sexual relations.
[They] desired to obtain men. Furthermore, six bhikṣuṇīs were traveling with a group of nuns; they constantly walked behind and alone along the edge of the road.
The other nuns questioned them, and they replied, "We wish to obtain men. The nuns censured them with disapproval and informed the bhikṣus, who in turn informed the World-Honored One.
He established the precept: "One should seek out another nun to cross together; one should gradually lift one's robes and enter the water, waiting [for the companion]."

If she enters the water quickly, causing her companion to fall behind, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. When entering the water, she should adjust her robe according to the depth of the water and wait for her companion.

If she enters the water too quickly and does not wait for her companion, it is a *sthūlātyaya*. Once she has reached the opposite shore, she should gradually lower her robe and wait for her companion.
If she does not gradually lower her robe to step onto the bank and does not wait for her companion, [it is a *sthūlātyaya*].
Thullaccaya. If one goes alone to a village, for each village reached, it is Saṅghādisesa. If one goes alone to a desolate place, upon hearing the sound of one drum-beat, it is Saṅghādisesa;
if one has not yet reached the village but is within less than the distance of one drum-beat, it is Thullaccaya.
Walking alone through a single boundary of a village, it is Dukkaṭa. If one makes the effort to go but does not actually depart, it is Dukkaṭa. If...
If they stay together overnight in a village and, when lying down, their outstretched hands do not reach one another, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If they travel together on a road and become separated beyond the range of sight or hearing, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. If they are separated from the range of sight but not the range of hearing, or separated from the range of hearing but not the range of sight, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
There is no offense if they cross by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), cross by boat, or cross over a bridge.
Crossing: crossing by stepping on a beam, crossing over stones, or [crossing] when a companion nun has passed away or has left the religious life;
or when there is danger to life, danger to the holy life, or danger from wild beasts; or when one is being led away by force, or is being swept away by water—[the same applies to] entering a village.
Two nuns may stay overnight in a place where they can reach each other by stretching out their hands.
