If one nun goes out to relieve herself, or to receive or recite the scriptures, or to cook soup, porridge, or rice for a sick nun, or if she passes away, the same rule applies to those traveling together.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, knowing that a man has a defiled mind, receives from him food fit for eating, solid food, or other items,
this bhikṣuṇī commits an offense involving the first rule, which must be relinquished— a saṃghāvaśeṣa (8).
At that time, grain was expensive and alms were difficult to obtain. Tiṣya Nanda went to a merchant’s house to beg for food.
The merchant’s mind was fixed upon his own business, yet he gave him a full bowl of rice and soup.
Subsequently, Tiṣya went to that house several times and obtained food. On another occasion, when the man saw the nun coming from afar, he thought to himself: "Just as..."
"I have previously and subsequently given him food worth five hundred gold coins—enough to purchase a woman.
He has now come forward, seized me, and wished to commit sexual misconduct. The nun cried out, "Do not! Do not!
Those nearby inquired into the matter and asked the nun whether she knew his intention in giving her food. She replied, "I know. He said, "If you knew, why did you..."
[The Buddha] called [the nuns]. At that time, the nuns, feeling resentment and reproach, informed the bhikṣus, who in turn informed the World-Honored One. He then established the precept:
"Permissible foods are roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, oil, sesame, black rock-honey, and fine powdered food. As for 'food,' it refers to rice and parched grain flour."

Regarding dry rice and other such items: as for "other things," this refers to gold, silver, precious gems, and the like. If one receives them from a man with a defiled mind, knowing him to have a defiled mind, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If the recipient is a son of a deva, a son of an asura, or even an animal capable of changing form, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If they are not capable of changing form, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*; for the other three [classes of practitioners], it is likewise.
A multitude of *duṣkṛta* (offenses of wrong-doing). There is no offense if one was unaware that the other possessed a defiled mind. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"If a nun has a defiled mind and the man has no defiled mind, she incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If the nun has no defiled mind and the man has a defiled mind, he incurs a *duṣkṛta*."
There is a bhikṣuṇī who instructs another bhikṣuṇī to speak as follows: "Sister, whether he has a defiled mind or an undefiled mind, what can that do to you?
As for yourself, being free from a defiled mind, if you receive food from him at the proper time and in a pure manner, you may accept it.
This bhikṣuṇī commits an offense of the first category, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* which must be relinquished before the Saṃgha. (9)
Tiṣya entered the city to beg for alms and returned with an empty bowl. The group of six nuns and Tiṣya’s mother spoke to him in such a manner [as to cause his distress].
Therefore, this rule was established. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense in cases such as speaking in jest.
10. Not relinquishing the practice of causing a schism in the Saṃgha; 11. Not relinquishing one's faction that has caused a schism in the Saṃgha; 12. Refusing to submit after being expelled;
13. Not relinquishing a malicious disposition. These four precepts are also the same as those for a bhikṣu.
If bhikṣuṇīs live in close association, engage together in misconduct, spread an evil reputation, and mutually conceal one another’s offenses, those bhikṣuṇīs should be admonished by saying:
"Sisters, do not live in close association, engage in misconduct, spread an evil reputation, and mutually conceal one another’s offenses. If you do not live in close association..."
Within the Buddha’s Dharma, she attains increased well-being and dwells in peace. When that bhikṣuṇī admonishes her [for this], she persists firmly and does not relinquish it.
That bhikṣuṇī should admonish her up to three times so that she may relinquish this matter. If she relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī has committed an offense involving three matters that must be relinquished, which is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (the fourteenth).

(Regarding the three matters: it is only after failing to relinquish [the offense] following the three admonitions that one incurs the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. As for what should be relinquished: one should likewise relinquish it so as not to commit an offense.)
There were two bhikṣuṇīs who lived in constant close association with one another, even to the point of covering each other’s offenses.

When the other bhikṣuṇīs admonished them, they did not reform. The Buddha therefore ordered the community of bhikṣuṇīs to perform a formal act of censure (*karmavācanā*) against them and established this precept.

“Close association” means frequently engaging in playful laughter together, frequently teasing one another, and frequently conversing. “Evil conduct” refers to planting flower trees oneself and instructing others to do so.
Regarding human races: irrigating, gathering, and stringing [garlands], and so forth;

even if a person or a youth sits upon the same bed or eats from the same vessel, or engages in singing, dancing, and instrumental music—such evil sounds and malicious words spread in all four directions, and there is no one who does not hear them. Regarding offenses:

with the exception of the eight *pārājika* dharmas, concealing other offenses constitutes this [offense]. After the third *karma-vācanā* is completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. The remainder is as [previously stated].
[Section] Ten. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one creates unwholesome conditions, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If there is an evil reputation, or if one causes distress to the community of nuns, or if they mutually conceal their offenses, all are *sthūlātyaya*. First, one should admonish them with gentle words as previously described."
If, when the community of bhikṣuṇīs is carrying out a formal reprimand against a bhikṣuṇī, another bhikṣuṇī instructs her by saying:
"You should not live separately; you should live together, for I have seen other bhikṣuṇīs living together as well."
"Living together while committing evil deeds, with a bad reputation spreading as they cover for one another's offenses, the Saṃgha, out of anger, has instructed you to live separately.
That bhikṣuṇī should admonish that other bhikṣuṇī, saying:
'Sister, do not instruct other bhikṣuṇīs by saying, "You should not live separately," for I also see other bhikṣuṇīs living together while committing evil deeds.'"
Their evil reputation has spread abroad, and they have covered for one another's offenses. Because of their anger, the Saṃgha instructed you to live separately;

yet now there are precisely these two bhikṣuṇīs who continue to dwell together, committing evil deeds, with their evil reputation spreading and covering for each other's offenses—there is no one else besides them.
If this bhikṣuṇī lives separately, it will lead to increase in the Buddha-dharma and a dwelling in peace and happiness.
When other bhikṣuṇīs admonish that bhikṣuṇī, if she persists and does not relinquish her position, those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her up to three times to make her relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well; if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī commits an offense involving the three dharmas.
The *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense involving forfeiture (the fifteenth).
Because the group of six nuns instructed those two nuns to speak in such a manner, this was established as a precept. The gravity of the offense is the same as previously stated.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one says, 'You should not act with discord; you should act with harmony.

Those who act with discord will not attain growth, whereas those who act with harmony shall attain growth,' [and if] all [the monks] commit a *sthūlātyaya*, and because the Saṃgha is angry, instructs them to act with discord, it is a *pāyattika*.
First, one should admonish them with gentle words as previously described."
If a bhikṣuṇī, on account of some trivial matter, becomes angry and displeased, and speaks thus: "I renounce the Buddha;
I renounce the Dharma; I renounce the Saṃgha. There are not only these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, but there are also other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life (brahmacarya).
We may also practice the holy life under them," that bhikṣuṇī should be admonished.
That bhikṣuṇī said, "Sister, do not hastily become angry and displeased over a mere trifle, and then speak these words:
'I renounce the Buddha; I renounce the Dharma; I renounce the Saṃgha. It is not only these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, that exist;
there are also other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life (brahmacarya). We may also practice the holy life under them. If...

When this bhikṣuṇī is being admonished by another bhikṣuṇī, if she persists and does not relinquish her position, that bhikṣuṇī should be admonished up to three times so that she may relinquish this matter.

If she relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well. If she does not relinquish it, this bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense of the third category, which must be relinquished before the Saṃgha (16).
This was originated by the group of six bhikṣuṇīs; therefore, it was established as a precept. The gravity of the offense is the same as previously stated.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If one says, 'I renounce the Buddha,' 'I renounce the Dharma,' 'I renounce the Saṃgha,' or 'I renounce the precepts,' it is all a sthūlātyaya.
If one says, 'It is not only the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, who know the Path,' and thereby reviles the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika. One should first attempt to restrain them with gentle words."
If a bhikṣuṇī delights in quarreling and does not properly remember the matter of the dispute, and later, out of anger, speaks these words:
"The Saṃgha has favoritism, anger, fear, and delusion," that bhikṣuṇī should be admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, saying: "Sister..."
"Do not take delight in quarreling. Do not improperly harbor matters of dispute. Later, out of anger, you said:
'The Saṃgha has attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; yet the Saṃgha is without attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion.
It is you who have attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion. When this bhikṣuṇī was being admonished by that bhikṣuṇī, she stubbornly maintained her position and would not relinquish it."
That bhikṣuṇī should be admonished three times for the purpose of relinquishing this matter. If she relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī has committed an offense involving three rules that must be relinquished, which is a saṃghāvaśeṣa (seventeenth).
This was originated by the bhikṣuṇī Kālī; therefore, it was established as a precept. The gravity of the offense is the same as previously stated.
○ The thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas. [In the *Mūla-vinaya*, these are thirty-three.]

1. Keeping extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*): The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that for nuns, twenty robes are permitted; five robes are to be maintained as one's own possession, while fifteen robes may be used after being formally dedicated through *śuddhikaraṇa*. If one keeps more than this, it is an offense of forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

For monks, there is no fixed limit; they may use them after dedicating them through *śuddhikaraṇa* without committing an offense. 2. Sleeping apart from the five robes for one night. 3. Keeping a robe for more than one month. 4.

Begging for a robe from someone who is not a relative. 5. Receiving more robes than permitted. 6. Seeking an increased price for a robe. 7. Seeking to have the price for a robe combined [with other funds]. 8. Soliciting a robe.
1. Exceeding six [repetitions]. 2. Accepting gold and silver nine times. 3. Buying and selling precious objects. 4. Engaging in trade. 5.
Keeping an alms bowl while seeking a better one. 6. Having a robe woven by one who is not a relative. 7. Seeking to have a fine robe woven. 8. Giving a robe and then angrily seizing it back.
9. Keeping medicine for more than seven days. 10. Keeping an *akālika-cīvara* (a robe offered at an urgent time) beyond the permitted period. 11. Diverting [the property of the Saṃgha].
If a nun takes monastic property for herself, it is treated in the same manner as for a bhikṣu.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having sought one thing, seeks another, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (nineteenth).
Stūlanandā went to the house of a donor seeking ghee. The donor bought ghee and gave it to her, but she said, "I do not need ghee; I need oil.
The donor criticized and complained about this, and therefore [the Buddha] established the rule: requesting other items is also like this.

One should relinquish them to the community of nuns—whether it be many or one person—but one must not relinquish them to a separate group. If one relinquishes them in such a manner, the relinquishment is invalid; [the offense is] a *duṣkṛta*.

It is a *duṣkṛta* offense. Once it has been relinquished, one should perform confession (*pratideśanā*). After the person receiving the confession has made the formal announcement (*jñapti*), one may then accept the confession.

One should say to that person: "Reprove your own mind. He shall reply: "So be it. The nun should then return the relinquished object to him by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).

If one does not return it, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one instructs another, saying "Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta*. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases:
if one needs ghee and asks for ghee; if one needs oil and asks for oil; or if one needs other items and asks for those other items.

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a donor’s gift intended for the Saṃgha is for a specific purpose, diverts it for another use, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture and expiation). (20)

The bhikṣuṇīs were reciting the precepts in the open air. A lay devotee provided materials for the construction of a hall for the recitation of the precepts. The bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves: "We have been content to sit and recite the precepts wherever we happen to be;
however, robes are difficult to obtain, and one ought to possess the five types of robes. They immediately took the materials and traded them for robes, which they divided among themselves.

Yet, they continued to recite the precepts in the open air. The lay devotee criticized and disparaged this, and therefore [the Buddha] established the rule: "One shall provide [materials] for the construction [of a hall]."
If one uses robes to construct a dwelling, whether using them for this location or that location, the offense is the same. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense if one asks the owner for permission to use them, or uses them according to their instructions, or if at the time of giving the items one says, "Use them as you please."
If this bhikṣuṇī, having received a gift intended for a specific purpose, seeks it for herself or for the Saṃgha, or diverts it for other uses,
it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (twenty-first).
The nuns who had long resided in Śrāvastī heard that the nun Anvaya was coming to beg for alms from house to house, and that she had obtained a great quantity of wealth, clothing, and food.
When the appointed time arrived, the nun did not arrive; they then took those goods, exchanged them for other items, and divided them among themselves.
Later, when the nun Anvaya came and entered the city to beg for alms, the lay devotees informed her that there was no food in the Saṃgha, and she went to the long-residing nuns.
Because they were asked about the reason for this and subsequently criticized one another, the following rule was established: To seek cloth for making robes and then use it for food;
to seek it for one purpose and then use it for another—these constitute an offense. For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense if one tells a layperson to use it as they wish, or if after a layperson has given an object, one says to them, "Use it as you wish. The same applies to all subsequent cases.
If a bhikṣuṇī diverts material goods donated by a donor for one purpose and uses them for another,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (22).
A householder asked the nun Anvaya, "Do you live in peace and happiness? She replied, "I find it noisy and am not happy. He asked again, "Is there no separate dwelling for you?

She replied, "There is none. He then gave her the value of a house. The nun thought, "Building a house involves many tasks and clothing is difficult to obtain," so she used the money for the house to purchase robes.
Because the householder criticized and complained about this, [the Buddha] established the rule.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when the donor has designated a specific object for a particular purpose, seeks it out for the Saṃgha and diverts it for another use,
it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (twenty-third).
A group of bhikṣuṇīs built a dwelling for them; they solicited wealth from various places, used it to purchase robes, and divided them among themselves. Therefore, the following rule was established:
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra alms-bowl beyond the permitted limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense (the twenty-fourth).

This was established because it originated with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs; therefore, the rule was enacted: on the very day one obtains a bowl, one should accept and maintain that one bowl on that same day, while the remainder must be given as a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*).
The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that one may keep [extra bowls] for one night.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that a bhikṣuṇī may possess sixteen bowls: one to be maintained, three to be given as pure gifts, four "excess bowls," and four "deficient bowls."
25. The fourth rule concerning alms bowls: If one keeps more than [the permitted number], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps many fine-colored vessels, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. (Twenty-five)
This [transgression] also arose among the group of six bhikṣuṇīs; therefore, it was prohibited. On the very day one obtains a vessel, one should accept those sixteen items that are necessary for use;
the remainder should be given as pure gifts (*śuddha-dāna*). The sixteen are: a large cauldron, its lid, a large basin, and a ladle;
a small cauldron, its lid, a small basin, and a ladle; a water jar, its lid, a basin, and a ladle; and a washing jar, its lid, a basin, and a ladle.
If a bhikṣuṇī promises a sick-nun’s robe and later does not give it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (26).
Cāndanīśūna, who constantly claimed to be free from thoughts of desire, said to another nun: "If you [experience] menstrual blood..."
[The blood] flows out. She takes this robe from me. At another time, when Śunā’s menstrual period begins and the other nuns’ periods also begin, they send a messenger to ask for the robe.
[If one] does not give it, that nun becomes resentful and reproaches her; therefore, [the rule] was established. Regarding "sickness-robe":
when the menstrual flow occurs, one wears an inner garment (*nivāsana*) to cover the body. Excluding the sickness-robe, other robes and [garments] are permitted.
If one does not give required items, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). There is no offense in the following cases: if one has no robes for illness; if one is making robes for illness;
or if that nun has broken the precepts, or there is danger to life, and so forth.
If a bhikṣuṇī accepts a non-seasonal robe and makes it into a seasonal robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (twenty-seventh).
This was established because of the group of six bhikṣuṇīs. "Seasonal" refers to after the retreat (*varṣā*) is concluded, when there is no *kaṭhina* robe. One.
[The Buddha said: "There is the *kāṭhina* robe; there are five months. 'At the improper time' means excluding these [five months]. To obtain an extra robe at any other time constitutes an offense.
There is no offense if it is an out-of-season robe received and treated as an out-of-season robe, or if it is an in-season robe received and treated as an in-season robe."

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: To make seasonal robes from non-seasonal cloth, or to divide non-seasonal robes as if they were seasonal robes, constitutes an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
Seasonal robes shall be divided among the monks who have completed the rainy season retreat; non-seasonal robes shall be divided among the monks present at that time.
If a bhikṣuṇī exchanges robes with another bhikṣuṇī and later, out of anger, takes them back herself or causes someone else to take them back, saying, "Sister, give me back my robe!
I will not give it to you. Your robe belongs to you; as for my robe, give it back to me! [This constitutes an offense.]
Naiḥsargika-pāyattika (28). This was established because it originated with Thullanandā.
Regarding "exchanging": exchanging cloth for cloth; or exchanging cloth for what is not cloth; or exchanging what is not cloth for cloth;
or exchanging what is not cloth for what is not cloth. [This includes] needles, knives, and thread.

Regarding fragmented objects, even down to a single pill of medicine: if one seizes and conceals them, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if one does not conceal them, it is a *duṣkṛta*. If one takes them and removes them from their place, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if one does not remove them from their place, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases: [if the object is lost or destroyed, or if one takes it for the sake of the Saṃgha, etc. (as specified in the full rule).

She speaks conciliatory words: "Sister, I regret it; return my robe. If she knows he intends to regret it and returns the robe, or if another nun tells him to return it, or if he returns it because there was no justification for his borrowing and wearing it, or if she knows beforehand that it will be lost.
If one fears it will be destroyed, or if that person has broken the precepts and so forth, or even if there is danger to life, one may take it away without concealing it.
If a bhikṣuṇī requests a heavy robe, its value shall not exceed four *khaṭa* of wool;
if it exceeds this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (twenty-ninth).
"Extra robes" refers to robes for warding off the cold. When seeking extra robes, the maximum limit is sixteen pieces.
There is no offense if one requests exactly four sets of *kappāsika* cloth, or fewer; nor is there an offense if one obtains them without having requested them.
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to beg for light clothing, the maximum value shall not exceed two and a half pieces of fine woolen cloth (*karpāsa*).
Should she exceed this, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (thirty).
"Light clothing" refers to clothing that wards off heat. To beg for light clothing, the maximum limit is ten pieces;
there is no offense beyond this, as explained above. Section 178: *Pāyattika* Dharmas. In the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, this is the 141st rule.
In the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, it is the 210th rule. In the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, it is the 180th rule.
1. Lying; 2. Slander; 3. Divisive speech; 4. Sleeping in the same room as a man; 5.
Staying more than three nights in the same room as a woman who has not received the precepts; 6. Reciting the Dharma together with one who has not received the precepts;
7. Speaking of another’s grave offense to outsiders; 8. Speaking of realized dharmas to outsiders; 9. Preaching the Dharma to a man for more than three sentences; 10. Digging [the earth].
1. [Destruction of] the earth; 2. Destroying a village of spirits; 3. Annoying others with discordant speech; 4. Resenting and reviling; 5.
Not putting away monastic bedding after spreading it; 6. Not putting away bedding from a monastic dwelling; 7.
Forcibly taking over a place where another is staying; 8. Dragging someone out of a room; 9. Sitting on a bed with detachable legs on an upper story; 10. [Using] water containing insects.
20. Pouring mud and grass over the roof; 21. Exceeding three meals during the retreat period; 22. Accepting an invitation for a single meal when it is not one's turn;
23. Eating separately from the community; 24. Accepting more than three bowls of food at an invitation; 25. Eating at an improper time.
25. Eating leftover food. 26. Taking food for oneself. 27. Going to another household without having informed [the preceptor].
28. Sitting down forcefully at a meal-giving household. 29. Sitting in a secluded place at a meal-giving household.
30. Sitting alone with a man. 31. Intentionally causing others not to receive food. 32. Receiving medicine in excess.
33. Observing military arrays; 34. Staying more than three nights among the army;
35. Observing military affairs; 36. Drinking alcohol; 37. Sporting in water; 38. Mutual tickling; 39. Not accepting admonition;
40. Terrifying others; 41. Bathing at improper times; 42. [The forty-second...]
43. Lighting a fire in an open space. 44. Hiding another’s belongings as a joke. 45. Wearing a pure gift (śuddhika) robe without first marking it with the dye of disfigurement (akāṣāya).
46. Failing to dye one’s robes with the color of disfigurement. 47. Taking the life of a living being. 48.

Drinking or using water containing insects. 49. Intentionally harassing another. 50. Concealing another’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*; excluding the eight *pārājika* offenses, which constitute a grave offense by their very nature). 51. [Continuation of the preceding item.]
Fifty-one: Initiating disputes. Fifty-two: Traveling with thieves. Fifty-three: Not relinquishing evil views. Fifty-four: Aligning with those who hold evil views. Fifty-five:
Keeping a *śrāmaṇerī* who has been expelled. Fifty-six: Refusing counsel and engaging in contentious questioning. Fifty-seven:
Slighting and reviling the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. Fifty-eight: Ignorance. Fifty-nine: Contradicting...
59. Reversing a formal act (*karmavācanā*). 60. Granting consent (*chanda*) and later regretting it. 61.
Listening in secret to a dispute and then reporting the subsequent words. 62. Striking a bhikṣuṇī out of anger. 63. Assaulting a bhikṣuṇī out of anger. 64.
Groundlessly accusing someone of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense out of anger. 65. Entering the palace precincts without authorization. 66. [The sixtieth.]
60. Taking precious objects; 61–67. Entering a village at an improper time; 68. Making a high bed; 69.
Storing a mattress stuffed with *tūla* cotton—these are all the same as for a bhikṣu.
If a bhikṣuṇī eats *śuka* (a type of herb), it is a pāyattika (seventy).
Stūlanandā took all the *śuka* from a garden; because the owner of the garden censured her, this rule was established. For the other four assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if one is ill and the illness is not cured by eating *śuka*, in which case eating it is permitted; or if it is applied as an ointment for a wound.
If a bhikṣuṇī shaves the hair of the three places, it is a pāyattika (seventy-one).
As with a courtesan or a female thief, the "three places" refer to the two orifices for excrement and urine, as well as the armpits.
To once move the blade constitutes one *pāyattika*. To pull it out, to cut it, or to burn it all constitute *duṣkṛta*; for a bhikṣu, this is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For the other three assemblies, it is *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if there is a sore that requires shaving away for the application of medicine.
If a bhikṣuṇī performs the purification with water, it should be limited to two finger-joints on each finger.
If she exceeds this, it is a pāyattika (seventy-two).
For the other two groups of women, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if there is grass or an insect inside and she pulls it out.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes a male organ out of lacquer, it is a *pāyattika* (73).

If one makes [a garment] out of various materials, it is a *pāyattika* offense in all cases. If it is not polished or treated, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. For the other two groups of women, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
There is no offense in cases where, due to illness, medicine must be worn, or where a cloth is used to block menstrual flow.
If a bhikṣuṇī slaps another, it is a pāyattika (74).
Whether with the palm of the hand or with the foot, the one who slaps commits a duṣkṛta; the one who receives the slap commits a pāyattika.
If two female organs slap each other, both commit a pāyattika; for the rest of the assembly of women, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when a bhikṣu is not ill, stands before him at the time of a meal to provide water or fans him with a fan,
it is a pāyattika (seventy-fifth).
There was an elder who, together with his wife, both went forth into homelessness. At mealtime, the former wife stood before him holding water and fanning him with a fan.
The bhikṣu said to her, "Step aside; I am ashamed before people. The nun replied, "I am standing right here, yet you say I am shameful?
You did such and such things to me in the past—why were you not ashamed then? She then struck him with the handle of the fan and spilled the water.
Because [the nun] poured water over his head and then entered the room, it was thus prescribed: at that time, the nuns did not dare to attend to the sick bhikṣus;
no one gave them water, and they did not dare to inquire after them. The Buddha said: "I permit the nuns to attend to the sick bhikṣus. If there is no water, I permit them to inquire."
If a bhikṣuṇī begs for raw grain, it is a pāyattika (seventy-six).
Begging for raw grain—whether sesame, rice, beans, or large and small wheat—in all such cases it is a pāyattika. For the other four assemblies, it is a dukkaṭa.
There is no offense if she begs from a relative, or if she begs from one who has left the household life, or if she obtains it without begging.
If a bhikṣuṇī voids excrement or urine upon living grass, it is a pāyattika (seventy-seventh).
Not far from a bhikṣuṇī’s vihāra, there was fine grass growing; laypeople frequently came to sit, lie down, and flirt there.
They disturbed the nuns who were practicing meditation. The nuns were troubled by this and placed refuse upon them. When the lay followers returned to play, they soiled their bodies and clothes;
everyone then reviled and censured them. Therefore, it was established as a rule: for the other four assemblies, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense in voiding excrement or urine in a place where no grass grows, or when it falls onto grass and the like.
If a bhikṣuṇī, after the night has passed, does not inspect her chamber-pot before discarding it outside the wall,
it is a pāyattika (78).
The group of six nuns used their vessels at night and, failing to inspect them in the morning, discarded their excrement outside the wall.
Early one morning, a high minister was traveling in his carriage to see King Bimbisāra; as his route passed by the side of the monastery, the excrement fell upon his head.
The minister intended to report this to the judicial authorities, but a Brahmin who was both deeply faithful and skilled in reading signs intervened to dissuade him.
He immediately went to the nunnery and told her not to do so again. Subsequently, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who established the precept:
"If one discards [something] at night without clearing one's throat or snapping one's fingers, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. For the other four assemblies, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if there were already tiles, stones, or various impurities present there."
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to watch or listen to music and performances, it is a pāyattika (seventy-ninth).
If she goes and sees it, it is a pāyattika; if she does not see it, it is a duṣkṛta. If she intends to leave but returns midway, and so forth, these are all duṣkṛtas.
For the other four assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta. There is no offense if she has something to report, or if she is summoned, or if she is on the way [to another destination].
Due to the fault of being in a secluded place, or at a lodging, or if she has been taken away by force, or if there is danger to her life and so forth—
should a bhikṣuṇī enter a village and stand and converse with a man in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika (eighty).
If her companion is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If she stands without speaking, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense if two nuns are her companions, or if she has a person capable of understanding as a companion, or if many women are standing together.
Whether he is not blind or deaf, whether he is walking or stationary, or even if he has fallen to the ground due to illness or is facing a life-threatening danger—
if a bhikṣuṇī enters a secluded place together with a man, it is a pāyattika (eighty-first).
If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village lane and sends her companion far away,
then stands in a secluded place with a man and whispers to him, it is a pāyattika (82).

If she sends her companion away from the place where they can see her but not from the place where they can hear her, or from the place where they can hear her but not from the place where they can see her,
it is a *duṣkṛta*. If a bhikṣuṇī sits inside the house of a layperson and departs without informing the host,
it is a *pāyattika* (83).
There was a nun who went to the house of a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*). The wife of the lay devotee spread out a single-seated bed for her and had her sit upon it;
she then left and entered the inner room. Without informing the host, the nun departed. A young brahmin (*māṇava*) came into the house, looked around, and not seeing anyone, took the bed away.
Therefore, it was established as a rule: if one foot is outside the door and so forth, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense. The rest [is as previously stated].
For the fourfold assembly, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if there is already another person sitting on the seat;
if one has requested the person sitting nearby to move; if the person sitting nearby tells them to leave; or if one is sitting on a stone, a wooden plank, a raised bank, a grass mat, or a mound;
or if the building is about to collapse or is on fire; or if there are venomous snakes, wild beasts, or bandits; or even in cases where life is at risk.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters the house of a layperson and sits down on a bed without informing the host,
it is a pāyattika (eighty-four).
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a minister who lacked faith and devotion. He possessed a private sitting couch upon which no one dared to sit.
Stūlanandā sat upon it without being asked; her menstrual blood defiled his bedding and cushions. The minister became resentful and angry, and thus he established a rule:
for the other four assemblies, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense if one sits on a seat that is one's regular place, or if the person is a relative.
[The Buddha said: "If there is someone with whom one is intimate and close, and they speak to [the bhikṣuṇī] to have her sit— whether on a stone, a wooden platform, or the like—
and if a bhikṣuṇī enters the interior of a layperson's house and, without informing the host,
spreads out a seat for herself and stays overnight, it is a pāyattika (85)."
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if it is an empty house, a house for performing meritorious acts, or the home of acquaintances and the like.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters a dark room together with a man, it is a *pāyattika* (86).
For the other four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if there is a lamp or fire facing a window, or in cases such as a threat to life.
If a bhikṣuṇī receives a statement without careful scrutiny and then speaks it to others, it is a *pāyattika* (87).
The bhikṣuṇī Cchanda told her disciple to fetch her robe, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case. The disciple accepted the task but did not examine it carefully;
she then said to the other bhikṣuṇīs, "My teacher has instructed me to steal the robes and bowl. When the bhikṣuṇīs questioned her and learned the truth, they censured her with indignation.

This matter was eventually reported to the Buddha, who established the precept. For the other four assemblies [of the Saṅgha], it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense. There is no offense in cases such as these.
It is indeed so. Or it may be spoken in jest, or even through error and the like.

If a bhikṣuṇī, on account of some minor matter, utters a curse such as, "May I fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma," or "If I have such a thing, may I fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma," or "If you have such..."
This matter also results in falling into the three evil realms and not being born within the Buddha-dharma; this is a *pāyattika* (eighty-eighth). The Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit you to invoke 'Namo Buddha. If I have such a matter, I say, 'Namo Buddha';
if you have such a matter, you also say, 'Namo Buddha. If there is speech involving cursing, it is a *pāyattika* offense; otherwise..."
For the fourfold assembly, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in a quarrel and, failing to properly retain the matter of the dispute, beats her breast and weeps,
it is a *pāyattika* (89).

To strike one’s chest once constitutes one *pāyattika*. For every single drop of a tear that falls, there is one *pāyattika*. For the remaining four groups [of monastics], it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense in the following cases:
if one strikes oneself because of choking while eating; or due to defecation or urination; or due to wind, cold, or heat; or from being smoked by fumes;
or if tears flow from the heart due to a sense of renunciation upon hearing the Dharma; or if tears come from applying medicine to a painful eye.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, lies down on the same bed with another person, it is a pāyattika (offense number ninety).
There is no offense if she is ill, or if she is bound, and so forth.
If a bhikṣuṇī lies down with another on the same mat and under the same blanket, except at other times, it is a pāyattika (91).
If they share the same mat but have separate blankets, or share the same blanket but have separate mats, it is a duṣkṛta. For the other four assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if, during cold weather, there is only one blanket available; in such a case, it is permitted for each person to wear an inner garment against their body.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that she arrived after those who were already residing there, or knowing that they arrived before her,
nevertheless recites the sūtras, inquires about their meaning, or provides instruction to them in order to cause them annoyance, it is a pāyattika (ninety-second).
There is no offense if one does not know [the rule]; or if one has previously given permission; or if the person is a close friend;
or if a close friend says, "Please teach him only"; or if the resident receives the scripture from the latecomer;
or if the latecomer receives the recitation from the resident; or if both receive it together from another; or if the other asks and this one answers; or if they recite together, and so forth.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not tend to a fellow bhikṣuṇī living with her who is ill, it is a pāyattika (93).
This excludes cases of illness involving those of the same Dharma; if the two teachers, or even close friends and acquaintances, do not tend to her, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
For the other four assemblies, it is *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if she herself is ill, or if there is danger to life, and so forth.
If a bhikṣuṇī, at the beginning of the rainy season retreat, permits another bhikṣuṇī to place a bed in her room,
and later, out of anger, drives her out, it is a pāyattika (94).

If one follows many people through many doors, there is a *pāyattika* offense for each individual door. If one takes out other clothing and belongings, or if one closes the door so that others cannot enter, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For the other four assemblies, it is also a *dukkaṭa*.

There is no offense if one does not follow the order of seniority out of anger, thereby causing a junior monk to leave; or if one has stayed two nights with an unordained person and causes them to leave on the third night.
If she violates the precepts, she shall even be subject to expulsion. If, however, due to such circumstances there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya), it is otherwise.
If a bhikṣuṇī wanders through human settlements during all seasons—spring, summer, or winter—except for other valid reasons, it is a pāyattika offense (ninety-five).
If it is for the sake of the Three Jewels or for the sake of a sick nun, one is permitted to receive the seven-day leave (*saptāha-kāla*) and go beyond the boundary.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the summer retreat (*varṣā*), does not depart [from the monastery], it is a *pāyattika* offense (96).
When the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is concluded, one should go forth [on tour] for at least one night. If one does not go forth, it is a *pāyattika*.
There is no offense in the following cases: if a layperson further invites one to stay; if there is a succession of invitations from various households; if male or female relatives invite one;
if one encounters illness and lacks an attendant to care for one; or if there is danger from water, up to being bound, or life-threatening danger, and so forth. (*Pañcavargīya-vinaya*)

It is said: If one does not accept an invitation for a fixed period, or if one does not go to a place where an invitation has been received because it is not a location suitable for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), there is no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī travels among people in a border region that is suspicious or dangerous, it is a *pāyattika* (97).
Regarding boundaries: if one enters a village while traveling from a distant location outside a city, for each individual boundary crossed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If traveling through a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*), it is a *pāyattika* for every ten *krośas*. If it is less than a village or less than ten *krośas*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one is summoned, or has something to report, or is being detained, or arrives first, or if there is subsequently a matter of fear.
[The Buddha] rose. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one flies, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī wanders among people in a place within the boundary that is suspected to be dangerous or fearful, it is a pāyattika (98)."
"Within the boundary" means surrounding the four sides of the city; whether an offense is committed or not is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī associates with a layman or the son of a layman, living together and engaging in improper conduct, and other bhikṣuṇīs admonish this bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister, do not associate with a layman or the son of a layman and live together."

"Venerable sister, you are acting in a manner that is not in accordance with the Dharma; you should live separately. By living separately, you will find increase and dwell in peace within the Buddha’s teaching.
When that bhikṣuṇī admonishes this bhikṣuṇī, she persists and does not relinquish her position.

That bhikṣuṇī should admonish her up to three times so that she may relinquish this matter. If, after being admonished up to three times, she relinquishes it, that is well; if she does not relinquish it...
[If one] does so, it is a *pāyattika* (99). As for "associating":

to speak, laugh, and joke with [the person] repeatedly. When the third *karmavācanā* is completed, it is a *pāyattika*. When the second *karmavācanā* is completed and [the act] is abandoned, there are two *duṣkṛtas*.
When the first *karmavācanā* is completed and [the act] is abandoned, there are two *duṣkṛtas*. When [the motion] has been announced (*jñapti*) and [the act] is abandoned, [there is one *duṣkṛta*].

One *duṣkṛta* offense: performing an act that is not in accordance with the rule before the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made is entirely a *duṣkṛta*. For the other four assemblies, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one desists at the first utterance; or when there is a formal censure by an illegal and discordant assembly (*adharma-vinīlaka-saṃgha*).
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to view the royal palace, its decorated painted halls, gardens, or bathing pools, it is a pāyattika (one hundred).
If she has gone and sees them, it is a pāyattika; if she does not see them, it is a duṣkṛta. All instances of making preparations to go, and so forth, are duṣkṛtas.

For the bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*; for the remaining four assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense in the following cases: when there is something to report; when one is summoned or invited;
when passing through on the way; when staying overnight; when being detained, and so forth; or when acting for the sake of the Saṃgha or the stūpa, or when examining and taking the model.
If a bhikṣuṇī bathes in a river, spring, canal, pond, or pool with her body exposed, it is a pāyattika (111).
For the other four assemblies, it is a dukkaṭa. There is no offense if she is seized by force.
If a bhikṣuṇī makes a bathing robe, it must be made according to the prescribed measurements. As for the measurements:
it should be six spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two and a half spans in width. If it exceeds these dimensions, it is a pāyattika (offense number 102).

A bathing robe (*udakasāṭikā*) is that which covers the body for bathing. If it exceeds the measurement in length but is sufficient in width, or if it is sufficient in length but exceeds the measurement in width, or if it exceeds both measurements:
if one makes it oneself, or instructs another to make it, and it is completed, it is a *pāyattika* offense;
if it is not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. If one has another make it, whether it is completed or not, it is always a *dukkaṭa* offense. For a bhikṣu, this is a *pāyattika*.

[For] the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*. There is no offense if one makes it according to the prescribed measure, makes it less than the measure, or if one obtains a finished garment and cuts it to conform to the Dharma, or if it is layered.

If a bhikṣuṇī sews a saṃghāṭī for more than five days—unless she is seeking a saṃghāṭī, or the kaṭhina robes have been suspended, or one of the six difficult circumstances has arisen—it is a pāyattika.

(Among the hundred and eight difficult circumstances, two—the non-human and the evil beast—are excluded; thus it is called "six difficulties," as the community of bhikṣuṇīs does not reside in araṇya hermitages.)
Thullanandā was tailoring a robe for a certain nun; because she wished to cause that nun to provide her with offerings for a long time, she did not sew it immediately.
At that time, a fire broke out at the monastery, and the clothing materials were burned. Therefore, it was prescribed: for monks and others, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense if there is no needle, thread, or scissors; or if they are insufficient in quantity; or if there is danger to life, and so forth.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not inspect her saṃghāṭī for more than five days, it is a pāyattika (104).

There was a nun who kept her saṃghāṭī in her room and failed to inspect, air-dry, or repair it; consequently, it became infested with insects, rotted, and its color faded. For this reason, the rule was established.
If one does not inspect other robes or necessary items every five days, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). For monks and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if the place where they are kept is secure; or if the person to whom they were entrusted is looking after them; or if one fears that inspection would result in their loss.
If a bhikṣuṇī creates an obstacle for the Saṃgha regarding robes, it is a pāyattika (105).
There was a former acquaintance and friend of Thullanandā who wished to provide food and offer robes to the Saṃgha.
She went and said to her, "The Saṃgha possesses great majesty and virtue; there are many donors making offerings, and you have many sources of support yourself. For now, simply provide food."

"One must give clothing; let one's relatives and old friends hear of this. The next day, observing the dignified and orderly deportment of the bhikṣuṇīs, he felt remorse and regretted not having given clothing.
When the bhikṣuṇīs questioned him and learned the reason, they reported it to the Buddha, who then established the precept: "To create obstacles by withholding other items [is an offense]."
Dukkata. To create an obstacle for another person is dukkata. For bhikṣus and others, it is dukkata.
If a bhikṣuṇī puts on another's robe without asking the owner, it is a pāyattika (106).
For monks and others, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense if one speaks with affectionate familiarity, saying, "Just put this on and go.
If a bhikṣuṇī gives a robe belonging to a śramaṇa to an outsider or a layperson, it is a *pāyattika* (107).
"White-robed ones" refers to householders. "Non-Buddhists" refers to renunciants outside of the Buddha's Dharma.

"Sramana robes" refers to dyed garments. If he accepts them, it is a *pāyattika*; if he does not accept them, it is a *dukkaṭa*. If he makes preparations with the intent to give them, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣu and others, it is likewise a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if giving to one's parents or to a stūpa.
Regarding laborers: for those who work on lecture halls or dwellings, one should calculate and provide them with wages for their food.

However, if they are seized by forceful means, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If one exchanges it for a nun’s robe, or uses it to repay a debt, there is no offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If a nun possesses preceptual virtue and someone requests a piece of a tattered *kāṣāya* to ward off calamities, she should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) give it to him."
If a bhikṣuṇī, with such an intention as this, obstructs the distribution of robes by the Saṃgha when it is being distributed according to the Dharma,
out of fear that her disciples will not receive any, it is a pāyattika (108).

For monks and others, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense in cases such as when it is not the proper time, or when the assembly is unlawful or divided, and thus one intentionally refrains [from the ceremony].

If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intention that the Saṃgha may not now emerge from the *kaṭhina* robe but shall do so later—desiring that the five privileges be relinquished for a long duration—commits this act, it is a *pāyattika* (109).
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta. There is no offense in cases such as departing at an improper time, or when the saṃgha is unlawfully divided.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with such an intention, obstructs the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha from not relinquishing the kaṭhina robe—desiring that they continue to enjoy the five privileges for a long time—it is a pāyattika (110).
If she explains it clearly, it is a *pāyattika*; if she does not explain it clearly, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī, "Settle this dispute for me," and does not employ the means to settle it, it is a *pāyattika* (111).

If one does not attempt to settle other minor disputes, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). If one does not attempt to settle a dispute concerning the person (*pudgala-vivāda*), or if one does not attempt to settle a dispute concerning others, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*. For monks and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill; if the words are not carried out; if the other party has broken the precepts and so forth; or if, due to these circumstances, there would be danger to life or similar threats.
If a bhikṣuṇī gives food with her own hands to a layperson or an outsider, it is a pāyattika (112).

The offenses and non-offenses are the same as those for the precept regarding the giving of robes. Furthermore, there is no offense if she places the food on the ground to give it, or causes another person to give it.
If a bhikṣuṇī acts as a messenger for a layperson, it is a pāyattika (113).
The group of six bhikṣuṇīs managed household affairs: they pounded grain, ground it, cooked rice, parched wheat, and boiled food; or they spread out beds, seats, and bedding;
or they swept the floors, fetched water, or accepted commissions from others. Laypeople mocked them and no longer showed them respect.
Out of reverence, this rule was established: for a bhikṣu, [this constitutes] an offense according to what has been transgressed; for the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

There is no offense if, when one's parents are ill, or if they have been imprisoned, one spreads out bedding and mats for them, sweeps the floor, fetches water, provides their necessities, or carries out their errands.
It is likewise if they are faithful *upāsakas* who are ill, and so forth. It is also not an offense if one is seized by those using force.
If a bhikṣuṇī spins thread with her own hands, it is a pāyattika (114).
For each turn [of the spindle], there is one pāyattika. For bhikṣus and others, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if she seeks thread herself to join together strands, or if she is constrained by force.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters the interior of a layperson's house and sits or lies down upon a small bed or a large bed,
it is a pāyattika (115).

Thullanandā went to the house of a lay devotee. While the householder’s wife had removed her jewelry and garments to enter the rear garden to bathe, she [Thullanandā] put on that woman’s jewelry and clothes and lay down upon the householder’s bed.

When the householder returned home and saw her suddenly, he thought she was his own wife; he immediately approached the bed, felt her body, and kissed her mouth. Only then did he realize her head was bald, and he asked: [The text continues with the inquiry.]
Knowing this to be censurable, it was therefore prescribed: "If a monk lies on his side upon a bed, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
For monks and others, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. There is no offense if he sits on a single seat, if he has spread many seats for the bhikṣuṇīs, or if he falls to the ground due to illness."
If one is coerced by force, etc.
*Zhongzhi vinaya shiyi jiyao*, Fascicle 16;
*Zhongzhi vinaya shiyi jiyao*, Fascicle 17.
Compiled by the ancient Wu śramaṇa Ouyi Zhixu:
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the house of a layperson and tells the host to prepare a seat for her to stay overnight,
yet departs the following day without taking leave of the host, it is a pāyattika (116).
A group of nuns arrived at a village without permanent dwellings and asked the householder for permission to stay overnight in his house.
At dawn, they departed without taking their leave. Later, the village house caught fire; the layperson, thinking there were people inside, did not go to extinguish it.

When the house was completely consumed by flames, he asked where the nuns were, and they replied that they had already left. Everyone then criticized them for this, and therefore the rule was established: [a nun] must exit the door [before departing].
*Pāyattika*. If one foot is inside [the house], etc., it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a *bhikṣuṇī*, etc., it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if there was already someone living inside the house; or if the house was previously empty; or if it was previously a house for meritorious purposes (*puṇya-śālā*);
or if a close friend said, "Just go; I shall speak to the owner on your behalf"; or if the house has collapsed; or if...
If there is a fire; or if there are venomous snakes or fierce beasts within; or if a thief enters;
or if one is seized by force, and so forth—if a bhikṣuṇī recites or practices worldly incantations or arts, it is a pāyattika (one hundred and seventeen).
If one transmits it orally or recites it from a written text, it is a *pāyattika* offense. For monks and others, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. There is no offense in the following cases:
when reciting spells for curing worms within the abdomen, spells for curing indigestion, or spells for neutralizing poison, for the purpose of protecting the body.
If a bhikṣuṇī teaches another person to recite and practice incantations, it is a pāyattika (118).
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman is pregnant, ordains her and grants her full admission,
it is a pāyattika (119).
When the three *karmavācanās* are completed, the preceptor nun commits a *pāyattika*. The rest may be understood by analogy. As for those who do not commit an offense:
if she was unaware; if she believed the words of that person; if she believed the words of a trustworthy person;

or if she believed the words of her parents—having granted the full ordination (*upasampadā*), if the woman later gives birth to a child and hesitates, fearing to hold or embrace it—the Buddha said: "If the child is not yet able to live independently apart from its mother, you are permitted [to hold it]."
All dharmas are like a mother; they nourish and raise one with milk. It is permitted to stay overnight with a woman who has not yet weaned her child.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman has returned home with a nursing infant, confers the full ordination upon her, it is a pāyattika (120).
There was a nun who, after ordaining another woman and returning her to her family, left the child behind at home. Later, the family sent the child back to her;
the nun then took the child into the village to beg for food. Laypeople criticized and disparaged this, and therefore [the Buddha] established the precept.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers full ordination upon one who is less than twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika (121).

The gravity of the offense is as previously stated. There is no offense if she was unaware, if the candidate herself says she is twenty or more, or if after the ordination she doubts and calculates the months of her pregnancy, the intercalary months, and the days of the fourteen-day *poṣadha* recitation. In these cases, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to a girl who is eighteen years old and has not completed two years of training in the precepts,
even though she has reached twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika (offense number 122).
If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to an eighteen-year-old girl who has completed two years of training in the precepts but has not been given the six rules,
once she has reached twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika (123).
If a śikṣamāṇā commits sexual misconduct, she should be expelled. If she has physical contact with a man with a defiled mind, her precepts are deficient and she should be given the precepts again.
If she steals five coins or more than five coins, takes the life of a human being, or claims for herself the attainment of the state of a superior person, she should be expelled.

If she steals less than five coins, takes the life of an animal, or intentionally utters a falsehood within the assembly [of monks], [she should be dealt with according to the gravity of the offense].
Eating at improper times, drinking alcohol, and violating the precepts: these require that the precepts be conferred again. The gravity of the offenses is the same as mentioned above.
If a bhikṣuṇī is an eighteen-year-old maiden, she shall be granted two years of training in the precepts and the six rules; once she has reached twenty, [she may receive full ordination].
If one confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) despite the community of monks not having granted permission, it is an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*); [this is the one hundred twenty-fourth rule].

This was established because nuns had brought into the order those who were blind, sightless, crippled, lame, deaf, mute, and so forth, thereby bringing disgrace upon the community of monks. Therefore, this regulation was made.
If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a woman who was previously married and returned home when she is ten years of age, she must undergo two years of training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*).
When she has reached twelve years of age, she may be granted full ordination (*upasampadā*). If she is less than twelve years of age and full ordination is granted, it is a *pāyattika* offense (125).

[This means that after marriage, one must be ten years old before becoming a *śikṣamāṇā*, and another two years before receiving the bhikṣuṇī precepts; it does not mean that her actual birth age is merely twelve.]
Because the bhikṣuṇīs ordained young women who had previously been married and, after receiving the precepts, engaged in flirtatious conversation with men, [the Buddha] established this rule:
"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a young woman who has previously been married, she must undergo two years of training in the precepts; only when she has reached the age of twelve may she be fully ordained."
If a bhikṣuṇī confers the full ordination upon someone without having informed the community of monks, it is a pāyattika (126).
If a bhikṣuṇī knows such a person and yet confers the full ordination upon them, it is a pāyattika (127).
Such a person is a courtesan. One should lead her five or six *yojanas* away and place her in a secure, hidden location;
otherwise, it is a *pāyattika*. There is no offense if one did not know [her identity] beforehand.
If a bhikṣuṇī ordains many disciples but does not instruct them in the two years of training in the precepts,
nor takes them under her care by means of the two dharmas, it is a pāyattika (128).
Regarding the two things: first, the Dharma; second, food and clothing. For a bhikṣu, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There is no offense if, after receiving full ordination, he departs, or if he has broken the precepts, and so forth.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not follow her preceptor (upādhyāyinī) for two years, it is a pāyattika (129). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one does not follow the preceptor for six years, it is a pāyattika; for bhikṣus and others, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if the preceptor permits her to leave, or if the preceptor has broken the precepts and so forth.
If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon another person without the consent of the Saṃgha, it is a *pāyattika* offense (130).
This rule was established because certain ignorant bhikṣuṇīs ordained others without knowing how to provide them with instruction.

One who wishes to ordain another must go before the Saṃgha and, maintaining proper deportment, make this formal announcement: "Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], from the Saṃgha..."
"I request ordination and the bestowal of full precepts. Thus one should say three times.

The bhikṣuṇīs should then examine this person to see whether she is capable of being instructed in the two years of training in the precepts and whether she can be sustained by these two matters. If she is not capable, they should say to her: "Sister..."

Cease from ordaining others. If there is one who possesses the wisdom and capability [to do so], perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) for them.

If the Saṃgha does not grant permission, to confer the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon another constitutes a *pāyattika*; to provide dependence (*niśraya*), or to maintain the other two groups [of followers], constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī who has not yet reached twelve years of seniority confers full ordination upon another, it is a pāyattika (131; [this refers to the bhikṣuṇī precepts:
having received the bhikṣuṇī vows, one must complete twelve years of summer retreat]).
If a bhikṣuṇī who is twelve years of age confers full ordination upon another person without the permission of the Saṃgha,
it is a pāyattika (132).
If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha has not authorized her to confer full ordination upon another, says, "The Saṃgha has favoritism,
anger, fear, and delusion; those who wish to authorize it do so, while those who do not wish to authorize it do not," she commits a pāyattika (133).
If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a woman whose parents or husband have not given their permission, it is a pāyattika (134).
The gravity of the offense is as previously stated; for a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta. There is no offense if she has no parents or husband.

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman has been distressed, angered, or resentful because she was in love with a young man, ordains her and grants her full admission (upasaṃpadā), it is a pāyattika (offense no. 135).
The gravity of the offense is as previously stated. There is no offense if one was unaware beforehand; or if, after the full ordination had been received, illness arose;
or if a bhikṣuṇī says to a śikṣamāṇā, "Sister, abandon this and train in that;
I shall grant you the full ordination," yet does not subsequently employ the means to grant the full ordination—this constitutes a pāyattika (136).
Thullanandā said to the śikṣamāṇā, "Learn this and abandon that; I shall confer the full ordination upon you.
She replied, "So be it. That śikṣamāṇā was wise and capable of inspiring others to practice.

Because Thullanandā wished to cause her to provide offerings through long-term persuasion and conversion, she did not provide the necessary arrangements for her to receive the full ordination. The śikṣamāṇā...
Because of that reproach, it was thus prescribed: for a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta offense. There is no offense if he is ill; or if there is no one else with whom he can live;
or if he lacks the five robes; or if the ten-member assembly is not present; or if [the person] is deficient in precepts, has broken the precepts, and so forth.
If a bhikṣuṇī says to a śikṣamāṇā, "Bring a robe and give it to me;
I shall confer the full ordination upon you," yet does not subsequently employ the proper means to confer the full ordination, it is a pāyattika (137).
If a bhikṣuṇī who has not yet reached twelve years of standing confers full ordination upon another, it is a pāyattika (138).
Because the nun An-yin frequently admitted disciples but was unable to instruct each one individually, this rule was established. (This is similar to the 131st precept in its gravity.)

The meaning of the origin of the *xiang* (auspicious rite): it may be that one is permitted to ordain only one disciple after waiting for that person to reach twelve years of age before allowing the ordination of another, just as, for example, a *bhikṣu* ordains only one person per year so as not to repeat the previous case.

If a bhikṣuṇī, having conferred full ordination upon a person, waits until after one night has passed before going among the community of bhikṣus to confer full ordination upon them, it is a pāyattika (offense no. 139).
After the bhikṣuṇīs have conferred full ordination, they may wait until the following day before going among the community of bhikṣus.

However, because those receiving full ordination might suffer from illnesses such as blindness, deafness, lameness, or paralysis, a rule was established: there is no offense if one confers full ordination on that very day and goes [to the bhikṣu-saṃgha] on that same day.
If she intends to go, but the path— whether by water or land— is cut off, or there are dangers such as wild beasts or even obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
and yet a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill does not go to receive instruction, it is a *pāyattika* (140).
There is no offense in cases concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha; nor is there an offense when attending to a sick person or when having made a formal entrustment.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not go before the community of bhikṣus every half-month to seek instruction, it is a pāyattika (141).
By means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation), one nun should be appointed to go and seek instruction. Two or three nuns should be appointed to go together.

Having gone into the midst of the great assembly of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*) and prostrated at the feet of the monks, they should bow their bodies, lower their heads, join their palms, and speak these words:
"The community of bhikṣuṇīs, being in harmony, prostrates at the feet of the community of monks and requests instruction. This should be said three times. They shall wait for the monks to speak.

The section on the precepts is concluded. [The monks] stood for a long time until they were exhausted. The Buddha said: "I allow you to entrust [the responsibility] to one great bhikṣu and then depart.

You should not entrust it to a guest bhikṣu, one who is traveling far, one who is ill, or one who lacks wisdom. Having made the entrustment, on the following day, one should go to inquire whether [the meal] is ready.
The bhikṣu should go at the appointed time, and the bhikṣuṇī should come at the appointed time. If neither goes nor welcomes [the other], both commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one hears that the instructor is coming, one should go out to meet him for half a yojana and provide whatever he requires; otherwise, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the entire community of bhikṣus is ill, one should send a messenger to pay respects and inquire after their health.

If the assembly is divided, or if the assembly is not in harmony, or if the assembly is incomplete, one should send a messenger to pay respects and inquire after their health. The same applies if it is the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
Even if one is afflicted by illness, or until the assembly is not yet full, one must still send a messenger to pay respects and inquire after their well-being.
If one does not go, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense in cases where the water or land routes are cut off, or when there are other such difficulties.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the summer retreat with the Saṃgha, does not go before the bhikṣu-saṃgha to perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for correction) regarding the three matters—
what has been seen, heard, or suspected— she commits a *pāyattika* offense (142).
The preceding rules are the same as above. On the fourteenth day, the community of bhikṣus performs the *pravāraṇā*; on the fifteenth day, the community of bhikṣuṇīs performs the *pravāraṇā*.
If a bhikṣuṇī observes the summer retreat (*varṣā*) in a place where there are no bhikṣus, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) [number 143].
On the day for receiving instruction, if there is no place to receive instruction, or if there is something doubtful but no one to consult, this rule is established.

For the other three assemblies, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. There is no offense in cases such as: observing the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in dependence upon the community of monks; passing away during that interval; traveling far away;
or being beset by calamities and the like.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing there is a bhikṣu saṃghārāma, enters it without having announced her presence, it is a pāyattika (144).
There was a bhikṣuṇī of great renown who passed away; other bhikṣuṇīs erected a stūpa for her within a bhikṣu monastery. All...
Numerous nuns came to stand nearby, laughing and conversing; some chanted while others lamented, thereby disturbing the bhikṣus who were practicing dhyāna.
The Elder Kapphiṇa destroyed their stūpa and cast it away. Those nuns all took up swords, staffs, tiles, and stones, coming to strike and hurl them at him.
Kapphiṇa flew into the air. The nuns reproached him, and they eventually reported the matter to the Buddha, who then established a precept.

Entering through a gate: a *pāyattika* offense. If one foot is inside the gate and so forth, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense if one was unaware beforehand; or if there are no other monks present;
or if one is paying homage to a Buddha-stūpa or a Śrāvaka-stūpa; or if one has been invited and passes through by way of that path;
or if one stays overnight there; or even in cases such as a threat to life.
If a bhikṣuṇī reviles a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika (145). If she is clearly understood [to have reviled him], it is a pāyattika;
if not clearly understood, it is a duṣkṛta. The subsequent rules are the same.
If a bhikṣuṇī delights in quarreling and does not properly keep in mind the matter of the dispute, and subsequently,
out of anger and displeasure, reviles the community of bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika (146).
If a bhikṣuṇī has a boil or various kinds of sores on her body and, without informing the community or others,
has a man break them open or bandage them, it is a pāyattika (147).
There is no offense in cases where one is seized by force. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If one wishes to have a man treat a disease, one should strike the *ghanṭā* (bell) to assemble the community of nuns. Once they have arrived, they should stand before the patient;
thereafter, the body should be wrapped in robes, leaving only that part exposed which requires treatment."
If a bhikṣuṇī, having previously accepted an invitation and already finished her meal, subsequently eats boiled rice, parched grain flour, cooked rice, fish, or meat, it is a pāyattika (148).
[This means that one who has already accepted a formal invitation for a full meal must not eat these five kinds of food; rather, she should go to accept that subsequent invitation for a full meal.]

A certain lay devotee prepared food and drink and invited the bhikṣuṇīs on the occasion of a festival. On that day, various lay devotees each brought rice and other offerings to the monastery to give to the bhikṣuṇīs.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had finished eating [at the monastery], they then went to the lay devotee’s house;

however, they were no longer able to eat much. The lay devotees criticized and complained about this, and therefore [the Buddha] established the rule: for every swallow, it is a pāyattika offense. For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Pāyattika. There is no offense if one accepts an invitation for non-food; or if it is an invitation for insufficient food; or if one was not previously invited;
or if one obtains further food while already at the meal; or if one accepts both the morning meal and the afternoon meal in that same household.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "It is permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to eat repeatedly. If she accepts an invitation and does not eat at all, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī gives rise to a mind of jealousy toward a household, it is a *pāyattika* (149)."
Tiṣyā was a disciple of Anurādha. They went together to the home of an old acquaintance, a donor.
Anurādha’s robes were neatly arranged and he maintained his dignified deportment; the donor felt great joy and immediately provided him with offerings.
When Anurādha returned to the monastery, he said to Tiṣyā, "This donor is deeply faithful and fond of giving. At that time, Tiṣyā was possessed by jealousy.
[Thinking thus: "The donor has firm faith; he is well-disposed toward you and provides offerings. The nuns felt resentment and reproached her. Therefore, it was established as a rule:
if [the matter] is clear, it is a *pāyattika*; if not clear, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For monks and others, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī applies fragrance by rubbing it onto her body, it is a pāyattika (150).
For bhikṣus and others, it is a duṣkṛta. There is no offense if she has such an illness or is constrained by force.
If a bhikṣuṇī smears sesame dregs upon her body, it is a pāyattika (151).
If a bhikṣuṇī causes another bhikṣuṇī to smear [sesame dregs] upon her body, it is a pāyattika (152).
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a śikṣamāṇā to rub her body, it is a pāyattika (153).
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a śrāmaṇerikā to rub her body, it is a pāyattika (154).
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a laywoman to anoint or massage her body, it is a pāyattika (155).
If a bhikṣuṇī wears a garment that covers the crotch, it is a pāyattika (156).

This causes the body to become coarse and large, leading householders to criticize and disparage [the practitioner]; therefore, it was prohibited. If one uses wool, cotton, silk, or similar materials [for this purpose], it is an *pāyattika* offense.

There is no offense in cases such as: having such an illness that one wears an inner garment for the illness, wears a *nirvāṇaka* (undergarment) over it, and then wears the *kāṣāya* (robe) over that; or being seized by those who are powerful.
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps ornaments for adorning the body belonging to a woman who has returned to lay life, except when there is a specific reason, it is a pāyattika (157).
There is a danger to life or a danger to the holy life; in such cases, she is permitted to wear ornaments while fleeing. Therefore, this excludes the case of a specific reason.
For monks, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī walks wearing leather sandals and carrying a parasol, except when there is a specific reason, it is a *pāyattika* (158).

When it rains, one may stay within a monastery. It is permitted to use a canopy made of tree bark, a leaf canopy, or a bamboo canopy. One may wear leather sandals; one may carry a canopy while wearing leather sandals and traveling from village to village. For each village, it is a *pāyattika*. In a place where there is no village, it is a *pāyattika* for every ten *krośas*. If it is less than a village boundary or less than ten *krośas*, it is a *dukkaṭa*. For monks and others, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense [in the following cases]: [The text continues with exemptions: ...if it is not raining; if one is ill; if one is on a journey; if one is crossing a river; if one is crossing a swamp; if one is crossing a field; if one is crossing a mountain pass; if one is crossing a path; if one is crossing a ditch; if one is crossing a moat; if one is crossing a wall; if one is crossing a fence; if one is crossing a thicket; if one is crossing a forest; if one is crossing a garden; if one is crossing a grove; if one is crossing a threshing floor; if one is crossing a threshing machine; if one is crossing a threshing cart; if one is crossing a threshing ox; if one is crossing a threshing buffalo; if one is crossing a threshing elephant; if one is crossing a threshing horse; if one is crossing a threshing donkey; if one is crossing a threshing goat; if one is crossing a threshing sheep; if one is crossing a threshing dog; if one is crossing a threshing cat; if one is crossing a threshing mouse; if one is crossing a threshing rat; if one is crossing a threshing snake; if one is crossing a threshing lizard; if one is crossing a threshing frog; if one is crossing a threshing fish; if one is crossing a threshing crab; if one is crossing a threshing tortoise; if one is crossing a threshing turtle;
