If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, travels by means of a vehicle,
even if coerced by force or even at the risk of her life, except for specific circumstances, it is a pāyattika (159).

The elderly, the sick, and those who ride in palanquins or carry-vehicles, as well as all women, are permitted to ride in vehicles when facing life-threatening danger or threats to their religious practice (*brahmacarya*).
This includes riding on elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, chariot-vehicles, or foot-vehicles. The gravity of the offense for violating this rule is the same as previously stated.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village without wearing a saṃkakṣikā (undershirt), it is a pāyattika (offense no. 160).

Because she exposed her chest, armpits, breasts, and waistband, laypeople criticized and disparaged her; therefore, it was prescribed that entering a village gate [without this garment] is a pāyattika.
If one foot is outside [the boundary] and so forth, it is a *duṣkṛta*. For a *bhikṣu* and others, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if there is a sore under the armpit, or if one is seized by force, or if there is danger to life, or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the house of a layperson at twilight without having been previously invited, it is a pāyattika (161).
If she enters the gate without being invited, it is a pāyattika. If one foot remains outside [the gate] and so forth, it is a duṣkṛta.
If she goes to the house of a layperson and departs without informing the host, upon exiting the gate, it is a pāyattika. If she makes preparations to depart and so forth, it is a duṣkṛta.
[The offense of] *duṣkṛta* for monks and others. There is no offense in cases such as being seized by force and entering without being invited;
or when that house is burning, collapsing, or contains venomous snakes and the like; or when one is seized by force and departs without speaking.
If a bhikṣuṇī opens the gate of a saṃghārāma at dusk and goes out without having entrusted herself to another bhikṣuṇī,
it is a pāyattika (162).

Regarding the matters of the Three Jewels, the matter of tending to the sick, and the permission to depart after entrusting one's affairs: to leave without having entrusted one's affairs constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

To have one foot inside [the boundary] and so forth constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense. For monks and others, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense in cases such as when the dwelling is destroyed by fire or other calamities.
If a bhikṣuṇī opens the gate of a saṃghārāma after sunset and leaves without having entrusted herself [to another], it is a pāyattika.

(163. This precept was originally established because thieves entered and plundered property; this precept was established because of escaping from prison. Ultimately, there were no two distinct rules; the compilers of the canon erred in dividing them into two.)
If a bhikṣuṇī neither enters the earlier retreat nor the later retreat, it is a pāyattika (164).

For the sake of the Triple Gem or for the purpose of tending to the sick, if she is unable to enter the earlier retreat, she is permitted to enter the later retreat. If she does not enter the earlier retreat, it is a duṣkṛta;
if she does not enter the later retreat, it is a pāyattika. (According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the same applies to bhikṣus; for the other three assemblies, it is a duṣkṛta.)
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers full ordination upon a woman who constantly leaks urine and feces and from whom mucus and saliva perpetually flow,
it is a pāyattika (offense number 165).
There is no offense if she was previously unaware; or if she acted upon the words of a trustworthy person; or if such an illness arose after she had received full ordination.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers full ordination upon a person with both sexual organs, it is a pāyattika (166).
Regarding those with dual sexual organs: male organs and female organs.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers full ordination upon one whose two channels are conjoined, it is a pāyattika (offense number 167).
Regarding the "convergence of two paths": this refers to the inability to distinguish between the urinary and fecal orifices.
If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers full ordination upon one who has debts or who faces difficulties due to illness, it is a pāyattika (offense no. 168).
A creditor may come to seize and detain [the debtor], and a sick person must always be attended and watched by others; one must not leave them alone.
Therefore, it is prescribed that even for a debtor who owes as little as one-sixteenth of a coin, or for a sick person who suffers from a constant headache, [one must remain in attendance].
If a bhikṣuṇī learns worldly arts and crafts to support her livelihood, it is a pāyattika (169).
If a bhikṣuṇī teaches worldly incantations to laypeople, it is a pāyattika (170).
The group of six nuns taught worldly arts and crafts to laypeople, saying: "You must not void excrement or urine toward the sun, the moon, or the shrines of the deities;
nor should you discard sweepings, rinse vessels with impure water, or stretch out your feet in those directions.
Furthermore, if you wish to build houses, plow fields, or engage in cultivation, you should face the sun, the moon, or the shrines of the deities. They added: "Today, such-and-such a star..."
It is auspicious to cultivate old friendships; it is auspicious to engage in planting; it is auspicious to build a house; it is auspicious to employ laborers;

it is auspicious to have a young child’s hair shaved; it is auspicious to let one's hair grow long; it is auspicious to collect wealth and goods; it is auspicious to travel far. Those with few desires criticized these practices, and eventually they reported them to the Buddha, who established the precept:
"If you wish to speak, you should say: 'Do not [make noise] toward a stūpa of the Buddha or a stūpa of a Śrāvaka, whether large or small.'"

This extends even to stretching out one's legs. If one wishes to enter a dwelling, plow fields, or engage in cultivation, one should go toward a Buddha stūpa or a Śrāvaka stūpa on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day, or on days when miraculous transformations are manifested.
It is appropriate to enter a stūpa or monastery to make offerings to the Saṃgha and receive the precepts of the fast (*upavāsa*).
For monks who do so [at other times], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī who has been subject to formal expulsion does not depart, it is a pāyattika (171).
For bhikṣus and others, it is a duṣkṛta. There is no offense if she complies and does not resist, humbles her mind and repents, or seeks the revocation of the formal act of expulsion;
or if she falls ill, lacks companions for the journey, or the water or land routes are cut off due to various difficulties.
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to ask a bhikṣu about the meaning [of the Dharma], and asks without first seeking permission, it is a pāyattika (172).
The bhikṣuṇī An-yin possessed great wisdom; she asked various bhikṣus about the meaning [of the Dharma], but the bhikṣus were unable to answer, and they all felt ashamed.
Therefore, it is established: if one wishes to inquire about the meaning, one must first seek permission to ask. To ask without having been granted permission constitutes a *pāyattika* offense;
for monks and others, it is a *dukkaṭa*. There is no offense in the following cases: if one has previously always received permission to ask; if there is a prior relationship of intimacy;

if a person of intimacy says, "Simply ask, and I shall seek [an answer] for you"; if the other party accepts [the question] from that [intimate person]; or if both parties receive [permission] from a third person.
[This is] the formal acceptance. If someone asks this, one should answer thus. Both persons shall recite it together, even if there are errors in the recitation and so forth.

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has arrived later than herself while she was already established there, or that she herself arrived later than another who was already established there, and desiring to annoy her, walks back and forth, stands, sits, or lies down before her, it is a pāyattika (173; the meaning is the same as the ninety-second precept mentioned previously).
For monks and others, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). There is no offense in the following cases: if one does not know; if one asks;

if one has already been permitted to walk in meditation (*caṅkrama*); if one is walking in meditation with another in turn; if the person is a close friend; if a close friend says, "Just go for your meditation walk, and I shall speak on your behalf";
if one has fallen to the ground due to illness; or if one is seized by force, even up to the point of life-threatening danger.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that there is a stūpa within a bhikṣu’s saṃghārāma, builds [another] one, it is a pāyattika (174).
For every brick for washing the feet, lump of clay, or clump of grass she takes, it is a pāyattika.
There is no offense if she did not know beforehand; or if she destroys the saṃghārāma intentionally; or if the stūpa was built first and the saṃghārāma was built later.
If a bhikṣuṇī sees a newly ordained bhikṣu, she should rise to meet him, pay respectful homage, inquire after his well-being, and invite him to sit.
To fail to do so, except for a specific reason, constitutes a pāyattika (offense number 175).
Or if one eats in a single sitting; or if one has performed the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhikṣā* (the ritual for leftover food) and does not eat; or if one is ill—[in these cases] it is permitted to say:
"Venerable sir, I have such a cause and condition that I am unable to rise and welcome you. For [failing to do so otherwise], the bhikṣus commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī sways her body while walking for the sake of appearance, it is a pāyattika (176). For a bhikṣu and others, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense in the following cases: if she has such an illness; if she is avoiding a staff, a wild elephant, or even thorns and brambles;
if she is crossing water or mud; or if she turns her body to check that her robes are properly arranged.
If a bhikṣuṇī adorns herself as a woman by applying perfumes or rubbing them upon her body, it is a pāyattika (177).

For bhikṣus and others, it is a duṣkṛta. There is no offense if she has such an illness, or if her parents or a devout upāsikā who is ill is imprisoned, and she washes, bathes, or combs their hair for them; or if she is constrained by force.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a non-Buddhist woman to apply perfume and massage her body, it is a pāyattika (178).
Furthermore, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "If the hair is long, it is a pāyattika. One should shave it once every half-month; if it exceeds this, it is called 'long hair'."
If there is no one to shave [the head], or if one is unable to shave due to being coerced by force, in all such cases there is no offense.
○ The eight *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas; in the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, there are eleven. First, milk; second, curd.
1. Fresh butter; 2. Refined butter; 3. Oil; 4. Molasses; 5. Honey; 6. Fish; 7. Meat; 8. Dried meat; 9. A family that provides for itself (regarding milk, curd, fish, meat, and dried meat:

for a bhikṣu, this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; regarding fresh butter, refined butter, oil, molasses, and honey: for a bhikṣu, this constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense; this applies equally to the bhikṣu regarding families that provide for themselves).
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill begs for ghee to eat, she commits an offense that requires confession and censure.
She should speak to another bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Sister, I have committed a censurable offense which ought not to be done; I now confess it to you, Sister.
This is called the method of repentance (1). Begging for oil (2), or honey (3), or black rock-honey (4) [is treated in the same manner].

If it be milk (5), or curd (6), or fish (7), or meat (8)—it is likewise. It is permitted to beg for these on behalf of one who is ill; it is also permitted to beg for them when one is ill oneself. This refers to obtaining something without having asked for it. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one knows for oneself that a certain illness will always recur at a specific time and that medicine will certainly be difficult to obtain then, there is no offense in requesting it in advance.
If one requests it when not ill and eats it when ill, it is a *vyatikrama* (transgression of the Vinaya).
If one requests it when ill and eats it when not ill, there is no offense. If one requests it when ill and eats it when ill, there is no offense."
If one begs for food when not ill and eats it when not ill, one should repent.

Regarding the rules of training for the community (*saṃghāvaśeṣa-dharmas*): these are the same as those for the bhikṣus (except for the two precepts concerning walking while swaying the body and defecating or urinating upon living grass or vegetables, which constitute *pāyattika* offenses).
○ The seven methods for settling disputes are the same as those for bhikṣus. ○ The method for leaving the household life and receiving the precepts consists of three parts:

(1) explaining the method for bestowing the śrāmaṇerī precepts; (2) explaining the method for bestowing the śikṣamāṇā precepts; (3) explaining the method for bestowing the bhikṣuṇī precepts). (△ Now, the first.)
The Bhikṣuṇī-khandhaka states: If one wishes to have one's hair shaved within a bhikṣuṇī monastery, one should inform the Saṃgha;
or, one should speak to each person individually so that they may be made aware. Only after this should the hair be shaved. The announcement should be made as follows:

Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen. This [person], so-and-so, wishes to have her hair shaved by the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen:
I shall shave the hair of so-and-so. Thus is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
If one wishes to receive the śrāmaṇerī precepts by taking ordination within the monastery, the ācāryī should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):

Regarding the hearing of the girl who is eighteen years old: she shall study the precepts for two years; when she reaches twenty years of age, she shall receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) among the bhikṣuṇīs.
If she is ten years old and has previously been married (meaning she has been married for a full ten years), she is permitted to study the precepts for two years.

May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the two-year training in the precepts. (Thus it is said three times.)
The śrāmaṇerikā should be moved from a place where she cannot hear to a place where she can see. The ācāryikā shall make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen. This śrāmaṇerikā [Name] now requests from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts, with Bhikṣuṇī [Name] as her upādhyāyikā.

Venerable Sisters, those of you who consent to the Saṃgha granting two years of training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerī so-and-so, with bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as her preceptor, remain silent.
Those who do not consent, speak. This is the first *karmavācanā* (the second and third are recited in the same manner).
The Saṃgha has consented to grant two years of training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerī so-and-so, with bhikṣuṇī so-and-so [as her preceptor].
The procedure for the *upādhyāyī* is concluded. Because the Saṃgha has remained silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Next, she is to be brought forward; having knelt long before the *ācāryī*, the six rules are conferred upon her.
Listen attentively, [Name]. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has taught six rules:

If a woman who is not of the Śākya clan engages in physical contact with a man who has a defiled mind, she violates the precepts and must receive the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not commit such an offense. Can you maintain this? (She replies, "I can.
One must not steal, even so much as a blade of grass or a leaf. If a *śikṣamāṇā* takes five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five *kārsāpaṇas*, whether taking it herself or instructing another to do so...

Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit such an offense. Can you maintain this? (Answer: "I can. You must not intentionally cut down living beings.

To do it oneself or to instruct another to do it—she is no longer a *śikṣamāṇā*, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.

If she takes the life of an animal that cannot undergo transformation, she violates the precepts; she must receive the precepts again. Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not commit such an offense.
Can you maintain this? (She replies: "I can. One must not speak falsely, even in jest. If a *śikṣamāṇā* is not truthful...

If one violates the precepts, the precepts should be conferred again. Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not violate them.
Can you maintain them? (He answers: "I can. One must not eat at improper times. If a śikṣamāṇā eats at an improper time, she violates the precepts;

the precepts should be conferred upon her again. Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not violate them. Can you maintain them? (He answers: "I can. One must not drink alcohol. If a śikṣamāṇā...

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The *śikṣamāṇā* is ranked below all *bhikṣuṇīs* and above all *śrāmaṇerīs*."

"Up to this point, do you have these various ailments? (The questions and answers are conducted one by one as previously described.

"Born! You are not a bhikṣuṇī; you are not a daughter of the Śākya clan. Within this [Saṃgha], for as long as life lasts, you must not do this.

She is not a bhikṣuṇī; she is not a daughter of the Śākya clan. Because she has concealed a grave offense, you must not commit these things for as long as you live.
Can you maintain this? (He replied, 'I can. You must not follow a suspended bhikṣu, nor even a park-keeper or a śrāmaṇera."

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that a bhikṣu has been formally accused by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the instructions of the Buddha, and that he is not compliant and has not made amends while the Saṃgha has not yet granted him restoration of communal residence, yet she nevertheless associates with him, that bhikṣuṇī should be admonished by the other bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Sister, do you know? The Saṃgha has now accused this bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the [instructions] of the Buddha..."
"Regarding what has been taught, you do not comply and do not repent; the Saṃgha has not yet granted you formal co-residence. You must not comply with this nun.
When that nun admonishes her, she persists and does not relinquish [her position]. That nun should be formally admonished up to three times so that she may relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well. If she does not relinquish it, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī; she is no longer a Śākyaputrī.
“Daughters of good family, because these have been enumerated, you must not transgress them for as long as life lasts. Can you uphold them? [She] replies, “I can.
“Daughter of good family, listen attentively. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has taught the four reliances (*niśraya*).
By relying upon these, a bhikṣuṇī may go forth and receive full ordination, becoming a bhikṣuṇī. She relies upon rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*); she may obtain...”
Having left the household life and received full ordination, you have become a bhikṣuṇī according to the Dharma. Can you maintain this throughout your entire life?
(She answers: "I can. If you obtain long-term benefits, such as robes offered by donors or robes made from rags, you may accept them.
Relying on alms-gathering, you have left the household life and received full ordination, becoming a bhikṣuṇī according to the Dharma. Can you maintain this throughout your entire life?

(Answering: "I am able. If one obtains long-term benefits; if food is assigned by the Saṃgha; if food is sent by a donor; food on the eighth day of the month; food on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the month;
food on the first day of the month; the regular food of the community of monks; or food offered at the invitation of a donor—one should accept it.
By sitting under a tree, one may go forth and receive full ordination, thereby accomplishing the state of a bhikṣuṇī. You are...

"Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts? (He answers, "I can. If one obtains long-term benefits—such as a separate room, a pointed-roof hut, a small cell, a stone cave, or two rooms with a single door—one should accept them.
(According to the *Nirgrantha-vinaya*, a nun should not reside in an *āraṇya* [forest hermitage], except within a royal garden. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:)
A nunnery should not be established outside the city walls; therefore, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that for a nun, there are only three things to rely upon.

By relying on medicinal substances that have become decomposed, one may go forth and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), thereby perfecting the status of a bhikṣuṇī. "Can you maintain this throughout your entire life? [She] replies, "I can.
If one obtains long-term benefits—namely, ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar—one should accept them. You have now completed the full ordination. This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).

The four *karmas* have been accomplished according to the Dharma; you have obtained a proper dwelling place. Your preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is according to the Dharma, your teacher (*ācārya*) is according to the Dharma, and the two assemblies of monks are complete and perfect according to the Dharma.
You should properly receive the instructions of the teaching. You ought to exhort and transform others to cultivate merit, repair stupas, and make offerings to the Sangha.
If your preceptor and teacher provide all instruction according to the Dharma, you must not oppose them.
"You should study, inquire, and recite the sūtras; you must diligently seek skillful means so that within the Buddha-dharma you may attain the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat.
Since you have first resolved to leave the household life, your efforts shall not be in vain."
The retribution will not cease. As for other matters not yet known, one should consult the Upādhyāya and Ācārya. (At this point, perform the *pariṇāmanā* [dedication of merit] as appropriate.
Let the person receiving the precepts go in front, with the other nuns following behind, and they shall depart.
If, when one wishes to receive the full ordination (upasampadā), there is the danger of bandits on the road, it is permitted to dispatch a messenger to receive the precepts on one's behalf.

The nuns' community shall perform a formal motion and announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) to dispatch one pure and unblemished bhikṣuṇī; furthermore, two or three other nuns shall be appointed to go together with her.
The nun acting as messenger prostrates at the feet of the monks, kneels with palms joined, and makes the three requests on their behalf. The monks should ask her: "What is her name?
Who is her preceptor-nun? Has she already trained in the precepts and is she pure? If she replies, "She has already trained in the precepts and is pure," [the procedure continues].
Furthermore, one should ask the companion nun: "Has she already trained in the precepts and is her conduct pure?

If she replies, "She has already trained in the precepts and is pure," then one should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of one motion and three proclamations). That messenger should then return to the nunnery and say:
"Sister, I have already conferred the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon you. One must not confer the ordination by means of a messenger for trivial reasons or on account of mere appearance.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "If a bhikṣuṇī once violates the precepts, she is no longer permitted to leave the household life or receive full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).

However, if after having renounced the precepts she undergoes a transformation of gender (*vyañjana-parivṛtti*) and becomes a male, it is not an offense to confer the bhikṣu precepts upon her. The *Sarvāstivāda-mātṛkā* states:

"If one commits an *anantarya-pārājika* (a grave offense unique to nuns) and subsequently undergoes a transformation of gender to become a male, he may be granted leave from the household life and receive full ordination."
○ Miscellaneous Rules.
The Bhikṣuṇī-khandhaka states: Kālodāyin reviled and struck bhikṣuṇīs, even resorting to deceitful speech and persuasion.

The Buddha permitted the community of bhikṣuṇīs to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) of "non-prostration" against him. He then complied with the bhikṣuṇīs and did not dare [to offend them].
This is contrary [to the rule]. When seeking to resolve a matter, one should not perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) without paying respect; it should be resolved.

As for the group of six bhikṣus who went to the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs and mutually mocked and teased the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, thereby disturbing those engaged in meditative seclusion, the Buddha said: "One should prohibit such behavior wherever there is disturbance and noise."
It was the same when nuns went to the dwelling place of the bhikṣus.

The śrāmaṇeras belonging to the group of six bhikṣus would go to the dwelling place of the nuns and, together with those śrāmaṇerīs and śikṣamāṇās, would mock and tease one another, disturbing those engaged in meditation.
The Buddha said: "They should be summoned and punished. If they do not reform, you should perform the *akaraṇīya-karman* (the act of non-prostration) against their two teachers."

[The Buddha] rebuked them. The six groups of bhikṣuṇīs had śrāmaṇerīs and śikṣamāṇās go to the dwelling places of the bhikṣus and, together with those śrāmaṇeras, mock and harass one another, thereby disturbing those engaged in meditation. The Buddha said: "They should be summoned and punished.
If they do not reform, the two preceptors of those śrāmaṇerīs and śikṣamāṇās should perform the formal act of 'relinquishing instruction' (śikṣā-niḥsaraṇa-karman) against them."
A bhikṣuṇī should not sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka); she is permitted to sit in the half-lotus posture. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"When a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣuṇī, he should regard her as a daughter; the bhikṣuṇī, for her part, should regard the instructor as the Buddha. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states:
If one encourages another to return to lay life, one incurs a *thullaccaya* offense. A small bowl for a *bhikṣu* is a large bowl for a *bhikṣuṇī*.

No *bhikṣuṇīs* should touch the children of others. The *Nidāna* states: "In times of famine when alms are difficult to obtain, it is permitted for a *bhikṣuṇī* to request permission from the community to travel back and forth to her parents' home;
this is performed through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal motion followed by three proclamations). This *bhikṣuṇī* [is thus authorized]."
Walking alone, there is no offense. When going to the homes of one's relatives, one may eat as one pleases. Furthermore, during times of abundance, one should not go to Muktika.
In any place where nuns eat, one seat must be reserved at the head of the assembly for the *upādhyāya*.
Even if a *śrāmaṇera* arrives later, he shall take that seat and eat, for he belongs to the senior group.

this is not necessarily so.

Postscript: Alas!
The study of the Vinaya has not been clear for a long time. If the Vinaya is not clear, how can the Teaching (Dharma) become clear?
If the Teaching is not clear, how can the School (Sect) become clear? The worthy ones have gone beyond it; the unworthy ones fall short of it. How much more so, moreover...
The conventional views of the vulgar have permeated our very bones and marrow; when spoken of in terms of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma, they are as startled as if by the Milky Way.
How could they possibly deign to cast their eyes upon the fragrant regulations of the Buddha’s world contained within these five hundred fascicles?

I am ashamed that my conduct in the gate of practice is sparse and deficient, thereby failing the Buddha-dharma; for this reason, I have kept my mouth shut in recent years and have not dared to debate with people of the age.

Regarding gain and loss, I rely upon the light from a single crack in the wall, borrowing the windows provided by the Buddhas and Patriarchs; thus, I may perhaps be called a guide for those with lame feet.
Should there be anyone who takes my intent as their own and practices it with devotion, they will surely reach the Cool Lake in peace and security—of this there is no doubt.
This colophon was written on the eighth day of the eighth month of the Gengyin year.

The Brahmajāla Sūtra states: "Whenever a superior or elder passes away, it is appropriate in all cases to invite a Dharma Master to chant the sūtras and vinaya to provide merit for their posthumous blessings.
Now, a single lecture on a sūtra lasts no more than a moment, yet it still brings boundless benefit and can provide merit for the afterlife."
How much more so when it is circulated via woodblocks, printed and distributed without end, passing from hand to hand in infinite succession.
The roots of goodness, merit, and karmic conditions thereof will fill all of space and pervade the entire Dharma-realm; they are truly inconceivable. An ancient said:

"To transmit a well-written work to one person is equivalent to ten good deeds; to transmit it to ten people is equivalent to a hundred good deeds; to transmit it to a great hero or a person of high nobility..."
If a person performs a thousand acts of goodness and disseminates them boundlessly, they shall achieve ten million acts of goodness that endure imperishably through re-publication. Alas!
If the merit of worldly virtuous writings is already such as this, how much more so for the Buddha’s scriptures, the Great Dharma that transcends the world?
From this one may gain awakening. It is further said: "All the fine words in the world have been fully spoken by the Buddha alone. How can one not regard this with urgency?
I, the Buddha’s disciple Yang Jingchao, with single-minded devotion prostrate before the eternally abiding Triple Gem:
Śākyamuni Bhagavān, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and all the great Bodhisattvas. May you compassionately accept me and take me under your care.

May the subtle influence of the Buddhas descend upon me as a blessing and bear witness to this vow (Jingchao): "In reverent accordance with the Buddha’s words, I have carved the woodblocks for the *Vinaya-jīyào*.
Relying on these supreme causes, may they serve to augment my merit in the afterlife; may all past obstructions be instantly eliminated, and may the ground of my mind be luminous."
May we swiftly escape saṃsāra and quickly proceed to the Land of Bliss; may we joyfully behold Amitābha and suddenly awaken to non-arising.
Returning to this Sahā world, may we deliver all those who have been our benefactors and enemies, so that we may together achieve the Buddha-way.
We pray only that the World-Honored One Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the assembly of the Pure Sea, and all the great Bodhisattvas will equally bestow their compassionate grace upon us.
May this humble aspiration be fulfilled.
